p.seg: 1.1 The Annals of the First Month of Spring
1: In the first month of spring:
the sun is in the constellation Yíngshì,
at dusk the constellation Shēn is in the meridian,
at dawn the constellation Wěi is in the meridian.
Its days are jiǎ and yǐ.
Its sovereign is Tàihào.
Its tutelary spirit is Gōumáng.
Its creatures are the scaly.
Its musical note is jué.
Its pitch-pipe is Tàicù.
Its number is eight.
Its taste is sour.
Its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the door.
The offering is first made of the spleen.
The east wind thaws the ice.
Hibernating creatures begin to stir and revive.
Fish rise up bearing ice.
Otters offer fish in sacrifice.
The wild geese arrive from the north.
The Son of Heaven resides in the left apartment of the Qīngyáng Hall,
rides in the phoenix carriage,
drawn by azure dragons,
bearing green banners,
wears green robes,
adorns himself with green jade,
and eats wheat and mutton.
His vessels are open and well-ventilated.
In this month,
the beginning of spring is established.
Three days before the beginning of spring,
the Grand Astrologer reports to the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such-and-such a day, spring begins.
The flourishing virtue resides in wood."
The Son of Heaven then purifies himself.
On the day of the beginning of spring,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials to welcome spring in the eastern suburbs.
Upon returning,
he then rewards the dukes, ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials at court.
He commands the prime minister to promulgate virtuous teachings and harmonious ordinances,
to distribute blessings and bestow favors,
reaching down to the myriad people.
Rewards and gifts are thus carried out,
with nothing inappropriate.
He then commands the Grand Astrologer
to uphold the statutes and observe the laws,
to oversee the movements of the heavens, sun, moon, and stars,
ensuring the lodgings and separations are without error,
and that the regular order is not lost,
taking the beginning as the constant rule.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven, on the first auspicious day, prays for grain to the Supreme Deity.
He then selects an auspicious morning,
the Son of Heaven personally loads the plow and share,
places them among the attendants of the charioteer and the guard,
and leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials to personally plow the imperial field.
The Son of Heaven pushes the plow three times,
the Three Dukes five times,
and the ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials nine times.
Upon returning,
holding a cup in the Great Chamber,
with the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials all in attendance,
he commands it to be called the "Feast of Toil."
In this month,
the celestial qi descends,
the terrestrial qi ascends,
heaven and earth are in harmony and unity,
and plants and trees flourish and stir.
The king proclaims the agricultural affairs:
he commands the field officers to reside in the eastern suburbs,
all to repair the boundaries and borders,
to examine and straighten the paths and roads,
to carefully survey the hills, mounds, slopes, dangers, plains, and lowlands,
the suitability of the land,
and what the five grains should be planted,
in order to instruct and guide the people,
and he must personally oversee it.
When the field affairs are put in order,
first establishing the standards and straightness,
the farmers will then not be confused.
In this month,
command the Director of Music to enter the school and practice dance.
Then revise the sacrificial codes,
command sacrifices to the mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
and do not use female animals as offerings.
Prohibit the felling of trees,
do not overturn nests,
do not kill infant insects, pregnant animals, young birds, or fledglings,
do not take fawns or eggs,
do not gather large crowds,
do not build city walls,
and cover exposed bones and bury skeletons.
In this month,
one must not raise armies,
raising armies will certainly bring heavenly calamity.
If military conflicts do not arise,
one must not be the first to start them.
Do not alter the way of heaven,
do not cut off the principles of earth,
do not disrupt the order of humanity.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out in the first month of spring,
then wind and rain will be untimely,
plants and trees will wither from drought,
and the state will have fear.
If the ordinances of autumn are carried out,
then the people will suffer great epidemics,
fierce winds and violent rains will frequently arrive together,
and weeds, tares, and wild grasses will flourish together.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out,
then floods will cause damage,
frost and snow will arrive in great force,
and the first plantings will not take root.
1.2 The Foundation of Life
2: That which gives birth to life in the beginning
is heaven and earth;
that which nurtures and completes it
is man.
He who can nurture what heaven gives birth to and not interfere with it is called the Son of Heaven.
The actions of the Son of Heaven
are for the purpose of preserving heaven's wholeness.
This is why offices are established.
Establishing offices is to preserve life.
The deluded rulers of the present age,
establish many offices but instead harm life,
thus losing the purpose for which they were established.
It is like those who arm themselves
to prepare against bandits;
now they arm themselves but instead attack themselves,
thus also losing the purpose for which they armed themselves.
Now, the nature of water is to be clear,
but soil muddies it,
so it cannot be clear.
The nature of man is to be long-lived,
but things disturb it,
so he cannot be long-lived.
Things are that by which
one nurtures one's nature,
not that by which one uses one's nature to nurture things.
The people of the present age,
the deluded ones mostly use their nature to nurture things,
thus they do not know what is light and what is heavy.
Not knowing what is light and what is heavy,
then the heavy becomes light,
and the light becomes heavy.
If it is like this,
then every action will end in failure.
To act like this as a ruler is perverse,
to act like this as a minister is chaotic,
to act like this as a son is reckless.
If a state has one of these three,
it will inevitably perish without hope.
Now suppose there is a sound here,
the ear listening to it would certainly be pleased,
but if listening to it would make one deaf,
one certainly would not listen.
Suppose there is a color here,
the eye looking at it would certainly be pleased,
but if looking at it would make one blind,
one certainly would not look.
Suppose there is a flavor here,
the mouth tasting it would certainly be pleased,
but if tasting it would make one mute,
one certainly would not taste it.
Therefore, the sage, regarding sounds, colors, and flavors,
if they are beneficial to his nature, he takes them;
if they are harmful to his nature, he discards them.
This is the way to preserve one's nature whole.
The wealthy and noble of the world,
regarding sounds, colors, and flavors, are mostly deluded;
day and night they seek them,
and if by luck they obtain them, they indulge in them.
Indulging in them,
how can their nature avoid injury?
If ten thousand men draw their bows and together shoot
at one target,
the target will certainly be hit.
The myriad things are multitudinous;
if they harm one life,
that life will certainly be injured;
if they benefit one life,
that life will certainly flourish.
Therefore, the sage's regulation of the myriad things
is to preserve their heaven-given nature whole.
When one's nature is whole, then spirit is harmonious,
eyes are clear,
ears are sharp,
the nose discerns odors,
the mouth is keen,
and all three hundred sixty joints are free and unimpeded.
Such a person:
speaks not, yet is trusted;
plans not, yet is fitting;
deliberates not, yet attains;
his essence communicates with Heaven and Earth,
his spirit pervades the cosmos;
toward things, there is none he does not receive,
none he does not encompass,
like Heaven and Earth themselves;
above, being the Son of Heaven, he is not arrogant;
below, being a commoner, he is not distressed;
this is what is called a person of whole virtue.
To be noble and wealthy yet not understand the Way
is precisely enough to become a calamity;
it is not as good as being poor and lowly.
For the poor and lowly, obtaining things is difficult;
even if they wished to exceed, how could they?
Going out, they use carriages;
entering, they use litters;
striving for self-indulgence—
this is called the mechanism for crippling lameness.
Fat meat and strong wine,
striving to strengthen oneself—
this is called the food that rots the intestines.
Delicate beauties with gleaming teeth,
the music of Zhèng and Wèi,
striving for self-pleasure—
this is called the axe that hacks at one's nature.
These three calamities
are brought about by nobility and wealth.
Therefore, among the people of old, there were those who refused nobility and wealth,
due to their valuing life;
it was not for boasting about reputation,
but for the substance of it.
Thus, this discourse cannot but be examined.
1.3 Valuing Oneself
The third says: Chuí was the utmost in skill.
Yet people do not love Chuí's fingers,
but love their own fingers,
because having them is beneficial.
People do not love the jade of the Kūnlún Mountains or the pearls of the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
but love their own single dull jade disc or small pearl,
because having them is beneficial.
Now, my life is possessed by me,
and its benefit to me is also great.
Consider its nobility or baseness—
even the rank of Son of Heaven is not enough to compare;
consider its lightness or heaviness—
even possessing all under Heaven is not enough to exchange for it;
consider its safety or peril—
if one morning it is lost,
one will never regain it for a lifetime.
These three aspects
are what those who possess the Way are cautious about.
There are those who are cautious yet end up harming themselves—
this is due to not comprehending the true nature of life and destiny.
Not comprehending the true nature of life and destiny,
what benefit is there in caution?
This is like a blind man loving his son,
yet unavoidably giving him chaff for a pillow;
this is like a deaf man raising an infant,
and at the sound of thunder taking him to look outside the hall;
there is little difference from not knowing caution at all.
Those who do not know caution—
for them, life and death, survival and perishing, what is permissible and what is not,
have never been distinguished.
Those who have never distinguished them,
what they call right has never been right,
what they call wrong has never been wrong;
they affirm what they call wrong,
and deny what they call right—
this is called great delusion.
Such people
are those whom Heaven brings calamity upon.
Using this to govern oneself,
one will surely die, surely meet disaster;
using this to govern a state,
it will surely be mutilated, surely perish.
Death, disaster, mutilation, and perishing
do not come of themselves;
delusion summons them.
Long life and longevity arriving constantly are also like this.
Therefore, those who possess the Way
do not examine what is summoned,
but examine what summons it;
then its arrival cannot be prevented.
This discourse cannot but be thoroughly understood.
Have Wū Huò swiftly pull an ox by its tail—
the tail will break, his strength exhausted,
yet the ox will not move—
this is going against it.
Have a child of five feet pull its nose ring,
and the ox will willingly go wherever—
this is following it.
The rulers and nobles of the world,
whether worthy or unworthy,
none do not desire long life and enduring vision,
yet daily they go against their life—
what benefit is there in desiring it?
Generally, the flourishing of life
is due to following it;
what makes life not follow
is desire;
therefore, the sage must first regulate desires.
A large room has much shade;
a high terrace has much sun;
much shade causes collapse;
much sun causes withering—
these are the calamities of imbalance between yīn and yáng.
Therefore, the former kings did not dwell in large rooms,
did not build high terraces;
their flavors were not numerous delicacies;
their clothing was not excessively hot.
Excessive heat causes the pores to block;
blocked pores cause the qì not to flow;
numerous delicacies cause the stomach to be full;
a full stomach causes internal blockage and distension;
internal blockage and distension, and qì not flowing—
can one attain long life by this?
In the past, when the former sage kings made parks, gardens, and ponds,
it was sufficient for viewing and exercising the body;
when they made palaces, rooms, terraces, and pavilions,
it was sufficient to avoid dryness and dampness;
when they made carriages, horses, clothing, and furs,
it was sufficient to ease the body and warm the bones;
when they made food, drink, sweet wine, and ale,
it was sufficient to please the taste and fill emptiness;
when they made music, sounds, and pleasures,
it was sufficient to calm the nature and amuse themselves.
These five things
are how the sage kings nurtured their nature;
it was not that they loved frugality and hated expense,
but that they regulated according to their nature.
1.4 Valuing Impartiality
The fourth says:
In the past, when the former sage kings governed all under Heaven,
they necessarily put impartiality first;
impartiality then brought peace to all under Heaven.
Peace is attained through impartiality.
Try observing the ancient records:
there have been many who attained all under Heaven;
they attained it necessarily through impartiality,
and lost it necessarily through partiality.
Generally, the establishment of a ruler
arises from impartiality.
Therefore, the "Hóng Fàn" says:
"Without partiality, without faction,
the kingly way is vast;
without partiality, without bias,
follow the king's righteousness;
let there be no personal preferences,
follow the king's way;
let there be no personal aversions,
follow the king's path."
All under Heaven is not the possession of one person;
it is the possession of all under Heaven.
The harmony of yīn and yáng
does not cause only one kind to grow;
sweet dew and timely rain
do not favor one thing alone;
the ruler of the myriad people
should not favor one person.
When Bó Qín was about to depart,
he asked how to govern Lǔ;
the Duke of Zhōu said:
"Benefit them, and do not seek benefit for yourself."
A man of Jīng lost a bow
but was unwilling to search for it,
saying:
"A man of Jīng lost it,
a man of Jīng will find it—
why search for it?"
Confucius heard of it and said:
"Remove the 'Jīng' and it would be acceptable."
Lǎo Dān heard of it and said:
"Remove the 'man' and it would be acceptable."
Thus, Lǎo Dān reached the utmost impartiality.
Heaven and Earth are great;
they give birth but do not claim as sons,
complete but do not possess;
the myriad things all receive their moisture and obtain their benefit,
yet none know from where they began—
Guǎn Zhòng fell ill.
Duke Huán went to inquire about him,
saying:
"Your illness, Father Zhòng,
is grave.
If the people of the state should lose you,
to whom should I entrust the state?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"In the past, I exhausted my strength and wisdom,
and still it was not enough to know such things.
Now that my illness is a matter of days,
how can I speak of it?"
Duke Huán said:
"This is a great matter.
I wish Father Zhòng to instruct me."
Guǎn Zhòng respectfully assented
and said:
"Whom does Your Lordship wish to appoint as chancellor?"
The Duke said:
"Would Bào Shūyá be suitable?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"He would not.
I, Yíwú, am close to Bào Shūyá.
Bào Shūyá's character
is pure, incorruptible, and upright.
When he sees those not his equal,
he does not associate with them.
Once he hears of someone's faults,
he never forgets them for the rest of his life."
"If it cannot be avoided,
then would Xí Péng be suitable?"
"Xí Péng's character
is to look up to those above and seek from those below.
He is ashamed not to equal Huángdì,
and pities those not his equal.
In matters of state,
there are things he does not hear;
in matters of things,
there are things he does not know;
in matters of people,
there are things he does not see.
If it cannot be avoided,
then Xí Péng would be suitable."
Now, the chancellorship
is a high office.
One who occupies a high office
should not desire petty scrutiny,
nor petty cleverness.
Hence it is said:
"A great carpenter does not carve;
a great chef does not set out dishes;
great courage does not fight;
a great army does not plunder."
Duke Huán acted with impartiality and rejected private grudges,
employed Guǎn Zhòng, and became chief of the Five Hegemons.
He acted with partiality and favored those he loved,
employed Shù Diāo, and worms crawled out the door.
When a person is young, they are foolish;
when they grow older, they become wise.
Thus, to be wise yet act with partiality
is not as good as to be foolish yet act with impartiality.
To be drunk all day yet pretend to be sober,
to seek private gain yet establish public good,
to be greedy and violent yet seek to be king—
even Shùn could not do such things.
1.5 "Rejecting Partiality"
The fifth says:
Heaven covers all without partiality;
Earth bears all without partiality;
the sun and moon shine on all without partiality;
the four seasons proceed without partiality.
They carry out their virtue, and the myriad things thereby achieve growth.
Huángdì said:
"Sounds should not be excessive;
colors should not be excessive;
clothing should not be excessive;
fragrances should not be excessive;
flavors should not be excessive;
dwellings should not be excessive."
Yáo had ten sons,
but he did not give the throne to his sons; instead, he entrusted it to Shùn.
Shùn had nine sons,
but he did not give the throne to his sons; instead, he entrusted it to Yǔ.
This is the utmost impartiality.
Duke Píng of Jìn asked Qí Huángyáng:
"Nányáng has no administrator.
Who would be suitable to take the position?"
Qí Huángyáng replied:
"Xiè Hú would be suitable."
Duke Píng said:
"Is Xiè Hú not your enemy?"
He replied:
"Your Lordship asked who is suitable,
not who is my enemy."
Duke Píng said:
"Good."
Thereupon, he employed him.
The people of the state praised this.
After some time had passed,
Duke Píng again asked Qí Huángyáng:
"The state has no commandant.
Who would be suitable to take the position?"
He replied:
"Wǔ would be suitable."
Duke Píng said:
"Is Wǔ not your son?"
He replied:
"Your Lordship asked who is suitable,
not who is my son."
Duke Píng said:
"Good."
Again, he thereupon employed him.
The people of the state praised this.
Confucius heard of it and said:
"Excellent!
Qí Huángyáng's judgment!
Recommending externally, he did not avoid his enemy;
recommending internally, he did not avoid his son."
Qí Huángyáng may be called impartial.
Among the Mohists, there was a Grand Master Fù Tūn.
He resided in Qín.
His son killed a man.
King Huì of Qín said:
"Your years are advanced, sir,
and you have no other sons.
I have already ordered the officials not to execute him.
I ask you, sir, in this matter, to comply with my wish."
Fù Tūn replied:
"The law of the Mohists says:
'One who kills a man shall die;
one who injures a man shall be punished.'
This is how killing and injuring people are prohibited.
Now, prohibiting killing and injuring people
is a great principle of the world.
Although Your Majesty grants this favor
and orders the officials not to execute him,
I, Fù Tūn, cannot fail to carry out the law of the Mohists."
He did not consent to King Huì
and thereupon had him executed.
A son is something people hold dear.
To suppress what one holds dear in order to carry out a great principle—
the Grand Master may be called impartial.
A chef blends flavors but does not dare to eat the food;
therefore, he can be a chef.
If a chef blended flavors and ate the food,
then he could not be a chef.
It is the same with kings and hegemons.
They punish the violent without partiality
and thereby enfeoff the worthy of the world;
therefore, they can be kings and hegemons.
If kings and hegemons punished the violent with partiality,
then they could not be kings and hegemons either.
2.1 "The Annals of Mid-Spring"
In the month of Mid-Spring:
The sun is in Kuí.
At dusk, Hú is at the zenith.
At dawn, Jiànxīng is at the zenith.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its sovereign is Tàihào.
Its spirit is Gōumáng.
Its creatures are the scaly.
Its note is Jué.
Its pitch-pipe is Jiázhōng.
Its number is eight.
Its flavor is sour.
Its smell is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the household deity.
The offering is first made of the spleen.
Rainwater begins.
Peach and plum trees blossom.
Cānggēng birds sing.
Eagles transform into doves.
The Son of Heaven resides in the Qīngyáng Grand Chamber,
rides in a carriage with bells,
drives azure dragons,
bears azure banners,
wears azure garments,
adorns himself with azure jade,
eats wheat and mutton,
and his vessels are open and penetrating.
In this month,
tender sprouts are stabilized,
the young and small are nurtured,
and orphans are cared for.
An auspicious day is chosen,
and the people are ordered to make offerings to the Earth Spirit.
Officials are commanded
to inspect the prisons,
remove fetters and shackles,
prohibit floggings and torture,
and halt lawsuits and disputes.
In this month,
the dark birds arrive.
On the day of their arrival,
a grand sacrifice of a bull, a sheep, and a pig is offered to the High Matchmaker.
The Son of Heaven personally attends,
with the empress and consorts leading the nine concubines in attendance.
Then, special honors are paid to the women of the Son of Heaven who are with child:
they are adorned with bow-cases,
and bows and arrows are presented before the altar of the High Matchmaker.
In this month,
day and night are equal.
Thunder begins to sound,
and lightning first appears.
All hibernating insects stir,
opening their burrows and beginning to emerge.
Three days before the first thunder,
bells are rung to warn the myriad people, saying:
"Thunder is about to sound.
If anyone does not guard their conduct,
their children will be born defective,
and there will surely be misfortune and disaster."
When day and night are equal,
measures of length and capacity are standardized,
balances and weights are adjusted,
bushels and pecks are verified,
and scales and levelers are corrected.
In this month,
farmers take a brief rest,
and repair their doors and gates.
The ancestral temples must be fully prepared.
No major undertakings are to be initiated
that would hinder agricultural work.
In this month,
do not drain rivers and marshes,
do not empty out ponds and pools,
and do not set fire to mountains and forests.
The Son of Heaven presents a lamb and opens the icehouse,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
On the first *dīng* day,
the Director of Music is ordered to enter the school and present offerings before beginning dance instruction,
and the Son of Heaven leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, and feudal lords to personally observe it.
On the second *dīng* day,
the Director of Music is again ordered to enter the school to practice music.
In this month,
sacrifices do not use live animals,
but instead use jade tablets and discs,
replacing them with hides and silks.
If the ordinances of autumn are carried out in mid-spring,
then the state will suffer great floods,
cold air will arrive in full force,
and enemies and soldiers will come to attack.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out,
then the yang energy will not prevail,
the wheat will not ripen,
and the people will frequently plunder one another.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then the state will suffer great drought,
warmth will arrive early,
and insects and pests will cause harm.
2.2 "Valuing Life"
The second says:
When sages deeply contemplate the world,
nothing is more valuable than life.
The ears, eyes, nose, and mouth
are servants of life.
Though the ears may desire sounds,
though the eyes may desire colors,
though the nose may desire fragrances,
though the mouth may desire flavors,
if they harm life, they must be stopped.
For these four faculties,
if something is not beneficial to life, it should not be done.
From this perspective,
the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth
cannot act arbitrarily;
they must be regulated.
This is like official duties:
they cannot be performed arbitrarily;
they must be regulated.
This is the method of valuing life.
Yáo offered the world to Zǐzhōu Zhīfù.
Zǐzhōu Zhīfù replied:
"It would be acceptable for me to become the Son of Heaven.
However, I happen to suffer from a deep-seated illness,
and I am just about to treat it.
I have no time for the affairs of the world."
The world is a weighty matter,
yet he did not let it harm his life.
How much more so for other things?
Only those who do not let the world harm their lives
are fit to be entrusted with the world.
The people of Yuè had killed three generations of their rulers.
Prince Sōu was troubled by this
and fled to a cave in Dānxué.
The state of Yuè was without a ruler.
They searched for Prince Sōu but could not find him,
until they tracked him to the cave in Dānxué.
Prince Sōu refused to come out,
so the people of Yuè smoked him out with mugwort,
and offered him the royal carriage.
Prince Sōu grasped the mounting cord and climbed into the carriage,
then looked up to heaven and cried out:
"O, rulership!
Can you not spare me?"
Prince Sōu did not hate being a ruler;
he hated the troubles of being a ruler.
Someone like Prince Sōu
can be said not to have harmed his life for the sake of a state.
This is precisely why the people of Yuè wanted him as their ruler.
The ruler of Lǔ heard that Yán Hé was a man who had attained the Way,
and sent someone with gifts to approach him first.
Yán Hé was guarding the village gate,
wearing coarse cloth clothes,
and feeding his oxen himself.
When the envoy of the ruler of Lǔ arrived,
Yán Hé received him personally.
The envoy said:
"Is this the home of Yán Hé?"
Yán Hé replied:
"This is Hé's home."
The envoy presented the gifts,
but Yán Hé said:
"I fear you may have heard incorrectly and will bring blame upon yourself,
so it would be better to verify it."
The envoy returned to verify the matter,
and when he came back to seek him,
Yán Hé could no longer be found.
Thus, someone like Yán Hé
did not hate wealth and honor;
he hated them because he valued life.
The rulers of the world
often use wealth and honor to arrogantly approach those who have attained the Way.
That they do not understand each other—
is this not lamentable?
Therefore it is said:
The essence of the Way
is used to maintain one's person;
its remnants
are used to govern the state;
its dregs
are used to rule the world.
From this perspective,
the achievements of emperors and kings
are but leftover matters for sages,
not the means to perfect the body and nurture life.
Nowadays, the gentlemen of the common world
often endanger their bodies and abandon their lives in pursuit of external things.
What do they seek to attain by this?
What do they seek to accomplish by this?
Whenever sages act,
they always examine what they seek to attain and what they seek to accomplish.
Suppose there were a person here
who used the pearl of the Marquis of Suí to shoot at a sparrow a thousand *ren* high.
The world would surely laugh at him.
Why is this?
Because what he used was heavy,
and what he sought was light.
Is life not far heavier than the pearl of the Marquis of Suí?
Zǐhuázi said:
"To fully preserve life is best;
to impair life is next;
death is next;
and forced life is worst."
Thus, what is called honoring life
means fully preserving it.
What is called fully preserving life
means that all six desires are satisfied appropriately.
What is called impairing life
means that the six desires are only partially satisfied appropriately.
A life of deficiency means one treats what is honorable in it with disregard.
The greater the deficiency,
the greater the disregard for what is honorable.
What is called death
is having no means of perception,
returning to the state before one was born.
What is called a constrained life
is when none of the six desires obtains what is proper for it,
and each obtains what it greatly detests.
Submission is this,
humiliation is this.
No humiliation is greater than unrighteousness.
Therefore, unrighteousness
is a constrained life.
Yet a constrained life is not solely unrighteousness.
Therefore it is said: a constrained life is not as good as death.
How do we know this is so?
For the ear to hear what it detests
is not as good as not hearing.
For the eye to see what it detests
is not as good as not seeing.
Therefore, one covers the ears at thunder,
and covers the eyes at lightning.
This is an analogy for it.
In all cases of the six desires,
if they all know what they greatly detest,
and yet cannot avoid it,
it is not as good as having no means of perception.
Having no means of perception
is what is meant by death.
Therefore, a constrained life is not as good as death.
One who craves meat
does not mean rotten rat.
One who craves wine
does not mean spoiled wine.
One who honors life
does not mean a constrained life.
2.3 "Qíng Yù" (Passions and Desires)
The third says:
Heaven gives birth to humans and endows them with greed and desires.
Desires involve passions,
and passions have moderation.
The sages cultivate moderation to restrain desires,
therefore they do not excessively indulge their passions.
Thus, the ear's desire for the five tones,
the eye's desire for the five colors,
the mouth's desire for the five flavors—
these are passions.
These three,
whether noble or base, foolish or wise, worthy or unworthy, are desired equally.
Even Shénnóng and Huángdì are the same as Jié and Zhòu in this.
What makes the sages different
is that they attain the proper measure of their passions.
Acting from valuing life leads to attaining the proper measure of passions.
Not acting from valuing life leads to losing the proper measure of passions.
These two
are the foundation of life and death, survival and perishing.
Common rulers impair their passions' proper measure,
therefore every action leads to ruin and failure.
Their ears cannot get enough,
their eyes cannot be satisfied,
their mouths cannot be filled.
Their bodies become completely swollen,
their sinews and bones heavy and sluggish,
their blood vessels blocked and congested.
The nine orifices become empty and desolate,
all losing their proper functions.
Even if they had Péng Zǔ,
he still could not help them.
Regarding material things,
they desire what cannot be obtained,
they seek what cannot be satisfied.
Greatly losing the root of life,
the people resent and criticize them,
and they also create great enemies.
Their will and energy are easily agitated,
unsteady and unstable.
Arrogant about their power, fond of cunning,
their hearts full of deceit and fraud,
they are slow to virtue and righteousness,
but swift to wicked profit.
Their persons thus fall into hardship and poverty.
Even if they later regret it,
what good will it do?
They draw near the clever and flattering,
and distance the upright and honest.
The state faces great danger.
Regretting past faults,
they still cannot turn back.
Hearing words, they are startled,
but do not grasp the cause.
A hundred illnesses arise in anger,
disorder and calamity arrive in time.
Ruling people in this manner
brings great worry to one's person.
The ear finds no pleasure in sounds,
the eye finds no pleasure in sights,
the mouth finds no sweetness in flavors.
There is no difference from death.
The ancients who attained the Way,
lived with long life,
and could long enjoy
sounds, sights, and flavors.
What is the reason?
Their principles were settled early.
Principles settled early means knowing early to be sparing,
knowing early to be sparing means the essence is not exhausted.
If autumn is cold early, then winter will surely be warm.
If spring has much rain, then summer will surely be dry.
Heaven and earth cannot have both,
how much less can humans?
Humans are the same as heaven and earth.
Though the forms of the myriad things differ,
their inherent principle is one body.
Therefore, the ancients who cultivated their persons and ruled the world
necessarily took heaven and earth as their model.
If many draw from the honored cup, it is quickly emptied.
The myriad things that draw upon the life of the greatly honored are many.
Therefore, the life of the greatly honored is often quickly exhausted.
It is not only that the myriad things draw from it,
but also that he diminishes his own life to benefit the people of the world,
yet in the end does not know it himself.
Though his achievements are accomplished outwardly,
his life is impaired inwardly.
His ears cannot hear,
his eyes cannot see,
his mouth cannot eat.
His heart is greatly disturbed,
he talks wildly and hallucinates.
On the verge of death,
confused, alarmed, and fearful,
he does not know what he is doing.
To use one's heart-mind in such a way—
is it not pitiable?
Those in the world who serve rulers
all consider Sūn Shū'áo's encounter with King Zhuāng of Chǔ as fortunate.
But from the perspective of one who possesses the Way, it is not so.
This was the fortune of the state of Chǔ.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was fond of traveling about and hunting,
galloping, shooting with bow and arrow,
leaving no joy untasted.
He placed all the labors within his borders and the worries of the feudal lords upon Sūn Shū'áo.
Sūn Shū'áo labored day and night without rest,
unable to make facilitating his own life his priority.
Thus he caused King Zhuāng's achievements to be recorded on bamboo and silk,
and transmitted to later ages.
2.4 "Dāng Rǎn" (On Being Influenced)
The fourth says:
Mòzǐ saw someone dyeing plain silk
and sighed, saying:
"Dyed in blue, it becomes blue;
dyed in yellow, it becomes yellow.
What goes in changes,
its color also changes.
With five dips, it is considered to have five colors."
Therefore, one cannot but be careful about dyeing.
It is not only dyeing silk that is like this;
states also have dyeing.
Shùn was dyed by Xǔ Yóu and Bó Yáng.
Yǔ was dyed by Gāo Yáo and Bó Yì.
Tāng was dyed by Yī Yǐn and Zhòng Huǐ.
King Wǔ was dyed by Tàigōng Wàng and Zhōu Gōng Dàn.
These four kings were dyed appropriately,
therefore they ruled the world,
were established as Sons of Heaven.
Their merit and fame overshadowed heaven and earth.
When raising up the world's benevolent, righteous, and illustrious men, one must mention these four kings.
Jié of Xià was dyed by Gān Xīn and Qí Zhǒng Róng.
Zhòu of Yīn was dyed by Chóng Hóu and È Lái.
King Lì of Zhōu was dyed by Guógōng Chángfù and Róng Yí Zhōng.
King Yōu was dyed by Guógōng Gǔ and Zhàigōng Dūn.
These four kings were dyed inappropriately,
therefore their states were destroyed and they died,
becoming objects of ridicule for the world.
When raising up the world's unrighteous and disgraceful men, one must mention these four kings.
Duke Huán of Qí was dyed by Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū.
Duke Wén of Jìn was dyed by Jiù Fàn and Xì Yǎn.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ was dyed by Sūn Shū'áo and Shěn Yǐn Zhēng.
King Hé Lú of Wú was dyed by Wǔ Yuán and Wén Zhī Yí.
King Gōu Jiàn of Yuè was dyed by Fàn Lǐ and Grand Master Zhǒng.
These five rulers were dyed appropriately,
therefore they became hegemon among the feudal lords,
and their merit and fame were transmitted to later ages.
Fàn Jí Shè was dyed by Zhāng Liǔ Shuò and Wáng Shēng.
Zhōng Háng Yín was dyed by Huáng Jí Qín and Gāo Qiáng.
King Fū Chāi of Wú was dyed by Wángsūn Xióng and Grand Steward Pǐ.
Zhì Bó Yáo was dyed by Zhì Guó and Zhāng Wǔ.
Shàng of Zhōngshān was dyed by Wèi Yì and Yuàn Cháng.
King Kāng of Sòng was dyed by Táng Yāng and Tián Bùyīn.
These six rulers were all improperly influenced,
so their states were all ruined and perished,
they themselves either died or were disgraced,
their ancestral temples received no blood sacrifices,
their posterity was cut off,
rulers and ministers were scattered and separated,
the people fled and wandered,
and when people in the world speak of greedy and violent men worthy of shame, they always name these six rulers.
Generally, one becomes a ruler not for the sake of the ruler's glory,
nor for the sake of the ruler's security,
but to carry out principles.
Carrying out principles arises from proper influence.
Thus, among the ancients, those skilled at being rulers
exerted themselves in evaluating men,
but were at ease in official affairs,
having grasped the essential method.
Those incapable of being rulers
injured their bodies and wasted their spirits,
troubled their minds and wearied their ears and eyes,
their states grew increasingly perilous,
their persons increasingly disgraced,
because they did not know the essential point.
Not knowing the essential point, they were improperly influenced.
Being improperly influenced,
how could principles arrive?
The six rulers are examples of this.
These six rulers
did not fail to value their states and love their persons,
but they were improperly influenced.
The causes of survival and perdition are not limited to this alone;
emperors and kings are likewise.
It is not only states that are subject to influence.
Confucius studied under Lǎo Dān, Mèng Sū Kuí, and Jìng Shū.
Duke Huì of Lǔ sent his steward Ràng to request from the Son of Heaven the rituals for the suburban and ancestral temples.
King Huán (or Píng) sent the scribe Jiǎo to go,
Duke Huì detained him,
and his descendants remained in Lǔ,
where Mòzǐ studied under them.
These two scholars,
though they had no noble rank to bring honor to men,
nor rewards and emoluments to benefit men,
when people in the world speak of those who are honored and glorious, they always name these two scholars.
Both have been dead a long time,
yet their followers have grown ever more numerous,
their disciples ever more abundant,
filling the world.
Kings, dukes, and great men follow them and bring them honor;
those who have beloved sons and younger brothers have them study under them,
and there is never a time when they are lacking or cut off.
Zǐgòng, Zǐxià, and Zēngzǐ studied under Confucius.
Tián Zǐfāng studied under Zǐgòng.
Duàngān Mù studied under Zǐxià.
Wú Qǐ studied under Zēngzǐ.
Qín Gǔlí studied under Mòzǐ.
Xǔ Fàn studied under Qín Gǔlí.
Tián Xì studied under Xǔ Fàn.
Later disciples of Confucius and Mòzǐ who became honored and glorious in the world are many;
they cannot be fully counted,
all because those who influenced them were proper.
2.5 "Merit and Fame"
The fifth discourse says:
If one follows the proper way,
merit and fame cannot be escaped,
just as a sundial and its shadow,
or a call and its echo.
A skilled angler draws fish from depths of ten fathoms,
because the bait is fragrant.
A skilled archer brings down birds from heights of a hundred fathoms,
because the bow is excellent.
A skilled ruler
makes the Mányí and Fántóng peoples with their strange customs and different practices all submit,
because his virtue is profound.
If the springs are deep, fish and turtles return to them.
If the trees are flourishing, flying birds return to them.
If the grasses are lush, birds and beasts return to them.
If the ruler is worthy, heroes and outstanding men return to him.
Therefore, the sage kings do not strive for those who return,
but strive for that which causes them to return.
Forced laughter is not joyful;
forced weeping is not sorrowful.
Forced adherence to the Way
may achieve small things,
but cannot achieve great things.
In a jar of vinegar, gnats gather
because there is sourness;
with plain water it certainly would not happen.
Using a cat to attract rats,
or ice to attract flies,
no matter how skillful, one cannot succeed.
Using rotten fish to drive away flies,
flies will come all the more, uncontrollably,
because one uses what attracts them to drive them away.
Jié and Zhòu used the method of driving away to attract them.
Though their punishments were heavy, their penalties severe, what good did it do?
When great cold arrives,
the people seek warmth as a benefit.
When great heat is above,
the people hasten toward coolness.
Thus, the people have no constant abode;
they gather where they see benefit,
and leave where there is none.
He who desires to be the Son of Heaven
must not fail to examine
where the people hasten.
In the present age,
it is extremely cold,
extremely hot,
yet the people have nowhere to hasten,
because the measures taken are equally bad.
He who desires to be the Son of Heaven,
what he shows the people
must not fail to be different.
If his conduct is not different,
even if disorder were twice that of today,
the people would still have nowhere to hasten.
If the people have nowhere to hasten,
then the kingly ruler is abandoned,
the tyrannical ruler is fortunate,
and the people are without hope.
Therefore, in the present age,
if there is a benevolent man,
he cannot but devote himself to this.
If there is a worthy ruler, he cannot but attend to this.
Worthiness and unworthiness cannot be shared or divided,
just as destiny cannot be changed,
or beauty and ugliness cannot be shifted.
Jié and Zhòu were honored as Sons of Heaven, rich in possessing the world;
they could harm all the people of the world,
yet they could not obtain a name for worthiness.
Guān Lóngpáng and Prince Bǐgān could die by having their waists and necks severed,
contending against their superiors' faults,
yet they could not bestow upon them a name for worthiness.
Fame inherently cannot be shared or divided;
it must come through the proper principle.
3.1 "The Annals of Late Spring"
The first discourse says:
In the month of late spring:
The sun is in the constellation Wèi.
At dusk, the Seven Stars are at the zenith.
At dawn, the Oxherd is at the zenith.
Its days are Jiǎ and Yǐ.
Its emperor is Tàihào.
Its spirit is Gōumáng.
Its creatures are the scaly.
Its musical note is Jué.
The pitch-pipe is Gūxiǎn.
Its number is eight.
Its flavor is sour.
Its odor is goatish.
Its sacrifice is to the door.
The offering is first the spleen.
The paulownia begins to flower.
Field mice transform into rú quails.
Rainbows begin to appear.
Duckweed begins to grow.
The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Qīngyáng Hall.
He rides in the luán carriage,
drives the azure dragons,
bears the azure banner,
wears azure garments,
and adorns himself with azure jade.
He eats wheat and mutton.
His vessels are open and penetrating.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven presents the jú-yellow garment to the former emperors.
He orders the boat overseer to inspect the boats,
five inspections and five reports,
then he reports to the Son of Heaven that the boats are fully prepared,
and the Son of Heaven then begins to ride in boats.
He presents the wěi fish in the ancestral temple,
and prays for the fullness of the wheat.
In this month,
the vital energy is just flourishing,
the yang energy disperses,
living things all emerge,
budding things fully extend,
and one must not restrain them.
The Son of Heaven spreads virtue and bestows favors.
He orders the officials
to open the granaries and storehouses,
bestow upon the poor and destitute,
relieve the needy and desperate,
open the treasuries,
bring out silks and cloth,
circulate them throughout the world,
encourage the feudal lords,
summon famous scholars,
and show courtesy to the worthy.
In this month, command the Minister of Works, saying:
"The seasonal rains are about to fall,
water from below will rise upward;
inspect the cities and towns,
survey the plains and fields all around;
repair and strengthen the dikes and embankments,
clear and dredge the ditches and canals,
open and clear the roads,
so that there are no obstructions or blockages;
traps and snares for hunting,
nets and birdlime,
and poisons for baiting animals,
must not be taken beyond the city gates."
In this month,
command the foresters
not to cut down mulberry or paper mulberry trees.
The turtledove preens its feathers,
and the hoopoe descends upon the mulberry trees.
Prepare the frames, reels, and baskets;
the queen and consorts observe purification,
personally face east
and pluck mulberry leaves themselves,
and forbid women from idly watching.
Reduce women's other duties,
encourage silkworm affairs;
once the silkworm work is completed,
divide the cocoons, weigh the silk, and assess the results,
to provide garments for suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices,
and none dare be negligent.
In this month,
command the master artisans
to order all craftsmen
to examine the stores in the five warehouses—
metals and iron, hides and sinews, horns and teeth, feathers and arrow shafts, fats and glues, cinnabar and lacquer—
so that none are of poor quality.
All craftsmen attend to their work;
supervisors daily exhort them not to violate the season,
nor to create extravagant and clever objects
that might unsettle the ruler's mind.
At the end of this month,
choose an auspicious day,
for a grand assembly of music,
and the Son of Heaven leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and senior officials
to personally attend and observe it.
In this month,
bring together the tethered bulls and stallions to mate with the mares in the pastures;
for sacrificial animals, foals, and calves,
record and document their numbers.
Order the people of the state to perform the exorcism,
disemboweling animals at the nine gates to ward off evil,
to bring the spring's vital energy to an end.
If these ordinances are carried out,
sweet rains will arrive for three ten-day periods.
If in late spring the ordinances of winter are practiced,
then cold air will frequently arise,
plants and trees will all wither,
and the state will experience great fear.
If the ordinances of summer are practiced,
then the people will suffer many epidemics and illnesses,
seasonal rains will not fall,
and the mountains and hills will yield no harvest.
If the ordinances of autumn are practiced,
then the heavens will often be overcast and gloomy,
excessive rains will fall early,
and weapons and armor will arise together.
3.2 "Fulfilling One's Destiny"
The second discourse says: Heaven gives birth to yin and yang, cold and heat, dryness and dampness;
the transformations of the four seasons,
the changes of the myriad things—
none fail to provide benefit,
none fail to cause harm.
The sage examines what is appropriate in yin and yang,
distinguishes the benefits of the myriad things to facilitate life.
Therefore, the essence and spirit dwell peacefully within the body,
and one's lifespan attains longevity.
Longevity means not cutting short and then extending it,
but fulfilling one's allotted span.
The task of fulfilling one's allotted span
lies in eliminating harm.
What is meant by eliminating harm?
Extreme sweetness, extreme sourness, extreme bitterness, extreme pungency, extreme saltiness—
if these five fill the body, they give rise to harm.
Great joy, great anger, great worry, great fear, great sorrow—
if these five affect the spirit, they give rise to harm.
Great cold, great heat, great dryness, great dampness, great wind,
great prolonged rain, great fog—
if these seven disturb the essence, they give rise to harm.
Therefore, in all matters of nurturing life,
nothing is as good as knowing the root;
knowing the root, then illness has no way to arrive.
When vital energy gathers, it must have a place to enter.
Gathering in feathered birds, it makes them soar;
gathering in running beasts, it makes them move swiftly;
gathering in pearls and jade, it makes them pure and bright;
gathering in trees, it makes them lush and tall;
gathering in sages, it makes them profoundly wise.
The coming of vital energy
relies on lightness to lift it,
relies on running to move it,
relies on beauty to refine it,
relies on growth to nurture it,
relies on wisdom to enlighten it.
Flowing water does not stagnate;
a door hinge does not become worm-eaten—because of movement.
The body's energy is likewise:
if the body does not move, the essence does not flow;
if the essence does not flow, the energy becomes stagnant.
Stagnation in the head causes swelling and wind ailments;
in the ears, causes blockage and deafness;
in the eyes, causes dimness and blindness;
in the nose, causes sniffling and congestion;
in the abdomen, causes distension and colic;
in the feet, causes atrophy and lameness.
Where the water is light, there are many bald and goitered people;
where the water is heavy, there are many swollen and lame people;
where the water is sweet, there are many handsome and beautiful people;
where the water is pungent, there are many ulcerous and boil-afflicted people;
where the water is bitter, there are many hunchbacked and stooped people.
In all eating, do not force richness;
in flavors, do not use intense tastes or strong drink—
these are called the beginning of illness.
If one can eat at proper times,
the body will certainly be free from calamity.
The way of eating in general
is to be neither hungry nor full—
this is called the protection of the five viscera.
The mouth must savor flavors,
harmonize the essence, compose the demeanor,
and guide it with spirit and energy.
All joints are content and joyful,
all receiving nourishment.
When drinking, one must swallow in small sips,
upright and straight, without contortion.
Nowadays, the world engages in divination and prayer,
hence diseases increasingly come.
It is like an archer:
if he shoots and misses,
he goes back to adjust the target—
what good does that do for hitting the mark?
Using boiling water to stop boiling
only makes the boiling increase without cease;
remove the fire, and it stops.
Thus, shamans, physicians, and poisonous drugs
are used to chase away and treat illness;
therefore, the people of old despised them,
for they address the branch, not the root.
3.3 "Putting Oneself First"
The third discourse says: King Tāng asked Yī Yǐn, saying:
"What must one do to take possession of the world?"
Yī Yǐn replied:
"If you desire to take possession of the world,
the world cannot be taken.
If it can be taken,
you must first take possession of yourself."
The root of all affairs
lies first in governing oneself,
cherishing one's great treasure.
Use what is new,
discard what is old,
and the pores and texture will become unobstructed.
Vital energy renews daily,
perverse energy completely departs,
and one lives out one's natural lifespan.
Such a one is called a true person.
In ancient times, the former sage kings
perfected themselves, and the world was perfected;
governed themselves, and the world was governed.
Thus, one skilled with echoes works not on the echo but on the sound;
one skilled with shadows works not on the shadow but on the form;
one who would govern the world works not on the world but on oneself.
The *Book of Songs* says: "The good man, the gentleman,
his demeanor is without fault.
His demeanor is without fault,
and he rectifies the four states."
This speaks of rectifying oneself.
Therefore, return to the Way, and one's person becomes good;
practice righteousness, and others become good;
delight in fulfilling the ruler's Way,
and the hundred officials are already governed,
and the myriad people are already benefited.
The achievement of these three
lies in non-action.
The way of non-action is called overcoming Heaven;
righteousness is called benefiting the self;
the ruler is called not acting for oneself.
Not acting for oneself means overseeing and listening;
benefiting the self means tranquility and calm;
overcoming Heaven means following one’s nature.
Following one’s nature leads to clarity, intelligence, longevity, and a long life;
tranquility and calm lead to progress in endeavors and joy in one’s homeland;
overseeing and listening lead to the blockage of wickedness and the absence of confusion.
Thus, if those above lose their way, the borders will be invaded by enemies;
if they lose their conduct internally,
their reputation will be tarnished externally.
Therefore, a pine tree a hundred ren tall,
if its roots are damaged below,
its top will wither above;
the states of Shāng and Zhōu,
if their plans fail in their hearts,
their commands will be obstructed by others.
Thus, when the heart attains, listening attains;
when listening attains, affairs attain;
when affairs attain, achievements and fame attain.
The Five Emperors prioritized the Way and then virtue,
thus their virtue was unsurpassed;
the Three Kings prioritized teaching and then punishment,
thus their affairs were unmatched in achievement;
the Five Hegemons prioritized affairs and then military force,
thus their military strength was unparalleled.
In the present age,
cunning schemes are employed simultaneously,
deceptive tactics are used in succession,
attacks and wars never cease,
and the number of fallen states and disgraced rulers grows ever larger,
because what is pursued is trivial.
Xiàhòu Xiàng fought with Yǒuhù at Gānzé but did not prevail;
the six ministers requested to attack again,
but Xiàhòu Xiàng said:
"It cannot be.
My land is not small,
my people are not few,
yet we fought and did not prevail—
this is because my virtue is shallow and my teachings are not good."
Thereupon, he sat without double mats,
ate without varied flavors,
did not play the qín and sè,
did not repair the bells and drums,
did not adorn his sons and daughters,
cherished his kin and respected his elders,
honored the worthy and employed the capable,
and within a year, the Yǒuhù clan submitted.
Thus, those who wish to overcome others must first overcome themselves;
those who wish to judge others must first judge themselves;
those who wish to understand others must first understand themselves.
The *Shī* says: "Holding the reins like weaving silk."
Confucius said:
"If one examines these words, one can govern the world."
Zǐgòng said:
"How hasty this is!"
Confucius said:
"It does not refer to haste,
but to acting here
and achieving patterns there.
The sage weaves and cultivates his own person,
and achieves patterns throughout the world."
Thus, Zǐhuázi said:
"When hills and mounds are formed, burrowers find peace;
when great waters and deep abysses are formed, fish and turtles find peace;
when pines and cypresses grow, travelers already find shade."
Confucius visited Lǔ Āigōng,
and Āigōng said:
"Someone told me:
'To govern the state,
one need only act in the hall.'
I consider this an impractical saying."
Confucius said:
"This is not an impractical saying.
I have heard:
'What is attained in oneself is attained in others;
what is lost in oneself is lost in others.'
Without stepping beyond the gate, yet the world is governed—
is this not only possible for those who know to reflect on themselves?"
3.4 "On Assessing People"
The fourth says: The ruler's way is simple;
the ruler's focus is near.
The highest is to reflect on oneself;
the next is to seek from others.
The farther one searches,
the more distant the results;
the more forcefully one seeks,
the farther one strays.
What does it mean to reflect on oneself?
Moderate the ears and eyes,
restrain desires and cravings,
discard clever schemes,
abandon artifice,
and let the mind wander in the realm of the infinite,
focus the heart on the path of spontaneity.
In this way, nothing can harm one's nature.
When nothing harms one's nature, one understands essence;
understanding essence leads to understanding spirit;
understanding spirit is called attaining the One.
All myriad forms,
attain the One and then are completed.
Thus, knowing the One,
one responds to things with transformation,
vast and profound,
unfathomable.
Virtuous conduct shines brightly,
comparable to the sun and moon,
unceasing.
Heroic scholars arrive in time,
distant lands come to pay tribute,
unblockable.
Will and energy flow freely,
unbound by anything,
unmanageable.
Thus, knowing the One,
one returns to simplicity,
desires are easily satisfied,
nourishment is taken sparingly and frugally,
unattainable by others.
Withdrawing from the world to find joy within,
the inner feelings pure and洁白,
immeasurable.
Threats cannot intimidate,
severity cannot frighten,
unsubduable.
Thus, knowing the One,
one can act appropriately to the task,
interact with the times,
limitless.
Actions and decisions follow numbers,
taking and giving adhere to principle,
unconfused.
Words leave nothing out,
penetrating skin and flesh,
unalterable.
Slanderers are impoverished,
the worthy rise to prominence,
unconcealable.
Thus, knowing the One,
one is like heaven and earth—
then what task cannot be accomplished,
what thing cannot be responded to?
It is like a charioteer:
reflecting on oneself,
the chariot becomes light, the horses swift,
reaching far distances and returning to feed without tiring.
In ancient times, the fallen rulers of old,
believing faults lay in others,
daily killed and punished without cease,
until they perished without realizing it.
The rising kings of the Three Dynasties,
believing faults lay in themselves,
daily achieved merits without decline,
until they became kings.
What does it mean to seek from others?
People are of the same kind but differ in wisdom;
the worthy and unworthy are distinct,
yet all use clever words and eloquent speech
to defend themselves—
this is why unworthy rulers bring chaos.
In assessing people generally,
when they are in favor, observe whom they respect;
when they are noble, observe whom they promote;
when they are wealthy, observe whom they support;
when listening, observe what they do;
when at rest, observe what they enjoy;
when learning, observe what they say;
when in hardship, observe what they do not accept;
when in lowly position, observe what they do not do;
delight them to test their integrity;
please them to test their biases;
anger them to test their restraint;
frighten them to test their uniqueness;
sadden them to test their humanity;
hardship them to test their will.
These eight observations and six tests
are how worthy rulers assess people.
In assessing people, one must also consider the six kin and four intimates.
What are the six kin?
Father, mother, elder brothers, younger brothers, wife, and children.
What are the four intimates?
Friends, old acquaintances, fellow villagers, and neighbors.
Internally, use the six kin and four intimates;
externally, use the eight observations and six tests—
then human truth and falsehood, greed and baseness, beauty and ugliness will not be missed.
It is like fleeing from rain
and mud—
there is no escape from it.
This is how the former sage kings understood people.
3.5 "The Way of the Circle"
The fifth says: The way of heaven is circular,
the way of earth is square;
the sage kings modeled themselves on this,
and thereby established the distinction between superior and inferior.
How can it be said that the way of heaven is circular?
The vital essence ascends and descends,
circling and revolving,
with nothing stagnant or lingering,
therefore it is said that the way of heaven is circular.
How can it be said that the way of earth is square?
The myriad things have different categories and different forms,
each has its allotted function,
and cannot substitute for one another,
therefore it is said that the way of earth is square.
The ruler holds to the circular,
the ministers occupy the square;
if the square and circular do not change,
then the state will flourish.
Day and night completing one cycle—this is the circular way.
The moon traversing the twenty-eight lunar mansions,
from Zhěn connecting to Jiǎo—this is the circular way.
The essence moves through the four seasons,
ascending and descending, each meeting the other—this is the circular way.
When things stir, they sprout;
sprouting, they are born;
born, they grow;
growing, they become large;
large, they mature;
mature, they then decline;
declining, they then perish;
perishing, they then are stored away—this is the circular way.
Clouds and vapor move westward,
billowing endlessly, ceaseless in winter and summer;
springs and streams flow eastward,
day and night without rest;
above they are not exhausted,
below they are not filled;
the small becomes large,
the heavy becomes light—this is the circular way.
Huángdì said:
"The sovereign has no constant abode;
having an abode is precisely having no abode."
This speaks of not being obstructed or hindered—this is the circular way.
Humans have nine orifices;
if one is occupied, then eight are empty;
if the eight remain empty for too long, the body perishes.
Therefore, if one assents and listens,
assent stops;
if one listens and looks,
listening stops.
This speaks of the unity;
the unity does not wish to linger;
if it lingers and halts, it leads to ruin—this is the circular way.
The unity is the most precious;
none know its origin,
none know its end,
none know its beginning,
none know its conclusion,
yet the myriad things take it as their ancestor.
The sage kings modeled themselves on this,
to order their nature,
to stabilize their correctness,
and to issue commands and decrees.
Commands issue from the ruler's mouth,
officials and positions receive and carry them out,
day and night without rest,
spreading and penetrating, reaching down to the utmost,
seeping into the people's hearts,
extending to the four directions,
circling around and returning,
arriving back at the ruler's place—this is the circular way.
If commands are circular, then what is permissible and impermissible, good and not good, have nothing obstructing them.
Having nothing obstructed means the ruler's way is unobstructed.
Therefore, commands are what the ruler uses as his life;
they determine the worthy and unworthy, safety and danger.
Humans have a physical body with four limbs;
they are able to use them
because when stimulated, they necessarily know;
if stimulated and they do not know,
then the physical body and four limbs cannot be used.
Ministers are likewise;
if commands and decrees do not stimulate them,
then they cannot be obtained and used.
Having them but not being able to use them is worse than not having them at all.
The ruler is one who uses what is not his own;
Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, and Wǔ were all like this.
When the former kings established high offices,
they necessarily made them square.
Being square, then duties are fixed;
duties fixed, then subordinates do not conceal from each other.
Yáo and Shùn
were worthy rulers;
they both took the worthy as their successors,
unwilling to give it to their own sons and grandsons,
just as establishing offices must make them square.
The rulers of the present age
all desire that their lineage not be lost,
and give it to their sons and grandsons;
establishing offices, they cannot make them square,
because they confuse them with private desires.
Why is this?
What they desire is distant,
but what they know is near.
Now, the five notes all respond to each other;
their distinctions are precise.
Gōng, Zhǐ, Shāng, Yǔ, Jué—
each occupies its place,
the notes are all harmoniously tuned,
and cannot violate each other;
this is why they do not interfere.
The worthy ruler's establishment of offices
is similar to this.
The hundred officials each occupy their duties, manage their affairs, and await the ruler;
the ruler is without unease.
Governing the state with this,
the state is without disadvantage;
preparing against calamity with this,
calamity has no way to arrive.
4.1 The Annals of the First Month of Summer
The first says: In the first month of summer:
The sun is in Bì;
at dusk, Yì is at the zenith;
at dawn, Wùnǚ is at the zenith.
Its days are Bǐng-Dīng.
Its sovereign is Yándì.
Its spirit is Zhùróng.
Its creatures are the feathered.
Its note is Zhǐ.
The pitch-pipe is Zhònglǚ.
Its number is seven.
Its nature is ritual.
Its affair is sight.
Its flavor is bitter.
Its smell is scorched.
Its sacrifice is to the hearth.
The offering is first the lungs.
Frogs croak.
Earthworms emerge.
Wángpú grows.
Bitter vegetables bloom.
The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the Bright Hall,
rides in a vermilion carriage,
drives red-maned horses,
carries vermilion banners,
wears red clothes,
adorns himself with red jade,
eats beans and chicken.
His vessels are tall and coarse.
In this month,
the beginning of summer is established.
Three days before the beginning of summer,
the Grand Historian reports to the Son of Heaven, saying:
"On such-and-such a day, summer begins;
the abundant virtue resides in fire."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the beginning of summer,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, and Grand Masters to welcome summer in the southern suburbs;
returning, he then bestows rewards,
enfeoffs marquises, celebrates and bestows gifts—
all are joyful and pleased.
He then commands the Music Master to practice and harmonize ritual and music.
He commands the Grand Commandant to assist the outstanding and eminent,
promote the worthy and good,
and recommend the tall and mature.
Bestowing ranks and issuing emoluments must match their positions.
In this month,
growth continues and height increases;
let there be no ruin or collapse.
Do not initiate earthworks,
do not mobilize the masses,
do not cut down large trees.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven begins to wear fine linen.
He commands the Field Overseer
to go out and inspect the fields and plains,
to encourage the farmers and urge the people,
so that none miss the season.
He commands the Minister of Education
to tour and inspect the counties and borderlands.
He commands the farmers to strive in their work,
and not to idle in the capital.
In this month,
drive away beasts so they do not harm the five grains.
Do not engage in large-scale hunting.
Farmers gather the wheat.
They present it as an offering. The Son of Heaven then tastes the wheat with pork,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
In this month, gather and store all kinds of medicinal herbs.
The delicate grasses die.
The wheat harvest arrives.
Conclude minor punishments,
adjudicate small offenses,
release those lightly imprisoned.
The silkworm work being completed,
the queen and consorts present the cocoons.
Then collect the cocoon tax,
based on the mulberry trees as the standard,
regardless of status, age, or rank,
to provide for the sacrificial robes of the suburban and ancestral temples.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven drinks the fermented spring wine,
accompanied by ritual and music.
If these ordinances are carried out,
sweet rain will arrive for three ten-day periods.
If autumn ordinances are implemented in early summer, then bitter rains will come frequently,
the five grains will not flourish,
and people from the four borders will flee into the fortifications.
If winter ordinances are implemented, then plants and trees will wither early,
and later there will be great floods, destroying the city walls.
If spring ordinances are implemented, then locusts and pests will cause damage,
violent winds will arrive,
and the flowering grasses will not bear fruit.
4.2 "Encouraging Learning"
The second says: Among the teachings of the former kings,
nothing is more honorable than filial piety,
nothing more illustrious than loyalty.
Loyalty and filial piety
are what rulers and parents greatly desire.
Illustriousness and honor
are what sons, ministers, and children greatly wish for.
Yet rulers and parents do not obtain what they desire,
sons, ministers, and children do not obtain what they wish for,
this arises from not understanding principle and righteousness.
Not understanding principle and righteousness
arises from not learning.
If a learner has a teacher who is accomplished and talented,
I have never known such a one not to become a sage.
Wherever a sage is present,
the world is well-ordered there.
If on the right, the right becomes weighty;
if on the left, the left becomes weighty.
Therefore, among the ancient sage-kings, none failed to honor their teachers.
Honoring teachers means not considering their nobility or baseness, poverty or wealth.
If this is done, then reputation becomes illustrious,
and virtuous conduct becomes manifest.
Thus, in the teaching of a teacher,
one does not contend over lightness or weight, honor or baseness, poverty or wealth,
but contends over the Way.
If the person is suitable,
then the affair is without unsuitability.
What is sought is fully obtained,
what is desired is fully achieved.
This arises from obtaining a sage.
Sages arise from diligent learning.
There has never been one who could become a great scholar or famous person without diligent learning.
This has never occurred.
Diligent learning lies in honoring teachers.
If teachers are honored, then their words are trusted,
and the Way is discussed.
Therefore, those who go to teach others are not transformed,
those who summon teachers are not transformed,
those who humble themselves are not heeded,
those who belittle teachers are not heeded.
If a teacher employs methods that do not transform and are not heeded
and forcefully teaches with them,
desiring the Way to be practiced and himself to be honored,
is that not far off?
If a learner is in a situation of not being transformed and not heeding,
and acts on his own,
desiring fame to be illustrious and himself to be secure,
this is like carrying rot and desiring fragrance,
it is like entering water and disliking wetness.
All persuasion is meant to please,
not to argue.
Persuaders of the present age
mostly cannot please,
but instead argue.
Being unable to please and instead arguing
is like saving a drowning person by weighing them down with a stone,
it is like curing illness by making them drink poison,
causing the age to become more chaotic;
unworthy rulers become deeply confused,
arising from this.
Therefore, the task of a teacher
lies in prevailing through principle,
lies in practicing righteousness.
If principle prevails and righteousness is established, then position is honored.
Kings, dukes, and great men dare not be arrogant toward them.
Up to the Son of Heaven,
he faces them without shame.
All encounters and matches
cannot be certain.
Abandoning principle and discarding righteousness to seek what is uncertain,
and desiring people to honor them,
is that not difficult?
Therefore, a teacher must prevail through principle and practice righteousness, then he will be honored.
Zēngzǐ said:
"When a gentleman walks on the road,
those who have a father can be recognized,
those who have a teacher can be recognized.
Those who have neither father nor teacher,
what more can be done for them!"
This says that serving a teacher is like serving a father.
Zēng Diǎn sent Zēng Shēn on an errand,
but he passed the deadline and did not return.
People all saw Zēng Diǎn and said:
"Could it be that he is afraid?"
Zēng Diǎn said:
"Even if he is afraid,
I am alive,
how dare he be afraid?"
When Confucius was in fear at Kuāng,
Yán Yuān arrived later. Confucius said:
"I thought you were dead."
Yán Yuān said:
"While you are alive,
how dare Huí die?"
Yán Huí's relation to Confucius
is like Zēng Shēn's serving his father.
The worthies of antiquity,
ah!
They honored their teachers like this,
therefore teachers exhausted their wisdom and the Way to teach.
4.3 "Honoring Teachers"
The third says: Shénnóng had teacher Xīzhū,
Huángdì had teacher Dànáo,
Emperor Zhuānxū had teacher Bóyífù,
Emperor Kù had teacher Bózhāo,
Emperor Yáo had teacher Zǐzhōu Zhīfù,
Emperor Shùn had teacher Xǔ Yóu,
Yǔ had teacher Dàchéng Zhì,
Tāng had teacher Xiǎochén,
King Wén and King Wǔ had teachers Lǚ Wàng and Zhōu Gōng Dàn,
Duke Huán of Qí had teacher Guǎn Yíwú,
Duke Wén of Jìn had teachers Jiùfàn and Suíhuì,
Duke Mù of Qín had teachers Bǎilǐ Xī and Gōngsūn Zhī,
King Zhuāng of Chǔ had teachers Sūnshū Áo and Shěnyǐn Shì,
King Hélǘ of Wú had teachers Wǔ Zǐxū and Wén Zhīyí,
King Gōujiàn of Yuè had teachers Fàn Lǐ and Dàfū Zhǒng.
These ten sages and six worthies
none failed to honor their teachers.
Now, if one's honor does not reach that of an emperor,
wisdom does not reach that of a sage,
yet desires not to honor teachers,
how can one attain it?
This is why the Five Emperors were cut off,
why the Three Dynasties perished.
Moreover, Heaven gives birth to humans,
and makes their ears able to hear,
but without learning, their hearing is no better than deafness;
makes their eyes able to see,
but without learning, their sight is no better than blindness;
makes their mouths able to speak,
but without learning, their speech is no better than muteness;
makes their minds able to know,
but without learning, their knowledge is no better than madness.
Therefore, all learning
is not about increasing abilities,
but about fulfilling innate nature.
Being able to fully preserve what Heaven has given birth to and not ruin it,
this is called good learning.
Zǐzhāng
was from a humble family in Lǔ;
Yán Zhuōjù
was a great robber of Liángfù;
they studied under Confucius.
Duàngān Mù
was a great horse trader of Jìn,
studied under Zǐxià.
Gāo Hé and Xiàn Zǐshí
were violent men of Qí,
pointed at in the villages,
studied under Master Mòzǐ.
Suǒlú Cān
was a great trickster of the east,
studied under Qíngǔlí.
These six men were
persons condemned to punishment, execution, or disgrace,
yet now not only are they spared from punishment, execution, and disgrace,
but through this they have become renowned scholars and illustrious figures in the world,
living out their full lifespans,
with kings, dukes, and great men according them ritual respect.
This is what they gained through learning.
In all learning,
one must strive to advance in one's studies,
the mind must be free from distraction,
diligently recite and memorize,
carefully attend to what one hears,
observe joy and pleasure,
inquire into the meaning of texts,
follow what the ears and eyes perceive,
not oppose one's will,
withdraw to ponder and consider,
seek what is called for,
timely engage in discussion and discourse,
in order to discourse on the Way,
not engaging in careless debate,
but always hitting the mark of the proper model.
When gaining it, do not be arrogant;
when losing it, do not feel ashamed;
one must return to the root.
In life, carefully nurture;
the way of careful nurturing
values nurturing the mind as most precious;
in death, respectfully offer sacrifices;
the method of respectful sacrifice
takes the timely seasons as its task;
this is how to honor the teacher.
Cultivate the garden plots,
diligently irrigate and soak,
devote effort to planting trees;
weave straw sandals,
tie nets for trapping,
bind rushes and reeds;
go to the fields and wilderness,
exert strength in plowing and weeding,
tend to the five grains;
proceed to the mountains and forests,
enter rivers and marshes,
catch fish and turtles,
seek birds and beasts;
this is how to honor the teacher.
Inspect the carriages and horses,
be cautious in driving;
adjust the clothing,
ensure it is light and warm;
when it comes to food and drink,
it must be clean and pure;
skillfully blend and harmonize,
strive for sweetness and richness;
one must be reverent and respectful;
harmonize one's countenance,
carefully consider one's words;
move swiftly and gracefully,
with strict solemnity;
this is how to honor the teacher.
In the learning of the noble person,
when discussing principles, one must cite the teacher to discourse on the Way;
in following and obeying, one must exert full effort to make it bright and clear.
If one follows and obeys without exerting full effort,
it is called betrayal;
if one discusses principles without citing the teacher,
it is called rebellion;
persons who betray and rebel,
wise rulers do not admit them into court,
and noble persons do not befriend them.
Therefore, teaching
is the greatest of righteous acts;
learning
is the height of knowledge.
Of the greatest righteous acts,
none is greater than benefiting others;
and benefiting others is greatest through teaching.
Of the height of knowledge,
none is greater than perfecting oneself;
and perfecting oneself is greatest through learning.
When one's person is perfected, then as a son one is filial without being commanded;
as a minister one is loyal without being ordered;
as a ruler one brings peace without being forced;
possessing great authority, one can become the correct standard for the world.
Therefore, Zǐgòng asked Confucius:
"How will later generations refer to you, Master?"
Confucius said:
"How am I worthy of being referred to?
If I must be described,
then it is loving learning without weariness,
loving teaching without fatigue—
perhaps only this."
When the Son of Heaven enters the Grand Academy
to sacrifice to the former sages,
he arranges by age, and those who once served as teachers are not treated as mere subjects—
this shows respect for learning and honoring teachers.
4.4 "Mistaken Disciples"
The fourth says: The teaching of an accomplished teacher
causes disciples to be at ease, joyful, relaxed, free, reverent, and serious.
If these six are attained through learning,
then the paths of depravity and deviation are blocked,
and the methods of principle and righteousness prevail.
If these six are not attained through learning,
then the ruler cannot command his ministers,
the father cannot command his sons,
and the teacher cannot command his disciples.
It is human nature
not to find joy in what makes one uneasy,
and not to gain from what one does not enjoy.
If doing something brings joy,
why wait for the worthy?
Even the unworthy will still be encouraged.
If doing something brings bitterness,
why wait for the unworthy?
Even the worthy cannot persist long.
Reflecting on human nature,
one then understands how to encourage learning.
Zǐhuázi said:
"The king delights in what makes him king,
and the doomed also delight in what dooms them.
Thus, boiling a beast is not enough to exhaust
the beast; savoring its dried meat is nearly enough."
Then the king has a taste for principle and righteousness,
and the doomed also have a taste for violence and arrogance.
Their tastes differ,
so their fortunes and misfortunes also differ.
Those who cannot teach:
Their will and spirit are not harmonious,
their choices and rejections frequently change,
they inherently lack constancy of heart,
as if cloudy or sunny, joyful or angry, without fixed place;
their speech and conversation daily shift,
acting willfully on their own,
their faults lie within themselves,
yet they refuse to acknowledge their own errors,
stubborn in their faults and self-opinionated,
impossible to correct or change;
when they see authority, kinship with power, or those with wealth and status,
they do not assess their talent,
do not examine their conduct,
but rush to teach them,
flatter and fawn upon them,
as if fearing they might not succeed;
disciples who dwell in cultivation and purity,
whose personal demeanor stands out from the crowd,
whose hearing and knowledge are broad and penetrating,
who approach learning with keen diligence,
and who are nearly completing their fundamental studies—
such disciples they then suppress,
make things difficult for and keep at a distance,
envy and detest;
disciples, when leaving, hope only to finish,
while staying, feel uneasy,
returning home, feel ashamed before parents and siblings,
going out, feel embarrassed before friends and fellow villagers;
this is what grieves the learner,
this is teacher and disciple harboring different hearts.
It is human nature
to dislike those different from oneself—
this is teacher and disciple creating mutual resentment and blame.
It is human nature
not to be close to those one resents,
not to praise those one detests.
The failure of learning and studies,
the abandonment of the Way and its methods,
arise from this.
Good teachers are not like this;
they regard disciples as themselves.
Reflecting on themselves to teach,
they then grasp the true essence of teaching.
What they impose on others
must be practicable for themselves.
If so, then teacher and disciple share the same body.
It is human nature
to love those like oneself,
to praise those like oneself,
to assist those like oneself.
The flourishing clarity of learning and studies,
the great practice of the Way and its methods,
