arise from this.
Those who cannot learn:
They follow the teacher with hardship yet desire the achievement of learning;
they follow the teacher superficially yet desire the depth of learning.
Plants, trees, chickens, dogs, oxen, horses—
one cannot treat them with abuse and insult;
if treated with abuse and insult,
they will also respond to people with abuse and insult.
How much more so with accomplished teachers and the words of the Way and its methods?
Thus, those who are incapable of learning:
when encountering a teacher, they are not attentive;
when applying their minds, they are not focused;
in their fondness for something, they are not profound;
in taking up a task, they are not diligent;
in debate and discussion, they are not precise;
in teaching others, they are not refined;
they harbor resentment toward their teacher,
are attached to common customs,
and entangle their spirits in worldly affairs;
they boast of their influence and delight in faults,
thus drowning in cleverness and cunning,
befuddled by petty gains,
and deluded by desires and cravings;
when asked about matters, their responses are contradictory;
when presented with complexity, they harbor divergent thoughts;
when faced with simplicity, they hold opposing views;
when separated, they cannot unite;
when united, they cannot separate;
when tasks arise, they are unable to accept them.
These are the troubles of those who are incapable of learning.
4.5 "Utilizing the Multitude"
The fifth says:
A good learner is like the King of Qí eating chicken:
he must eat thousands of its feet before he is satisfied;
even if he is not full,
it is as if he still has feet to eat.
All things inherently have their strengths,
and all things inherently have their weaknesses.
So too with people.
Therefore, a good learner
borrows the strengths of others to make up for his own weaknesses.
Thus, one who borrows from others can thereby possess the world.
Do not be ashamed of inability,
do not despise ignorance.
Being ashamed of inability
and despising ignorance
is a fault;
not being ashamed of inability
and not despising ignorance
is noble.
Even Jié
and Zhòu still had qualities to be respected and adopted—
how much more so for the worthy?
Therefore, a learned scholar says:
"Debate and discussion must not be neglected."
If debate and discussion can be conducted appropriately,
this is teaching.
Teaching is a great form of discussion.
If debate and discussion cannot be conducted appropriately,
it is like going out in coarse cloth
and returning in brocade robes.
A Róng person is born among the Róng,
grows up among the Róng, and speaks the Róng language,
not knowing from whom he received it;
a Chǔ person is born in Chǔ,
grows up in Chǔ, and speaks the Chǔ language,
not knowing from whom he received it.
Now, if a Chǔ person were to grow up among the Róng,
or a Róng person were to grow up in Chǔ,
then the Chǔ person would speak the Róng language,
and the Róng person would speak the Chǔ language.
From this perspective,
I do not know that a ruler of a fallen state cannot become a worthy ruler—
it is merely that the environment in which he grew up is not suitable.
Therefore, the environment in which one grows up must not be overlooked.
Under heaven, there is no fox of pure white fur,
yet there are robes of pure white fur—
they are made by gathering many white hairs.
To draw from the multitude—
this is how the Three Sovereigns
and Five Emperors achieved great merit and fame.
In general, the reason a ruler is established
is because he emerges from the multitude.
Once established, if he abandons the multitude,
he grasps the branches but loses the root.
Grasping the branches but losing the root—
one never hears of peaceful stability in such a case.
Thus, with the courage of the multitude, one need not fear even Mèng Bēn;
with the strength of the multitude, one need not fear even Wū Huò;
with the vision of the multitude, one need not fear even Lí Lóu;
with the wisdom of the multitude, one need not fear even Yáo
and Shùn.
To rely on the multitude—
this is the great treasure for one who rules people.
Tián Pián said to the King of Qí:
"Mèng Bēn nearly mastered the art of dealing with troubles,
yet the borders were not troubled;
the kings of Chǔ and Wèi,
though their words were not eloquent,
had their territories well-prepared,
and their soldiers well-trained and ready—
this was achieved through the multitude."
5.1 "Records of Mid-Summer"
The first says: In the month of mid-summer:
the sun is in Jīng,
at dusk the constellation Kàng is at the zenith,
at dawn the constellation Wēi is at the zenith.
Its days are Bǐng-Dīng.
Its sovereign is Yán Dì.
Its deity is Zhù Róng.
Its creatures are the feathered ones.
Its musical note is Zhǐ.
The pitch-pipe is Ruíbīn.
Its number is seven.
Its flavor is bitter.
Its odor is scorched.
Its sacrifice is to the hearth.
The offering is first made with lungs.
Minor Heat arrives.
Praying mantises are born.
The jú bird begins to sing.
The mockingbird falls silent.
The Son of Heaven resides in the Bright Hall's Grand Ancestral Temple,
rides in a vermilion carriage,
drives red-maned horses,
bears vermilion banners,
wears vermilion robes,
adorns himself with red jade,
and eats beans and chicken.
His vessels are tall and coarse.
He nurtures the strong and vigorous.
In this month,
he commands the Music Master
to repair drums large and small,
tune qins, sè, pipes, and flutes,
prepare shields, axes, spears, and feathers,
adjust yús, shēngs, xūns, and chís,
and set in order bells, chimes, zhùs, and yǔs.
He orders the officials
to pray and sacrifice to the mountains, rivers, and all sources for the people,
conduct the Great Rain Sacrifice to the Emperor,
using grand music.
Then he commands all districts
to perform rain sacrifices to the various lords and ministers who benefited the people,
to pray for abundant grain.
Farmers then present millet.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven tastes millet with young chickens,
presents cherries as delicacies,
and first offers them in the ancestral temple.
He orders the people not to cut indigo for dyeing,
not to burn charcoal,
and not to sun-dry cloth.
Gates and alleys are not closed,
and tolls are not levied at passes and markets.
He lightens the sentences of heavy prisoners,
and increases their food.
He separates the roaming mares from their herds,
then tethers the spirited colts,
and regulates the horse officials.
In this month,
the day reaches its longest.
Yīn and Yáng contend,
and life and death divide.
The nobleman observes purification and abstinence,
dwelling in places where he must cover his body,
seeking stillness without agitation,
abstaining from music and beauty,
with no advancement of desires,
diluting flavors,
not seeking harmony,
withdrawing from cravings and desires,
calming his heart and energy,
keeping all officials quiet,
and affairs without haste,
so as to stabilize what is achieved by the calm Yīn.
Deer shed their antlers.
Cicadas begin to sing.
Pinellia sprouts,
and hibiscus blooms.
In this month,
do not use fire in the southern direction.
One may dwell in high, bright places,
may gaze afar,
may climb mountains and hills,
and may reside in terraces and pavilions.
If in midsummer the ordinances of winter are carried out,
then hail and sleet will damage the grain,
roads will become impassable,
and violent soldiers will arrive.
If the ordinances of spring are carried out,
then the five grains will ripen late,
various insect pests will arise in season,
and the state will suffer famine.
If the ordinances of autumn are carried out,
then plants and trees will wither and fall,
fruits will mature early,
and the people will suffer calamity from epidemics.
5.2 "The Great Music"
The second says: The origins of music are ancient indeed.
It is born from measurement and proportion,
and rooted in the Supreme Unity.
The Supreme Unity gives rise to the Two Modes,
and the Two Modes give rise to Yīn and Yáng.
Yīn and Yáng transform and change,
one ascending, one descending,
combining to form patterns.
In a state of primal chaos,
they separate and then reunite,
reunite and then separate again;
this is called the constant way of Heaven.
Heaven and Earth are like a turning wheel:
when it ends, it begins again;
when it reaches an extreme, it returns.
Nothing fails to find its proper place.
The sun, moon, stars, and constellations,
some moving swiftly, some slowly,
the sun and moon differing,
each completes its course.
The four seasons arise in succession,
some hot, some cold,
some short, some long,
some yielding, some firm.
All things that emerge
are created by the Supreme Unity,
and transformed by Yīn and Yáng.
When the sprout first stirs,
it congeals and takes form.
Where forms and bodies have their place,
none is without sound.
Sound arises from harmony,
and harmony arises from appropriateness.
From harmony and appropriateness, the ancient kings established music,
and it was born from this.
When the world is at peace,
and all things are tranquil,
all transformed by those above,
then music can be achieved.
To achieve music requires tools;
one must regulate desires.
If desires are not depraved,
then music can be pursued.
To pursue music requires method;
it must arise from balance.
Balance arises from impartiality,
and impartiality arises from the Dào.
Thus, only those who have attained the Dào
can be spoken to about music!
In states that perish and people who are slaughtered,
it is not that there is no music,
but their music is not joyful.
A drowning man is not without laughter,
a criminal is not without song,
a madman is not without martial display;
the music of a chaotic age
resembles this.
When ruler and minister lose their positions,
father and son lose their proper places,
husband and wife lose their proper relationship,
and the people groan,
to take this as music—
how can it be so?
All music
is the harmony of Heaven and Earth,
the attunement of Yīn and Yáng.
Heaven is what first gave birth to humans;
humans had no part in it.
Heaven causes humans to have desires;
humans cannot but seek them.
Heaven causes humans to have aversions;
humans cannot but avoid them.
Desires and aversions are received from Heaven;
humans have no part in them.
They cannot be altered,
cannot be changed.
Among the scholars of the world,
there are those who condemn music;
from what does this arise?
The Great Music
is what brings joy and delight to ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger.
Joy arises from balance,
and balance arises from the Dào.
The Dào—
look at it, you do not see it;
listen to it, you do not hear it;
it cannot be described in form.
If one knows the seeing of not-seeing,
the hearing of not-hearing, the form of no-form,
then one is close to knowing it.
The Dào
is the most refined essence;
it cannot be given form,
cannot be given a name.
If forced to name it, it is called the Supreme Unity.
Thus, the One issues commands,
and the Two obey and listen.
The ancient sages chose the Two and modeled themselves on the One;
thereby they knew the nature of all things.
Therefore, one who can use the One to hear governance
delights ruler and minister,
harmonizes near and far,
pleases the common people,
and unites clan and kin.
One who can use the One to govern his own person
avoids calamity,
completes his lifespan,
and preserves his Heaven-given nature.
One who can use the One to govern his state
drives away treachery and evil,
attracts the worthy,
and achieves great transformation and accomplishment.
One who can use the One to govern the world
ensures that cold and heat are appropriate,
wind and rain timely,
and becomes a sage.
Thus, to know the One is to be enlightened;
to exalt the Two is to be deluded.
5.3 "Extravagant Music"
The third says: All people live by their life,
but do not know why they live.
All people know by their knowing,
but do not know why they know.
To know why one knows is called understanding the Dào;
not to know why one knows is called discarding a treasure.
Those who discard the treasure are sure to encounter misfortune.
The rulers of the world
mostly consider pearls, jade, spears, and swords as treasures.
The more treasures they have, the more the people resent them,
the more the state is endangered,
and the more their own persons are imperiled and burdened.
This misses the true nature of treasure.
The music of a chaotic age is the same as this.
The sounds of wood and leather are like thunder;
the sounds of metal and stone are like thunderclaps;
the sounds of strings, bamboo, song, and dance are like clamor.
Using these to startle the heart's energy,
agitate the ears and eyes,
and unsettle the vital nature—
this is possible,
but to consider this as music is to have no joy.
Thus, the more extravagant the music,
the more depressed the people become,
the more chaotic the state,
the more debased the ruler,
and this too misses the true nature of music.
In general, what the ancient sage-kings valued in music
was its joy.
Xià Jié and Yīn Zhòu created extravagant music:
the sounds of great drums, bells, chimes, pipes, and flutes,
considering enormity as beauty,
multitude as spectacle,
strange, extraordinary, and bizarre,
what the ear had never before heard,
what the eye had never before seen,
striving only to outdo each other,
with no use of measure or proportion.
When Sòng declined,
it created the Thousand Bells.
When Qí declined,
it created the Great Lǚ.
When Chǔ declined,
it created Shaman Music.
Extravagant it was indeed,
but from the perspective of one who possesses the Dào,
it missed the true nature of music.
To miss the true nature of music
means the music is not joyful.
When music is not joyful,
the people are sure to resent it,
and their lives are sure to be harmed.
The relationship between their lives and such music
is like that between ice and the blazing sun or hot coals—
it turns back to wound itself.
This arises from not knowing the true nature of music,
and instead striving for extravagance.
Music has its nature,
comparable to how the body and limbs have their inherent disposition;
having an inherent disposition means there must be a way to nurture it.
Cold, heat, toil, rest, hunger, and satiety—
these six are not moderation.
All nurturing
involves observing what is not moderate and making it moderate.
If one can long remain in moderation,
then growth and development occur.
Life itself
is fundamentally tranquil in its nature;
it is only through external stimuli that awareness arises,
stimuli that activate it.
If one pursues [these stimuli] without turning back,
becoming controlled by insatiable desires,
then being controlled by insatiable desires will inevitably cause one to lose one’s innate nature.
Moreover, when desires are insatiable,
there will certainly arise minds of greed, baseness, perversity, and disorder,
and deeds of licentiousness, excess, treachery, and deceit.
Thus, the strong plunder the weak,
the many oppress the few,
the brave bully the timid,
the robust scorn the young—
all this arises from this.
5.4 “Appropriate Tones”
The fourth says: The ear’s nature desires sounds,
but if the mind is not pleased,
even the five tones are before it, it does not listen.
The eye’s nature desires colors,
but if the mind is not pleased,
even the five colors are before it, it does not see.
The nose’s nature desires fragrances,
but if the mind is not pleased,
even fragrances are before it, it does not smell.
The mouth’s nature desires flavors,
but if the mind is not pleased,
even the five flavors are before it, it does not eat.
Those that desire
are the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth;
what determines pleasure or displeasure
is the mind.
The mind must be peaceful and harmonious before there is pleasure;
the mind must be pleased before the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth have the means to desire.
Therefore, the essential task of music lies in harmonizing the mind,
and harmonizing the mind lies in practicing moderation.
Now, music has its moderation,
and the mind also has its moderation.
Human nature
desires longevity and hates early death,
desires safety and hates danger,
desires honor and hates disgrace,
desires ease and hates toil.
When these four desires are fulfilled,
and these four aversions are removed,
then the mind is in moderation.
The fulfillment of these four desires
lies in following principle.
Following principle to govern the body ensures the preservation of life;
preservation of life leads to longevity.
Following principle to govern the state ensures the establishment of laws;
establishment of laws leads to the submission of all under heaven.
Therefore, the essential task of moderating the mind lies in following principle.
Now, tones also have their moderation.
If too loud, the will becomes agitated;
listening to loudness with agitation, the ears cannot contain it;
if they cannot contain it, they become blocked;
if blocked, they vibrate.
If too soft, the will becomes dissatisfied;
listening to softness with dissatisfaction, the ears are not filled;
if not filled, they do not reach;
if they do not reach, they become hollow.
If too high-pitched, the will becomes precarious;
listening to high pitch with precariousness, the ears become strained to the extreme;
if strained to the extreme, they do not discern;
if they do not discern, they become exhausted.
If too low-pitched, the will becomes debased;
listening to low pitch with debasement, the ears do not gather;
if they do not gather, they do not concentrate;
if they do not concentrate, they become angry.
Therefore, tones that are too loud, too soft, too high-pitched, or too low-pitched are all not moderate.
What is moderation?
The mean is the moderation of tones.
What is the mean?
Not exceeding the jūn in size,
not exceeding the shí in weight—
this is the mean in size and weight.
The huángzhōng note’s gōng,
is the foundation of tones,
the mean between high and low pitch.
The mean is moderation;
listening to moderation with moderation brings harmony.
In music, there should be no excess;
what is balanced and harmonious is correct.
Thus, the music of a well-governed age is peaceful and joyful,
reflecting its equitable governance;
the music of a chaotic age is resentful and angry,
reflecting its perverse governance;
the music of a perishing state is sorrowful and mournful,
reflecting its perilous governance.
All music is connected to governance
and transforms customs and mores;
once customs are settled, music transforms them.
Therefore, in an age ruled by the Way,
observe its music and know its customs; observe its customs and know its governance;
observe its governance and know its ruler.
Thus, the former kings necessarily relied on music to convey their teachings.
The se zither of the “Qīngmiào”
had red strings and widely spaced sound holes,
one singing followed by three sighs—
there was something surpassing mere sound.
In the ceremony of the great sacrifice,
the dark-colored zuń vessel was placed above, and raw fish on the sacrificial stand,
the grand broth was not seasoned—
there was something surpassing mere flavor.
Therefore, when the former kings instituted rites and music,
it was not merely to delight the ears and eyes or to satisfy the desires of the mouth and belly,
but to teach the people to balance likes and dislikes
and to practice principle and righteousness.
5.5 “Ancient Music”
The fifth says: The origins of music are ancient,
and it must not be abolished.
There is restrained music and extravagant music,
proper music and licentious music.
The worthy prosper through it,
the unworthy perish through it.
In ancient times, when Zhūxiángshì governed the world,
there was much wind and the yáng energy accumulated excessively,
all things scattered and disintegrated,
fruits did not ripen,
so Shì Dá made a five-stringed se zither
to draw in yīn energy
and stabilize all living beings.
The music of ancient Gétiānshì
featured three men holding ox tails, stamping their feet, and singing eight pieces:
the first called “Zàimín,”
the second called “Xuánshēn,”
the third called “Suì Cǎomù,”
the fourth called “Fèn Wǔgǔ,”
the fifth called “Jìng Tiāncháng,”
the sixth called “Dá Dìgōng,”
the seventh called “Yī Dìdé,”
the eighth called “Zǒng Wànwù zhī Jí.”
At the beginning of ancient Táotángshì’s time,
yīn energy was excessive, stagnant, and accumulated deeply,
the yáng path was obstructed,
not following its proper order,
the people’s vital energy was depressed, blocked, and stagnant,
their sinews and bones constricted and not free,
so they created dances to channel and guide it.
In ancient times, Huángdì ordered Líng Lún to create the pitch standards.
Líng Lún went from the west of Dàxià
to the northern side of Ruǎnyú,
took bamboo from the valley of Xièxī,
selected those with hollow internodes of uniform thickness,
cut between two nodes to a length of three inches and nine-tenths, and blew into them,
producing the huángzhōng note’s gōng,
called “Shěshǎo.”
Then he made twelve tubes,
took them to the foot of Ruǎnyú,
listened to the calls of the fenghuang,
and distinguished the twelve pitch standards.
The male calls were six,
the female calls also six;
compared to the huángzhōng note’s gōng, they matched perfectly.
The huángzhōng note’s gōng
could generate all of them;
therefore it is said that the huángzhōng note’s gōng
is the foundation of the pitch standards.
Huángdì also ordered Líng Lún and Róng Jiāng to cast twelve bells,
to harmonize the five tones,
to perform the “Yīngsháo,”
and in the second month of spring,
on the day of yǐmǎo,
when the sun was in Kuí,
they began to play it,
naming it “Xiánchí.”
Emperor Zhuānxù was born at Ruòshuǐ,
but actually dwelled at Kōngsāng,
then ascended to become emperor.
In accordance with Heaven’s harmony,
the proper winds then blew,
their sound like a bustling, chilly, clanging resonance.
Emperor Zhuānxū enjoyed its sounds,
so he ordered Fēilóng to create music imitating the sounds of the eight winds,
naming it "Chéng Yún,"
to offer sacrifices to the Supreme God.
He then ordered the eel to lead the music performance,
and the eel lay down,
using its tail to drum on its belly,
producing a resonant sound.
Emperor Kù commanded Xián Hēi to compose melodies, singing
"Jiǔ Zhāo," "Liù Liè," and "Liù Yīng."
Chuí crafted drums, bells, chimes, flutes, pipes, xūn, chí, táo, and hammered bells.
Emperor Kù then ordered people to clap or beat drums,
strike bells and chimes,
and blow flutes, pipes, and chí.
He also commanded phoenixes and celestial pheasants to dance to it.
Emperor Kù was greatly pleased,
and used it to glorify imperial virtue.
When Emperor Yáo ascended the throne,
he ordered Zhì to create music.
Zhì imitated the sounds of mountains, forests, streams, and valleys to compose songs,
then covered a pottery vessel with deer hide to drum on it,
and struck stones against stones,
to emulate the sound of the Supreme God's jade chimes,
thereby summoning the dance of a hundred beasts.
Gǔsǒu then blended the five-stringed se,
creating a fifteen-stringed se.
It was named "Dà Zhāng,"
to offer sacrifices to the Supreme God.
When Shùn ascended the throne,
he ordered Yán to blend the se created by Gǔsǒu,
adding eight more strings,
making it a twenty-three-stringed se.
Emperor Shùn then ordered Zhì to revise "Jiǔ Zhāo," "Liù Liè," and "Liù Yīng,"
to illuminate imperial virtue.
When Yǔ ascended the throne,
he toiled diligently for the world,
working day and night without rest,
dredging great rivers,
clearing blockages,
carving through Lóngmén,
channeling Liáo Shuǐ to guide the Hé River,
dredging the Sān Jiāng and Wǔ Hú,
directing them into the Eastern Sea,
to benefit the common people.
He then ordered Gāo Yáo to compose "Xià Yuè" in nine movements,
to manifest his achievements.
When Tāng of Yīn ascended the throne,
the Xià dynasty acted without virtue,
oppressing the myriad people,
invading and diminishing the feudal lords,
disregarding proper measures,
causing the world to suffer.
Tāng then led six provinces to punish Jié's crimes,
achieving great success and fame,
bringing peace to the common people.
Tāng then ordered Yī Yǐn to compose "Dà Hù,"
singing "Chén Lù,"
and revising "Jiǔ Zhāo" and "Liù Liè,"
to display his goodness.
King Wén of Zhōu resided in Qí,
and the feudal lords, abandoning Yīn's three excesses, supported King Wén.
Sàn Yíshēng said:
"Yīn can be attacked."
King Wén did not permit it.
Zhōu Gōng Dàn then composed a poem, saying:
"King Wén is above,
shining in the heavens,
Zhōu, though an old state,
its mandate is renewed,"
to praise King Wén's virtue.
When King Wǔ ascended the throne,
he led six armies to attack Yīn,
but before the six armies arrived,
he defeated them with sharp troops at Mùyě.
Upon returning,
he presented captives and trophies at the Great Temple in the capital,
and ordered Zhōu Gōng to compose "Dà Wǔ."
When King Chéng ascended the throne,
the people of Yīn rebelled,
and the king ordered Zhōu Gōng to lead a punitive expedition against them.
The Shāng people used elephants,
wreaking havoc in the Eastern Yí lands,
so Zhōu Gōng led troops to drive them out,
reaching south of the Jiāng River,
and composed "Sān Xiàng,"
to celebrate his virtue.
Thus, the origins of music are ancient,
not created for a single era alone.
6.1 "Jì Xià Jì"
It is said: In the month of Jì Xià:
the sun is in Liǔ,
at dusk the heart star is in the center,
at dawn the Kuí star is in the center.
Its days are Bǐng and Dīng.
Its emperor is Yán Dì.
Its deity is Zhùróng.
Its creatures are feathered.
Its musical note is Zhǐ.
The pitch pipe corresponds to Lín Zhōng.
Its number is seven.
Its flavor is bitter.
Its odor is scorched.
Its sacrifice is to the stove.
Offer lungs first.
Cool winds begin to arrive.
Crickets dwell in the eaves.
Hawks then learn to hunt.
Rotten grass transforms into fireflies.
The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Bright Hall,
rides in a vermilion carriage,
drives red-maned horses,
carries vermilion banners,
wears vermilion robes,
adorns himself with red jade,
eats beans and chicken.
His vessels are tall and coarse.
In this month,
order the fishing masters to hunt flood dragons
and capture alligators, raise turtles and capture giant softshell turtles.
Then command the foresters to gather timber and reeds.
In this month,
order the four supervising officials to collect fodder from all counties to nourish sacrificial animals.
Command the people to all exert their efforts,
to serve the August Heaven and Supreme God,
the famous mountains and great rivers, the deities of the four directions, to offer sacrifices to the spirits of ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain,
to pray for blessings for the people.
In this month,
order the women officials to dye fabrics,
with intricate patterns and designs,
following established methods,
without any errors,
black, yellow, blue, and red,
all must be of fine quality,
and none dare to falsify,
to provide garments for suburban and temple sacrifices,
to make banners and insignia, to distinguish the degrees of nobility and rank.
In this month,
trees are flourishing,
and yin energy is about to begin its punishment, so order the foresters to inspect the mountains and trees, and do not allow any felling.
Do not undertake earthworks,
do not assemble feudal lords,
do not raise armies or mobilize the masses.
Do not initiate major undertakings,
to nurture yang energy.
Do not issue orders that interfere with the seasons,
to hinder the affairs of Shénnóng.
Floodwaters are abundant,
command Shénnóng,
to inspect the achievements.
Initiating major undertakings will bring heavenly calamities.
In this month,
the soil is moist and the heat is oppressive,
heavy rains occur seasonally,
burn weeds and channel water,
beneficial for killing grass,
as if with boiling water,
it can fertilize the fields,
and enrich the soil.
If these commands are followed,
sweet rains will arrive three times this month,
over thirty-two days.
If spring commands are followed in Jì Xià,
then grain kernels will shed,
the state will suffer from wind-induced coughs,
and the people will migrate.
If autumn commands are followed,
then hills and marshes will flood,
crops will not ripen,
and many women will suffer disasters.
If winter commands are followed,
then cold energy will be untimely,
hawks and falcons will hunt early,
and the four borders will retreat into fortifications.
Central Earth:
Its days are Wù and Jǐ.
Its emperor is Huáng Dì.
Its deity is Hòutǔ.
Its creatures are naked.
Its musical note is Gōng.
The pitch pipe corresponds to Huáng Zhōng's Gōng.
Its number is five.
Its flavor is sweet.
Its odor is fragrant.
Its sacrifice is to the household god.
The offering is made first to the heart.
The Son of Heaven resides in the Great Ancestral Temple's Great Chamber,
rides in the great carriage,
drives yellow-maned horses,
bears a yellow banner,
wears yellow robes,
adorns himself with yellow jade,
and eats millet and beef.
His vessels are round and covered.
6.2 "Musical Pitches"
The second says:
Huángzhōng gives birth to Línzhōng,
Línzhōng gives birth to Tàicù,
Tàicù gives birth to Nánlǚ,
Nánlǚ gives birth to Gūxiǎn,
Gūxiǎn gives birth to Yìngzhōng,
Yìngzhōng gives birth to Ruíbīn,
Ruíbīn gives birth to Dàlǚ,
Dàlǚ gives birth to Yízé,
Yízé gives birth to Jiázhōng,
Jiázhōng gives birth to Wúyì,
Wúyì gives birth to Zhònglǚ.
Divide what is born into three parts,
add one part to generate the upper pitch;
divide what is born into three parts,
remove one part to generate the lower pitch.
Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, Tàicù, Jiázhōng, Gūxiǎn, Zhònglǚ, and Ruíbīn are upper pitches; Línzhōng, Yízé, Nánlǚ, Wúyì, and Yìngzhōng are lower pitches.
In the age of great sages and perfect order,
the qi of heaven and earth
combines to produce wind.
When the sun arrives, the moon concentrates this wind,
giving birth to the twelve pitches.
At the winter solstice in midwinter,
Huángzhōng is born.
In late winter, Dàlǚ is born.
In early spring, Tàicù is born.
In mid-spring, Jiázhōng is born.
In late spring, Gūxiǎn is born.
In early summer, Zhònglǚ is born.
At the summer solstice in midsummer,
Ruíbīn is born.
In late summer, Línzhōng is born.
In early autumn, Yízé is born.
In mid-autumn, Nánlǚ is born.
In late autumn, Wúyì is born.
In early winter, Yìngzhōng is born.
When the winds and qi of heaven and earth are correct,
the twelve pitches are established.
In the month of Huángzhōng,
do not undertake earthworks,
carefully avoid uncovering covers,
to secure the closure of heaven and earth.
Uncovering covers and stores,
mobilizing the masses,
causes yang qi to leak out,
which is called opening the chambers of heaven and earth.
In the month of Dàlǚ,
the count is nearing its end,
the year is about to begin anew,
so focus on agriculture, and the people
should not be employed for other tasks.
In the month of Tàicù,
the heavenly qi descends, yang qi begins to grow,
heaven and earth are harmonious, plants and trees stir vigorously.
Order the farmers to break ground,
and do not miss the season.
In the month of Jiázhōng,
be lenient, generous, peaceful, and harmonious,
practice virtue and avoid punishments,
do not undertake any projects,
to harm the multitude of living things.
In the month of Gūxiǎn,
clear the roads and open the paths,
repair and improve ditches and canals.
Proclaim this order,
and auspicious qi will swiftly arrive.
In the month of Zhònglǚ,
do not gather large crowds,
but tour to encourage agricultural work.
Plants and trees are just growing,
do not disturb the people's hearts.
In the month of Ruíbīn,
yang qi is above,
comfort the strong and nurture the excellent.
If the court is not tranquil,
plants and trees will wither early.
In the month of Línzhōng,
plants and trees are full and abundant,
yin is about to begin its punitive phase.
Do not initiate major undertakings,
to preserve yang qi.
In the month of Yízé,
revise laws and rectify punishments,
select soldiers and sharpen weapons,
interrogate and punish the unjust,
to pacify distant regions.
In the month of Nánlǚ,
hibernating insects all crouch in their burrows,
sealing their entrances. Urge farmers to harvest and gather,
not daring to slack off,
striving for abundance.
In the month of Wúyì,
swiftly judge the guilty,
apply the law without pardon,
do not delay lawsuits and disputes,
but act with urgency.
In the month of Yìngzhōng,
yin and yang do not communicate,
closing up to become winter.
Regulate mourning rites,
distinguish burial garments, and determine the people's final arrangements.
6.3 "The Origins of Music"
The third says:
Kǒng Jiǎ of the Xiàhòu clan was hunting at Fù Mountain in Dōngyáng,
when a great wind arose, darkening the sky.
Kǒng Jiǎ became lost
and entered a commoner's house.
The mistress was just giving birth.
Some said,
"The ruler's arrival on this day is auspicious;
this child will surely have great fortune."
Others said,
"He cannot bear it;
this child will surely have misfortune."
The ruler then took the child and returned,
saying:
"If I make him my son,
who would dare bring him misfortune?"
When the child grew to adulthood,
a curtain moved, splitting a rafter,
and an axe fell, cutting off his foot.
He thus became a gatekeeper.
Kǒng Jiǎ said:
"Alas!
There is affliction;
it is fate, is it not!"
He then composed the song "Broken Axe,"
which truly began the Eastern music.
When Yǔ was traveling on his work,
he saw a woman of Túshān.
Yǔ did not meet with her but went to inspect the southern lands.
The woman of Túshān then sent her maid to wait for Yǔ at the southern slope of Túshān.
The woman then made a song,
singing, "Waiting for the man, oh alas!"
This truly began the Southern music.
Duke Zhōu and Duke Shào drew inspiration from it,
making it the "Zhōunán" and "Shàonán."
King Zhāo of Zhōu personally led an expedition against Jīng.
Xīn Yúmí was tall and strong,
serving as the king's right-hand guard.
On the return crossing of the Hàn River,
the bridge collapsed,
and the king and Duke Cài fell into the Hàn River.
Xīn Yúmí rescued the king and carried him north across the river,
then returned to rescue Duke Cài.
Duke Zhōu then enfeoffed him in the Western Dí,
and he became the Elder Lord.
Yǐn Zhěngjiǎ moved his dwelling to Xīhé,
but still longed for his old home.
This truly began the Western music.
The Elder Lord continued this music while dwelling in the Western Mountains.
Duke Mù of Qín drew inspiration from it,
which truly began the Qín music.
The Yǒusōng clan had two beautiful maidens,
for whom a nine-tiered tower was built.
When they ate and drank, drums were always played.
The Lord on High ordered a swallow to go and observe them.
Its cry was like "yì yì."
The two maidens loved it and fought to catch it,
covering it with a jade basket.
After a short while,
they opened it to look,
and the swallow had left two eggs,
then flew north
and did not return.
The two maidens made a song, one stanza
saying,
"The swallow, the swallow has flown away,"
which truly began the Northern music.
All music
arises from the human heart.
When stirred within the heart, it manifests as sound in music;
the music forms externally and transforms internally.
Therefore, by hearing its sounds, one can understand its customs;
by examining its customs, one can understand its aspirations;
by observing its aspirations, one can understand its virtue.
Prosperity and decline, worthiness and unworthiness, noble and petty men—all are revealed in music,
unable to be concealed.
Thus it is said: music provides a profound means of observation.
When the soil is exhausted, grass and trees do not grow;
when the waters are turbulent, fish and turtles do not grow large;
when the age is corrupt, rituals become excessive and music becomes licentious.
The sounds of Zhèng and Wèi,
the music of Sāngjiān,
these are what disordered states delight in,
what declining virtue takes pleasure in.
When wayward, frivolous, excessive, and dissolute music emerges,
then dissipated, unrestrained energies and wicked, arrogant hearts are stirred;
once stirred, all manner of treacheries and evils arise from this.
Therefore, the noble man returns to the Way to cultivate virtue,
rectifies virtue to produce music,
and harmonizes music to achieve accord.
When music is harmonious, the people turn toward righteousness.
6.4 "Regulating Music"
Fourth:
If one wishes to observe perfect music,
it must be in a state of perfect order.
Where governance is substantial, its musical governance is substantial;
where governance is meager, its musical governance is meager;
in chaotic times, music becomes negligent.
Now, even with doors and windows closed,
it can move heaven and earth,
all within a single room.
Thus, in the time of Chéng Tāng,
there was grain that grew in the courtyard,
appearing at dusk
and by dawn had grown as thick as an arm.
His historian requested to divine the reason.
Tāng dismissed the diviner, saying:
"I have heard that auspicious signs are the forerunners of blessing,
but if one sees an auspicious sign and acts unworthily, the blessing will not come;
ominous signs are the forerunners of disaster,
but if one sees an ominous sign and acts virtuously, the disaster will not come."
Thereupon, he attended court early and retired late,
inquired after the ill and mourned the dead,
and diligently pacified and comforted the people.
After three days, the grain vanished of itself.
Thus, disaster is where blessing relies;
blessing is where disaster lurks.
This is what the sage alone perceives;
how can the multitude know its ultimate principle?
When King Wén of Zhōu had been established as ruler for eight years,
in the sixth month of the year,
he lay ill for five days, and then an earthquake occurred.
East, west, south, and north,
it did not extend beyond the borders of the state.
All the officials requested:
"We have heard that earthquakes
are due to the ruler.
Now, the king has been ill for five days, and an earthquake has occurred, not extending beyond the Zhōu borders on all sides.
All the ministers are fearful and ask to transfer it."
King Wén said:
"How would you transfer it?"
They replied:
"By mobilizing the people and undertaking works
to enlarge the state's walls,
perhaps it could be transferred."
King Wén said:
"No.
When Heaven displays an ominous sign,
it is to punish the guilty.
I must have committed some fault,
thus Heaven punishes me thus.
Now, if I deliberately mobilize the people to enlarge the walls,
that would compound my fault.
It cannot be." King Wén said,
"Through this, it may prosper.
Let us reform our conduct and redouble our goodness to transfer it;
perhaps then we may be spared."
Thereupon, he carefully regulated the ceremonial ranks and hides
to engage with the feudal lords;
he refined his decrees
and silks
to honor the eminent scholars;
he distributed ranks, grades, and fields
to reward the meritorious, and so proceeded with his ministers.
Not long after practicing this,
his illness ceased.
King Wén had been ruler for eight years when the earthquake occurred;
after it occurred, forty-three years passed,
and altogether King Wén ruled for fifty-one years before his end.
This is how King Wén halted calamity and dispelled omens.
In the time of Duke Jǐng of Sòng,
Mars was in the Heart constellation.
The duke was afraid
and summoned Zǐ Wéi to inquire,
saying:
"Mars is in the Heart constellation;
what does this mean?"
Zǐ Wéi said:
"Mars
is Heaven's punishment;
the Heart constellation
is the celestial division corresponding to Sòng.
Disaster is about to befall your person.
Nevertheless,
it can be transferred to the prime minister."
The duke said:
"The prime minister assists in governing the state;
to transfer death to him
would be inauspicious."
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the people."
The duke said:
"If the people die,
for whom would I be ruler?
I would rather die alone."
Zǐ Wéi said:
"It can be transferred to the harvest."
The duke said:
"If the harvest is harmed, the people will starve;
if the people starve, they will die.
For a ruler to seek to kill his people to preserve himself,
who would take me as their ruler?
My fate is surely at its end;
say no more."
Zǐ Wéi retreated,
faced north, bowed twice, and said:
"I dare to congratulate you, my lord.
Heaven, though on high, hears what is below.
You have spoken three supremely virtuous words;
Heaven must reward you thrice.
Tonight, Mars will shift three lunar mansions,
and you will gain twenty-one years of life."
The duke said:
"How do you know this?"
He replied:
"With three good statements,
there must be three rewards.
Mars will shift three mansions;
each mansion traverses seven stars;
each star shifted corresponds to one year.
Three times seven is twenty-one;
therefore I say you will gain twenty-one years of life.
I request to wait below the steps to observe it.
If Mars does not shift,
I ask to die for it."
The duke said:
"Very well."
That night, Mars indeed shifted three mansions.
6.5 "Clarifying Principles"
Fifth:
The Five Emperors and Three Kings exhausted the essence of music.
The rulers of disordered states,
who have never understood music,
are merely ordinary rulers.
To have received Heaven's favor and become ruler,
yet never to have attained the substance of rulership—
this is called great sorrow.
It is like sitting straight in a chamber facing west:
what one calls straight
is actually not straight.
All life is not transformed by a single breath;
all growth is not accomplished by a single thing;
all completion is not achieved by a single form.
Thus, where many upright things accumulate,
their blessings reach everywhere;
where many wicked things accumulate,
their disasters reach everywhere.
Then the winds and rains are untimely,
the sweet rains do not fall,
the frost and snow are unseasonable,
the cold and heat are improper,
yīn and yáng lose their order,
the four seasons shift their nodes,
the people become dissolute and unstable,
beasts miscarry and do not breed,
plants and trees remain stunted and do not flourish,
the five grains spoil and do not ripen.
To make music in such a state—
what would it be like?
Thus, in the transformation of extreme disorder,
ruler and minister harm each other,
elder and youth kill each other,
father and son are cruel to each other,
brothers slander each other,
friends betray each other,
husband and wife revile each other,
daily endangering one another,
losing human order,
hearts like those of beasts,
cultivating wickedness and coveting profit,
knowing neither righteousness nor principle.
The forms of clouds:
some resemble dogs, horses, white swans, or numerous chariots;
some have shapes like humans,
with blue garments and red heads,
motionless—
these are called Tiānchōng;
some have shapes like suspended red cauldrons,
these are called Yúnjīng;
some resemble numerous horses fighting,
these are called Huámǎ;
some resemble many upright flowers growing tall,
yellow above and white below,
these are called the Banner of Chīyóu.
As for the sun,
there are eclipses,
double halos,
coronas and parhelia,
dimness,
failure to cast shadows,
multiple suns appearing together,
daytime blindness,
and nighttime visibility.
As for the moon,
there are partial eclipses,
halos and parhelia,
partial blindness,
four moons appearing together,
two moons appearing together,
a small moon supporting a large moon,
a large moon supporting a small moon,
the moon eclipsing stars,
and emergence without light.
As for the stars,
there is Yínghuò (Mars),
comets,
Tiānbàng,
Tiānchán,
Tiānzhú,
Tiānyīng,
Tiāngān,
thief stars,
fighting stars,
and guest stars.
As for the vapors,
some rise but do not reach the sky,
descend but do not reach the earth;
some are full above and thin below,
resembling the waves of water,
or the ridges of mountains;
yellow in spring,
black in summer,
blue in autumn,
red in winter.
As for ominous phenomena,
there are creatures born like belts,
ghosts throwing themselves at the battlements,
rabbits giving birth to pheasants,
pheasants also giving birth to quails,
locusts gathering in the state,
their sounds clamorous,
wandering snakes moving east and west in the state,
horses and oxen speaking,
dogs and pigs mating,
wolves entering the state,
people descending from the sky,
markets with dancing owls,
the state with flying creatures,
horses growing horns,
roosters with five legs,
pigs born without eyes,
chicken eggs mostly infertile,
altars of the soil relocated,
pigs giving birth to dogs.
If a state has such things,
and its ruler does not know to be alarmed and urgently reform,
the Supreme Deity will send down calamities,
and disasters will surely come swiftly.
Its destruction, death, and demise,
utter extinction without survivors,
dispersal, wandering, and famine will be imminent.
All these are born in disordered states,
too numerous to count;
even exhausting all the bamboo of Jīng and Yuè
could not record them all.
Thus, Zǐhuázi said:
"The people of chaotic times
have uneven lifespans, a hundred ailments;
the people suffer many epidemics,
the roads are full of swaddled infants,
the blind, bald, hunchbacked, and lame—
ten thousand strange things arise."
Thus, how can the ruler of a chaotic age
hear the highest music?
Not hearing the highest music,
his joy is not joyful.
7.1 The Annals of Early Autumn
It is said:
In the month of early autumn:
the longest day has passed for forty-six days.
The sun is in Yì,
at dusk Dǒu is at the zenith,
at dawn Bì is at the zenith.
Then autumn begins. Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Its emperor is Shàohào.
Its deity is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are the furry ones.
Its musical note is Shāng.
The pitch-pipe corresponds to Yízé.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is pungent.
Its odor is rank.
Its sacrifice is at the gate.
The offering is first made with liver.
Cool winds arrive.
White dew descends.
Cold cicadas sing.
Hawks then sacrifice birds.
Executions begin to be carried out.
The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the Zǒngzhāng Hall,
rides in a military chariot, drawn by white-maned horses,
bears a white banner,
wears white garments,
adorns himself with white jade,
eats hemp and dog meat.
His vessels are angular and deep.
In this month,
autumn is established.
Three days before the establishment of autumn,
the Grand Historian informs the Son of Heaven,
saying:
"On such-and-such a day autumn begins,
the abundant virtue is in metal."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the establishment of autumn,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, feudal lords, and high officials to welcome autumn in the western suburbs.
Upon returning,
he rewards military commanders and warriors at court.
The Son of Heaven then commands generals and marshals
to select soldiers, sharpen weapons,
and train the brave and outstanding;
entrusting authority solely to those with merit,
to campaign against the unrighteous;
interrogating and punishing the violent and arrogant,
to clarify good and evil;
patrolling those distant regions.
In this month,
command the officials
to revise laws and regulations,
repair prisons,
prepare fetters and handcuffs,
prohibit wickedness,
be cautious of crimes and evils,
and strive to capture offenders.
Command the judges
to examine wounds and injuries,
inspect fractures and assess verdicts;
adjudicate lawsuits,
ensuring they are just and fair;
execute the guilty,
strictly enforcing penalties.
Heaven and earth begin to turn severe,
and one must not be indulgent.
In this month,
farmers present the new grain.
The Son of Heaven tastes the new harvest,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
Command all officials
to begin gathering and storing.
Complete dikes and embankments,
carefully block up leaks,
to prepare for floods.
Repair palaces and buildings,
mend walls and enclosures,
and fortify city walls.
In this month,
do not enfeoff marquises or appoint high officials, do not grant lands,
issue heavy currency, or send out great envoys.
If these ordinances are carried out,
cool winds will arrive for thirty days.
then Yin energy will greatly prevail,
shelled insects will damage the grain,
and armed soldiers will come.
If the ordinances of spring are carried out,
then the state will suffer drought,
Yang energy will return,
and the five grains will not ripen.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then there will be many fires,
heat and cold will be irregular,
and the people will suffer many malarial diseases.
7.2 "On the Use of Arms"
The second says:
The ancient sage kings had righteous armies but never abolished arms.
The origins of arms are ancient,
coexisting with the beginning of humanity.
All arms are
a manifestation of authority;
authority is
a manifestation of force.
That humans possess authority and force is inherent to their nature.
Nature is what is received from Heaven,
not something humans can create.
The martial cannot alter it,
and the skillful cannot change it.
The origins of arms are indeed ancient.
Huángdì and Yándì in antiquity already used water and fire [in warfare];
Gònggōng certainly instigated rebellion;
the Five Emperors certainly contended with one another.
They rose and fell in succession,
with the victors holding power.
It is also said, "Chīyóu created weapons."
Chīyóu did not create weapons;
he merely improved their implements.
Before the time of Chīyóu,
people already stripped trees to fight, with the victor becoming the chief.
When a chief was still insufficient to govern them,
they established lords.
When lords were still insufficient to govern them,
they established the Son of Heaven.
The establishment of the Son of Heaven arose from lords,
the establishment of lords arose from chiefs,
and the establishment of chiefs arose from contention.
The origins of contention and strife are ancient indeed.
They cannot be prohibited,
they cannot be stopped.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings had righteous armies but never abolished arms.
If a household lacks angry flogging,
then the faults of children and infants will immediately appear;
if a state lacks punishments and penalties,
then the people's mutual encroachments will immediately appear;
if the world lacks punitive campaigns,
then the mutual violence among the feudal lords will immediately appear.
Therefore, angry flogging cannot be abolished in the household,
punishments and penalties cannot be abolished in the state,
punitive campaigns cannot be abolished in the world—
it is only a matter of skillful or clumsy application.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings had righteous armies but never abolished arms.
If someone dies from choking on food,
and one wishes to prohibit all eating in the world,
that is perverse.
If someone dies from riding in a boat,
and one wishes to prohibit all boats in the world,
that is perverse.
If someone loses their state through the use of arms,
and one wishes to abolish all arms in the world,
that is perverse.
Arms cannot be abolished;
they are like water and fire.
Used skillfully, they bring fortune;
used unskillfully, they bring calamity.
It is the same for those skilled in using medicine:
obtaining good medicine saves people,
obtaining bad medicine kills people.
Righteous armies are a great, good medicine for the world.
Moreover, the origins of arms are remote;
there has never been a moment when they were not used.
Noble and base, old and young, worthy and unworthy—all are the same in this;
it is only a matter of great or subtle manifestation.
Examine the subtle manifestations of arms:
harboring [hostility] in the heart without expressing it is arms;
glaring fiercely is arms;
changing countenance is arms;
arrogant speech is arms;
pushing and pulling is arms;
forming alliances and rebelling is arms;
extravagant fighting is arms;
the attacks and battles of three armies are arms.
These eight are all arms,
differing only in subtlety or greatness.
Those in the present age who advocate abolishing arms with fervent arguments
use arms their entire lives without realizing it—perverse!
Therefore, though their arguments may be forceful,
though their discourse may be eloquent,
though their literary learning may be broad,
they still will not be heeded.
Therefore, the ancient sage kings had righteous armies
but never abolished arms.
If arms are truly righteous,
used to punish tyrannical rulers and relieve the suffering people,
then the people's delight in them
is like a filial son seeing a loving parent,
like a starving person seeing fine food.
The people, shouting and rushing towards them,
are like a powerful crossbow shooting into a deep ravine,
like accumulated floodwaters losing their restraining dikes.
Even a mediocre ruler would be unable to keep his people,
let alone a tyrannical ruler?
7.3 "On Quelling Disorder"
The third says:
The age we live in
is exceedingly turbid;
the suffering of the black-haired people
cannot be increased further.
The Son of Heaven's line is already severed,
the worthy are cast down and hidden,
the worldly rulers act wantonly,
alienated from the people,
leaving the black-haired people with nowhere to voice their grievances.
If there are worthy rulers and outstanding scholars in the world,
they should examine this discourse;
then their armies will be righteous.
The people of the world,
on the verge of death, will live;
on the verge of disgrace, will be honored;
on the verge of suffering, will find ease.
If worldly rulers act wantonly,
then even average men will flee their rulers and abandon their kin,
let alone the unworthy?
Therefore, when righteous armies arrive,
worldly rulers will be unable to keep their people,
and parents will be unable to restrain their children.
All those who act as leaders for the people of the world
should consider nothing more important than promoting the Way and suppressing those without the Way,
rewarding the righteous and punishing the unrighteous.
In the present age,
many scholars condemn offensive warfare.
Condemning offensive warfare, they advocate defensive rescue.
Advocating defensive rescue means the aforementioned methods of promoting the Way and suppressing those without the Way, rewarding the righteous and punishing the unrighteous, cannot be implemented.
For the leaders of the world's people,
benefit and harm lie in examining this discourse.
Offensive warfare and defensive rescue are essentially the same thing,
yet people's choices differ.
Using argument and persuasion to decide it,
ultimately yields no settled conclusion.
If one is truly ignorant,
that is perversity;
if one knows but deceives one's own heart,
that is falsehood.
False and perverse scholars,
however eloquent, are useless.
To condemn what one chooses and choose what one condemns,
is to benefit them but instead harm them,
to give them security but instead endanger them.
Those who create the world's lasting troubles and bring great harm to the black-haired people—
such arguments run deep.
Those whose hearts are set on benefiting the people of the world
cannot but thoroughly examine this discourse.
Now, the matter of offensive warfare
is none other than attacking those without the Way and punishing the unrighteous.
Attacking those without the Way and punishing the unrighteous—
then no fortune is greater,
no benefit for the black-haired people is thicker.
To prohibit this
is to suppress those with the Way and attack the righteous; it is to thwart the deeds of Tāng and Wǔ and perpetuate the faults of Jié and Zhòu.
The reason all people detest acting without the Way and unrighteously
is because of the punishment;
the reason they aspire to act with the Way and righteously
is because of the reward.
Now, if those without the Way and unrighteous survive,
their survival is their reward;
if those with the Way and acting righteously are impoverished,
their impoverishment is their punishment.
Rewarding the unworthy and punishing the worthy—
to desire that the people be well-governed,
is that not difficult?
Therefore, those who disorder the world and harm the black-haired people—
such arguments are the greatest.
7.4 "On Prohibiting Blockades"
The fourth says:
The intention behind defensive rescue
is none other than defending those without the Way and rescuing the unrighteous.
Defending those without the Way and rescuing the unrighteous—
then no calamity is greater,
no harm to the people of the world is deeper.
All defensive rescue
primarily uses persuasion,
secondarily uses arms.
Using persuasion, they gather many followers, forming groups.
Day and night they ponder it,
exhausting their minds and spirits.
Rising, they recite it;
lying down, they dream of it.
They make their own lips parched and lungs dry,
wasting their spirit and injuring their soul.
Above, they cite the achievements of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors to please their minds;
below, they cite the strategies of the Five Hegemons and famous scholars to validate their affairs.
Holding court early and retiring late,
they inform those who control the armies,
He speaks to the masses to clarify his Way.
If the Way is fully explained but not practiced,
then he must resort to arms.
Resorting to arms,
will inevitably lead to conflict, and conflict
in its nature,
will certainly result in killing,
which is to kill innocent people to promote those without the Way and without righteousness.
If those without the Way and without righteousness persist,
they perpetuate the harm of the world and halt the benefits of the world.
Even if they wish to win by luck,
disaster will begin to grow.
The law of the former kings says:
"Reward those who do good,
punish those who do evil."
This is the Way of antiquity,
and cannot be changed.
Now, without distinguishing between righteousness and unrighteousness,
and hastily advocating rescue and defense,
nothing is more unrighteous than this,
and nothing harms the people of the world more than this.
Therefore, those who advocate offensive warfare cannot
be condemned,
but offensive warfare cannot
be advocated;
rescue and defense cannot
be condemned,
but rescue and defense cannot
be advocated.
Only righteous armies are permissible.
If the army is righteous,
offensive warfare is permissible,
and rescue and defense are permissible.
If the army is unrighteous,
offensive warfare is impermissible,
and rescue and defense are impermissible.
If Xià Jié and Yīn Zhòu were without the Way to this extent,
it was due to luck;
if Wú Fūchāi and Zhì Bóyáo invaded and plundered to this extent,
it was due to luck;
if Jìn Lì, Chén Líng, and Sòng Kāng were evil to this extent,
it was due to luck.
If Jié and Zhòu had known that their states would perish and they would die,
with no descendants left,
I doubt they would have been so without the Way as to reach this point;
if King Fūchāi of Wú and Zhì Bóyáo had known that their states would become ruins,
and they themselves would be executed,
I doubt they would have been so evil, without the Way, invading and plundering to this extent;
if Jìn Lì had known he would die at the hands of Jiàng Lìshì,
if Chén Líng had known he would die at the hands of Xià Zhēngshū,
if Sòng Kāng had known he would die in Wēn, I doubt they would have been so evil as to reach this point.
These seven rulers,
great yet without the Way and unrighteous:
the innocent people they slaughtered
cannot be counted in the tens of thousands;
the deaths of the strong, the young, the old, and the unborn
filled the plains in great numbers;
they filled deep valleys and great gorges,
threw them into great waters,
piled up ashes,
filled moats and dangerous passes,
exposed them to flying arrows,
trampled on white blades,
and added to them the suffering of cold, hunger, and starvation.
Up to the present age,
this has become even worse,
so exposed bones are countless,
piled into mounds like mountains.
If there are enlightened rulers and benevolent men in the world,
who deeply reflect on this,
they can feel heartache,
they can feel sorrow.
Examining how this arose,
it arises from the abandonment of those with the Way,
and the unrestrained actions of those without the Way.
The unrestrained actions of those without the Way
are due to luck.
Therefore, the calamity of the world
does not lie in rescue and defense,
but in the luck of the unworthy.
When the theory of rescue and defense is proposed,
the unworthy become even luckier,
and the worthy become even more doubtful.
Therefore, what brings great chaos to the world is not discussing righteousness and hastily advocating rescue and defense.
7.5 "Huáichǒng"
The fifth says:
Whenever a gentleman speaks,
it is not merely for argument's sake;
when a scholar debates,
it is not merely for talk's sake.
He must align with principle before speaking,
and he must accord with righteousness before debating.
Therefore, when speaking of righteousness, kings, dukes, and great men become more fond of principle, and scholars and common people practice righteousness more.
When the Way of righteousness and principle is made clear,
then the methods of tyranny, deceit, invasion, and plunder cease.
Tyranny and deceit are opposed to righteousness and principle,
their forces cannot both win,
they cannot coexist.
Therefore, when the army enters the enemy's territory,
the people know where to seek shelter,
and the common people know they will not die.
When reaching the outskirts of cities and towns,
they do not harm the five grains,
do not dig up graves,
do not cut down trees,
do not burn stockpiles,
do not set houses on fire,
do not take the six domestic animals.
They capture prisoners and respectfully return them,
to make clear what is good and evil;
they keep faith with the people as promised,
to deprive the enemy of resources. If even then there are those who harbor resentment, act recklessly, persist in error, and refuse to listen, then using military force is permissible.
First, issue a proclamation saying:
"The army has come
to save the people from death.
Your ruler above is without the Way,
arrogant, negligent, and indolent,
greedy, cruel, and oppressive to the masses,
willful and self-serving,
rejecting the sagely institutions,
slandering and vilifying the former kings,
repudiating and criticizing the old classics,
above not complying with Heaven,
below not benefiting the people,
levying taxes without limit,
demanding endlessly,
killing the innocent without guilt,
rewarding and赏赐不当.
Such a person
is one whom Heaven will punish,
whom people will仇敌,
and is unfit to be a ruler.
Now the army has come
to punish those unfit to be rulers,
to remove the people's仇敌and comply with the Way of Heaven.
If any people oppose the Way of Heaven and defend the people's仇敌,
they will be executed and their families exterminated without pardon.
Those who can bring their families to comply
will be rewarded with their families'禄;
those who can bring their villages to comply
will be rewarded with their villages'禄;
those who can bring their townships to comply
will be rewarded with their townships'禄;
those who can bring their cities to comply
will be rewarded with their cities'禄;
those who can bring their states to comply
will be rewarded with their states'禄."
Therefore, when conquering a state, do not harm its people,
only punish those who must be punished.
Promote its outstanding scholars and enfeoff them as marquises,
select its worthy and virtuous and honor and elevate them,
seek out its orphans and widows and relieve and comfort them,
meet its elders and respect and礼敬them.
Increase their禄,
raise their ranks.
Judge its criminals and pardon and release them;
distribute the gold from the treasury,
scatter the grain from the granaries,
to pacify and安抚the masses,
not keeping the wealth for oneself;
inquire about its丛社and great sacrifices,
those the people do not wish to abolish and restore them,
adding extra礼敬in the sacrifices.
Thus, the worthy take pride in their名声,
the elders are pleased with the礼敬,
and the people cherish their德.
If there were someone now
who could give life to one person,
the world would certainly strive to serve him.
A righteous army gives life to many more than one person,
who would not be pleased?
Therefore, when a righteous army arrives,
the people of neighboring states flock to it like flowing water,
the people of the state to be punished look to it like parents,
the farther it travels,
the more people it gains,
without crossing blades, the people submit as if transformed.
8.1 "Zhòngqiū Jì"
The first says:
In the mid-autumn month:
the sun is in Jiǎo,
at dusk Qiānniú is at the zenith,
at dawn Zīxī is at the zenith.
Its days are Gēng and Xīn.
Its emperor is Shàohào.
Its deity is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are the hairy ones.
Its musical note is Shāng.
The pitch pipe is Zhōngnǚlǚ.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is pungent.
Its odor is fishy.
Its sacrifice is at the gate.
The offering is first of the liver.
Cool winds arise.
Migrating geese arrive.
The dark swallows return.
Flocks of birds store up food.
The Son of Heaven resides in the Zǒngzhāng Grand Temple,
rides in a military chariot,
drives white-maned horses,
bears white banners,
wears white clothes,
adorns himself with white jade,
eats hemp and dog.
His vessels are angular and deep.
In this month,
care is given to the aged and decrepit,
they are provided with stools and canes,
and thin gruel and drink are distributed.
Then the Director of Attire is ordered
to prepare and arrange the ceremonial robes,
the patterns and embroideries having fixed standards,
the making having small and large sizes,
the measurements having short and long lengths,
the clothing having set quantities,
all must follow the old ways,
caps and sashes having fixed rules.
The officials are ordered,
to strictly enforce all punishments,
executions and killings must be appropriate,
none may be wrongful or perverted,
if wrongful or perverted and inappropriate,
they will in turn suffer calamity.
In this month,
the Chief of Sacrifices is ordered,
to inspect the sacrificial animals:
examine their completeness;
check their fodder;
observe their fatness or leanness,
scrutinize their colors,
they must be matched by category;
measure their size,
look at their length,
all must meet the standard.
When these five are fully appropriate,
the Supreme Deity will ◇◇ enjoy them.
The Son of Heaven then performs the exorcism,
to ward off auxiliary illnesses,
and to circulate the autumn qi.
With dog, he tastes the hemp,
first offering sacrifice in the ancestral temple.
In this month,
one can build city walls,
establish capitals and towns,
dig cellars and pits,
repair granaries and storehouses.
Then the officials are ordered
to urge the people to gather in the harvest,
to store up vegetables,
to accumulate much.
They encourage the planting of wheat,
none should miss the season,
if any miss the season, punishment is carried out without doubt.
In this month,
day and night are equal.
Thunder begins to cease its sound.
Hibernating insects all crouch in their burrows, sealing their entrances.
The killing qi gradually grows strong,
the yang qi daily declines.
Water begins to dry up.
When day and night are equal,
then the standards of length and capacity are unified,
the steelyard and scales are balanced,
the weights and stone measures are corrected,
the bushels and pecks are standardized.
In this month,
customs and markets are regulated,
merchants and travelers are attracted,
goods and valuables are brought in,
to facilitate the people's affairs.
From all directions they come in multitude,
from distant regions all arrive,
then goods and wealth are not lacking,
the ruler has no shortage for use,
and all affairs are accomplished.
In all undertakings, do not oppose the numbers of Heaven,
but must follow its seasons,
and act according to their categories.
If these ordinances are carried out,
white dew will fall for thirty days.
If in mid-autumn the ordinances of spring are carried out,
then autumn rain will not fall,
plants and trees will flourish and bloom,
and the state will have great fear.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then the state will suffer drought,
hibernating insects will not hide,
and the five grains will sprout again.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out,
then wind disasters will arise frequently,
the ceasing of thunder will come early,
and plants and trees will die prematurely.
8.2 "On Awe-Inspiring Power"
The second says:
Righteousness,
is the guiding principle of all affairs,
it is the source from which ruler and minister, superior and inferior, closeness and distance arise,
it is where order and chaos, safety and danger, surpassing and being surpassed lie.
To surpass and be surpassed,
do not seek it in others,
but must turn back to oneself.
Human nature desires life and hates death,
desires honor and hates disgrace.
If the way of life and death, honor and disgrace is one,
then the soldiers of the three armies can be made to be of one mind.
In general, an army desires to be numerous,
and its mind desires to be unified,
if the three armies are of one mind then orders can make them invincible.
If orders can make them invincible,
then their soldiers under Heaven are also invincible.
The ultimate armies of antiquity,
made the people value orders.
Valued above all under Heaven,
esteemed by the Son of Heaven.
They were stored in the people's hearts,
quickened in their flesh and skin,
deeply painful and firmly held,
unshakable,
nothing could move them.
If so, how could the enemy be sufficient to overcome?
Therefore it is said: if its orders are strong, its enemy is weak;
if its orders are trustworthy, its enemy is subdued.
If victory is first achieved here,
then it will surely be achieved there.
In general, arms
are the instruments of ill omen under Heaven;
courage,
is the virtue of ill omen under Heaven.
To take up instruments of ill omen,
to practice virtue of ill omen,
is still a matter of having no alternative.
To take up instruments of ill omen necessarily involves killing,
killing,
is the means by which life is given;
to practice virtue of ill omen necessarily involves awe,
awe,
is the means by which intimidation is achieved.
The enemy intimidated, the people live,
this is why righteous armies are exalted.
Therefore the ultimate armies of antiquity,
before the talented people had even assembled,
their awe was already made known,
the enemy was already subdued,
must they necessarily use drumsticks, shields, and spears?
Therefore those skilled in making awe known,
do so before it is unleashed,
before it is communicated,
profoundly dark and obscure,
none know their true state,
this is called the sincerity of ultimate awe.
In general, arms desire swiftness, speed, and seizing the initiative.
The way to desire swiftness, speed, and seizing the initiative
lies in knowing the distinction between slowness, delay, lagging behind and swiftness, speed, seizing the initiative.
Swiftness, speed, and seizing the initiative,
this is what decides the victory of righteous armies.
And they cannot long remain in place,
knowing they cannot long remain in place,
then one knows the ground where hares start and ducks rise, where death and stupor lie.
Even if there are the perils of rivers and seas, they are crossed;
even if there are the obstructions of great mountains, they are breached;
concentrating qi and focusing essence,
the mind has no thoughts,
the eyes have no sights,
the ears have no sounds,
unified entirely in martial action.
Rǎn Shū vowed to die at the hands of Tián Hóu,
and the state of Qí was all afraid;
Yù Ràng was determined to die at the hands of Xiāngzǐ,
and the Zhào clan were all terrified;
Chéng Jīng sought death at the hands of the ruler of Hán,
and the people of Zhōu were all fearful;
how much more for a state of ten thousand chariots,
if it has sincere determination,
then what enemy can there be?
Blades have not yet crossed, yet the desire is already achieved.
When the enemy is filled with dread, fear, and terror,
their spirit is utterly exhausted and dissipated,
all as if possessed by a mad soul,
their form and nature separated,
walking without knowing where they are going,
running without knowing where they are headed,
even if they have perilous passes and strong fortresses,
sharp weapons and keen armaments,
their hearts dare not rely on them,
their minds dare not settle upon them—
this is why Xià Jié died at Náncháo.
Now, if one strikes wood with wood, it splits;
if one throws water into water, it disperses;
if one throws ice into ice, it sinks;
if one throws mud into mud, it sinks in—
this is the principle of swiftness and slowness, of what comes first and what follows.
Now, in warfare there is a great essential:
to know that in planning against things, one must plan for what they do not plan for and cannot prohibit—then one will attain it.
Zhuānzhū was such a man;
alone, he raised his sword and struck, and that was all—
the King of Wú was accomplished in one move.
How much more so with righteous armies,
where the many number tens of thousands,
the few number several thousand,
who closely tread the paths,
opening the way against the enemy—
then how could the officers merely be discussed alongside Zhuānzhū?
8.3 《Simplified Selection》
Thirdly:
There is a saying in the world:
"Driving market folk to fight
can overcome the enemy's well-paid, trained troops;
the old, weak, and weary people
can overcome the enemy's elite soldiers and practiced talents;
scattered and bound captives
can overcome the enemy's well-ordered battle formations;
hoes, harrows, and plain clubs
can overcome the enemy's long spears and sharp weapons."
This is the argument of those who do not understand warfare.
Suppose there is a sharp sword here:
if one thrusts with it but does not hit,
if one strikes with it but does not reach,
it is no different from a poor sword;
for this reason, to fight using a poor sword is unacceptable.
Selecting the excellent and elite,
having sharp and keen weapons and armaments,
yet deploying them at the wrong time,
employing them inappropriately—
they are no different from poor troops;
for this reason, to wage war using poor troops is unacceptable.
Wángzǐ Qìngjì and Chénnián still desired the sharpness of their swords.
Selecting the excellent and elite,
having sharp and keen weapons and armaments,
and ordering capable generals to lead them—
in ancient times, there were those who became kings and those who became hegemons by this means:
Tāng, Wǔ, Qí Huán, Jìn Wén, and Wú Hélǘ are such examples.
Yīn Tāng had seventy excellent chariots,
six thousand men resolved to die,
and on the day Wùzǐ fought at Chéng,
he captured Tuīyí and Dàxī,
ascended from Míngtiáo,
then entered the gates of Cháo,
and thus possessed Xià.
Once Jié had fled,
then he practiced great benevolence and kindness,
to comfort the black-haired people;
he reversed Jié's affairs,
promoted the worthy and good,
followed what the people delighted in;
those near and far came to him,
therefore he ruled the world.
King Wǔ had three thousand tiger-warriors,
three hundred selected chariots,
and on the day Jiǎzǐ, at Mùyě, he accomplished his task and Zhòu was captured.
He exalted the positions of the worthy,
advanced the surviving elders of Yīn,
and inquired about what the people desired;
he bestowed rewards extending even to birds and beasts,
carried out punishments without sparing the Son of Heaven,
treated Yīn as his own like Zhōu,
regarded others as himself;
the world praised his virtue,
the myriad people delighted in his righteousness,
therefore he was established as the Son of Heaven.
Duke Huán of Qí had three hundred excellent chariots,
ten thousand trained troops,
using them as the head of his army,
he roamed unhindered within the seas,
and none in the world could stop him;
south he reached Shíliáng,
west he reached Fēnghào,
north he reached Lìngzhī.
Zhōngshān destroyed Xíng,
the Dí people extinguished Wèi,
Duke Huán reestablished Xíng at Yíyí,
and reestablished Wèi at Chǔqiū.
Duke Wén of Jìn created five chariots with five pairs of warriors,
a thousand keen troops,
who first engaged the enemy,
and none of the feudal lords could withstand him;
he returned Zhèng's ramparts,
oriented Wèi's field ridges eastward,
and honored the Son of Heaven at Héngyōng.
Wú Hélǘ selected five hundred men of great strength,
three thousand men with swift feet,
using them as the front formation,
he fought with Jīng,
fought five battles and won five victories,
thus possessing Yǐng.
He campaigned east to Bìlú,
campaigned west to Bā and Shǔ,
pressed north against Qí and Jìn,
and his commands were carried out in the central states.
Therefore, in general, the advantage of terrain and perilous passes
is desired for their convenience;
weapons, armor, and equipment
are desired for their sharpness;
selecting, training, and testing talents
is desired for their excellence;
commanding and leading officers and people
is desired for their training.
These four things
are aids to righteous armies.
They respond to changes of the times,
cannot be forced and are not sufficient to rely on exclusively.
This is one strategy for victory.
8.4 《Decisive Victory》
Fourthly:
Now, warfare has its root and trunk:
it must be righteous,
it must be wise,
it must be courageous.
Righteousness makes the enemy isolated;
the enemy isolated, then high and low are empty,
the people disintegrate and scatter;
isolated, then fathers and brothers resent,
the worthy criticize,
and disorder arises within.
Wisdom knows the changes of the times;
knowing the changes of the times, then one knows the transformations of emptiness and solidity, prosperity and decline;
knows the methods of what comes first and what follows, far and near, advancing and retreating.
Courage enables decisive judgment;
able to judge decisively, then one can be like thunder, lightning, whirlwind, and torrential rain;
can be like collapsing mountains, breaking dikes, splitting and crumbling, falling and crashing;
like the strike of a bird of prey,
seizing in combat, then it kills;
hitting wood, then it shatters.
This is attained through wisdom.
Now, the people are not constantly courageous,
nor are they constantly timid.
Having spirit, they are solid;
solid, then they are courageous;
lacking spirit, they are empty;
empty, then they are timid.
Timidity, courage, emptiness, solidity—
their origins are very subtle,
and cannot be unknown.
Courageous, then they fight;
timid, then they flee.
Those who fight and win
fight because of their courage;
those who fight and flee
fight because of their timidity.
Timidity and courage are not constant,
suddenly coming and going,
and none know their direction—
only the sage alone sees the reason for this.
Therefore, Shāng and Zhōu rose because of this,
Jié and Zhòu fell because of this.
The reason for the difference between skill and clumsiness
lies in increasing the people's spirit or robbing the people's spirit,
in being able to make the masses fight or being unable to make the masses fight.
Though the army be large,
though the troops be many,
it is of no benefit to victory.
The army large and troops many, yet unable to fight—
the multitude is not as good as few.
Now, the multitude brings great fortune,
but it also brings great calamity.
It is like fishing in a deep abyss:
the fish one catches are large,
but the harm one encounters is also large.
Those skilled in using troops
ensure that within all borders,
none do not join the fight;
even servants, carters, and untrained conscripts,
across several hundred lǐ square,
all come to join the battle—
circumstances make it so.
As for opportunity,
it lies in carefully observing the timing of battle and having means to restrain and lure the enemy.
In all matters of warfare,
the key lies in adaptation.
Adaptation means
using the enemy's terrain as one's own stronghold,
and turning the enemy's plans to one's own advantage.
If one can understand adaptation and act accordingly, victory will be inexhaustible.
Inexhaustible victory is called divine,
and the divine ensures invincibility.
In warfare,
the highest value is invincibility.
Invincibility depends on oneself,
while the opportunity for victory depends on the enemy.
The sage focuses on what lies within his own control,
not on what depends on the enemy.
Thus, by employing invincible strategies against a vulnerable enemy,
