military affairs will be free from error.
All victories in warfare
stem from the enemy's mistakes.
An army that capitalizes on the enemy's mistakes
must be concealed and subtle,
must accumulate strength and concentrate forces.
Concealment overcomes exposure,
subtlety overcomes obviousness,
accumulation overcomes dispersion,
and concentration overcomes division.
All beasts that seize, claw, and bite
rely on their teeth, horns, claws, and fangs,
but they always do so from a position of lowliness, concealment, and obscurity—
this is how they achieve victory.
8.5 "Cherishing Men of Worth"
The fifth says:
To clothe others
is because they are cold;
to feed others
is because they are hungry.
Hunger and cold
are great afflictions for people.
To relieve them
is a great act of righteousness.
When people are in distress and poverty,
it is even worse than hunger and cold.
Therefore, a worthy ruler must pity those in distress
and grieve for those in poverty.
In this way, his reputation will become illustrious,
and men of worth will be gained for the state.
Long ago, Duke Mù of Qín was riding in a chariot when it broke down,
and the right horse broke free and was taken by villagers.
Duke Mù went himself to seek it
and saw the villagers about to eat it on the southern slope of Qí Mountain.
Duke Mù sighed and said:
"Eating the meat of a fine horse without drinking wine immediately
is harmful to people. I fear it will harm you!"
Thereupon, he provided wine for all to drink and then left.
One year later,
during the battle of Hányuán,
the men of Jìn had already surrounded Duke Mù's chariot.
Liáng Yóumǐ of Jìn had already seized the left trace horse of Duke Mù's chariot,
and Lù Shí, on the right of Duke Huì of Jìn, brandished his spear and struck Duke Mù's armor—
six layers of it were pierced.
More than three hundred villagers who had once eaten horse meat on the southern slope of Qí Mountain
exerted all their strength to fight fiercely for Duke Mù beneath his chariot,
and thus they greatly defeated Jìn
and captured Duke Huì to bring him back. This is what the Odes meant by saying:
"When a ruler treats gentlemen with correctness,
he practices his virtue;
when he treats lowly people with generosity,
they exhaust their strength for him."
How can a ruler not strive to practice virtue and cherish the people?
Practicing virtue and cherishing the people makes the people devoted to their superiors,
and when the people are devoted to their superiors, they are all willing to die for their ruler.
Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào had two white mules that he cherished greatly.
Xú Qú of Yángchéng, an officer at the Guǎngmén gate,
knocked at the gate at night and requested an audience, saying:
"Your servant Xú Qú is ill,
and the physician instructed him:
'If you obtain the liver of a white mule, the illness will cease;
if not, you will die.'"
The usher entered to report this.
Dǒng Ānyú, who was attending at his side,
said angrily:
"Ha!
Xú Qú expects our lord's mule—
I request that he be punished immediately."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"To kill a man to save an animal—
is that not inhumane?
To kill an animal to save a man—
is that not humane?"
Thereupon, he summoned the cook to kill a white mule
and take its liver to give to Xú Qú of Yángchéng.
Not long after,
Zhào raised troops to attack Dí.
The officers of the Guǎngmén gate,
seven hundred on the left
and seven hundred on the right,
all were the first to ascend and captured armored heads.
How can a ruler not cherish men of worth?
When enemies come,
it is to seek advantage.
If they come and meet death,
then they gain no advantage by advancing, and retreat becomes advantageous.
If all enemies consider retreat advantageous,
then blades need not clash.
Thus, if the enemy gains life from me,
then I meet death from the enemy.
If the enemy meets death from me,
then I gain life from the enemy.
To gain life from the enemy
versus the enemy gaining life from me—
how can this not be carefully examined?
This is the essence of warfare.
Survival or destruction, life or death,
is determined solely by understanding this.
9.1 "The Annals of Late Autumn"
The first says:
In the month of late autumn:
The sun is in the constellation Fáng.
At dusk, the constellation Xū is at the zenith;
at dawn, the constellation Liǔ is at the zenith.
The day is under the stem Gēng-Xīn.
Its emperor is Shàohào.
Its deity is Rùshōu.
Its creatures are the hairy ones.
Its musical note is Shāng.
The pitch-pipe is Wúyì.
Its number is nine.
Its flavor is pungent.
Its odor is rank.
Its sacrifice is to the gate.
The offering is first made of liver.
The migratory geese arrive.
The guest sparrows enter the great waters and become clams.
Chrysanthemums bear yellow blossoms.
Jackals sacrifice beasts and kill birds.
The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Zǒngzhāng Hall.
He rides in a war chariot,
drawn by white piebald horses,
bearing a white banner,
wearing white robes,
adorned with white jade,
and eats hemp seeds and dog meat.
His vessels are angular and deep.
In this month,
he reiterates strict orders.
He commands all officials, noble and humble,
to devote themselves to storing,
to align with the hidden treasures of Heaven and Earth,
with nothing being dispersed outward.
He commands the Chief Minister
that, with the agricultural tasks fully gathered,
he should compile the essentials of the five grains
and store the harvest from the imperial fields in the divine granary, with reverence and meticulous care.
In this month,
when frost first descends,
all artisans rest.
Then he commands the officials:
"The cold air is gathering,
and the people's strength cannot endure it—
let them all enter their dwellings."
On the first Dīng day,
he orders the Director of Music to enter the school to practice wind instruments.
In this month,
he offers the great sacrifice to the Supreme Deity,
presents the sacrificial animals,
and reports the preparations to the Son of Heaven.
He assembles the feudal lords.
He regulates the hundred districts.
He receives the calendar for the coming year and the laws on the light or heavy taxes levied by the feudal lords on the people.
The quotas of tribute and duties
are determined according to distance and what the land produces appropriately,
to supply the affairs of the suburban and ancestral temple sacrifices,
with nothing held privately.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven instructs in hunting
to practice the five weapons.
He selects horses.
He orders the charioteers and the seven grooms all to harness the chariots, bearing banners and flags.
They receive chariots according to rank,
arranged in order outside the screen.
The Minister of Education inserts his rod,
faces north, and administers the oath.
The Son of Heaven then dons stern attire and stern accoutrements,
grasping his bow and holding arrows to shoot.
He orders the chief priest
to sacrifice the game to the four directions.
In this month,
the plants and trees turn yellow and fall,
and firewood is cut to make charcoal.
All hibernating insects crouch in their burrows,
sealing their entrances.
Then the enforcement of punishments is hastened,
leaving no guilty person unpunished.
Salaries and provisions that are inappropriate are withdrawn.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven tastes the newly harvested rice with dog meat,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out in late autumn,
the state will suffer great floods,
weapons will be stored away and disasters will occur,
and the people will suffer from nasal congestion.
If the ordinances of winter are carried out,
the state will be plagued by thieves and bandits,
its borders will be unsettled,
and its territory will be divided.
If the ordinances of spring are carried out,
warm winds will arrive,
the people’s spirit will become lax,
and military campaigns will inevitably arise.
9.2 "Conforming to the People"
The second says:
The former kings first conformed to the people’s hearts,
thus achieving merit and fame.
Those who, through virtue, won the people’s hearts and thereby established great merit and fame were numerous in ancient times.
Those who lost the people’s hearts yet achieved merit and fame have never existed.
To win the people, there must be a way.
In a state of ten thousand chariots,
or a town of a hundred households,
there are none among the people who are not pleased.
Take what pleases the people, and the people are won.
Are the things that please the people many?
This is the key to winning the people.
In the past, when Tāng conquered the Xià and brought order to the world,
there was a great drought,
and for five years there were no harvests.
Tāng then prayed with his own body at Sānglín,
saying:
"If I alone am guilty,
let it not extend to the myriad people.
If the myriad people are guilty,
let it rest upon me alone.
Do not, because of one man’s inadequacy,
cause the Lord on High and the ghosts and spirits to harm the lives of the people."
Thereupon he cut off his hair,
pared his nails,
and offered his own body as a sacrifice,
to pray for blessings from the Lord on High.
The people were greatly pleased,
and rain fell in abundance.
Thus, Tāng understood the transformations of the ghosts and spirits
and the transmission of human affairs.
King Wén, dwelling in Qí, served Zhòu,
enduring injustice, humiliation, and constant deference,
attending court morning and evening without fail,
presenting tributes appropriately,
and conducting sacrifices with reverence.
Zhòu was pleased,
and commanded King Wén to be called the Earl of the West,
granting him a territory of a thousand lǐ.
King Wén bowed twice and kowtowed, then declined, saying:
"I wish to plead on behalf of the people for the abolition of the roasting punishment."
King Wén did not dislike the thousand-lǐ territory,
but by pleading for the abolition of the roasting punishment for the people’s sake, he surely desired to win the people’s hearts.
Winning the people’s hearts is worth more than a thousand-lǐ territory,
thus it is said that King Wén was wise.
The King of Yuè, bitter over the disgrace of Kuàijī,
wished to deeply win the people’s hearts,
in order to seek death against Wú.
He did not rest comfortably on his pillow and mat,
did not savor rich flavors,
did not look upon beauty,
and did not listen to bells and drums.
For three years he toiled his body and exerted his strength,
until his lips were parched and his lungs dry.
He intimately attended to his ministers,
and nurtured the common people below,
to win their hearts.
If there were delicacies insufficient to share,
he dared not eat them;
if there was wine, he poured it into the river,
to share it with the people.
He personally plowed to eat,
and his wife personally wove to clothe themselves.
He forbade extravagant flavors,
forbade layered robes,
and forbade dual colors.
From time to time he traveled on the roads,
with food carried in his carriage,
to visit the orphaned, widowed, elderly, weak, sick, impoverished, and those with sorrowful, haggard, and destitute appearances,
and he always personally fed them.
Then he gathered his high officials and told them,
saying:
"I wish once to test the will of Heaven with Wú.
Now the states of Wú and Yuè
mutually destroy each other,
with officers and ministers treading on liver and lungs,
dying on the same day,
and I, with the King of Wú, locking necks and crossing arms to fall together—this is my greatest wish.
If this cannot be achieved,
and considering internally, my state is insufficient to harm Wú,
and externally, serving the various lords cannot harm it,
then I will abandon the state,
dismiss my ministers,
grasp my sword and bare my blade,
change my appearance,
alter my name,
take up broom and dustpan to serve as a subject,
and with the King of Wú contend for a morning’s death.
Though I know my neck and waist will be severed,
head and feet separated,
limbs torn apart,
and I will be humiliated before the world,
my resolve will surely be carried out."
Then, on another day, he indeed fought with Wú at Wǔhú,
and the Wú army was greatly defeated.
He then tightly besieged the royal palace,
the city gates could not be defended,
Fūchāi was captured,
the Wú prime minister was executed,
and within two years Wú was destroyed and he became hegemon.
This is because he first conformed to the people’s hearts.
Qí Zhuāngzǐ requested to attack Yuè,
and asked Hézi about it.
Hézi said:
"Our former lord left a command, saying:
'Do not attack Yuè,
for Yuè is a fierce tiger.'"
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"Though it is a fierce tiger,
now it is already dead."
Hézi then reported this to Xiāozǐ.
Xiāozǐ said:
"Though dead, it is regarded as alive."
Therefore, in all undertakings,
one must first examine the people’s hearts, and only then can one act.
9.3 "Knowing the Scholar"
The third says:
Suppose there is a thousand-lǐ horse here,
but without an excellent groom,
it is as if not obtained.
The excellent groom and the horse,
only when they match each other can they achieve success.
This is like the drumstick and the drum.
Now, scholars also have their thousand-lǐ,
lofty integrity and dying for righteousness—
this is the scholar’s thousand-lǐ.
One who can make a scholar achieve his thousand-lǐ,
only the worthy can do so.
Jìng Guō Jūn was fond of Jì Màobiàn.
Jì Màobiàn, as a person, was much criticized,
and the disciples were displeased.
Shìwèi admonished Jìng Guō Jūn about this,
but Jìng Guō Jūn would not listen,
so Shìwèi resigned and left.
Mèng Cháng Jūn privately advised Jìng Guō Jūn,
but Jìng Guō Jūn became greatly angry and said:
"Exterminate your kind!
If ruining my household
can accommodate Jì Màobiàn,
I will not refuse to do so."
Thereupon he housed him in the best quarters,
ordered his eldest son to serve him,
and provided him with morning and evening meals.
After several years,
King Wēi passed away,
and King Xuān ascended the throne.
Jìng Guō Jūn’s relationship
was very poor with King Xuān,
so he resigned and went to Xuē,
accompanied by Jì Màobiàn.
Not long after they stayed,
Jì Màobiàn bid farewell and departed,
requesting an audience with King Xuān.
Jìng Guō Jūn said:
"The king’s displeasure with me is extreme;
if you go,
you will surely die there."
Jì Màobiàn said:
"I certainly do not seek to preserve my life."
He insisted on going,
and Jìng Guō Jūn could not stop him.
Jì Màobiàn traveled
to Qí,
and when King Xuān heard of it,
he concealed his anger and awaited him.
Jì Màobiàn went to see King Xuān.
The king said:
"Are you the one whom Lord Jìng Guō listens to and loves?"
Jì Màobiàn replied:
"Loved, I may be;
listened to, I am not.
When Your Majesty was still the crown prince,
I said to Lord Jìng Guō:
'The crown prince's physiognomy is unkind;
his jaw is overly prominent, and he looks like a pig.
One like this will turn against you.
It would be better to depose the crown prince
and instead establish Wèi Jī's infant son, Jiàoshī.'
Lord Jìng Guō wept and said:
'That cannot be;
I cannot bear to do it.'
Had Lord Jìng Guō listened to me and acted accordingly,
he certainly would not have the troubles of today.
This is the first instance.
When we arrived at Xuē,
Zhāoyáng requested to exchange several times the amount of land for Xuē.
I again said:
'You must agree to this.'
Lord Jìng Guō said:
'I received Xuē from the former king.
Even if I incur the dislike of the later king,
how could I alone face the former king?
Moreover, the former king's temple is in Xuē.
How could I give the former king's temple to Chǔ?'
Again, he refused to listen to me.
This is the second instance."
King Xuān sighed deeply,
his countenance moved,
and said:
"Has Lord Jìng Guō's regard for me reached such an extent!
I was young,
and truly did not know this.
Sir, would you be willing to come
and bring Lord Jìng Guō to me?"
Jì Màobiàn replied:
"I respectfully obey."
Lord Jìng Guō came,
wearing King Wēi's robes,
donning his cap,
and girding his sword.
King Xuān personally welcomed Lord Jìng Guō in the suburbs,
wept upon seeing him.
When Lord Jìng Guō arrived,
the king then requested him to serve as prime minister.
Lord Jìng Guō declined,
but was compelled to accept.
After ten days,
he pleaded illness,
strongly declined,
and after three days, his resignation was accepted.
At that time,
Lord Jìng Guō could be said to truly know how to recognize men.
Because he could truly know men,
he was not deterred by their faults.
This is why Jì Màobiàn disregarded life and pleasure, and hastened toward hardship and danger.
9.4 "Examining Oneself"
The fourth says:
Whenever things are as they are,
there must be a reason.
To know that they are so but not know the reason,
even if correct, is the same as not knowing;
one will ultimately be confounded.
The reason why the former kings, famous scholars, and enlightened teachers surpassed the common people is because of their understanding.
Water emerges from the mountains and flows to the sea;
it is not that water dislikes the mountains and desires the sea,
but that high and low make it so.
Grain grows in the fields and is stored in granaries;
it is not that grain has desires,
but that men all make it so.
Therefore, Zǐlù captured a pheasant but then released it.
Zǐ Lièzǐ learned archery and hit the target;
he asked Guān Yǐnzǐ about it.
Guān Yǐnzǐ said:
"Do you know why you hit the target?"
He replied:
"I do not know."
Guān Yǐnzǐ said:
"Not yet."
He withdrew and practiced for three years,
then asked again.
Guān Yǐnzǐ said:
"Do you know why you hit the target?"
Zǐ Lièzǐ said:
"I know it now."
Guān Yǐnzǐ said:
"Now it is permissible;
hold to it and do not lose it."
It is not only archery;
the survival of a state,
the fall of a state,
the worthiness of a person,
the unworthiness of a person—
all also have their reasons.
Therefore, the sage does not examine survival or fall, worthiness or unworthiness,
but examines their reasons.
Qí attacked Lǔ,
demanding the Cén Dǐng.
The lord of Lǔ sent another tripod instead.
The marquis of Qí did not believe it and returned it,
considering it not genuine,
and sent a man to tell the lord of Lǔ:
"If Liǔxià Jì considers it genuine,
we will accept it accordingly."
The lord of Lǔ requested this of Liǔxià Jì.
Liǔxià Jì replied:
"Your lordship's bribe
to desire the Cén Dǐng
is to save the state from calamity.
I too have a 'state' here—
to ruin my 'state' to save your lordship's state—
this is difficult for me."
Thereupon, the lord of Lǔ sent the genuine Cén Dǐng.
Moreover, Liǔxià Jì can be said to be skilled in persuasion;
not only did he preserve his own 'state,'
but he also preserved the lord of Lǔ's state.
King Mǐn of Qí, having lost his state, dwelled in Wèi.
One day while walking,
he said to Gōng Yùdān:
"I have lost my state,
yet I do not know the reason.
The reason for my losing it—
what indeed was it?
I should already know."
Gōng Yùdān replied:
"I thought Your Majesty already knew;
does Your Majesty truly not yet know?
The reason Your Majesty lost your state
is because of your worthiness.
The kings of the world are all unworthy,
and they hated Your Majesty's worthiness;
therefore, they joined forces to attack you.
This is why Your Majesty lost your state."
King Mǐn sighed with emotion and said:
"Is worthiness truly so bitter?"
This too is not knowing the reason;
this is Gōng Yùdān's error.
King Shòu of Yuè had four sons.
The king of Yuè's younger brother was named Yù;
he wanted to kill them all
to become the successor.
He hated three of them and killed them;
the people of the state were displeased,
greatly criticizing the ruler.
He hated the remaining one and wanted to kill him,
but the king of Yuè would not listen.
That son, fearing he would certainly die,
relying on the people's desire to expel Yù,
surrounded the royal palace.
The king of Yuè sighed and said:
"I did not listen to Yù's words,
and thus incurred this calamity."
He too did not know the reason for his downfall.
9.5 "Spiritual Penetration"
The fifth says:
Some say the dodder plant has no roots.
The dodder is not rootless;
its root is not attached—
it is the poria cocos.
The lodestone attracts iron;
something draws it.
Trees close together rub against each other;
something pushes them.
The sage faces south and stands,
with a heart of love and benefit for the people.
Before the commands are issued, all under heaven crane their necks and stand on tiptoe—this is spiritual penetration with the people.
As for harming others, people are likewise.
Now, those who attack
sharpen the five weapons,
wear fine clothes and eat delicacies;
the day of departure is set.
Those who are to be attacked are unhappy—
it is not that they have heard of it,
but that the spirits have forewarned them.
One's body is in Qín,
but one's beloved is in Qí;
when they die, one's will and vital breath are unsettled—
the essence may travel back and forth.
Virtue is the master of the myriad people.
The moon is the root of all yin.
When the moon is full, clams and oysters are plump, and all yin is abundant;
when the moon wanes, clams and oysters are empty, and all yin diminishes.
The moon takes form in the heavens, while all yin transforms in the depths;
the sage manifests virtue within himself, and the four borders are all governed by benevolence.
Yǎng Yóujī shot at a rhinoceros,
hit a stone,
and the arrow sank to its feathers—such was his sincerity toward the rhinoceros.
Bó Lè learned to judge horses,
and everything he saw was a horse—such was his sincerity toward horses.
The butcher Dīng of Sòng delighted in carving oxen,
and everything he saw was a dead ox;
for three years he did not see a live ox;
he used his knife for nineteen years,
and its edge was as if newly sharpened—he followed their grain, such was his sincerity toward oxen.
Zhōng Zǐqī heard someone striking a chime stone at night and felt sorrow, so he sent for the person and asked:
"Why do you strike the chime stone so sorrowfully?"
The reply was:
"My father unfortunately killed someone and could not live;
my mother was allowed to live but was made to brew wine for the state;
I myself was allowed to live but was made to strike the chime stone for the state.
I have not seen my mother for three years.
Previously, when I worked at the Shè residence, I saw my mother,
but considering how to redeem her, I had no wealth,
and my person is firmly owned by the state.
That is why I am sorrowful."
Zhōng Zǐqī sighed and said:
"How sorrowful! How sorrowful!
The heart is not the arm, nor is the arm the mallet or the stone.
Sorrow resides in the heart, and wood and stone respond to it.
Thus, the noble person is sincere in this and manifests in that,
moved within himself and elicits response from others—must one always force explanations?"
There was a man named Shēn Xǐ in Zhōu who had lost his mother.
Hearing a beggar singing outside his gate, he felt sorrow,
and his countenance changed.
He told the gatekeeper to bring in the singing beggar,
awoke to himself and asked:
"Why do you beg?"
Speaking with her, it turned out to be his mother.
Thus, parents toward their children,
and children toward their parents,
are one body divided in two,
sharing the same breath yet breathing separately.
Like plants having flowers and fruits,
like trees having roots and heartwood,
though in different places, they connect,
hidden intentions reach each other,
pain and illness bring mutual aid,
worries and thoughts stir mutual feeling,
in life they rejoice together,
in death they grieve together—this is called the bond of flesh and blood.
Spirit emerges from loyalty and responds to the heart;
when two essences meet,
must words be necessary?
10.1 "The Annals of Early Winter"
It is said:
In the month of early winter:
The sun is in the Tail constellation,
at dusk the Rooftop constellation is at the zenith,
at dawn the Seven Stars constellation is at the zenith.
Its days are Rén and Guǐ.
Its sovereign is Zhuānxū.
Its spirit is Xuánmíng.
Its creatures are the shelled.
Its musical note is Yǔ.
The pitch-pipe is Yìngzhōng.
Its number is six.
Its flavor is salty.
Its odor is rotten.
Its sacrifice is to the wayfarer.
Offer the kidneys first.
Water begins to freeze,
earth begins to harden.
Pheasants enter the great waters and become clams.
Rainbows hide and are not seen.
The Son of Heaven resides in the left chamber of the Dark Hall,
rides in a black carriage,
drives black horses,
carries black banners,
wears black clothes,
adorns himself with dark jade,
eats millet and pork.
His vessels are large and deep.
In this month, winter is established.
Three days before the establishment of winter,
the Grand Historian informs the Son of Heaven,
saying:
"On such-and-such a day, winter is established;
the abundant virtue is in water."
The Son of Heaven then fasts.
On the day of the establishment of winter,
the Son of Heaven personally leads the Three Dukes, Nine Ministers, and Grandees to welcome winter in the northern suburbs.
Upon returning, he rewards those who died in service and comforts the orphaned and widowed.
In this month,
he orders the Grand Diviner
to pray and offer sacrifices with tortoise shells and milfoil stalks, interpreting the cracks and signs,
examining the hexagrams for good or ill fortune.
Then, those who flatter superiors and disrupt the law are investigated and punished, with no concealment.
In this month,
the Son of Heaven begins wearing furs.
He orders the officials, saying:
"The qi of heaven ascends,
the qi of earth descends,
heaven and earth do not communicate,
closing to form winter."
He commands all officials to carefully cover and store.
He orders the Minister of Education to inspect stockpiles and accumulations, ensuring nothing is left uncollected;
to reinforce city walls,
guard gates and wards,
repair bolts and locks,
secure keys,
fasten seals,
prepare the borders,
fortify strongholds,
watch passes and bridges,
block footpaths,
regulate mourning rites,
distinguish burial garments,
examine the thickness of inner and outer coffins, and plan the dimensions—size, height, lowness, thickness—of burial mounds, according to the ranks of noble and humble.
In this month,
he orders the Master of Artisans to assess work.
Display sacrificial vessels,
check standards and measurements,
do not create extravagant or clever objects to unsettle the ruler's mind;
craftsmanship must be of the highest quality.
Objects are inscribed with the artisan's name to examine their sincerity;
if an artisan's work is improper,
punishment must be carried out to thoroughly investigate the circumstances.
In this month,
the great drinking ceremony and winter sacrifice are held.
The Son of Heaven prays to the heavenly ancestors for the coming year.
Animals are greatly slaughtered,
sacrifices are made at the public altars and at gates and wards, offerings and prayers are made to ancestors and the five household gods,
and farmers are rewarded with rest.
The Son of Heaven orders generals and commanders to discuss military affairs, practicing archery, charioteering, and tests of strength.
In this month,
he orders the Water Conservator and Fishing Master to collect taxes from springs, ponds, and marshes,
and no one dares to encroach upon or exploit the masses and myriad people,
lest the Son of Heaven incur resentment below.
If there are such cases,
punish without pardon.
If the ordinances of spring are carried out in early winter,
then freezing will not be solid,
earth's qi will leak out,
and many people will flee into exile.
If the ordinances of summer are carried out,
then the state will have many violent winds,
winter will not be cold,
and hibernating insects will reappear.
If the ordinances of autumn are carried out,
then snow and frost will be untimely,
small military conflicts will arise frequently,
and land will be encroached upon and diminished.
10.2 "Moderation in Funerals"
The second says:
To understand life thoroughly
is the essential task of the sage;
to understand death thoroughly
is the ultimate achievement of the sage.
To understand life
means not harming life with material things;
this is called nurturing life.
To understand death
means not harming the dead with material things;
this is called giving peace to the dead.
These two things
are what the sage alone determines.
All things born between heaven and earth
must inevitably die.
This is unavoidable.
The filial son's reverence for his parents,
the loving parent's affection for their child,
pierces to the bone and marrow;
it is their nature.
For those they revere and love,
to die and be cast into ditches and gullies
is something human feeling cannot bear to do.
Therefore, there is the principle of burying the dead.
Burial
means concealment,
which loving parents and filial sons treat with caution.
To be cautious
means to consider with the mind of the living.
To consider for the dead with the mind of the living,
nothing is better than leaving them undisturbed,
nothing is better than leaving them unexposed.
To leave them unexposed and undisturbed,
nothing is better than having nothing worth coveting;
having nothing worth coveting—this is called secure concealment.
The ancients had burials in vast wilderness or deep mountains that remained secure,
not because of pearls, jade, or state treasures,
but because burial must involve concealment.
If burial is shallow, foxes and badgers will dig it up;
if deep, it will reach springs and water.
Therefore, all burials must be on high hills
to avoid the danger of foxes and the dampness of water springs.
This is good,
but to forget the calamity of traitors, thieves, robbers, and rebels
—is this not deluded?
It is like a blind musician avoiding a pillar, only to bump hard into a stake.
The dangers of foxes, water springs, traitors, thieves, robbers, and rebels
are the great stakes.
If loving parents and filial sons avoid these,
they grasp the true principle of burial.
Making good inner and outer coffins
is to avoid ants, snakes, and insects.
Now, in this age of great disorder,
rulers increasingly lavish
their burials, not out of consideration for the dead,
but for the living to show off to one another.
Extravagance is considered glorious,
frugality is considered shameful.
They do not take convenience for the dead as their purpose,
but merely strive for the praise or blame of the living.
This is not the heart of loving parents and filial sons.
Though a father is dead,
a filial son's reverence for him does not slacken;
though a son is dead,
a loving parent's affection for him does not cease.
To bury those they love and revere
with what the living greatly desire
in order to give them peace—
how can this be?
As for the people's pursuit of profit,
they brave flying arrows,
tread upon naked blades,
wade through blood and gore to obtain it.
Ignorant rustics
will bear to wrong parents, brothers, and close friends to seek profit.
Now, without such danger,
without such disgrace,
the profit is very great:
riding in carriages, eating meat,
benefits extending to sons and grandsons.
Even a sage could not prevent this,
let alone in an age of disorder?
The larger the state,
the wealthier the family,
the more lavish the burial.
Pearls in the mouth, jade suits, pearls, jade, curios, treasures, and valuables,
bells, tripods, pots, and basins,
chariots, horses, clothing, coverings, spears, and swords
are too numerous to count.
All the implements for sustaining life
are included without exception.
The burial chamber with layered timbers,
multiple layers of inner and outer coffins,
piled stones and charcoal
encircling the outside.
When wicked men hear of this,
they spread the word to one another.
Even if the ruler uses severe authority and heavy penalties to prohibit it,
it still cannot be stopped.
Moreover, the longer the dead have been buried,
the more distant the living become;
the more distant the living become,
the more negligent the guardians become;
the more negligent the guardians become, while the burial goods remain as before, the situation is inherently insecure.
The common practice in conducting funerals:
they carry the coffin on a large hearse,
with feather pennants, banners, and flags like clouds, and feather canopies to oversee it, pearls and jade to equip it,
embroidered patterns and designs to adorn it.
Tens of thousands of rope-pullers on left and right march it,
and military discipline must be established before it can proceed.
Viewed as a spectacle for the world,
it is beautiful and extravagant;
viewed as treatment for the dead,
it is unacceptable.
If it were truly convenient for the dead,
then even if it impoverished the state and wearied the people,
loving parents and filial sons would not refuse to do it.
10.3 "Giving Peace to the Dead"
The third says:
In this age, they make burial mounds
as high and large as mountains,
plant trees on them like forests,
set up gate towers, courtyards, make palace halls, and construct guest and host platforms as if they were capital cities.
To display wealth to the world, this is acceptable; to do this for the dead is not.
For the dead,
gazing upon ten thousand years is like a blink.
Human lifespan,
at its longest, does not exceed a hundred years;
middle longevity does not exceed sixty.
To plan for the infinite dead with the span of a hundred or sixty years—their circumstances are certainly not commensurate.
To plan for the dead with the infinite in mind,
then one grasps it.
Suppose there were a person here
who erected a stone inscription on a burial mound, saying:
"The objects within this
contain very many pearls, jade, curios, wealth, goods, treasures, and precious vessels.
You must not fail to dig it up.
If you dig it up, you will surely become greatly wealthy,
riding in carriages and eating meat for generations."
People would surely laugh at him together,
considering him greatly deluded.
The lavish burials of this age resemble this.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been a state that did not perish;
if there are no states that do not perish,
then there are no tombs that are not dug up.
From what ears and eyes have heard and seen,
Qí, Jīng, and Yān have perished,
Sòng and Zhōngshān have already perished,
Zhào, Wèi, and Hán have all perished;
they are all former states.
From these upward, perished states are too numerous to count.
Therefore, of ancient great tombs, none have not been dug up.
Yet the world all competes to make them—
is this not lamentable?
The ruler's unruly people,
the father's unfilial sons,
the elder brother's disrespectful younger brothers,
all are those driven out by their villages with pots and ladles,
who fear the toil of plowing, sowing, and gathering firewood,
unwilling to manage human affairs,
but pray for the pleasure of fine clothes and extravagant food.
When their cunning and cleverness are exhausted,
and they have no means to achieve it,
then they gather bands of many followers
in deep mountains, vast marshes, forests, and thickets,
to assault, rob, and plunder.
They also look for famous mounds and great tombs with rich burials,
seek lodging nearby,
to secretly dig them up,
ceaselessly day and night,
determined to gain profit,
and divide it among themselves.

To have those they love and revere, yet let traitors, thieves, robbers, and rebels inevitably disgrace them in the end—this is a grave matter for filial sons, loyal ministers, loving fathers, and close friends.
Yáo was buried at Gǔlín,
with trees planted all around;
Shùn was buried at Jìshì,
and the market stalls did not change their trade;
Yǔ was buried at Kuàijī,
without troubling the people and laborers.
Therefore, the former kings buried the dead with frugality and moderation,
not because they begrudged the expense,
not because they disliked the labor,
but because they considered the dead.
What the former kings detested
was only the disgrace of the deceased.
If lavish, it is bound to bring disgrace;
if frugal, it will not be lavish.
Therefore, the burials of the former kings
were necessarily frugal, harmonious, and unified.
What is meant by "harmonious"?
What is meant by "unified"?
If buried in the mountains and forests, they harmonized with the mountains and forests;
if buried on slopes or lowlands, they unified with the slopes or lowlands.
This is what is called loving the dead.
Now, those who love the dead are many,
but those who know how to love the living are few.
Thus, before Sòng perished, the eastern tomb was dug up;
before Qí perished, Duke Zhuāng's tomb was dug up.
Even when the state was peaceful and secure, it was like this;
how much more so after a hundred generations when the state has already perished?
Therefore, filial sons, loyal ministers, affectionate fathers, and friends must not fail to examine this.
To love them but instead harm them, to give them peace but instead endanger them—
is this not what is meant here?
The Odes say:
"I dare not face a tiger barehanded,
nor dare I cross a river without a boat.
People know one thing,
but none know the other."
This speaks of not knowing how to analogize.
Thus, they oppose each other to criticize,
and oppose each other to affirm.
What they criticize is precisely what they affirm,
and what they affirm is precisely what they criticize.
Right and wrong are not yet determined,
yet joy, anger, and strife
are instead put to use.
I do not criticize strife, nor do I criticize contention,
but I criticize the reasons for strife and contention.
Therefore, all those who engage in strife and contention
do so only after right and wrong have been determined.
Now, many do not first determine right and wrong but instead hasten to strife and contention;
this is a great delusion.
When Jìsūn of Lǔ had a funeral,
Confucius went to offer condolences.
Entering the gate, he turned left,
following the guest's position.
The host used a yúfán jade to place in the coffin,
and Confucius strode straight across the courtyard,
ascended the steps rapidly,
and said:
"To use precious jade in the burial
is like exposing the bones on the central plain."
Striding straight across the courtyard and rapidly ascending the steps
was contrary to ritual;
nevertheless, it was to correct an error.
10.4 "Different Treasures"
The fourth says:
The people of antiquity were not without treasures,
but what they treasured was different.
When Sūnshū Áo fell ill,
and was about to die,
he admonished his son, saying:
"The king has repeatedly offered me fiefs,
but I have not accepted them.
When I die,
the king will then enfeoff you,
but you must not accept fertile land.
Between Chǔ and Yuè, there is a place called Qǐnzhīqiū.
This land is not fertile,
and its name is very inauspicious.
The people of Jīng fear ghosts,
and the people of Yuè believe in omens.
What can be held long
is only this place."
After Sūnshū Áo died,
the king indeed offered his son fertile land,
but the son declined,
requesting Qǐnzhīqiū instead.
Thus, to this day, it has not been lost.
The wisdom of Sūnshū Áo
lay in knowing how to turn disadvantage into advantage,
in knowing how to take what others detest as his own delight.
This is how those who possess the Way differ from the vulgar.
Wǔ Yuán fled,
and Jīng urgently sought him. He ascended Tàiháng and gazed toward Zhèng, saying:
"This state,
with its perilous terrain and its people full of cunning,
its ruler is a vulgar ruler,
not worth joining forces with."
He left Zhèng and went to Xǔ,
where he met Duke Xǔ and asked where to go.
Duke Xǔ did not respond,
but spat toward the southeast.
Wǔ Yuán bowed twice and received the gift, saying:
"I know where to go."
Thereupon, he went to Wú.
Passing through Jīng,
he reached the river
and wished to cross.
He saw an old man
paddling a small boat,
just about to fish,
and approached him with a request.
The old man ferried him across the river.
When asked his name and clan,
he refused to tell.
Wǔ Yuán untied his sword and offered it to the old man,
saying:
"This is a sword worth a thousand pieces of gold;
I wish to present it to you, old man."
The old man refused to accept it, saying:
"According to the laws of Jīng,
whoever captures Wǔ Yuán
will be enfeoffed as a zhíguī,
receive a salary of ten thousand dàn,
and a thousand yì of gold.
In the past, when Zǐxū passed by,
I still did not seize him;
why would I now take your thousand-gold sword?"
After Wǔ Yuán passed through Wú,
he sent people to search for him on the river, but could not find him. Whenever he ate, he would make offerings to him,
praying:
"Old man of the river!
Heaven and earth are vast,
and the multitude is great;
what is there that you would not do?
Yet you act without purpose.
You act, yet without acting for a purpose.
Your name cannot be heard,
your person cannot be seen;
is this not the old man of the river?"
A rustic of Sòng,
while plowing, obtained a piece of jade
and presented it to Sīchéng Zǐhǎn.
Zǐhǎn did not accept it.
The rustic pleaded:
"This is the treasure of a rustic;
I beg the Prime Minister to grant me the favor of accepting it."
Zǐhǎn said:
"You consider jade a treasure;
I consider not accepting it a treasure."
Therefore, the elders of Sòng said:
"Zǐhǎn was not without treasure;
what he treasured was different."
Now, if you show a child a hundred pieces of gold and a ball of glutinous rice,
the child will certainly take the ball of glutinous rice;
if you show a rustic the Héshì Jade and a hundred pieces of gold,
the rustic will certainly take the hundred pieces of gold;
if you show a worthy the Héshì Jade and the ultimate words of the Way and virtue,
the worthy will certainly take the ultimate words.
The more refined one's wisdom,
the more refined what one chooses;
the cruder one's wisdom,
the cruder what one chooses.
10.5 "Different Uses"
The fifth says:
All things are different,
but their uses for humans vary;
this is the source of order and chaos, survival and destruction, life and death.
Thus, a state may be vast and immense,
its soldiers strong and wealthy,
but it is not necessarily secure;
one may be noble and exalted,
but not necessarily illustrious;
it lies in how they are used.
Jié and Zhòu used their talents and brought about their own downfall,
while Tāng and Wǔ used their talents and achieved kingship.
Tāng saw a man praying over a net,
set up on all four sides,
and his prayer was:
"Those who fall from heaven,
those who emerge from earth,
those who come from the four directions,
all fall into my net."
Tāng said:
"Alas!
This exhausts them all.
If not Jié, who would do such a thing?"
Tāng removed three sides of the net,
leaving only one side,
and changed the prayer, saying:
"In the past, spiders made webs,
and now people learn to weave.
Those who wish to go left, go left;
those who wish to go right, go right;
those who wish to go high, go high;
those who wish to go low, go low;
I will take only those who defy fate."
The states south of the Hàn River heard of this and said:
"The virtue of Tāng extends even to birds and beasts."
Forty states submitted to him.
If one sets up nets on all four sides,
one may not necessarily catch birds;
Tāng removed three sides,
leaving only one side,
and thereby netted forty states—
it was not merely about catching birds.
King Wén of Zhōu had people dig a pond,
and they unearthed the bones of a dead person.
The officials reported this to King Wén,
who said:
"Rebury them."
The officials said:
"These have no master."
King Wén said:
"He who possesses the world
is the master of the world;
he who possesses a state
is the master of that state.
Am I not his master now?"
He then ordered the officials to rebury the bones with proper clothing and a coffin.
When the world heard of this, they said:
"King Wén is virtuous indeed,
his kindness extends even to dried bones,
how much more so to living people?"
Some obtain treasures and thereby endanger their states;
King Wén obtained decayed bones and thereby made clear his intent.
Thus, for the sage, nothing is without its use.
When a disciple of Confucius came from afar,
Confucius, leaning on his staff, asked him:
"Is your grandfather well?"
Then, holding his staff upright, he bowed and asked:
"Are your parents well?"
Setting his staff aside, he asked:
"Are your brothers well?"
Taking a few steps back, he turned and asked:
"Are your wife and children well?"
Thus, Confucius, with a staff six feet long,
illustrated the distinctions of noble and humble,
and clarified the principles of closeness and distance.
How much more so could this be done with high rank and generous salary?
The ancients valued archery
for nurturing the young and caring for the aged.
People today value archery
for attacking, fighting, invading, and seizing.
In its lesser form, it is used to rob the weak and oppress the few,
making plunder their chief aim.
When a benevolent person obtains malt sugar,
they use it to nourish the sick and sustain the elderly.
When Zhí and Jué obtain malt sugar,
they use it to pick locks and break bolts.
11.1 The Annals of Midwinter
It is said:
In the month of Midwinter:
The sun is in Dǒu,
at dusk the Eastern Wall is at the zenith,
at dawn Zhěn is at the zenith.
Its day is Rén-Guǐ.
Its emperor is Zhuānxū.
Its spirit is Xuánmíng.
Its creatures are the shelled.
Its musical note is Yǔ.
The pitch-pipe is Huángzhōng.
Its number is six.
Its flavor is salty.
Its odor is putrid.
Its sacrifice is to the wayfarer.
The offering is first made to the kidneys.
The ice grows thicker.
The earth begins to split.
The hé dàn does not call.
Tigers begin to mate.
The Son of Heaven resides in the Dark Hall of the Grand Temple,
rides in a dark carriage,
drives black horses,
bears dark banners,
wears black clothes,
adorns himself with dark jade,
eats millet and pork.
His vessels are large and covered.
He commands the officials, saying:
"Do not undertake earthworks,
do not open stored reserves,
do not mobilize the masses,
so as to secure the closing of heaven and earth."
If stored reserves are opened,
and the masses are mobilized,
the earth's energy will leak out,
this is called opening the chambers of heaven and earth.
Then all hibernating creatures will die,
the people will suffer many epidemics and diseases,
and death will follow.
This month is called the Month of Unobstructedness.
In this month,
command the eunuch director
to reiterate the palace regulations,
inspect the gates and alleys,
secure the rooms and chambers,
ensuring they are tightly closed.
Reduce women's work,
do not allow excess.
Even noble relatives and close attendants
are not exempt from these prohibitions.
Then command the Grand Vintner:
"The glutinous rice and ordinary rice must be uniform,
the yeast and malt must be timely,
the soaking and steaming must be clean,
the water and springs must be fragrant,
the pottery vessels must be excellent,
the heat and timing must be precise.
Employ all six materials,
with the Grand Vintner overseeing,
ensuring there are no errors."
The Son of Heaven then commands the officials
to pray and sacrifice to the four seas, great rivers, famous plains, deep marshes, wells, and springs.
In this month,
if there are farmers who do not gather and store their harvests,
or if oxen, horses, livestock, or beasts are left to roam,
they may be taken without inquiry.
In the mountains, forests, marshes, and wetlands,
those who can gather wild food or hunt birds and beasts
are instructed by the Field Overseer.
If there are those who encroach upon or seize from others,
they are punished without pardon.
In this month,
the day reaches its shortest.
Yīn and Yáng contend,
all living things are in flux.
The gentleman fasts and abstains,
residing in seclusion,
seeking tranquility of body,
avoiding music and beauty,
restraining desires and cravings,
calming his form and nature,
keeping affairs still,
awaiting the settling of Yīn and Yáng.
The yún grass begins to grow.
The lì plant sprouts.
Earthworms coil.
Elk shed their antlers.
Springs begin to stir.
When the day is shortest,
then cut timber and trees,
and take bamboo for arrows.
In this month,
one may dismiss officials who have no duties,
and discard utensils that have no use.
Plaster the gate towers, courtyards, gates, and alleys,
and build prisons.
This is to assist heaven and earth in their closing and storing.
If in Midwinter the ordinances of Summer are carried out,
then the state will suffer drought,
hazy mists will appear,
and thunder will sound.
If the ordinances of Autumn are carried out,
then the weather will bring sleety rain,
melons and gourds will not ripen,
and the state will face great military campaigns.
If the ordinances of Spring are carried out,
then insect pests will cause damage,
springs and streams will diminish and dry up,
and the people will suffer many epidemics and plagues.
11.2 Ultimate Loyalty
It is said:
Utterly loyal words are offensive to the ear and unsettling to the mind.
If not a worthy ruler, who can listen to them?
Thus, what pleases a worthy ruler
is what an unworthy ruler condemns.
All rulers detest violent coercion,
yet they daily bring it upon themselves.
What good does detesting it do?
Suppose there is a tree here,
and one wishes it to be beautiful.
If someone waters it from time to time,
one dislikes it,
but if one cuts at its roots oneself,
then certainly no living tree will remain.
To detest hearing loyal words
is precisely cutting at one's own roots.
King Zhuāng'āi of Jīng hunted in Yúnmèng,
shot at a rhinoceros,
and hit it.
Shēn, Lord Zǐ Péi, rushed the king and seized it.
The king said:
"How violent and disrespectful!"
He ordered the officials to execute him.
The ministers on both sides all came forward to remonstrate, saying:
"Zǐ Péi is a worthy man,
and moreover a minister a hundred times more loyal to the king.
There must be a reason for this.
We beg the king to investigate."
Within three months,
Zǐ Péi fell ill and died.
Jīng raised an army,
fought Jìn at Liǎngtáng,
won a great victory over Jìn,
and upon returning, rewarded those who had merit.
Shēn Gōng Zǐ Péi's younger brother came forward and requested a reward from the officials, saying:
"Others had merit on the battlefield;
my elder brother had merit beneath the chariot."
The king said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"My elder brother incurred the charge of violent disrespect,
risking the crime of death by the king's side.
His foolish heart was set on being loyal to the king's person,
and preserving a lifespan of a thousand years.
My elder brother once read in an old record:
'Whoever kills a suísì,
will die within three months.'
Therefore, my elder brother, alarmed and fearful, contended for it,
and thus suffered the penalty and died."
The king ordered someone to open the archives and look,
and indeed it was found in the old records.
He then richly rewarded him.
Shēn Gōng Zǐ Péi's loyalty can be called sublime conduct.
The meaning of sublime conduct is such that
if others know of it, it does not serve as encouragement,
and if others do not know of it, it does not lead to discouragement.
No conduct is loftier than this.
The King of Qí suffered from a boil,
and sent someone to Sòng to fetch Wén Zhì.
Wén Zhì arrived,
examined the king's illness,
and said to the crown prince:
"The king's illness can certainly be cured.
However,
if the king's illness is cured,
he will certainly kill Zhì."
The crown prince said:
"Why?"
Wén Zhì replied:
"If I do not anger the king, the illness cannot be treated;
if I anger the king, Zhì will certainly die."
The crown prince kowtowed and urgently pleaded:
"If you can cure the king's illness,
I and my mother will plead with the king even at the risk of death.
The king will surely show favor to me and my mother.
I beg you, sir, not to worry."
Wén Zhì said:
"Very well.
I will risk death for the king."
He made an appointment with the crown prince,
but failed to appear three times when he was supposed to go,
so the King of Qí was already angry.
When Wén Zhì arrived,
he did not remove his shoes before climbing onto the bed,
stepped on the king's clothes,
and asked about the king's illness.
The king was angry and did not speak to him.
Wén Zhì then used harsh words to further anger the king.
The king shouted and rose,
and the illness was then cured.
The king was greatly angered and displeased,
and intended to have Wén Zhì boiled alive.
The crown prince and the queen urgently pleaded for him but could not succeed.
Indeed, Wén Zhì was boiled alive in a cauldron.
He was boiled for three days and three nights,
yet his complexion did not change.
Wén Zhì said:
"If you truly wish to kill me,
then why not cover it,
to cut off the yīn and yáng energy?"
The king had it covered,
and Wén Zhì then died.
Being loyal in a well-ordered age is easy;
being loyal in a corrupt age is difficult.
Wén Zhì was not unaware that curing the king's illness would lead to his own death.
He acted for the crown prince, undertaking difficulty to fulfill his duty.
11.3 "Loyalty and Integrity"
Thirdly:
When a scholar's sense of honor cannot be insulted, it is of great importance.
When it is of great importance, it is esteemed above wealth and honor.
Profit is insufficient to sway his mind.
Even if he is nominally a feudal lord,
actually possessing ten thousand chariots,
it is insufficient to shake his heart.
If truly insulted, then there is no reason to take pleasure in life.
Such a man,
if he has power, will certainly not act selfishly;
if he holds office, will certainly not act corruptly;
if he leads troops, will certainly not flee in defeat.
Loyal ministers are likewise.
If it benefits the ruler and is advantageous to the state,
they dare not refuse or avoid it, even to the point of giving their lives and leaving their families to follow it. If a state has scholars like this,
then it can be said to have men of worth.
Such men are inherently difficult to find,
and the worry is that even if one obtains them, one may not be wise.
The King of Wú wanted to kill Prince Qìngjì, but no one could kill him.
The King of Wú was troubled by this.
Yāolí said:
"I can do it."
The King of Wú said:
"How can you possibly do it?
I once pursued him along the river with six horses,
but could not catch up;
shot arrows at him,
filling his left and right hands,
but could not hit him.
Now you, when you draw your sword, cannot even lift your arm;
when you board a chariot, cannot even mount the handrail.
How can you possibly do it?"
Yāolí said:
"A scholar worries about not being brave;
why worry about not being able?
If the king can truly assist me,
I request to certainly be able."
The King of Wú said:
"Very well."
The next morning, he falsely accused Yāolí of a crime,
seized his wife and children,
burned them and scattered their ashes.
Yāolí fled,
and went to Wèi to see Prince Qìngjì.
Prince Qìngjì happily said:
"The King of Wú's lack of virtue,
you have witnessed it,
and the feudal lords know it.
Now that you have escaped and left him is also good."
Yāolí stayed with Prince Qìngjì for a while,
then said to Prince Qìngjì:
"Wú's lack of virtue grows worse.
I request to go with you, prince, to seize the state."
Prince Qìngjì said:
"Good."
Then he and Yāolí crossed the river together.
In the middle of the river,
Yāolí drew his sword and stabbed Prince Qìngjì.
Prince Qìngjì seized him
and threw him into the river.
When he floated up, he grabbed him and threw him in again,
doing this three times.
Finally, he said:
"You are a scholar of renown in the world.
I grant you the favor of achieving your fame."
Yāolí did not die,
and returned to Wú.
The King of Wú was greatly pleased,
and offered to share the state with him.
Yāolí said:
"That cannot be.
I request to certainly die."
The King of Wú tried to stop him.
Yāolí said:
"To kill one's wife and children, burn them, and scatter their ashes,
for the convenience of the task,
I consider this unkind.
To kill a new lord for the sake of an old lord,
I consider this unrighteous.
To be seized and thrown into the river,
three times entering and emerging,
only because Prince Qìngjì granted me favor and did not kill me—
I am already disgraced.
To be unkind and unrighteous,
and moreover already disgraced,
I cannot live."
The King of Wú could not stop him,
and indeed he fell on his sword and died.
Yāolí can be said to have been unmoved by reward.
Thus, facing great profit without changing his righteousness,
he can be called incorruptible.
Being incorruptible, he did not forget his disgrace because of honor and wealth.
Duke Yì of Wèi had a minister named Hóng Yǎn,
who was sent on a mission.
The Dí people attacked Wèi.
Its people said:
"Those to whom the lord gives position and salary
are cranes;
those whom he honors and enriches
are palace attendants.
Let the lord send the palace attendants and cranes to fight.
How can we fight?"
They then scattered and fled.
The Dí people arrived,
caught up with Duke Yì at Róngzé,
killed him,
ate all his flesh,
and only left his liver.
Hóng Yǎn arrived,
reported his mission to the liver,
finished,
cried out to heaven and wept,
exhausted his grief and stopped,
saying:
"I request to be the outer covering."
He then killed himself, first removing the contents of his abdomen,
and placed Duke Yì's liver inside.
Upon hearing this, Duke Huán said:
"When Wèi perished,
it was considered to be without the Way.
Now that it has ministers like this,
it cannot be allowed to perish."
Thereupon, he reestablished Wèi at Chǔqiū.
Hóng Yǎn can be called loyal indeed,
sacrificing his own life and body to follow his lord.
Not only did he follow his lord,
but he also caused the ancestral temples of Wèi to be reestablished,
with sacrifices continuing without interruption.
He can be said to have achieved merit.
11.4 "Dāngwù"
The fourth says:
To be discerning but not in proper argumentation,
trustworthy but not in accordance with principle,
courageous but not in accordance with righteousness,
law-abiding but not in accordance with what is essential,
is like being confused and riding a swift horse,
or being mad and wielding the sword Wú Gānjiàng.
Those who bring great chaos to the world
are certainly these four types.
What is valued in discernment
is that it follows proper argumentation;
what is valued in trustworthiness
is that it adheres to principle;
what is valued in courage
is that it acts in righteousness;
what is valued in law-abidingness
is that it aligns with what is essential.
A disciple of Zhí asked Zhí:
"Do robbers also have a Way?"
Zhí said:
"How could they not have a Way?
To accurately guess what is inside a gate,
and hit the hidden treasure—that is sageliness;
to enter first—that is courage;
to exit last—that is righteousness;
to know the right timing—that is wisdom;
to divide the spoils equally—that is benevolence.
One who does not master these five
and yet can become a great robber
does not exist in the world."
He exhaustively criticized the Six Kings and Five Hegemons,
considering that Yáo had a reputation for lack of kindness,
Shùn had conduct of unfiliality,
Yǔ had intentions of indulgence and drunkenness,
Tāng and Wǔ had deeds of exile and killing,
and the Five Hegemons had schemes of violence and chaos.
The world praises them,
and people conceal their faults,
which is delusion.
Therefore, when he died, he held a golden mallet to be buried with him,
saying:
"When I go down and meet the Six Kings and Five Hegemons,
I will knock their heads."
Discernment like this is worse than no discernment.
In Chǔ, there was a man named Zhígōng.
His father stole a sheep, and he reported it to the authorities.
The authorities arrested his father and were about to execute him.
Zhígōng requested to die in his place.
When he was about to be executed,
he told the officer:
"My father stole a sheep, and I reported it—
is that not trustworthy?
My father was to be executed, and I took his place—
is that not filial?
If one who is both trustworthy and filial is executed,
will there be anyone in the state who is not executed?"
The King of Jīng heard this
and did not execute him.
Confucius heard of it and said:
"How strange is Zhígōng's trustworthiness!
He used one father to gain two reputations."
Therefore, Zhígōng's trustworthiness
is worse than no trustworthiness.
In Qí, there were two men who admired courage.
One lived in the eastern suburb,
the other in the western suburb.
They met suddenly on the road and said:
"Shall we drink together?"
After several rounds of drinking,
they said:
"Shall we get some meat?"
One said:
"Your meat?
My meat?
Why bother seeking other meat?
Let us just prepare some sauce."
Thereupon, they drew knives and ate each other's flesh,
until they died.
Courage like this is worse than no courage.
Zhòu had two older brothers from the same mother.
The eldest was called Wēizǐ Qǐ,
the next was called Zhòngyǎn,
and the next was called Shòudé.
Shòudé was Zhòu,
and he was much younger.
When Zhòu's mother gave birth to Wēizǐ Qǐ and Zhòngyǎn, she was still a concubine,
but later she became the wife and gave birth to Zhòu.
Zhòu's father and mother wanted to make Wēizǐ Qǐ the crown prince,
but the Grand Historian, according to the law, argued:
"There is a son by the wife,
and one cannot set up a son by the concubine."
Thus, Zhòu became the heir.
To apply the law like this
is worse than having no law.
11.5 "Cháng Jiàn"
The fifth says:
The reason why wisdom differs among people
lies in their long-term vision and short-term vision.
The present in relation to the past
is like the past in relation to the future.
The present in relation to the future
is also like the present in relation to the past.
Therefore, by carefully understanding the present, one can know the past;
by knowing the past, one can know the future.
Past, present, and future are one.
Thus, the sage knows a thousand years above
and a thousand years below.
King Wén of Jīng said:
"Guǎn Ráo often confronts me with righteousness,
opposes me with ritual,
and when I am with him, I feel uneasy.
But when I neglect him, I gain nothing.
If I do not confer a rank on him in my lifetime,
later generations will have sages
who will criticize me."
Thereupon, he conferred on him the rank of Grandee.
"Shén Hóu Bó is good at nurturing my desires;
whatever I want, he does it before me.
When I am with him, I feel at ease.
But when I neglect him, I lose nothing.
If I do not distance myself from him in my lifetime,
later generations will have sages
who will criticize me."
Thereupon, he sent him away.
Shén Hóu Bó went to Zhèng,
flattered the ruler of Zhèng,
and did what he desired before he asked.
After three years, he took control of Zhèng's government,
but after five months, the people of Zhèng killed him.
Thus, the sages of later generations
caused King Wén to act virtuously in his time.
Duke Píng of Jìn cast a large bell.
When the bell was completed, he had artisans listen to it,
and they all considered it harmonious.
He then showed it to Shī Kuàng. Shī Kuàng said:
"It is not harmonious.
Please recast it."
Duke Píng said:
"The artisans all consider it harmonious.
Why do you think it is not harmonious?"
Shī Kuàng said:
"If there are no connoisseurs of music in later generations, then it is fine. But if there are connoisseurs of music,
they will know that the bell is not harmonious.
I secretly feel ashamed for you."
When it came to Shī Juān,
he indeed knew that the bell was not harmonious.
Thus, Shī Kuàng wanted to tune the bell well
for the connoisseurs of music in later generations.
Lǚ Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in Qí,
and Zhōu Gōng Dàn was enfeoffed in Lǔ.
The two rulers were very friendly with each other.
They asked each other, "How will you govern your state?"
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"Respect the worthy and honor achievement."
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"Be close to relatives and honor kindness."
Tàigōng Wàng said:
"From now on, Lǔ will decline."
Zhōu Gōng Dàn said:
"Although Lǔ will decline,
the one who possesses Qí will certainly not be from the Lǚ clan."
Afterward, Qí grew larger day by day,
until it became a hegemon,
but after twenty-four generations, Tián Chéngzǐ took possession of Qí.
Lǔ declined day by day,
until it barely survived,
and after thirty-four generations, it perished.
Wǔ Qǐ governed the region west of the Yellow River,
when Wáng Cuò slandered him before Marquis Wǔ of Wèi.
The Marquis sent someone to summon him.
When Wǔ Qǐ reached Ànmén,
he stopped his carriage to rest. Gazing toward the west of the Yellow River,
tears streamed down his face.
His attendant said to Wǔ Qǐ:
"I observe your intentions,
and you seem to regard abandoning the world as discarding a worn-out sandal.
Yet now, as you leave the west of the Yellow River, you weep.
Why is this?"
Wǔ Qǐ wiped away his tears and replied to him:
"You do not understand.

If the ruler knew me and allowed me to fully utilize my abilities, Qín could certainly be destroyed, and the west of the Yellow River could become a foundation for kingship. Now, the ruler listens to the words of slanderers and does not know me.
It will not be long before the west of the Yellow River is taken by Qín,
and the state of Wèi will henceforth decline."
Wǔ Qǐ indeed left Wèi and entered Chǔ.
After some time,
the entire west of the Yellow River fell to Qín,
Wèi daily grew weaker, and Qín daily grew stronger.
This is what Wǔ Qǐ foresaw and wept over.
Gōngshū Cuó of Wèi fell ill.
King Huì went to inquire about him
and said:
"Alas, Gōngshū's illness
is grave indeed!
What will become of the altars of soil and grain?"
Gōngshū replied:
"I have a retainer, Gōngsūn Yāng.
I wish Your Majesty would entrust the state's affairs to him.
If you are unwilling to heed him,
do not allow him to leave the state."
The King did not respond.
Upon leaving, he said to his attendants:
"Is it not lamentable?
With Gōngshū's wisdom,
he now tells me I must entrust the state's affairs to Gōngsūn Yāng.
How perverse!"
After Gōngshū died,
Gōngsūn Yāng traveled west to Qín.
Duke Xiào of Qín listened to him,
and Qín indeed became strong,
while Wèi indeed became weak.
It was not Gōngshū Cuó who was perverse,
but rather the King of Wèi.
The trouble with the perverse
is that they invariably regard the non-perverse as perverse.
12.1 "The Annals of the Final Month of Winter"
It is said:
In the final month of winter:
The sun is in the constellation Wùnǚ.
At dusk, the constellation Lóu is at the zenith.
At dawn, the constellation Dī is at the zenith.
Its days are Rén and Guǐ.
Its sovereign is Zhuānxū.
Its spirit is Xuánmíng.
Its creatures are those with shells.
Its musical note is Yǔ.
The pitch pipe corresponds to Dàlǚ.
Its number is six.
Its flavor is salty.
Its odor is putrid.
Its sacrifice is to the spirit of the road.
The offering is first made with kidneys.
Wild geese head north.
Magpies begin to build nests.
Hens brood and pheasants call.
The Son of Heaven resides in the right chamber of the Dark Hall.
He rides in a dark carriage,
drawn by black horses,
bearing a dark banner,
wears black robes,
adorns himself with dark jade,
and eats millet and pork.
His vessels are large and deep.
He orders the officials to perform the great exorcism,
sacrifice at the gates,
and bring out the earthen ox
to send off the cold air.
Birds of prey are fierce and swift.
Then the sacrifices to the mountains and rivers are completed,
as well as those to the great ministers of the sovereign and the spirits of heaven and earth.
In this month,
he orders the fishing master to begin fishing,
and the Son of Heaven goes in person.
He then tastes the fish,
first offering it in the ancestral temple.
Ice is at its peak,
and the waters and marshes are solidly frozen.
He orders the collection of ice.
After the ice has been stored,
he commands the people to be informed
to bring out the five grains.
He orders the Minister of Agriculture
to plan for paired plowing,
repair plows and shares,
and prepare farming tools.
He orders the music master
to hold a grand concert and then conclude.
He then orders the four overseers
to collect firewood
for the ancestral temple and the various sacrifices.
In this month,
the sun completes its course,
the moon completes its cycle,
the stars revolve through the heavens,
the count of days is nearly at an end,
and the year is about to begin anew.
Focus is on agriculture, and the people
are not to be employed for other tasks.
The Son of Heaven, together with his ministers, revises the state's statutes,
discusses the seasonal ordinances,
and prepares for the coming year's arrangements.
He then orders the Grand Historian
to rank the feudal lords
and assign them sacrificial animals,
to be offered to the Supreme Emperor of Heaven and the spirits of soil and grain.
He orders the states of the same surname
to supply animals for the ancestral temple.
He commands the steward to record the landholdings of ministers down to the common people and assign them sacrificial animals,
to be offered in sacrifices to the mountains, forests, and famous rivers.

All the people within the nine provinces under heaven must contribute their efforts to supply the sacrifices to the Supreme Emperor of Heaven, the spirits of soil and grain, the ancestral temple, mountains, forests, and famous rivers.
When these ordinances are carried out,
this is called the completion of one cycle,
thirty-two days.
If the ordinances of autumn are practiced in the final month of winter,
then white dew will fall early,
shelled creatures will cause calamities,
and the four neighbors will enter their strongholds for protection.
If the ordinances of spring are practiced,
then fetuses and newborns will suffer many injuries,
the state will have many chronic illnesses,
and this is called perversity.
If the ordinances of summer are practiced,
then floods will ruin the state,
seasonal snow will not fall,
and ice and frost will melt away.
12.2 "The Integrity of Scholars"
It is said:
The way of a scholar as a person
is to face principle without shunning difficulty,
confront peril while forgetting personal gain,
discard life to act righteously,
and regard death as a homecoming.
One who is like this
cannot be made a friend by a feudal lord,
nor a subject by the Son of Heaven.
At best, such a person can stabilize the world;
at the next level, stabilize a single state.
This must be achieved through such people.
Therefore, a ruler who wishes to achieve great merit and fame
must diligently seek such people.
A worthy ruler toils in seeking people
but rests in governing affairs.
In Qí, there was a man named Běiguō Sāo
who set up nets,
bound reeds,
and wove sandals and shoes
to support his mother, yet it was still insufficient.
He went to Yànzǐ's gate and said to him:
"I wish to beg for means to support my mother."
Yànzǐ's attendant said to Yànzǐ:
"This is a worthy man of Qí.
In his integrity, he will not serve as a subject to the Son of Heaven,
nor befriend feudal lords.
He does not improperly take from profit,
nor improperly avoid harm.
Now he begs for means to support his mother.
This is in accord with your principles, Master.
You must give to him."
Yànzǐ sent someone to give him grain from the granary and gold from the treasury,
but he declined the gold and accepted the grain.
After some time,
Yànzǐ fell under suspicion by the ruler of Qí
and fled the state.
Passing by Běiguō Sāo's door, he took his leave.
Běiguō Sāo bathed and came out to see Yànzǐ, saying:
"Where are you going, Master?"
Yànzǐ said:
"I am suspected by the ruler of Qí,
and I am fleeing the state."
Běiguō Sāo said:
"Master, do your best."
Yànzǐ mounted his carriage,
heaved a deep sigh, and lamented:
"Is it not fitting that I am fleeing?
I also know scholars too little."
Yànzǐ departed.
Běiguōzi summoned his friend and told him:
"I was moved by Yànzǐ's righteousness,
and once begged from him the means to support my mother.
I have heard it said:
'He who provides for one's parents,
should personally face their difficulties.'
Now Yànzǐ is under suspicion,
I will use my death to clear his name."
He put on his robes and cap,
ordered his friend to carry a sword and follow with a bamboo box,
went to the ruler's court,
and requested the gatekeeper to announce:
"Yànzǐ
is a worthy man of the world.
If he leaves now, Qí will surely be invaded.
Rather than see the state invaded,
it is better to die first.
I beg to entrust my head to clear Yànzǐ's name."
Then he said to his friend:
"Place my head in the box,
and present it as an entrustment."
He withdrew and cut his own throat.
His friend then presented it as entrusted.
His friend said to the onlookers:
"Běiguōzi died for the state's sake;
I will die for Běiguōzi."
He also withdrew and cut his own throat.
The ruler of Qí heard of this,
was greatly alarmed,
mounted a relay carriage and personally pursued Yànzǐ,
reaching him at the outskirts of the state,
and requested him to return.
Yànzǐ, having no alternative, returned.
Hearing that Běiguō Sāo had died to clear his name,
he said:
"Was my fleeing not fitting?
It shows how greatly I failed to recognize true scholars."
12.3 "Jié Lì"
The third says:
It is easy to have followers when noble and rich,
difficult when poor and lowly.
When Jìn Wéngōng was in exile,
wandering throughout the world,
destitute and lowly,
yet Jièzǐtuī did not leave him—
he had the means to retain him.
When he returned to the state with ten thousand chariots,
and Jièzǐtuī left him—
he lacked the means to retain him.
Able in the difficult,
unable in the easy—
this is why Wéngōng did not become king.
When Jìn Wéngōng returned to the state,
Jièzǐtuī refused to accept reward,
and composed a poem himself:
"There was a dragon flying,
circling all under heaven.
Five snakes followed it,
serving as its aides.
The dragon returned to its home,
gaining its proper place.
Four snakes followed it,
gaining its dew and rain.
One snake was ashamed,
and died dried up in the wilds."
He hung the writing at the duke's gate,
and hid at the mountain's foot.
Wéngōng heard of it and said:
"Alas!
This must be Jièzǐtuī."
He vacated his residence, changed his garments,
and ordered the officers and commoners:
"Whoever can find Jièzǐtuī,
will be ennobled as a high minister,
with a fief of a million acres."
Someone met him in the mountains,
carrying a cauldron and wearing a rain hat,
and asked him:
"May I ask where Jièzǐtuī is?"
He replied:
"If Jièzǐtuī does not wish to be seen but to hide,
how would I alone know?"
Then turned his back and walked away,
never to be seen again for life.
Are not people's hearts
vastly different?
Those of the present age who chase profit,
rise early and retire late,
lips parched and throats dry,
thinking of it day and night,
still cannot obtain it.
Now having obtained it, they urgently flee from it—
Jièzǐtuī was far removed from worldly customs.
In the east there was a scholar named Yuán Jīngmù,
who was about to go on a journey,
but starved on the road.
A robber from Húfǔ named Qiū,
saw him and came down, offering a pot of food to feed him.
Yuán Jīngmù ate three mouthfuls before he could see,
and said:
"Who are you?"
He said:
"I am Qiū, a man of Húfǔ."
Yuán Jīngmù said:
"Alas!
Are you not a robber?
Why do you feed me?
By my principles, I cannot eat your food."
He supported himself with both hands on the ground and vomited it,
but it would not come out,
and he choked, then fell to the ground and died.
When the people of Zhèng descended from Xí,
when Zhuāng Qiāo ravaged Yǐng,
when the people of Qín besieged Chángpíng—
Hán, Jīng, and Zhào—
the generals and nobles of these three states were mostly arrogant,
their soldiers and masses were mostly strong,
yet they violently attacked and killed each other,
the weak bowed and begged to avoid death,
until finally they ate each other in turn,
not distinguishing righteousness,
hoping by luck to stay alive.
If Yuán Jīngmù had eaten and not died,
he would have hated the unrighteousness and refused not to die.
Compared to these who conspired together,
was he not far removed?
12.4 "Chéng Lián"
The fourth says:
A stone may be broken,
but its hardness cannot be taken away;
cinnabar may be ground,
but its redness cannot be taken away.
Hardness and redness
are inherent in their nature.
Nature
is received from Heaven,
not chosen and made so.
The self-respecting among heroic scholars
cannot be defiled with污秽,
just like this.
Long ago, when Zhōu was about to rise,
there were two scholars
living in Gūzhú,
named Bóyí and Shūqí.
The two said to each other:
"We hear in the west there is a regional lord,
who seems to be a man of the Way.
Why then do we remain here?"
The two traveled west to Zhōu,
reaching Qíyáng,
but King Wén had already died.
King Wǔ succeeded to the throne.
Observing Zhōu's virtue,
the king sent Shūdàn to meet Jiāogé at Cìsìnèi,
and made an alliance with him, saying:
"Increase your wealth by three grades,
and appoint you to a high office."
They made three copies of the same text,
smeared with the blood of a sacrifice,
buried one at Cìsìnèi,
and each took one copy.
He also sent Bàozhāogōng to meet Wēizǐ Kāi below Gòngtóu,
and made an alliance with him, saying:
"Be a senior marquis for generations,
preserve the constant sacrifices of Yīn,
oversee the Sānglín sacrifices,
and have Mèngzhū as your private domain."
They made three copies of the same text,
smeared with the blood of a sacrifice,
buried one below Gòngtóu,
and each took one copy.
Bóyí and Shūqí heard of this,
looked at each other and laughed, saying:
"Alas,
how strange!
This is not what we call the Way.
In ancient times, when Shénnóngshì possessed the world,
he sacrificed seasonally with utmost reverence but did not pray for blessings. Towards people,
he was loyal, trustworthy, and governed fully without making demands.
He delighted in correctness and acted correctly,
delighted in order and brought order,
did not use others' ruin to achieve his own success,
nor use others' lowliness to elevate himself.
Now Zhōu sees Yīn's corruption and chaos,
and hastily sets itself up as correct and orderly,
using schemes above and practicing bribery,
relying on hills to preserve its might.
They slaughter victims and swear alliances to show trust,
use Cìsìnèi and Gòngtóu to display their actions,
proclaim dreams to please the masses,
kill and attack to seek profit.
To succeed Yīn in this way
is to replace violence with chaos."
I have heard that the ancient scholars,
when encountering times of order,
did not shirk their responsibilities,
and when encountering times of chaos,
did not seek to merely survive.
Now the world is dark,
and the virtue of Zhōu has declined.
Rather than staying with Zhōu and tarnishing myself,
it is better to withdraw to preserve the purity of my conduct."
The two men traveled north,
and starved at the foot of Shǒuyáng Mountain.
In human nature, there is nothing that is not valued,
and nothing that is not disregarded.
What is valued, one desires to preserve;
what is disregarded is used to nurture what is valued.
Bóyí and Shūqí,
these two scholars,
both abandoned their lives to uphold their principles,
having determined what to value and what to disregard beforehand.
12.5 "Not Being Subjugated"
The fifth says:
The world is lighter than one's own person,
yet scholars offer their persons for others.
Those who offer their persons for others,
are of such importance,
yet people do not understand them.
How then can they be appreciated?
Wise rulers must personally understand scholars,
so scholars exhaust their strength and wisdom,
speak frankly and contend,
without avoiding the hardships,
as Yùràng and Gōngsūn Hóng exemplify.
At that time,
Zhì Bó and Mèngcháng Jūn understood this.
The rulers of the world,
rejoice when gaining a hundred lǐ of land,
and all within the four borders congratulate them;
yet when gaining scholars, they do not rejoice,
nor do they know to congratulate each other,
failing to comprehend the distinction between what is light and what is heavy.
Tāng and Wǔ,
though lords of a thousand chariots,
had scholars all flock to them.
Jié and Zhòu,
though Sons of Heaven,
had scholars all abandon them.
Kǒngzǐ and Mòzǐ,
were scholars of common cloth;
yet lords of ten thousand chariots,
and rulers of a thousand chariots,
could not compete with them for scholars.
From this perspective,
nobility, wealth, and greatness are insufficient to attract scholars;
one must personally understand them before it is possible.
Yùràng's friend said to Yùràng:
"Your actions are quite perplexing.
