You once served the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
and when the feudal lords destroyed them entirely,
you did not seek revenge for them.
Yet when it comes to the Zhì clan,
you insist on seeking revenge for them.
Why is that?"
Yùràng said:
"I will tell you the reason.
The Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
when I was cold, did not clothe me;
when I was hungry, did not feed me;
and often made me share provisions with a thousand others;
they treated me as one of the masses.
Those who treat me as one of the masses,
I also serve as one of the masses.
As for the Zhì clan, it was not so.
When going out, they provided me with a carriage;
when entering, they ensured I had ample provisions;
in the grand court of many people,
they always showed extra courtesy to my place;
they treated me as a scholar of the state.
Those who treat me as a scholar of the state,
I also serve as a scholar of the state."
Yùràng,
a scholar of the state,
still cared about how others treated him,
how much more so would an average person?
When Mèngcháng Jūn was forming an alliance,
Gōngsūn Hóng said to Mèngcháng Jūn:
"You should send someone west to observe the King of Qín.
If the King of Qín is a ruler fit for an emperor,
you may fear you cannot even become his minister,
how could you have leisure to form an alliance to oppose him?
If the King of Qín is an unworthy ruler,
then forming an alliance to oppose him would not be too late."
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"Good.
I wish to ask you to go."
Gōngsūn Hóng respectfully agreed,
and went to Qín with ten carriages.
King Zhāo of Qín heard of this,
and wanted to shame him with words,
to observe Gōngsūn Hóng.
Gōngsūn Hóng met King Zhāo,
and King Zhāo said:
"How large is the territory of Xuē?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"A hundred lǐ."
King Zhāo laughed and said:
"My state,
has territory several thousand lǐ,
yet I still dare not cause trouble.
Now Mèngcháng Jūn's territory is only a hundred lǐ,
and yet he wants to cause trouble for me, is that permissible?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"Mèngcháng Jūn values scholars,
while Your Majesty does not value scholars."
King Zhāo said:
"How does Mèngcháng Jūn value scholars?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"Righteous, not submitting to the Son of Heaven,
not befriending feudal lords,
when successful, not ashamed to be a ruler,
when unsuccessful, unwilling to be a minister;
there are three such men.
Capable of governance, fit to be teachers of Guǎn Zhòng and Shāng Yāng;
persuasive in righteousness, their advice followed;
able to make their lord a hegemon or king;
there are five such men.
If a stern lord of ten thousand chariots
insults his envoy,
the envoy will retreat and commit suicide,
and must stain his clothes with his blood;
there are seven such men as myself."
King Zhāo laughed and apologized, saying:
"Why must you be like this?
I am well-disposed toward Mèngcháng Jūn, and wish you to carefully convey my intentions."
Gōngsūn Hóng said: "Respectfully, I will."
Gōngsūn Hóng can be said to be unsubjugated.
King Zhāo,
is a great king.
Mèngcháng Jūn,
is a lord of a thousand chariots.
To uphold the righteousness of a thousand chariots and not be humiliated,
can be called a true scholar.
12.6 "Preface"
In the eighth year of Qín,
the year being Tūn Tān,
in autumn,
on the first day of the month, Jiǎzǐ,
on that day,
a good man inquired about the "Twelve Annals."
Wénxìn Hóu said:
"I once learned how Huángdì instructed Zhuānxū:
'There is the great circle above,
the great square below;
if you can emulate them,
you will be a parent to the people.'
I have heard that in the clear ages of antiquity,
they modeled themselves on heaven and earth.
All the 'Twelve Annals'
record order and chaos, survival and destruction,
and allow one to know longevity, premature death, fortune, and misfortune.
Measure it against heaven above,
verify it against earth below,
examine it among people in between;
if so, then right and wrong, permissible and impermissible, will have nowhere to hide.
Heaven is called compliance,
compliance maintains life;
earth is called stability,
stability maintains peace;
man is called trustworthiness,
trustworthiness maintains obedience.
When these three are all in place,
action follows without effort.
Action
is acting according to principle.
Follow its patterns,
adhere to its principles,
and pacify selfishness.
For selfish seeing blinds the eyes,
selfish hearing deafens the ears,
selfish thinking deranges the heart.
If these three are all selfishly set, then wisdom has no way to be impartial.
If wisdom is not impartial,
then fortune daily declines,
and calamity daily grows,
as can be known by watching the sun decline westward."
Zhào Xiāngzǐ was traveling in his park,
and came to a bridge.
The horse retreated and refused to advance.
Qīng Píng was his carriage attendant.
Xiāngzǐ said:
"Go forward and look under the bridge;
it seems there is someone there."
Qīng Pīng approached to look under the bridge.
Yù Ràng was lying there,
pretending to be a dead man.
He shouted at Qīng Pīng:
"Go away!
I, an elder, have matters to attend to."
Qīng Pīng said:
"Since youth, I have been your friend.
You are about to undertake a great deed,
and if I speak of it,
I would violate the way of friendship.
Yet you intend to harm my lord,
and if I do not speak of it,
I would violate the duty of a subject.
For one like me, only death is acceptable."
He then withdrew and took his own life.
Qīng Pīng did not delight in death;
he valued upholding the integrity of a subject
and abhorred abandoning the principles of friendship.
Qīng Pīng and Yù Ràng may be called true friends.
13.1 "The Beginning"
One says: Heaven and earth have a beginning.
Heaven is subtle and thus forms,
earth is solid and thus takes shape.
The harmony of heaven and earth
is the great principle of life.
It is known through cold and heat, sun and moon, day and night;
it is explained through different forms, different capacities, and different aptitudes.
Things combine to form and separate to generate.
Understanding combination and formation,
understanding separation and generation,
then heaven and earth are in balance.
Balance means
that one must examine their nature and situate their forms.
Heaven has nine fields,
earth has nine provinces,
the land has nine mountains,
the mountains have nine passes,
the marshes have nine great lakes,
the winds have eight grades,
the waters have six great rivers.
What are the nine fields?
The center is called Jūntiān,
its stars are Jiǎo, Kàng, and Dī.
The east is called Cāngtiān,
its stars are Fáng, Xīn, and Wěi.
The northeast is called Biàntiān,
its stars are Jī, Dǒu, and Qiānniú.
The north is called Xuántiān,
its stars are Wùnǚ, Xū, Wēi, and Yíngshì.
The northwest is called Yōutiān,
its stars are Dōngbì, Kuí, and Lóu.
The west is called Hàotiān,
its stars are Wèi, Mǎo, and Bì.
The southwest is called Zhūtiān,
its stars are Zīxī, Shēn, and Dōngjǐng.
The south is called Yántiān,
its stars are Yúguǐ, Liǔ, and Qīxīng.
The southeast is called Yángtiān,
its stars are Zhāng, Yì, and Zhěn.
What are the nine provinces?
Between the Hé and Hàn rivers is Yùzhōu,
the land of Zhōu.
Between the two Hé rivers is Jìzhōu,
the land of Jìn.
Between the Hé and Jǐ rivers is Yǎnzhōu,
the land of Wèi.
The east is Qīngzhōu,
the land of Qí.
Above the Sì river is Xúzhōu,
the land of Lǔ.
The southeast is Yángzhōu,
the land of Yuè.
The south is Jīngzhōu,
the land of Chǔ.
The west is Yōngzhōu,
the land of Qín.
The north is Yōuzhōu,
the land of Yān.
What are the nine mountains?
Kuàijī,
Tàishān,
Wángwū,
Shǒushān,
Tàihuà,
Qíshān,
Tàiháng,
Yángcháng,
Mèngmén.
What are the nine passes?
Dàfén,
Míng'è,
Jīngruǎn,
Fāngchéng,
Xiáo,
Jǐngxíng,
Cīchù Lìngcī,
Gōuzhù,
Jūyōng.
What are the nine great lakes?
Wú's Jùqū,
Chǔ's Yúnmèng,
Qín's Yánghuá,
Jìn's Dàlù,
Liáng Zhèng's Pútián,
Sòng's Mèngzhū,
Qí's Hǎiyú,
Zhào's Jùlù,
Yān's Dàzhāo Zhāoyú.
What are the eight winds?
Northeast is called Yánfēng,
east is called Tāofēng,
southeast is called Xūnfēng,
south is called Jùfēng,
southwest is called Qīfēng,
west is called Liáofēng,
northwest is called Lìfēng,
north is called Hánfēng.
What are the six great rivers?
Héshuǐ,
Chìshuǐ,
Liáoshuǐ,
Hēishuǐ,
Jiāngshuǐ,
Huáishuǐ.
Within the four seas,
east to west measures twenty-eight thousand lǐ,
north to south measures twenty-six thousand lǐ,
waterways measure eight thousand lǐ,
and the area receiving water also measures eight thousand lǐ.
There are six major valleys,
six hundred famous rivers,
three thousand land channels,
and tens of thousands of small streams.
Within the four extremes,
east to west measures five hundred million nine thousand seven hundred lǐ,
north to south also measures five hundred million nine thousand seven hundred lǐ.
The multitude of stars travels with heaven,
yet the celestial pivot, the polar star, does not move.
At the winter solstice, the sun travels the distant path,
circling the four extremes,
named Xuánmíng.
At the summer solstice, the sun travels the near path,
and ascends to a higher position.
Beneath the pivot, there is no day or night.
South of the Báimín,
beneath the Jiànmù tree,
at midday there is no shadow,
and shouts produce no echo—
this is the center of heaven and earth.
Heaven, earth, and the myriad things
are like a single person's body;
this is called the great unity.
The multitude of ears, eyes, noses, and mouths,
the multitude of grains, cold and heat—
this is called the multitude of differences.
Thus, the myriad things are complete.
Heaven pours forth the myriad things,
and the sage observes them,
to contemplate their categories.
The explanation lies in why heaven and earth take form,
why thunder and lightning arise,
the essence of yīn and yáng and material things,
and why people, birds, and beasts dwell in peace.
13.2 "Corresponding Categories"
Two says: Whenever an emperor or king is about to rise,
heaven must first show an auspicious sign to the people below.
In the time of Huángdì,
heaven first showed large earthworms and large mole crickets.
Huángdì said, "The earth's energy prevails."
The earth's energy prevailed,
so his color honored yellow,
and his affairs followed earth.
In the time of Yǔ,
Heaven first manifested that plants and trees did not wither in autumn and winter.
Yǔ said, “The Wood element prevails.”
Since the Wood element prevailed,
its favored color was green,
and its affairs corresponded to Wood.
In the time of Tāng,
Heaven first manifested metal blades born from water.
Tāng said, “The Metal element prevails.”
Since the Metal element prevailed,
its favored color was white,
and its affairs corresponded to Metal.
In the time of King Wén,
Heaven first manifested fire: red birds carrying cinnabar writings gathered at the Zhōu altar.
King Wén said, “The Fire element prevails.”
Since the Fire element prevailed,
its favored color was red,
and its affairs corresponded to Fire.
What will succeed Fire is inevitably Water.
Heaven will first manifest that the Water element prevails.
Since the Water element prevails,
its favored color will be black,
and its affairs will correspond to Water.
When the Water element arrives, if one does not understand the cycle is complete,
it will shift to Earth.
Heaven acts in its seasons,
yet does not assist the farmers below.
Things of the same kind inherently summon each other;
when their vital energies are the same, they unite;
when sounds match, they resonate.
Thus, when the gong note is struck, other gong notes respond;
when the jué note is struck, other jué notes respond.
Pour water on level ground,
and it flows to the damp areas.
Spread fire among evenly placed firewood,
and it catches where it is driest.
Mountain clouds resemble grass and thickets;
water clouds resemble horned fish scales;
drought clouds resemble smoke and fire;
rain clouds resemble water ripples.
All things manifest their origins to show people.
Thus, dragons are used to summon rain;
forms are used to pursue shadows.
Where armies are stationed,
thorns and brambles are sure to grow.
As for the origins of fortune and misfortune,
the masses consider them fate,
but how can they know their true source?
If nests are overturned and eggs destroyed,
then the phoenix will not come.
If animals are disemboweled and their fetuses eaten,
then the qílín will not come.
If marshes are drained and fish exhausted,
then the turtle and dragon will not dwell there.
Things that follow the same principle
are too numerous to record.
A son does not conceal from his father;
a minister does not conceal from his ruler.
When in accord, they come;
when at odds, they depart.
Thus, though the ruler is honored,
if he calls white black,
the minister cannot obey.
Though the father is dear,
if he calls black white,
the son cannot follow.
Huángdì said:
“Vast and obscure,
relying on Heaven’s majesty,
I share the same vital energy as the origin.”
Thus it is said: sharing the same vital energy is superior to sharing the same righteousness;
sharing the same righteousness is superior to sharing the same strength;
sharing the same strength is superior to sharing the same dwelling;
sharing the same dwelling is superior to sharing the same name.
Emperors share the same vital energy;
Kings share the same righteousness;
Hegemons share the same strength;
those who toil share the same dwelling, which is shallow;
those who perish share the same name, which is coarse.
The coarser one’s wisdom,
the coarser what they share;
the more refined one’s wisdom,
the more refined what they share.
Therefore, in all matters of intention, one must be refined.
Refinement
is how the Five Emperors and Three Kings succeeded.
When things are perfected, aligned, and of the same kind, they all find harmony.
Thus, when Yáo did good, all good came to him;
when Jié did wrong, all wrong came to him.
The “Shāng Zhēn” says:
“Heaven sends down calamities and spreads auspicious signs,
each having its proper role,”
meaning that fortune and misfortune are summoned by people themselves.
Thus, when a state is in disorder, it is not merely disorderly;
it is sure to attract invaders.
Disorder alone does not necessarily lead to ruin,
but attracting invaders leaves no means of survival.
In all uses of military force,
it is used for advantage,
and used for righteousness.
Attacking a disordered state makes it yield easily;
when it yields easily, the attacker gains advantage.
Attacking a disordered state is righteous;
when it is righteous, the attacker gains honor.
With both honor and advantage,
even a mediocre ruler would do it,
let alone a worthy ruler.
Thus, ceding territory and offering precious vessels,
using humble words and submitting,
are insufficient to stop an attack;
only good governance is sufficient.
With good governance, those seeking advantage will not attack,
and those seeking fame will not invade.
When people attack or invade,
it is either for advantage or firmly for fame.
If neither fame nor gain is attainable,
even if a state is strong and large,
why would anyone attack it?
The explanation lies in Shǐ Mò’s arrival causing cessation of the attack on Wèi;
Jiǎnzǐ of Zhào can be said to have understood action and stillness.
13.3 “Dispelling Prejudice”
Third Discourse:
Those who listen in this world
often have prejudices.
Having prejudices means their listening is inevitably perverse.
The causes of prejudice are many,
but the essence lies in what people like
and what people dislike.
One looking east cannot see the western wall;
one gazing south cannot see the north—
the mind is fixed on one place.
A man who lost his axe
suspected his neighbor’s son.
He saw the boy’s walking as stealing the axe,
his expression as stealing the axe,
his speech as stealing the axe—
every movement and manner seemed that of a thief.
Later, digging in a valley, he found his axe.
Another day, seeing his neighbor’s son again,
none of his movements or manner resembled a thief.
The neighbor’s son had not changed;
he himself had changed.
This change had no other cause
than his prejudice.
In Zhū’s old method,
armor skirts were made of silk.
Gōngxī Jì said to the ruler of Zhū:
“It would be better to use woven cords.
What makes armor secure
is that the holes are filled.
Now the holes are filled,
but only half the strength is utilized.
With cords it is not so;
when the holes are filled, all strength is utilized.”
The ruler of Zhū thought this right
and said:
“How shall we obtain the cords?”
Gōngxī Jì replied:
“If those above use them, the people will make them.”
The ruler of Zhū said:
“Good.”
He gave the order
that officials must use cords for armor.
Gōngxī Jì, knowing his advice was adopted,
had his whole household make cords.
Someone slandered him, saying:
“The reason Gōngxī Jì wants cords used
is that his household makes many cords.”
The ruler of Zhū was displeased
and thereupon ordered again
that officials must not use cords for armor.
This was the ruler of Zhū’s prejudice.
If using cords for armor is beneficial,
even if Gōngxī Jì makes many cords,
what harm is there?
If using cords is not beneficial,
even if Gōngxī Jì makes none,
what good is it?
Making cords or not
should not affect the evaluation of Gōngxī Jì’s advice.
The intention behind using cords
must be examined.
In Lǔ there was an ugly man.
His father went out and saw Shāng Duō,
then returned and told his neighbor:
“Shāng Duō is not as good as my son.”
Now his son was extremely ugly,
and Shāng Duō was extremely handsome.
That he considered the extremely handsome inferior to the extremely ugly
was due to the prejudice of love.
Thus, to know the ugliness in beauty,
and the beauty in ugliness,
only then can one truly know beauty and ugliness.
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"One who gambles with tiles is at ease;
one who gambles with belt hooks is anxious;
one who gambles with gold is fearful.
The skill is the same,
yet one becomes fearful
because he attaches importance to external things.
When one attaches importance to external things,
his inner self becomes shallow."
The people of Lǔ can be said to have attached importance to external things.
The explanation lies in the Qí man's desire to obtain gold,
and the mutual jealousy among the Mò practitioners of Qín,
both of which had their particular faults.
Lǎodān, however, understood this.
If one stands alone like a planted tree,
he will certainly not conform to the vulgar,
so how could he be broadened?
13.4 "Hearing Words"
The fourth says: Whenever hearing words, one must examine them.
If one does not examine them, then good and bad will not be distinguished.
If good and bad are not distinguished,
there is no greater disorder.
The Three Dynasties distinguished good from bad,
hence they ruled.
Now the world declines ever more,
and the Way of the sage kings is abandoned and cut off.
Most rulers of the age amplify their pleasures,
enlarge their bells and drums,
and extravagantly build their terraces, pavilions, parks, and enclosures,
thereby seizing people's wealth;
they lightly send people to their deaths
to vent their anger;
the old and weak freeze and starve,
the young and strong die prematurely and become emaciated,
utterly exhausted and destitute,
and are further subjected to death or captivity;
they attack guiltless states to demand land,
and execute innocent people to seek profit;
yet they desire the ancestral temples to be secure and the altars of soil and grain to be free from danger—
is this not difficult?
Now if someone says:
"That family has many goods,
their house walls are damp,
the guard dog is dead,
the situation allows tunneling in,"
then he will certainly be condemned.
But if one says:
"A certain state is suffering famine,
its city walls are low,
its guards and equipment are few,
it can be attacked and seized,"
then he is not condemned—
this is to not understand analogy.
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
"The past cannot be reached,
the future cannot be awaited;
one who makes his age wise and enlightened
is called the Son of Heaven."
Therefore, in the present age,
if there is one who can distinguish good from bad,
his becoming king would not be difficult.
Good and bad are rooted in righteousness,
not in personal affection.
Affection and benefit as a Way are great indeed.
Those who drift on the sea,
after traveling for ten days or a month,
are delighted to see something resembling a human.
And after a full year,
they are delighted to see something they once saw in the Central States.
The longer one is away from people,
the deeper one misses them!
The people of a disordered age
have also been long separated from the sage kings.
Their wish to see them
knows no pause day or night.
Therefore, worthy kings and outstanding scholars who wish to care for the black-haired people
must not neglect this.
Achievement precedes reputation,
action precedes achievement,
words precede action.
If one does not understand affairs, how can he hear words?
If one does not understand circumstances, how can he assess words?
When one speaks empty words to others,
is there a distinction?
Or is there no distinction?
Zàofǔ first learned from Dàdòu,
Péngmén first learned from Gānyíng.
Driving from Dàdòu,
archery from Gānyíng,
they did not change what others considered their nature.
Not changing it
is how they could travel far and pursue swiftly,
how they could eliminate harm and prohibit violence.
All people must also have something to train their minds,
then they can listen and understand.
If they do not train their minds,
they train through study and inquiry.
One who does not study yet can listen and understand—
such a person has never existed in past or present.
The explanation lies in Báiguī's criticism of Huìzǐ,
Gōngsūn Lóng's persuading Yānzhāowáng to cease warfare and his response at the empty Luò meeting,
Kǒng Chuān's disputing Gōngsūn Lóng,
and Dí Jiǎn's challenging Huìzǐ's methods.
The arguments of these four scholars
all have many reasons,
and must be distinctly examined.
13.5 "Attentive Listening"
The fifth says:
In the past, Yǔ would catch up his hair three times while bathing once,
and rise three times during one meal,
to show courtesy to men of the Way,
thereby understanding his own shortcomings.
Understanding his own shortcomings,
he then did not contend with things.
He waited with ease and calm,
letting them express themselves naturally;
he followed their nature,
letting them speak for themselves.
The rulers of perished states did the opposite:
they considered themselves worthy and looked down on others.
Looking down on others, the persuaders would maintain appearances without reaching the essence,
and the listeners, self-satisfied, would gain nothing.
Even possessing all under heaven, what benefit was there?
This is making darkness bright,
disorder orderly,
defeat success,
danger peace.
Thus Yīn and Zhōu perished,
Bǐgān died,
all perverse and insufficient to mention.
Therefore, the nature of a ruler
errs not in what he doubts,
but in what he does not doubt;
errs not in what he does not know,
but in what he thinks he knows.
Thus, even if he does not doubt,
even if he already knows,
he must examine it by law,
measure it by standards,
verify it by numbers.
If so, then right and wrong will not be mistaken,
and actions will not err.
How did Yáo obtain worthies under heaven and test Shùn?
How did Shùn obtain worthies under heaven and test Yǔ?
They judged by ear alone.
That the ear can judge
returns to the true nature of life.
Now the confused
not only do not know to return to the true nature of life,
they further do not know to observe how the Five Emperors and Three Kings succeeded.
Then how can they know their age is not viable?
How can they know they themselves fall short?
The highest knows,
the next knows that he does not know.
If one does not know, he asks;
if he cannot, he learns.
The "Zhōu Zhēn" says:
"If one reflects on this,
it is not too late to learn virtue."
Learning from worthies and inquiring—
this is why the Three Dynasties flourished.
Not knowing yet considering oneself knowing—
this is the source of all misfortunes.
Reputation does not stand without cause,
achievement does not accomplish itself,
a state does not exist in vain—
there must be worthies.
The Way of worthies
is profound and hard to know,
subtle and hard to see.
Therefore, seeing a worthy without awe means not being inwardly alarmed,
not being inwardly alarmed means not knowing deeply.
Not deeply understanding what the worthy says—
there is no greater inauspiciousness.
If the ruler is worthy and the age orderly, then worthies are in high position;
if the ruler is unworthy and the age disordered, then worthies are in low position.
Now that the Zhōu house is already destroyed,
and the Son of Heaven is already cut off,
there is no greater disorder than having no Son of Heaven.
Without a Son of Heaven, the strong overcome the weak,
the many oppress the few,
they harm each other with weapons,
with no rest—
the present age is exactly this.
Therefore, in the present age,
to seek men of the Way,
one must search within the four seas, in the mountains and valleys, in remote and secluded places;
only then might one be fortunate enough to find them.
Once they are obtained, what desire cannot be fulfilled?
What undertaking cannot be accomplished?
Tàigōng fished at Zīquán,
encountering the era of Zhòu,
thus King Wén obtained him and became king.
King Wén
was a lord of a thousand chariots;
Zhòu
was the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven lost him, while the lord of a thousand chariots gained him—
this was a matter of knowing and not knowing.
As for the common masses,
they can be employed without waiting for understanding,
and commanded without waiting for courtesy.
But as for men of the Way,
they must be treated with courtesy and understanding,
and only then can their wisdom and abilities be fully utilized.
The explanation lies in Shèng Shū’s persuasion of Zhōu Gōng,
which can be said to be capable of listening;
Duke Huán of Qí’s meeting with Xiǎochén Jì,
and Marquis Wén of Wèi’s meeting with Tián Zǐfāng,
can all be said to be capable of treating scholars with courtesy.
13.6 "Devotion to Fundamentals"
The sixth says:
Let us examine the records of antiquity:
the ministers of the Three Kings
all enjoyed illustrious reputations,
and their realities were all secure—
this was because their achievements were great.
The Book of Songs says:
"Dark clouds gather densely,
rising thick and heavy;
rain falls on our public fields,
and then reaches our private lands."
The ministers of the Three Kings
were all able to extend the public to benefit the private.
The ministers of mediocre rulers
desire fame and reality just like the ministers of the Three Kings,
yet their reputations are all disgraced,
and their realities are all endangered—
this is because they lack public achievements.
They all worry that they themselves are not honored in the state,
but do not worry that their lord is not honored in the world;
they all worry that their families are not wealthy,
but do not worry that their state is not great.
This is why they seek honor but end up more disgraced,
seek security but end up more endangered.
The root of security, danger, honor, and disgrace lies with the lord;
the root of the lord lies in the ancestral temple;
the root of the ancestral temple lies in the people;
the order or chaos of the people lies with the officials.
The Book of Changes says:
"Returning to the proper path,
what fault is there?
Auspicious."
This means that if the root is not different, then actions will ultimately bring joy.
Now, holding office leads to neglect and disorder,
facing wealth leads to greed and acquisition,
being close to the ruler leads to flattery and sycophancy,
leading troops leads to exhaustion and cowardice.
To place high hopes on the lord with such conduct—
is this not difficult?
Suppose there is a person here
who finds self-cultivation and careful accounting shameful,
and when facing material wealth, takes everything for himself.
If such a person becomes wealthy,
if not through theft, then there is no other way.
Thus, honor and wealth do not come of themselves;
they arise from achievements and merit.
Now, if achievements are very slight but expectations are high,
this is deception;
if there are no achievements yet one seeks honor and wealth,
this is fraud.
The ways of fraud and deception
are not followed by the noble person.
People often argue:
"If the ruler employs me, the state will surely have no troubles."
But employing oneself may not necessarily be so;
and nothing compares to being virtuous oneself.
If even oneself still has troubles,
employing oneself in the state—
how can it be without troubles?
Oneself
is what one can control.
To abandon what one can control
and seize what one cannot control—
this is perverse.
One may not yet be able to govern the state or manage officials,
but as for serving parents at home,
and making friends abroad,
these can certainly be achieved.
If serving parents is not yet filial,
and making friends is not yet sincere,
these are what one has not yet attained.
How can one excel in them?
Thus, in evaluating others, do not judge by what they have not yet attained,
but employ what they have already attained;
then one can know what they have not yet attained.
In ancient times, those who served their lord
first demonstrated their abilities before taking office,
and first examined their feelings before accepting.
Even if the lord gave excessively,
the ministers did not take without reason.
The Greater Odes says:
"God is watching over you;
do not waver in your heart."
This speaks of the conduct of loyal ministers.
The explanation lies in Lord Zhèng’s inquiry into Bèi Zhān’s righteousness,
and Bó Yí’s response to Lord Sì of Wèi about not imposing heavy taxes.
These two gentlemen both came close to understanding the fundamentals.
13.7 "On Greatness"
The seventh says:
In the past, Shùn wanted to unify past and present but did not succeed,
yet it was enough to establish his rule.
Yǔ wanted to become emperor but did not succeed,
yet it was enough to correct diverse customs.
Tāng wanted to succeed Yǔ but did not succeed,
yet it was enough to subdue the four wilds.
King Wǔ wanted to equal Tāng but did not succeed,
yet it was enough to make the kingly way prevail.
The Five Hegemons wanted to succeed the Three Kings but did not succeed,
yet it was enough to become leaders among the feudal lords.
Kǒng Qiū and Mò Dí wanted to practice the great way in the world but did not succeed,
yet it was enough to achieve illustrious fame.
Thus, even if the great righteousness is not fully achieved,
there is still achievement in what is accomplished.
The Book of Xià says:
"The virtue of the Son of Heaven is vast and far-reaching,
both sage and divine,
both martial and civil."
Thus, effort lies in affairs,
and affairs lie in greatness.
If the land is vast, there will be Chángxiáng, Bùtíng, Qímǔ, Qúndǐ, Tiāndí, and Bùzhōu;
if the mountains are great, there will be tigers, leopards, bears, and vipers;
if the waters are great, there will be flood dragons, giant turtles, alligators, sturgeons, and yellow fish.
The Book of Shāng says:
"In a temple of five generations,
one can observe strange things;
in a leader of ten thousand men,
one can give rise to schemes."
If a room is empty, there will be no ponds;
if a well is small, there will be no large fish;
if a forest is new, there will be no tall trees.
Generally, for the success of any endeavor,
it must be broad, vast, numerous, and enduring—
this is certain.
Jìzǐ said:
"Swallows and sparrows contend for a good spot under the same roof,
mother and chicks feed each other,
happily enjoying themselves together,
thinking themselves secure.
If the chimney cracks,
and flames rise to burn the beams,
the swallows and sparrows show no change in expression.
Why is this?
It is because they do not know disaster is about to befall them.
Is this not foolish?
Few are the ministers who avoid the wisdom of swallows and sparrows.
As for those who serve as ministers,
advancing their ranks, emoluments, and wealth,
fathers, sons, brothers colluding together within a state,
happily enjoying themselves,
yet endangering their altars of soil and grain—
their chimney is near,
yet they never realize it.
Their wisdom is no different from that of swallows and sparrows.
Thus it is said:
'When the world is in great chaos,
no state is secure;
when a state is in complete chaos,
no family is secure;
when a family is in total chaos,
no person is secure.'
This refers to this.
Thus, the stability of the small must rely on the great,
and the security of the great must rely on the small.
Small and great, noble and humble,
mutually rely on each other,
and only then can all find joy."
The stability of the humble and small lies in the noble and great.
The explanation lies in Bó Yí persuading Lord Sì of Wèi with the art of kingship,
Dù Hè persuading Lord Zhāowén of Zhōu to pacify the world,
and Kuāng Zhāng challenging Huìzǐ about making the King of Qí a true king.
14.1 "Filial Conduct"
The first says:
In governing the world and administering the state,
one must attend to the root before dealing with the branches.
What is called the root
does not refer to plowing, weeding, planting, or cultivating;
it means attending to the people.
Attending to the people
does not mean making the poor rich
or the few numerous;
it means attending to the root.
In attending to the root, nothing is more important than filial piety.
If the ruler is filial,
then his name will be illustrious and glorious,
his subjects will obey and listen,
and the world will praise him.
If ministers are filial,
then they will serve their ruler loyally,
hold office with integrity,
and face death in times of peril.
If scholars and common people are filial,
then they will plow and weed diligently,
defend and fight steadfastly,
and will not retreat in defeat.
Filial piety
is the root task of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors
and the guiding principle of all affairs.
To hold one method and have all goodness arrive, all evil depart, and the world follow—
this is only filial piety.
Therefore, in evaluating people, one must start with those who are close and then extend to those who are distant,
must start with those who are important and then extend to those who are insignificant.
If there is a person here
who behaves toward the close and important
and does not neglect the insignificant and distant,
then this is being sincere and careful in the way of filial piety,
which is how the former kings governed the world.
Therefore, loving one’s parents,
one dare not hate others;
respecting one’s parents,
one dare not slight others.
When love and respect are fully expressed in serving one’s parents,
their radiance extends to the common people,
reaching to the four seas.
This is the filial piety of the Son of Heaven.
Zēngzǐ said:
"The body
is the legacy of one’s parents.
In using the legacy of one’s parents,
how dare one not be respectful?
If one’s dwelling and conduct are not dignified,
it is not filial.
If serving one’s ruler is not loyal,
it is not filial.
If holding office is not respectful,
it is not filial.
If friendship is not sincere,
it is not filial.
If in battle formations one is not brave,
it is not filial.
If these five conducts are not fulfilled,
disaster will reach one’s parents.
How dare one not be respectful?"
The Shāngshū says:
"Of the three hundred punishments,
none is heavier than that for unfiliality."
Zēngzǐ said:
"There are five things by which the former kings governed the world:
honoring virtue,
honoring the noble,
honoring the aged,
respecting elders,
and being kind to the young.
These five
are how the former kings stabilized the world.
Honoring virtue
is because it is close to sagehood.
Honoring the noble
is because they are close to the ruler.
Honoring the aged
is because they are close to one’s parents.
Respecting elders
is because they are close to elder brothers.
Being kind to the young
is because they are close to younger brothers."
Zēngzǐ said:
"What parents give life to,
the child dare not destroy.
What parents establish,
the child dare not abolish.
What parents make whole,
the child dare not impair.
Therefore, using a boat instead of swimming,
taking the main road instead of shortcuts,
being able to keep the limbs whole
to preserve the ancestral temple—
this can be called filial."
There are five ways of nurturing:
building palaces and rooms,
making beds and mats comfortable,
moderating food and drink—
this is the way to nurture the body.
Displaying the five colors,
applying the five hues,
arranging patterns and designs—
this is the way to nurture the eyes.
Correcting the six pitch-standards,
harmonizing the five notes,
blending the eight sounds—
this is the way to nurture the ears.
Cooking the five grains,
preparing the six domestic animals,
harmonizing flavors through frying and seasoning—
this is the way to nurture the mouth.
Harmonizing one’s expression,
pleasing one’s speech,
being respectful in advancing and retreating—
this is the way to nurture the will.
These five
are used in succession and in order;
this can be called good nurturing.
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn descended the hall and injured his foot.
After it healed, for several months he did not go out,
and still had a worried expression.
His disciples asked him:
"Master, you descended the hall and injured your foot.
After it healed, for several months you have not gone out,
and still have a worried expression.
May we ask the reason?"
Yuèzhèng Zǐchūn said:
"Excellent that you ask this.
I heard it from Zēngzǐ,
and Zēngzǐ heard it from Zhòngní:
Parents give birth to one whole,
and the child should return whole.
Not damaging one’s body,
not impairing one’s form—
this can be called filial.
A gentleman does not take half a step and forget this.
I forgot the way of filial piety,
therefore I am worried."
Thus it is said:
The body is not one’s private possession;
it is the legacy of one’s strict parents.
The fundamental teaching for the people is called filial piety;
the practice of filial piety is called nurturing.
Nurturing is possible,
but respect is difficult.
Respect is possible,
but ease is difficult.
Ease is possible,
but completion is difficult.
After parents have passed away,
to conduct oneself respectfully,
leaving no bad name for one’s parents—
this can be called able to bring it to an end.
Ritual is to tread this path;
righteousness is to accord with this;
trustworthiness is to be faithful to this;
strength is to be strong in this.
Music arises from following this;
punishments arise from opposing this.
14.2 The Original Flavor
The second says:
Seek it at the root,
and within ten days you will surely obtain it;
seek it at the branches,
and you will labor without success.
The establishment of merit and fame
depends on grasping the root of affairs,
on obtaining the transformation of worthies.
If not for worthies, who would understand the transformation of affairs?
Therefore it is said: The root lies in obtaining worthies.
A woman of the Yǒushēn clan was picking mulberry leaves
and found an infant in a hollow mulberry tree.
She presented it to her ruler.
The ruler ordered a cook to raise him.
Examining the reason for this,
it is said:
"His mother lived by the Yī River.
When she was pregnant,
she dreamed that a spirit told her:
'When the mortar emits water, go east.
Do not look back.'
The next day,
she saw the mortar emitting water.
She told her neighbors,
went east for ten lǐ,
and looked back to see her village completely submerged in water.
Her body then transformed into a hollow mulberry tree."
Therefore he was named Yī Yǐn.
This is the story of how Yǐ Yǐn was born in a hollow mulberry tree. He grew up to be virtuous.
Tāng heard of Yǐ Yǐn,
and sent someone to request him from the Yǒushēn clan.
The Yǒushēn clan refused.
Yǐ Yǐn also wished to join Tāng.
Tāng then asked to take a wife in marriage.
The Yǒushēn clan was pleased,
and sent Yǐ Yǐn as an attendant to accompany the bride.
Thus, when a worthy ruler seeks a man of the Way,
there is nothing he will not do; when a man of the Way seeks a worthy ruler,
there is no path he will not take;
only when they find each other do they find joy.
They become close without scheming,
trust each other without pacts,
exhaust their wisdom and strength for one another,
brave dangers and endure hardships,
and delight in doing so—
this is how great achievements and fame are fully accomplished.
Certainly, it is not only
when a scholar is isolated and self-reliant,
or when a ruler is assertive and fond of acting alone,
that his name and reputation will surely fade and extinguish,
and his altars of soil and grain will surely be endangered.
Thus, Huángdì established four sides to seek advice,
and Yáo and Shùn obtained Bóyáng and Xù'ěr before they succeeded.
In general, the virtue of a worthy man can be known through such means.
Bóyá played the qin,
and Zhōng Zǐqī listened to him.
Just as he was playing and his mind was on Tàishān,
Zhōng Zǐqī said:
"How splendid is your qin playing,
as lofty as Tàishān."
A short while later,
when his mind was on flowing water,
Zhōng Zǐqī again said:
"How splendid is your qin playing,
as vast as flowing water."
When Zhōng Zǐqī died,
Bóyá broke his qin and severed its strings,
and never played the qin again for the rest of his life,
believing there was no one in the world worth playing for again.
Not only the qin is like this;
worthy men are also so.
Even if there is a worthy man,
but he is not treated with propriety,
how can the worthy give his full loyalty?
It is like a poor driver—
a fine steed will not run a thousand li on its own.
When Tāng obtained Yǐ Yǐn,
he purified him at the ancestral temple,
fumigated him with reeds,
lit a torch fire,
and smeared him with the blood of a sacrificial pig.
The next day,
he held court and met him.
Yǐ Yǐn spoke to Tāng about the ultimate flavors,
and Tāng said:
"Can these be prepared?"
He replied:
"Your state is small,
and cannot supply them;
only after becoming the Son of Heaven can they be supplied.
Now, the creatures of the three groups:
those dwelling in water are fishy,
those preying on flesh are rank,
those eating grass are gamy.
But even foul odors can be made delicious,
each having its method.
The foundation of all flavors
begins with water.
The five flavors and three materials,
through nine boilings and nine transformations,
are governed by fire.
Sometimes swift, sometimes slow,
eliminating fishiness, removing rankness, and dispelling gaminess—
each must be overcome by its proper means,
without losing their principles.
In the art of harmonizing,
one must use sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, and salty,
in sequence and quantity,
their proportions extremely subtle,
each with its own origin.
The transformations within the cauldron
are exquisite, delicate, and fine,
beyond what words can describe,
beyond what the mind can comprehend.
It is like the subtleties of archery and charioteering,
the transformations of yīn and yáng,
the measures of the four seasons.
Thus, enduring without spoiling,
cooked without becoming mushy,
sweet without being cloying,
sour without being sharp,
salty without being overpowering,
pungent without being harsh,
mild without being bland,
rich without being greasy.
The finest meats:
the lips of the xīngxing,
the roasted huānhuān,
the crest of the xuānyàn,
the wrist of the shùdàng,
the tender parts of the yak and elephant.
West of Liúshā,
south of Dānshān,
there are the eggs of the phoenix,
eaten by the people of Wò.
The finest fish:
the zhuān of Dòngtíng,
the ér of the Eastern Sea.
The fish of Lǐshuǐ,
named the Zhūbiē,
with six legs,
and pearls of a hundred greens.
The fish of Guànshuǐ,
named the Yáo,
shaped like a carp but with wings,
often flying from the Western Sea at night,
to swim in the Eastern Sea.
The finest vegetables:
the píng of Kūnlún,
the blossoms of the Shòumù.
East of Zhǐgū,
in the land of Zhōngróng,
there are leaves of the red tree and the dark tree.
South of Yúmào,
on the cliffs of the southern extreme,
there is a vegetable,
named the Jiāshù,
its color like jade.
The yún of Yánghuá.
The celery of Yúnmèng.
The jīng of Jùqū.
The grass of Jìnyuān,
named Tǔyīng.
The finest seasonings:
the ginger of Yángpǔ,
the cinnamon of Zhāoyáo,
the bamboo shoots of Yuèluò,
the fermented sauce of zhān and wěi fish,
the salt of Dàxià,
the dew of Zǎijiē,
its color like jade,
the eggs of Chángzé.
The finest grains:
the grain of Xuánshān,
the millet of Bùzhōu,
the jì of Yángshān,
the black millet of the Southern Sea.
The finest waters:
the dew of Sānwēi;
the well of Kūnlún;
the hill of Jùjiāng,
named Yáoshuǐ;
the waters of Yuēshān;
the mountain of Gāoquán,
on which there is a gushing spring;
the plains of Jìzhōu.
The finest fruits:
the fruit of the shātáng;
north of Chángshān,
above the cast abyss,
there are a hundred fruits,
eaten by the multitude of emperors;
east of Jīshān,
where the green birds dwell,
there is the sweet orange;
the oranges of Jiāngpǔ;
the pomelos of Yúnmèng.
The stone ears of Hànshàng.
These are the means to obtain them.
The finest horses:
the steeds of Qīnglóng,
the mounts of Yífēng.
Unless one first becomes the Son of Heaven,
one cannot obtain and possess them.
One cannot force becoming the Son of Heaven;
one must first understand the Way.
The Way lies in stopping with others and residing in oneself.
When oneself is perfected, the Son of Heaven is perfected;
when the Son of Heaven is perfected, the ultimate flavors are possessed.
Thus, examining the near is how one knows the distant;
perfecting oneself is how one perfects others.
The Way of the sage kings is essential—
how could it involve excessive and numerous labors!"
14.3 "Shǒu Shí"
Third:
The sage in handling affairs
seems slow but is urgent, seems delayed but is swift, awaiting the right moment.
Wáng Jìlì died in distress,
and King Wén grieved for him,
never forgetting the humiliation of Yǒulǐ,
but the time was not yet right.
King Wǔ served him,
diligent day and night without rest,
also never forgetting the disgrace at the royal gate,
and after twelve years of rule,
he accomplished the affair of Jiǎzǐ.
The right moment is truly hard to come by.
Tàigōng Wàng,
a scholar from the Eastern Yi,
wished to bring order to the age but lacked a lord,
and hearing of King Wén's worthiness,
he fished in the Wèi River to observe him.
Wǔ Zǐxū wished to see the King of Wú but could not.
A guest spoke of him to Prince Guāng,
who, upon seeing him, disliked his appearance,
refused to listen to his words, and dismissed him.
The guest pleaded with Prince Guāng,
and Prince Guāng said:
"His appearance happens to be what I detest most."
The guest reported this to Wǔ Zǐxū,
and Wǔ Zǐxū said:
"This is easily remedied.
I wish to have the prince stay in the hall,
behind layered curtains, and let him see only my clothes and hands,
and allow me to persuade him."
The prince agreed.
When Wǔ Zǐxū had spoken halfway,
Prince Guāng lifted the curtains,
grasped his hand, and sat with him.
After the speech concluded,
Prince Guāng was greatly pleased.
Wǔ Zǐxū believed that the one who would possess the state of Wú must be Prince Guāng,
and withdrew to farm in the wilderness for seven years.
Prince Guāng succeeded King Liáo of Wú as king,
and employed Zǐxū.
Zǐxū then established laws and institutions,
honored the worthy and virtuous,
selected and trained soldiers,
and practiced warfare;
after six years,
he achieved a great victory over Chǔ at Bójǔ,
winning nine battles in a row,
pursuing the defeated enemy for a thousand li,
causing King Zhāo to flee to Suí,
and thus capturing Yǐng,
personally shooting into the royal palace,
and whipping the grave of King Píng of Jīng three hundred times.
His earlier farming
was not because he forgot his father's vengeance,
but because he awaited the right moment.
A Mohist named Tián Jiū wished to see King Huì of Qín,
but remained in Qín for three years without gaining an audience.
A guest spoke of him to the King of Chǔ,
and he went to see the King of Chǔ,
who was pleased with him,
and gave him the credentials of a general to go to Qín,
where, upon arrival,
he was able to see King Huì.
He told others:
"The way to reach Qín
was actually through Chǔ?"
Things are such that what seems near may be far, and what seems far may be near.
So it is with timing.
Having the worthiness of Tāng and Wǔ but lacking the times of Jié and Zhòu,
one cannot succeed;
having the times of Jié and Zhòu but lacking the worthiness of Tāng and Wǔ, one also cannot succeed.
The sage's perception of timing
is like the shadow that follows a step, inseparable.
Therefore, when a person of the Way has not yet encountered the right moment,
they hide and scatter,
diligently awaiting the time.
When the time arrives,
some rise from commoners to become Son of Heaven,
some from a state of a thousand chariots gain the world,
some from lowly positions assist the three kings,
and some from ordinary men take revenge on a state of ten thousand chariots.
Thus, what the sage values most
is timing alone.
When water freezes solid,
Hòujì does not sow;
Hòujì's sowing must await spring.
Therefore, though a person may be wise, if they do not encounter the right moment,
they achieve nothing.
When leaves are lush and beautiful,
picking them all day yields little,
but after autumn frost descends,
all forests wither.
The difficulty or ease of affairs
lies not in their size,
but in knowing the timing.
During the crisis of Zhèng Zǐyáng,
a mad dog caused the collapse;
during the crisis of Qí's Gāo and Guó,
a lost ox caused the collapse;
the masses used these to kill Zǐyáng, Gāo, and Guó.
At such times,
even dogs and oxen can lead the people,
let alone humans leading them?
When hungry horses fill the stable,
they are silent,
for they have not seen fodder;
when hungry dogs fill the kennel,
they are silent,
for they have not seen bones;
but when they see bones or fodder,
their movement cannot be restrained.
The people in chaotic times
are silent,
for they have not seen a worthy person;
but when they see a worthy person, they rush forth uncontrollably.
What rushes forth is not their form,
but their hearts.
When Qí, as the Eastern Emperor, was beset by the world, Lǔ seized Xúzhōu;
when Hándān, with its Shòulíng, was beset by the people, Wèi seized Jiǎnsì.
Though Lǔ and Wèi were small, they achieved their aims against great states,
because they encountered the right moment.
Therefore, worthy rulers and outstanding scholars who wish to care for the black-haired people
should act in chaotic times.
Heaven does not grant twice,
time does not linger long,
one cannot excel in two things at once,
success lies in seizing the moment.
14.4 "Righteous Rewards"
Fourth:
When spring's energy arrives, plants and trees grow;
when autumn's energy arrives, plants and trees shed.
Growth and shedding are caused by something,
not by nature itself.
Thus, when the cause arrives,
things cannot but act;
when the cause does not arrive,
things have nothing to act upon.
The ancients understood what caused things,
so nothing was left unused.
The power of rewards and punishments
is what the ruler uses to cause action.
If what is added is righteous,
then the ways of loyalty, trust, affection, and love become evident.
Long evident, they grow stronger,
and the people accept them as their nature.
This is called the completion of teaching.
Once teaching is complete, even heavy rewards and strict punishments cannot alter it.
Thus, a good teacher
does not rely on rewards and punishments to complete teaching;
teaching is completed, and rewards and punishments cannot alter it.
Using rewards and punishments improperly has the same effect.
The ways of deceit, falsity, violence, disorder, greed, and cruelty arise,
persist long without ceasing,
and the people hate them as their nature.
The people of Róng, Yí, Hú, Mò, Bā, and Yuè are like this;
even heavy rewards and strict punishments cannot restrain them.
When the people of Yǐng built walls with two boards,
Wú Qǐ changed it and was disliked,
but changing rewards and punishments brought peace and joy to the people;
the people of Dī Qiāng,
when captured,
do not worry about being bound,
but worry about dying without being cremated;
all these are formed by perversity.
Therefore, where rewards and punishments are applied,
one must be careful.
Otherwise, they may harm the people.
In the past, when Duke Wén of Jìn was about to fight the people of Chǔ at Chéngpú,
he summoned Jiù Fàn and asked:
"The Chǔ are many, we are few;
what can we do?"
Jiù Fàn replied:
"I have heard that a ruler fond of elaborate rites
lacks refinement;
a ruler fond of frequent warfare
lacks deceit.
Your Lordship should simply use deceit."
Duke Wén reported Jiù Fàn's words to Yōng Jì,
and Yōng Jì said:
"Draining a pond to catch fish,
will you not catch them?
But next year there will be no fish.
Burning a marsh to hunt,
will you not catch game?
But next year there will be no beasts.
Deceit and falsity as a way,
though they may succeed for now,
will not work again later,
and are not a lasting method."
Lord Wén followed the advice of Jiù Fàn,
and defeated the Chǔ army at Chéngpú.
Upon returning, he distributed rewards,
placing Yōng Jì first.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
"The victory at Chéngpú
was due to Jiù Fàn's strategy.
You used his advice yet reward him after others—
perhaps this is not right!"
Lord Wén said:
"Yōng Jì's words
are beneficial for a hundred generations.
Jiù Fàn's words
addressed the needs of a single moment.
How can one place the needs of a moment before the benefits of a hundred generations?"
Confucius, hearing of this, said:
"Facing peril, he used deception,
which sufficed to repel the enemy.
Upon returning, he honored the worthy,
which sufficed to repay virtue.
Though Lord Wén did not persist in this to the end,
it sufficed to make him a hegemon."
When rewards are substantial, the people will shift toward them;
when the people shift, success is achieved.
Success achieved through deception—
that success will be destroyed,
that victory will turn to defeat.
There have been many victors in the world,
yet only five became hegemons.
Lord Wén was one of them,
because he understood what leads to victory.
To be victorious yet not know what leads to victory
is the same as having no victory.
Qín triumphed over the Róng but was defeated at Xiáo;
Chǔ triumphed over the various Xià states but was defeated at Bójǔ.
King Wǔ understood this principle,
thus with one victory he became king over all under heaven.
When deception fills the state,
it cannot be secure;
the peril is not only external.
When Zhào Xiāngzǐ broke out of a siege,
he rewarded five men for their merit,
placing Gāo Shè first.
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"During the siege of Jìnyáng,
Shè performed no great feat.
Why reward him first?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"My state was in peril,
the altars of soil and grain endangered,
and I myself was in distress and constraint.
Among those who associated with me yet did not neglect the rites between ruler and minister, only Shè did so.
Therefore, I place him first."
Confucius, hearing of this, said:
"Xiāngzǐ may be called skilled at rewarding.
By rewarding one man, all ministers under heaven dare not neglect ritual."
For leading the six armies, he could not be replaced.
To the north, he conquered Dài;
to the east, he pressured Qí.
He ordered Zhāng Mèngtán to scale the walls and travel in secret,
to join Wèi Huán and Hán Kāng at the appointed time to attack Zhì Bó,
cut off his head to make a drinking vessel,
and thus settled the three families.
Was this not due to using rewards and punishments appropriately?
14.5 "Long-term Strategy"
Fifth Discourse:
Order and chaos, survival and destruction,
safety and peril, strength and weakness—
there must be a specific encounter,
and only then can success be achieved;
if each exists alone, it cannot be established.
Thus, though Jié and Zhòu were unworthy,
their destruction encountered Tāng and Wǔ;
encountering Tāng and Wǔ was due to Heaven,
not because Jié and Zhòu were unworthy.
Though Tāng and Wǔ were worthy,
their kingship encountered Jié and Zhòu;
encountering Jié and Zhòu
was due to Heaven,
not because Tāng and Wǔ were worthy.
If Jié and Zhòu had not encountered Tāng and Wǔ,
they might not have been destroyed;
if Jié and Zhòu had not been destroyed,
though unworthy,
their disgrace would not have reached this extent.
If Tāng and Wǔ had not encountered Jié and Zhòu,
they might not have become kings;
if Tāng and Wǔ had not become kings,
though worthy,
their renown would not have reached this extent.
Thus, a ruler who achieves great merit
is not heard of as unworthy;
a ruler who destroys his state is not heard of as worthy.
Compare it to a skilled farmer:
he distinguishes the suitability of the land,
diligently attends to plowing and weeding,
yet a harvest is not certain;
however, if there is a harvest,
it must be due to such a man.
It begins with encountering timely rain;
encountering timely rain
is due to Heaven,
not something a skilled farmer can bring about.
The state of Yuè suffered a great famine;
the king was alarmed
and summoned Fàn Lǐ to consult.
Fàn Lǐ said:
"Why should Your Majesty worry?
This famine
is Yuè's fortune and Wú's calamity.
The state of Wú is very wealthy with abundant resources;
its king is young,
of shallow wisdom and slight ability,
fond of fleeting fame,
and gives no thought to future troubles.
If Your Majesty sends generous gifts and humble words to request grain from Wú,
then food can be obtained.
Once food is obtained,
in the end Yuè is sure to possess Wú.
So why should Your Majesty worry?"
The King of Yuè
said: "Excellent."
He then sent someone to request food from Wú.
The King of Wú was about to grant it.
Wǔ Zǐxū came forward to remonstrate:
"You must not give it.
Wú and Yuè
share borders and are neighboring territories;
the roads are easy and people move freely.
They are states that are enemies and adversaries in war.
If Wú does not destroy Yuè,
Yuè is sure to destroy Wú.
As for states like Yān, Qín, Qí, and Jìn,
situated among mountains or on land,
how could they cross the five lakes and nine rivers, traverse seventeen passes to possess Wú?
Therefore it is said: if Wú does not destroy Yuè,
Yuè is sure to destroy Wú.
Now to transport grain to them,
to give them food,
is to nourish our adversary and sustain our enemy.
Resources will be exhausted and the people alarmed;
regret will be too late.
It is better not to give but to attack them,
for this accords with the inevitable course.
This is how our former kings became hegemons."
Moreover, famine
is a cyclical event,
like deep pools and slopes—
what state does not have them?
The King of Wú said:
"Not so.
I have heard:
'Righteous armies do not attack those who submit;
the benevolent feed the hungry.'
Now they submit, yet to attack them
is not the action of a righteous army;
they are hungry, yet not to feed them
is not the essence of benevolence.
To be neither benevolent nor righteous,
even if I gained ten Yuè,
I would not do it."
He then gave them food.
Within three years, Wú also suffered famine.
He sent someone to request food from Yuè.
The King of Yuè refused to give it,
and instead attacked.
Fūchāi was captured.
The King of Chǔ wanted to seize Xī and Cài.
He first pretended to be friendly with the Marquis of Cài,
and plotted with him, saying:
"I wish to obtain Xī.
What should I do?"
The Marquis of Cài said:
"The wife of the Marquis of Xī
is my wife's sister.
I request to host a feast for the Marquis of Xī and his wife,
and you, sire, come along.
We can then take advantage to launch a surprise attack."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Agreed."
Thereupon, he and the Marquis of Cài entered Xī under the pretext of a feast,
and taking advantage of the situation,
they seized Xī.
On the return,
they stopped in Cài,
and also seized Cài.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ fell ill.
He summoned the heir and told him:
"After I die and am buried,
put on mourning garments and ascend Xiàwū Mountain to look out."
The crown prince respectfully assented.
After Jiǎnzǐ died,
was buried,
and mourning garments were worn,
he summoned his ministers and told them:
"I wish to ascend the Xiàwū to gaze afar."
The ministers all remonstrated, saying:
"To ascend the Xiàwū to gaze afar
is an excursion.
To wear mourning garments on an excursion
is not permissible."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"This was the command of our late lord,
I dare not disregard it."
The assembled ministers respectfully assented.
Xiāngzǐ ascended the Xiàwū to observe the customs of Dài.
Their pleasures were exceedingly fine.
Thereupon Xiāngzǐ said:
"Our late lord must have intended this to instruct me."
Upon returning,
he considered how to seize Dài,
and first sought to ingratiate himself with them.
The lord of Dài was fond of women.
He requested to give his elder sister to him as a wife.
The lord of Dài agreed.
After his sister had gone,
the means to ingratiate himself with Dài were multiplied ten-thousandfold.
The horse commandery was suitable for horses.
The lord of Dài presented fine horses to Xiāngzǐ.
Xiāngzǐ invited the lord of Dài and requested to toast him.
The horse commandery was exhausted.
He first ordered several hundred dancers to conceal weapons among their plumes.
He first prepared a large metal ladle.
When the lord of Dài arrived,
and the wine was in full swing,
he overturned the ladle and struck him with it.
With one blow,
his brains were smeared on the ground.
The dancers took up their weapons and fought,
killing all his attendants.
Thereupon, he used the lord of Dài's carriage to fetch his wife.
His wife, hearing of this from afar,
sharpened a hairpin and stabbed herself with it.
Therefore, the Zhào clan to this day has the testimony of the hairpin-stabbing and the name of the overturned ladle.
These three lords
each obtained what they had from a source.
They did not fully adhere to principle,
yet later generations praise them,
because they had merit.
To have merit in this and be without fault,
even becoming king is possible.
14.6 "Being Cautious About Men"
The sixth says:
The great establishment of merit and fame
is due to Heaven.
For this reason, one cannot be incautious about men.
That Shùn encountered Yáo
was due to Heaven.
Shùn plowed at Lìshān,
made pottery by the riverbank,
fished at Léizé.
All under Heaven delighted in him,
outstanding scholars followed him—
this was due to men.
That Yǔ encountered Shùn
was due to Heaven.
Yǔ traveled throughout all under Heaven,
seeking worthy men,
working for the benefit of the black-haired people.
Wherever waters, floods, rivers, and marshes were stagnant, blocked, and could be made passable,
Yǔ did it all—
this was due to men.
That Tāng encountered Jié,
and Wǔ encountered Zhòu,
was due to Heaven.
Tāng and Wǔ cultivated themselves, accumulated goodness, and acted righteously,
taking the worries and sufferings of the people upon themselves—
this was due to men.
Shùn's plowing and fishing—
his worthiness or lack thereof was the same as when he became Son of Heaven.
When he had not yet encountered his time,
he, with his followers,
dug for the earth's resources,
took advantage of water's benefits,
wove cattails and reeds,
knit nets,
his hands and feet calloused without rest,
only then avoiding the calamity of freezing and starvation.
When he encountered his time,
he ascended to become Son of Heaven.
Worthy scholars returned to him,
the myriad people praised him.
Men and women,
all in great numbers and earnestness,
none did not revere and delight in him.
Shùn himself made a poem, saying:
"Under the vast heaven,
all is the king's land.
To the shores of the land,
all are the king's servants."
This shows he possessed it all.
To possess it all—
his worthiness was not increased.
To possess none of it—
his worthiness was not diminished.
The times made it so.
When Bǎilǐ Xī had not yet encountered his time,
he fled Guó and was captured by Jìn.
He fed oxen in Qín,
was sold for the price of five sheepskins.
Gōngsūn Zhī obtained him and was delighted,
presenting him to Duke Mù.
After three days,
he requested to entrust him with affairs.
Duke Mù said:
"To buy him for five sheepskins and entrust him with affairs—
would we not be laughed at by all under Heaven?"
Gōngsūn Zhī replied:
"To trust a worthy and employ him
is the ruler's wisdom.
To yield to a worthy and serve beneath him
is the minister's loyalty.
The ruler becomes a wise ruler,
the minister becomes a loyal minister.
If he is truly worthy,
within the borders they will submit,
enemy states will fear.
Who then will have leisure to laugh?"
Duke Mù then employed him.
His plans were never inappropriate,
his actions always successful—
not because his worthiness increased.
Had Bǎilǐ Xī, though worthy,
not obtained Duke Mù,
he certainly would not have had this fame.
How can we know there is no Bǎilǐ Xī in the world today?
Therefore, rulers who desire to seek scholars
cannot but strive to be broad.
When Confucius was in distress between Chén and Cài,
for seven days he tasted no food,
his vegetable soup had no grain.
Zǎiyǔ was exhausted,
yet Confucius played the zither and sang inside the room,
while Yán Huí selected vegetables outside.
Zǐlù and Zǐgòng spoke together, saying:
"Our Master was twice driven from Lǔ,
his traces erased in Wèi,
trees were felled because of him in Sòng,
he is in distress between Chén and Cài.
Those who kill our Master are without crime,
those who insult our Master are not restrained.
Yet our Master plays the zither, sings, drums, and dances,
never ceasing the sound.
Can it be that a gentleman's lack of shame is like this?"
Yán Huí had nothing to reply,
entered and told Confucius.
Confucius, looking displeased, pushed aside his zither,
sighed deeply and said:
"Yóu and Cì
are petty men.
Summon them here,
I will speak to them."
Zǐlù and Zǐgòng entered.
Zǐgòng said:
"One like this can be said to be in distress."
Confucius said:
"What words are these?
A gentleman penetrating the Way is called 'penetrating';
being blocked from the Way is called 'distress'.
Now I, Qiū, embrace the Way of benevolence and righteousness,
and have encountered the calamity of a chaotic age.
This is my proper place.
How can it be called distress?
Therefore, examining within and finding no fault against the Way,
facing difficulty and not losing one's virtue.
When the great cold arrives,
frost and snow have fallen,
I thereby know the luxuriance of the pine and cypress.
In the past, Duke Huán obtained it in Jǔ,
Duke Wén obtained it in Cáo,
the King of Yuè obtained it at Kuàijī.
The straits of Chén and Cài—
for me, Qiū, are they not fortunate!"
Confucius, with fervor, turned back to his zither and sang,
Zǐlù, with vigor, grasped a shield and danced.
Zǐgòng said:
"I do not know the height of heaven,
nor the depth of earth."
Those in ancient times who attained the Dào,
were joyful even in poverty,
joyful even in success.
Their joy was not about poverty or success.
Having attained the Dào in this,
then poverty and success become one,
like the orderly succession of cold, heat, wind, and rain.
Thus, Xǔ Yóu found contentment at Yǐngyáng,
and Gòng Bó attained it at Gòngshǒu.
14.7 "Meeting and Suiting"
The seventh discourse says:
In all meetings and suitings,
if the time is not suitable,
one must wait for suitability before acting.
Thus, birds that fly wing-to-wing die in the trees,
fish that swim side-by-side die in the sea.
Confucius traveled throughout the realm,
twice sought audiences with the lords of the age,
went to Qí and reached Wèi,
met with over eighty rulers,
had three thousand disciples who presented themselves as students,
and seventy accomplished followers.
Among these seventy,
if the lord of a ten-thousand-chariot state could employ even one, he could serve as a teacher.
It was not that there were no capable men,
yet with this, his travels only reached the position of Minister of Justice in Lǔ.
This is why the Son of Heaven's line was sometimes cut off,
and why the feudal lords fell into great disorder.
In disorder, the foolish are often favored by fortune,
and when favored, they are inevitably unequal to their tasks.
Holding a position long without being equal to it,
then fortune turns into calamity.
The greater the fortune,
the greater the calamity,
and the calamity does not fall on them alone.
Therefore, the noble man does not dwell in fortune,
does not act recklessly,
but must first examine himself thoroughly before taking a position,
and only then act after taking the position.
All who are capable of listening to persuasion,
must be proficient in discussion and argument.
Few are the lords of the age who can recognize discussion and argument,
so how can their encounters not be reckless?
All who are capable of listening to music,
must be proficient in the five notes.
Few are the people who can understand the five notes,
so how can their preferences not be reckless?
There was a guest who performed playing the yuè for the King of Yuè.
His rendering of the five notes—yǔ, jué, gōng, zhǐ, shāng—was flawless,
but the King of Yuè did not appreciate it.
He played rustic music instead, and the king appreciated that.
The way of persuasion also has cases like this.
There was a woman who became someone's wife.
Someone told her parents:
"When marrying, one cannot be sure of bearing children.
Clothing and utensils,
you can hide outside,
to prepare for childlessness."
Her parents thought this right,
and so instructed their daughter to always hide things outside.
Her mother-in-law and father-in-law found out,
saying:
"To be our daughter-in-law and have an outward heart,
she cannot be kept."
They therefore sent her away.
The woman's parents,
considering the one who advised them as loyal for planning on their behalf,
regarded him well all their lives,
never understanding the true reason.
The destruction of ancestral temples,
the loss of the realm,
also arise from this.
Therefore it is said: Meeting and suiting have no constancy.
Persuasion,
is a matter of chance.
As with people's response to beauty,
none do not delight in the beautiful,
yet the beautiful may not necessarily be encountered.
Thus, Mómǔ was taken by Huángdì,
Huángdì said:
"I charge you with virtue, do not forget it;
I give you correctness, do not let it decline.
Even if ugly, what harm is there?"
As with people's response to flavors,
none do not delight in sweetness and crispness,
yet sweetness and crispness may not necessarily be accepted.
King Wén was fond of pickled calamus root,
Confucius heard of it and tried it,
wrinkling his brow as he ate it,
and only after three years could he bear it.
There was a man with a great stench,
his relatives, brothers, wife, concubines, acquaintances—none could live with him.
He suffered by himself and lived by the sea.
A man by the sea delighted in his stench,
following him day and night, unable to leave.
Delight also has cases like this.
In Chén there was an ugly man,
named Dūnqià Chóumí.
He had a prominent forehead and broad face,
his complexion like soaked red earth,
with drooping eyes down to his nose,
long elbows and crooked limbs.
The Marquis of Chén saw him and greatly delighted in him,
employing him externally to govern his state,
and internally to manage his person.
When Chǔ assembled the feudal lords,
the Marquis of Chén was ill and could not go,
so he sent Dūnqià Chóumí to offer apologies.
The King of Chǔ, curious about his name, received him first.
The guest entered; his appearance was repulsive, his speech was repulsive, his name was repulsive.
The King of Chǔ was angered,
assembled his great officers and told them:
"The Marquis of Chén,
if he did not know this man was unfit to be sent,
that is ignorance;
if he knew and still sent him,
that is insult.
Insult and ignorance combined—
we cannot but attack."
He raised an army to attack Chén,
and after three months, Chén was lost.
Ugliness enough to startle men,
speech enough to lose a state,
yet his friendship sufficed for the Marquis of Chén as if he had no superior,
and even to the point of ruin, his friendship did not wane.
When those who should not meet with favor do meet with it,
then necessarily those who should meet with favor are cast aside.
This is why states fall into disorder and ages into decline.
The people of the realm,
their suffering, sorrow, toil, and hardship all arise from this.
In general, the root of employing men:
the highest is by their intent,
next by their deeds,
next by their achievements.
If these three cannot be done,
the state will inevitably be maimed and lost,
hordes of calamities will arrive in force,
the ruler's person will inevitably meet with death and disaster,
and if he reaches seventy or ninety years of age, it is still but fortune.
Descendants of worthies and sages,
who instead bring calamity upon the people,
thereby harm their own persons—
how could they alone [suffer]?
14.8 "Necessarily Oneself"
The eighth discourse says:
External things cannot be counted on,
thus Lóng Páng was executed,
Bǐgàn was slain,
Jīzǐ went mad,
È Lái died,
and Jié and Zhòu perished.
No ruler does not wish his ministers to be loyal,
yet loyalty is not necessarily trusted.
Thus Wǔ Yún was cast into the river,
Cháng Hóng died, and his blood, stored for three years, turned to jade.
No parent does not wish his child to be filial,
yet filiality is not necessarily loved.
Thus Xiàojǐ was doubted,
and Zēngzǐ grieved.
Zhuāngzǐ was walking in the mountains,
and saw a tree, very beautiful, tall and large,
with luxuriant, flourishing branches and leaves.
Woodcutters stopped beside it but did not take it.
He asked the reason,
and they said:
"It is of no use whatsoever."
Zhuāngzǐ said:
"This tree, by being useless, gets to live out its natural lifespan."
Coming out of the mountains,
and reaching a town,
he lodged at an old friend's home.
The old friend was pleased,
prepared wine and meat,
and ordered a servant boy to kill a goose to feast him.
The servant boy asked:
"One goose can honk,
one goose cannot honk.
Which should I kill?"
The master of the house said:
"Kill the one that cannot honk."
The next day,
a disciple asked Zhuāngzǐ:
"Yesterday, the tree in the mountains, by being useless, got to live out its natural lifespan.
Now, the master's goose, by being useless, died.
How will you, Master, position yourself?"
Zhuāngzǐ laughed and said:
"I, Zhōu, will position myself between usefulness and uselessness.
Between usefulness and uselessness—
it seems right but is not,
so one still cannot avoid entanglement.
As for those who embody the Way and its Virtue, it is not so:
they are neither startled nor slandered,
now a dragon, now a serpent,
they transform along with the times,
and are unwilling to be fixed in their actions;
now ascending, now descending,
they take harmony as their measure,
and drift and wander in the ancestral source of the myriad things,
using things but not being used by things—
how then could they possibly be encumbered?
This is what Shénnóng and Huángdì followed as their model.
As for the nature of the myriad things and the transmissions of human relations, it is not so:
completion leads to destruction,
greatness leads to decline,
sharpness leads to being blunted,
honor leads to loss,
straightness leads to being bent,
union leads to separation,
love leads to ruin,
great wisdom leads to scheming,
lack of worth leads to deception—
how then could one possibly be certain of anything?"
There was a man named Niú Quē, a great Confucian scholar of the upper lands.
He went down to Hándān,
and encountered robbers in the midst of the Ǒushā area.
The robbers demanded the goods in his bags,
and he gave them;
they demanded his carriage and horses,
and he gave them;
they demanded his clothing and coverings, and he gave them.
Niú Quē then walked away on foot.
The robbers said to each other:
"This man is a prominent figure in the world.
Now that we have humiliated him like this,
he is certain to report us to the ruler of ten thousand chariots.
The ruler of ten thousand chariots will certainly use the power of the state to execute us.
We will surely not survive.
It would be better for us to join together, pursue him, and kill him,
in order to eliminate the traces."
Thereupon they joined together and hurried after him,
traveled thirty lǐ,
caught up with him and killed him.
This happened because they knew who he was.
Mèng Bēn was crossing a river.
He went ahead of the others by five [people],
and the boatman became angry.
Using his oar, he struck Mèng Bēn on the head,
not knowing at the time that it was Mèng Bēn.
In the middle of the river,
Mèng Bēn glared at the boatman,
his hair stood on end,
his eyes seemed to split open,
and his temples bristled.
Everyone in the boat was thrown about and fell into the river.
If the boatman had known it was Mèng Bēn,
he would not have dared to look him straight in the face,
let alone be the first to cross,
and even more so, to insult him!
This happened because he did not know who he was.
Knowing and not knowing
are both insufficient to rely on.
Only harmony and attunement come close.
Yet even this cannot be certain,
for there are those who do not distinguish harmony and attunement,
so even harmony and attunement cannot avoid [misfortune].
Sīmǎ of Sòng Huán had a precious pearl.
Having committed a crime, he fled into exile.
The king sent someone to ask where the pearl was.
He said, "I threw it into the pond."
Thereupon they drained the pond to search for it,
but did not find it,
and the fish all died.
This illustrates how misfortune and fortune are interconnected.
Zhòu committed evil deeds in Shāng,
and calamity filled heaven and earth.
What good was harmony and attunement then?
Zhāng Yì was fond of being respectful.
Whether at gates, alleys, curtains, or screens, wherever crowds gathered, he would hasten to be respectful;
towards carriage drivers, servants, relatives by marriage, and young children, there was none he did not treat with respect,
in order to stabilize his person.
Yet he did not live out his natural lifespan,
but died from internal heat.
Shān Bào was fond of techniques.
He withdrew from the vulgar and abandoned the dusty world,
did not eat the grains,
did not wear clothes for warmth,
dwelt in mountain forests and rocky caves,
in order to preserve his life.
Yet he did not live out his full years,
but was eaten by a tiger.
Confucius was traveling on the road and stopped to rest.
His horse broke loose
and ate someone's crops.
The rustic seized his horse.
Zǐgòng requested to go and persuade him.
He exhausted his words,
but the rustic would not listen.
There was a rustic who had just begun to serve Confucius, who said:
"Allow me to go and persuade him."
Thereupon he said to the rustic:
"You do not farm in the Eastern Sea,
and I do not farm in the Western Sea.
How could my horse not eat your grain?"
The rustic was greatly pleased.
They said to each other:
"Persuasion can also be as eloquent as this—
how is it that the previous person was not like this?"
They untied the horse and gave it to him.
If persuasion as unprincipled as this can still work,
how can one be certain about external things?
In conducting himself, the gentleman
respects others but does not necessarily expect to be respected;
he loves others but does not necessarily expect to be loved.
Respecting and loving others
depends on oneself;
being respected and loved
depends on others.
The gentleman insists on what depends on himself,
not on what depends on others.
Insisting on what depends on oneself, he will never fail to encounter [the proper response].
15.1 "Being Cautious in Greatness"
Part One says:
The worthy ruler, the greater he becomes, the more apprehensive;
the stronger he becomes, the more fearful.
Generally, greatness
means making neighboring states small;
strength
means overcoming one's enemies.
Overcoming one's enemies creates much resentment;
making neighboring states small creates much trouble.
With much trouble and much resentment,
though the state is strong and great,
how can it not be apprehensive?
How can it not be fearful?
Therefore, the worthy ruler thinks of danger in times of safety,
thinks of extremity in times of success,
thinks of loss in times of gain.
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
