"As if facing a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice"—
this speaks of being cautious in affairs.
Jié acted without the Way,
violent, cruel, stubborn, and greedy.
All under heaven trembled in fear and were troubled by him.
Those who spoke did not agree,
they were confused and contentious,
and their true sentiments were difficult to ascertain.
Gān Xīn wielded power,
oppressed and trampled the feudal lords,
and extended this to the common people.
The worthy and good were stifled and resentful.
He killed that Lóng Páng
in order to subdue the multitude of malcontents.
The masses were in turmoil,
all had thoughts of distancing themselves,
none dared to speak frankly,
and their lives were as if startled.
The great ministers shared the troubles,
and, not being supported, they rebelled.
Jié increasingly considered himself worthy,
boasted of his errors and praised his wrongs.
The way of the ruler was repeatedly blocked,
and the people of the state greatly collapsed.
Tāng then became alarmed and fearful,
concerned that all under heaven was not at peace.
He wished to send Yī Yǐn to observe the vastness of the Xià,
but feared he would not be trusted,
so Tāng accordingly personally shot at Yī Yǐn.
Yī Yǐn fled to Xià for three years,
then returned and reported at Bó, saying:
"Jié is deluded by Móxǐ,
is fond of those [women] Wǎn and Yǎn,
and does not pity his multitudes.
The will of the multitudes cannot endure it;
superiors and inferiors hate each other;
the resentment of the people's hearts has accumulated.
They all say:
'Heaven above does not pity us;
the mandate of Xià is about to end.'"
Tāng said to Yī Yǐn:
"What you have told me about the vastness of Xià is entirely as in the ode."
Tāng made a covenant with Yī Yǐn,
to show his determination to destroy Xià.
Yī Yǐn went again to observe the vastness of Xià,
and listened to Móxǐ.
Móxǐ said:
"Last night the Son of Heaven dreamed that there was a sun in the west
and a sun in the east.
The two suns fought with each other;
the western sun was victorious,
the eastern sun was not victorious."
Yī Yǐn reported this to Tāng.
Shāng suffered from drought,
yet Tāng still raised an army
to honor his covenant with Yī Yǐn.
Therefore, he ordered the army to set out from the east of the capital,
and advance towards the west.
Before blades could clash, Jié fled,
and was pursued to Dàshā,
where his body was torn apart,
and he was executed for all to see.
Unable to accept upright remonstrance,
though he later regretted it,
what could be done?
Tāng was established as the Son of Heaven,
and the people of Xià were greatly pleased,
as if they had gained a loving parent.
Officials did not change their positions,
farmers did not leave their fields,
merchants did not alter their shops,
and they felt as close to Yī as they had to Xià.
This is called utmost impartiality,
this is called utmost peace,
this is called utmost trust.
He fully carried out the covenant of Yī Yǐn,
not avoiding drought or calamity,
and Yī Yǐn was honored by Shāng for generations.
When King Wǔ defeated Yīn,
and entered Yīn,
before descending from his chariot,
he ordered the descendants of Huángdì to be enfeoffed at Zhù,
the descendants of Emperor Yáo at Lí,
and the descendants of Emperor Shùn at Chén.
After descending from his chariot,
he ordered the descendants of the Xià rulers to be enfeoffed at Qǐ,
and established the descendants of Chéng Tāng in Sòng to continue the sacrifices at Sānglín.
King Wǔ then grew fearful,
sighed, and shed tears,
ordering Zhōu Gōng Dàn to summon the surviving elders of Yīn,
and inquired about the reasons for Yīn's downfall,
and also asked what pleased the masses and what the people desired.
The surviving elders of Yīn replied:
"We wish to restore the governance of Pán Gēng."
King Wǔ then restored the governance of Pán Gēng;
he distributed the grain from Jùqiáo,
and disbursed the wealth from Lùtái,
to show the people he had no selfish motives;
he released prisoners and pardoned crimes,
distributed wealth and canceled debts,
to relieve the impoverished;
he restored Bǐ Gān's tomb,
purified Jīzǐ's residence,
and honored Shāng Róng's neighborhood,
so that scholars passing by would bow,
and chariots passing by would halt;
within three days,
those who had strategized with him were enfeoffed as feudal lords,
the senior officials were rewarded with lands and households,
and the common officials were relieved of taxes;
then (at the Jì River) he crossed the river,
and returned west to report at the ancestral temple;
he then released his horses at Huàshān,
and released his oxen at Táolín,
so the horses were never ridden again,
and the oxen were never used again;
he smeared the blood of sacrifice on drums, banners, armor, and weapons,
and stored them in the treasury,
never to be used again in his lifetime.
This was the virtue of King Wǔ.
Thus, the outer gates of the Zhōu dynasty's Bright Hall remained unclosed,
showing the world that nothing was hidden.
Only by hiding nothing can one guard the ultimate treasure.
When King Wǔ defeated Yīn,
he captured two prisoners and questioned them,
saying:
"Does your state have any omens?"
One prisoner replied:
"Our state has an omen.
Stars appearing during the day and blood raining from the sky—
these are the omens of our state."
The other prisoner replied:
"These are indeed omens.
However,
they are not the greatest ones.
The omens of our state,
the greatest ones,
are that sons do not obey fathers,
younger brothers do not obey elder brothers,
and the ruler's commands are not carried out.
These are the greatest omens."
King Wǔ rose from his mat and bowed twice to them.
This was not to honor the prisoners,
but to honor their words.
Thus, the Yìjīng says:
"Treading on a tiger's tail with caution,
ultimately brings good fortune."
When Zhào Xiāngzǐ attacked Dí,
and captured Zuǒrén and Zhōngrén,
he sent an envoy to report the victory.
Xiāngzǐ was eating a ball of rice at the time,
and wore a worried expression.
His attendants said:
"Two cities captured in a single day—
this is something others would celebrate.
Why do you look worried now?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"Even the greatest rivers,
do not overflow for more than three days;
a fierce storm does not last a full morning,
and the sun at its zenith does not linger.
Now, the virtue and conduct of the Zhào clan
have not accumulated significantly,
yet two cities are captured in a single day.
Will our downfall not soon follow?"
When Confucius heard of this, he said:
"The Zhào clan will surely prosper!"
Worry is what leads to prosperity,
while joy is what leads to downfall.
Victory is not the difficult part;
maintaining it is the difficult part.
Wise rulers use this to maintain victory,
so their blessings extend to later generations.
Qí, Jīng, Wú, and Yuè all once achieved victory,
but ultimately met their downfall,
because they did not understand how to maintain victory.
Only rulers who possess the Dào can maintain victory.
Confucius had the strength
to lift the bar of a city gate,
yet he refused to be known for his physical power;
Mòzǐ, in defense and attack,
made Gōngshū Bān submit,
yet he refused to be known for his military knowledge.
Those skilled at maintaining victory
use strategy to strengthen the weak.
15.2 "Quán Xūn"
The second says:
Profit cannot be twofold,
and loyalty cannot be dual.
If minor gains are not abandoned, major gains cannot be attained;
if minor loyalty is not abandoned, great loyalty cannot be achieved.
Thus, minor gains
are the ruin of major gains;
minor loyalty
is the thief of great loyalty.
The sage discards the minor and chooses the major.
Long ago, Jīng Gōngwáng fought Jìn Lìgōng at Yānlíng,
the Jīng army was defeated,
and Gōngwáng was wounded.
During the battle,
Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn was thirsty and asked for a drink.
The attendant Yáng Gǔ brought him a vessel of wine.
Zǐfǎn scolded him:
"Ugh!
Away!
This is wine."
The attendant Yáng Gǔ replied:
"It is not wine."
Zǐfǎn said:
"Quickly, away!
It is wine."
Yáng Gǔ again said:
"It is not wine."
Zǐfǎn took it and drank.
Zǐfǎn, by nature, loved wine,
and could not resist its sweetness,
so he became drunk.
After the battle ended,
Gōngwáng wished to resume fighting and plan the next move,
so he sent someone to summon Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn.
Zǐfǎn excused himself on grounds of a heart ailment.
Gōngwáng rode to see him,
entered the tent,
smelled the odor of wine, and returned,
saying:
"In today's battle,
I myself was wounded,
and what I relied upon was Sīmǎ.
Yet Sīmǎ is in such a state—
this is to forget the altars of Jīng and show no concern for my people.
I cannot resume the battle."
Thereupon, he withdrew the army and left,
and executed Sīmǎ Zǐfǎn as a punishment.
Thus, when the attendant Yáng Gǔ offered the wine,
it was not to make Zǐfǎn drunk,
but his heart was filled with loyal affection for him.
Yet it was precisely this that caused his death.
Thus it is said: minor loyalty
is the thief of great loyalty.
Long ago, Jìn Xiàngōng sent Xún Xī to borrow a passage through Yú to attack Guó.
Xún Xī said:
"I request to use the jade disc of Chuíjí and the steeds of Qūchǎn
to bribe the Duke of Yú,
and ask for passage through his territory.
It will surely be granted."
Xiàngōng said:
"The jade disc of Chuíjí
is the treasure of my ancestors;
the steeds of Qūchǎn
are my finest horses.
If he accepts our gifts but does not grant us passage,
what shall we do?"
Xún Xī said:
"Not so.
If they do not grant us passage,
they certainly will not accept our gifts.
If they accept our gifts and grant us passage,
then it is as if the treasure were taken from the inner treasury and stored in the outer treasury,
and the horses were taken from the inner stables and placed in the outer stables.
What is there for Your Lordship to worry about?"
Duke Xiàn agreed.
He then sent Xún Xī with the finest horses from Qūchǎn as court gifts,
adding the jade disc of Chuíjí,
to request passage through Yú to attack Guó.
The Duke of Yú, coveting the treasure and horses, wished to consent.
Gōng Zhīqí remonstrated, saying:
"You must not consent.
The relationship between Yú and Guó
is like that between a carriage and its side supports.
The carriage relies on the supports,
and the supports also rely on the carriage.
Such is the situation between Yú and Guó.
The ancients have said:
'When the lips are gone, the teeth feel the cold.'
Guó's survival depends on Yú,
and Yú's survival also depends on Guó.
If we grant them passage,
then Guó will perish in the morning and Yú will follow in the evening.
How can we grant them passage?"
The Duke of Yú did not listen,
and granted them passage.
Xún Xī attacked Guó
and conquered it.
Returning, he attacked Yú,
and conquered it as well.
Xún Xī, holding the jade disc and leading the horses, reported back.
Duke Xiàn, pleased, said:
"The jade disc is still the same,
however,
the horses' teeth have grown a bit longer."
Thus it is said that small gains are the ruin of great gains.
In the state of Zhōngshān there was a place called Qiúyóu.
Zhì Bó wished to attack it but had no way to do so,
so he cast a large bell,
with a carriage width of two tracks, and presented it to them.
The lord of Qiúyóu planned to cut down embankments and fill in ravines to welcome the bell.
Chìzhāng Mànzhī remonstrated, saying:
"The Book of Odes says:
'Only by following principles can a state be settled.'
Why would we receive this from Zhì Bó?
Zhì Bó's character is greedy and untrustworthy.
He certainly wishes to attack us but has no way to do so,
therefore he made this large bell,
with a carriage width of two tracks, to present to you, my lord.
If you, my lord, cut down embankments and fill in ravines to welcome the bell,
his army will surely follow."
He did not listen.
After a while,
he remonstrated again.
The lord said:
"A great state is showing us favor,
and you oppose it.
This is inauspicious.
Let it be."
Chìzhāng Mànzhī said:
"For a minister to be disloyal and unfaithful
is a crime;
but if loyalty and faithfulness are not heeded,
it is permissible to distance oneself."
He broke the axle of his carriage and departed.
He reached Wèi, and seven days later Qiúyóu perished.
The desire for the bell prevailed.
When the desire for the bell prevails, then sound advice for preserving Qiúyóu is blocked.
In general, when listening to advice,
one must carefully examine what prevails,
therefore the highest priority is to first prevail.
Lord Chāngguó led the armies of five states to attack Qí.
Qí sent Chù Zǐ to command,
meeting the allied forces at Jìshàng.
The King of Qí wished to fight,
and sent a messenger to Chù Zǐ,
shaming and rebuking him, saying:
"If you do not fight,
I will certainly exterminate your kind,
and dig up your ancestral graves."
Chù Zǐ was distressed by this,
and wished for the Qí army's defeat.
Then, when the allied forces engaged in battle,
as the battle commenced,
he sounded the gongs to retreat,
and the troops fled in defeat.
The allied forces pursued them,
and Chù Zǐ then left with a single chariot,
none knowing where he went,
nor hearing any news of him.
Dá Zǐ then led the remaining troops,
stationing them at Qínzhōu.
Having no means to give rewards,
he sent someone to request funds from the King of Qí.
The King of Qí angrily said:
"You wretched scoundrel,
how can I give you funds?"
Engaging the Yān forces in battle,
they were greatly defeated,
Dá Zǐ died,
and the King of Qí fled to Jǔ.
The Yān forces pursued the defeated army into the state,
and they vied for much gold at Měitáng.
This is an example of coveting small gains and thereby losing great gains.
15.3 "Esteeming the Worthy"
Third:
Men of the Way are inherently arrogant toward rulers,
and unworthy rulers are also arrogant toward men of the Way.
Daily they grow more arrogant toward each other;
when will they ever find mutual accord?
It is like the debates between the Ru and Mo schools or the rivalry between Qí and Jīng.
Worthy rulers are not like this.
Even if the scholar is arrogant toward him,
he treats him with ever greater courtesy.
How then can the scholar not turn to him?
When scholars turn to him,
the world follows.
The term "Dì" (Emperor)
means "to befit the world";
the term "Wáng" (King)
means "to be where the world goes."
Those who have attained the Way,
though honored as Son of Heaven, are not arrogant or haughty;
though possessing all under Heaven, they do not boast or show off;
though lowly as commoners, they are not dispirited or cowed;
though poor without food or clothing, they are not anxious or fearful.
Profound is their inherent sincerity,
clear is their unwavering conviction,
resolute is their inevitable constancy,
compliant are they in transformation with yīn and yáng,
steadfast is the firmness of their hearts,
empty and open are they, free from artifice,
far-reaching is the ambition of their will,
deep and unfathomable are they,
firm and unyielding is their integrity,
cautious are they, unwilling to be self-righteous,
pure as a swan, ashamed to use cunning schemes,
detached are they,
disdaining worldly praise and blame. They take Heaven as their model,
virtue as their conduct,
the Way as their guiding principle.
They transform along with things, without ever reaching an end,
their essence fills Heaven and Earth without exhaustion,
their spirit envelops the cosmos without bounds.
None know their beginning,
none know their gate,
none know their origin,
none know their source.
Their greatness has no outside,
their smallness has no inside.
This is called the ultimate nobility.
Scholars who are like this,
even the Five Emperors could not make them friends,
nor the Three Kings make them teachers.
But if one discards the airs of an emperor or king,
then one may come close to attaining them.
Yáo did not receive Shàn Quǎn as an emperor,
but faced north and inquired of him.
Yáo was the Son of Heaven,
Shàn Quǎn was a commoner.
Why did he treat him with such extreme courtesy?
Shàn Quǎn was a man who had attained the Way.
Those who have attained the Way
cannot be treated with arrogance.
Yáo considered that in virtue, conduct, wisdom, and understanding he was not Shàn Quǎn's equal,
therefore he faced north and inquired of him.
This is called ultimate impartiality.
If not ultimate impartiality, who could treat the worthy with such courtesy?
Zhōu Gōng Dàn was the son of King Wén,
the younger brother of King Wǔ,
and the uncle of King Chéng.
Yet he paid court to seventy men in narrow alleys and beneath humble windows.
King Wén initiated this but did not complete it,
King Wǔ continued it but did not achieve it,
Zhōu Gōng Dàn, embracing the young sovereign, brought it to completion.
Therefore he is called King Chéng (the Accomplisher),
not only because he personally humbled himself before scholars.
Duke Huán of Qí went to see the minor official Jì,
three times in one day, yet could not get an audience.
His attendants said:
"The lord of ten thousand chariots,
going to see a common scholar,
three times in one day without gaining an audience—
this can stop now."
Duke Huán said:
"That is not so.
When a scholar is arrogant about salary and rank,
he inevitably looks down on his lord;
when a lord is arrogant about hegemony and kingship,
he also looks down on his scholars.
Even if you, Master, are arrogant about salary and rank,
how dare I be arrogant about hegemony and kingship?"
Thereupon he went to see him,
and could not be stopped.
Many in the world point to Duke Huán's personal conduct;
although his personal conduct was not cultivated,
he still achieved hegemony.
If he had truly practiced this principle and cultivated his personal conduct,
he would have been close to true kingship.
Zǐchǎn served as prime minister of Zhèng.
When he went to see Húqiūzǐ Lín,
he always sat among his disciples according to seniority,
thus setting aside his prime ministerial status at the gate.
To be prime minister of a state of ten thousand chariots and yet be able to set it aside,
discussing intentions and evaluating conduct,
and seeking connection with others through sincerity of heart—
was this not only Zǐchǎn?
Thus, during his eighteen years as prime minister of Zhèng,
only three people were punished,
and two were executed.
Peaches and plums hanging over the road, no one picked them;
awls and knives left on the road, no one took them.
Marquis Wén of Wèi went to see Duàngān Mù.
He stood until weary but did not dare to rest.
Returning, he saw Zhái Huáng,
and sat sprawled on the hall floor while speaking with him.
Zhái Huáng was displeased.
Marquis Wén said:
"Duàngān Mù would not accept an official post if offered,
nor would he accept a salary if granted.
Now you desire an office and have the position of prime minister;
you desire a salary and have that of a high minister.
Having already received my substantial gifts,
you now demand my ritual respect as well—
is that not rather difficult?"
Therefore, when a worthy ruler treats people,
he shows ritual respect to those unwilling to accept substantial gifts.
In respecting scholars, nothing is higher than restraining one's desires.
When desires are restrained, then orders are carried out.
Marquis Wén may be said to have been fond of respecting scholars.
Being fond of respecting scholars, he therefore defeated Chǔ to the south at Liándī;
defeated Qí to the east at the Great Wall,
captured the Marquis of Qí,
and presented him to the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven rewarded Marquis Wén with the rank of High Minister.
15.4 "Requiting Kindness"
Fourth: A state may be small,
but if its food is sufficient to feed the worthy of the world,
its chariots sufficient to carry the worthy of the world,
its wealth sufficient to show ritual respect to the worthy of the world,
and it joins with the worthy of the world as companions,
this is how King Wén became king.
Now even if one cannot yet become king,
to use this to achieve security
is also easy, is it not?
This is how Zhào Xuānmèng was saved,
how Lord Zhāowén of Zhōu became illustrious,
and how Lord Mèngcháng repelled the Chǔ army.
Those in ancient times who achieved great merit and fame, secured the state, and preserved themselves—
their way had no other secret;
it necessarily came from this.
Capable scholars cannot be bent by arrogance and willfulness.
Long ago, when Zhào Xuānmèng was going up to Jiàng,
he saw under a twisted mulberry tree
a starving man lying unable to rise.
Xuānmèng stopped his chariot,
prepared food for him,
cleansed him and fed him.
The starving man swallowed twice before he could see.
Xuānmèng asked him:
"Why are you starving like this?"
He replied:
"I served as an official in Jiàng,
and on returning my provisions ran out.
I was ashamed to beg and hated to steal,
so I ended up like this."
Xuānmèng gave him one or two pieces of dried meat.
The man bowed and received it but did not dare eat it.
Asked the reason,
he replied:
"I have an old mother;
I will give this to her."
Xuānmèng said:
"Eat this now,
I will give you more."
Then he bestowed on him two bundles of dried meat and a hundred coins,
and then departed.
Two years later,
Duke Líng of Jìn wanted to kill Xuānmèng.
He stationed armed men in a side room to await him,
and then served wine to Xuānmèng.
Xuānmèng realized this,
and left midway through the drinking.
Duke Líng ordered the men in the side room to quickly pursue and kill him.
One man pursued swiftly,
reaching Xuānmèng first.
Seeing Xuānmèng's face, he said:
"Ah,
it is you, my lord!
I beg to return and die for you."
Xuānmèng said:
"What is your name?"
Turning to run back, he replied:
"What use is a name!
I am the starving man under the twisted mulberry tree."
He turned back, fought, and died.
Thus Xuānmèng survived.
This is what the Documents mean by
"Virtue, however small, is never insignificant."
Xuānmèng's virtue toward one scholar saved his own life;
how much more if he had shown virtue to ten thousand men?
Therefore the Odes say:
"Valiant are the martial men,
bulwark of the lords and princes";
"Numerous are the officers,
with whom King Wén secured peace."
How can a ruler not strive to cherish scholars?
Scholars are difficult to know;
only by broadening contact can it be done.
Broaden contact, and none can remain hidden.
Zhāng Yí
was a collateral descendant of the Wèi clan.
He was about to travel west to Qín,
passing through Eastern Zhōu.
A guest spoke to Lord Zhāowén about him, saying:
"Zhāng Yí of the Wèi clan
is a man of talent.
He is about to travel west to Qín.
I hope you will treat him with ritual respect."
Lord Zhāowén met him and said:
"I hear you are going to Qín.
My state is small,
insufficient to detain a guest.
Even if you travel,
are you certain to find opportunity?
If you, sir, do not find opportunity,
I ask that you return for my sake.
Though my state is small,
I ask to share it with you."
Zhāng Yí turned and stepped back,
facing north and bowing twice.
When Zhāng Yí departed,
Lord Zhāowén saw him off and provided him funds.
Arriving in Qín,
after staying a while,
King Huì was pleased and made him prime minister.
Of all the benefactors Zhāng Yí had in the world,
none was like Lord Zhāowén.
Zhōu
was a state of a thousand chariots,
yet its weight surpassed that of ten thousand chariots.
He made King Huì of Qín take him as teacher.
At the meeting at Féngzé,
the King of Wèi once held the reins for him,
the King of Hán served as his attendant on the right,
and his name and title are not forgotten to this day.
This was due to Zhāng Yí's efforts.
Previously, while Lord Mèngcháng was in Xuē,
the people of Chǔ attacked it.
Chúnyú Kūn was on a mission from Qí to Chǔ.
On his return,
he passed through Xuē.
Lord Mèngcháng had people treat him with ritual respect and personally escorted him to the outskirts.
He said to Chúnyú Kūn:
"The people of Chǔ are attacking Xuē.
If you, Master, do not show concern,
I will have no means to serve you again."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"I respectfully heed your command."
Arriving in Qí,
he completed his report.
The King said:
"What did you see in Chǔ?"
He replied:
"Chǔ is very stubborn,
and Xuē also does not assess its own strength."
The King said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"Xuē does not assess its own strength,
yet it built a pure temple for the former king.
Chǔ is stubborn and attacks Xuē;
Xuē's pure temple will certainly be endangered.
Therefore I say Xuē does not assess its own strength,
and Chǔ is also very stubborn."
The King of Qí showed understanding in his expression,
and said:
"Alas!
The ancestral temple of my late father is there."
He swiftly raised troops to rescue it,
and thus Xuē was preserved intact.
The plea made in stumbling haste,
the audience obtained while seated,
though slight, were indeed slight.
Therefore, a skilled persuader
lays out the situation,
speaks of the method,
and when seeing another's urgency,
feels as if he himself were in peril and distress—
how could he rely on forceful strength?
To rely on forceful strength is crude.
If the persuasion is not heeded,
the responsibility lies not solely with the one being persuaded,
but also with the persuader.
15.5 "Shùn Shuō" (Persuasion Through Accord)
The fifth says:
A skilled persuader is like a clever craftsman
who uses another's strength as his own;
he follows along with their coming,
and follows along with their going;
he establishes no fixed form or image,
but grows and develops along with them;
his words echo like a resonance;
he aligns with their flourishing and decline,
thereby guiding them to their destination.
Though the other's strength be great,
though their talent be vigorous,
he can control their fate.
Shouting with the wind,
one's voice is not increased in speed;
gazing from a high place,
one's eyesight is not made clearer;
it is because what one relies on is advantageous.
Huì Àng went to see King Kāng of Sòng.
King Kāng stamped his feet, cleared his throat, and said hastily:
"What I, the solitary one, delight in is courage and strength;
I do not delight in those who advocate benevolence and righteousness.
What will you, guest, use to instruct me?"
Huì Àng replied:
"I have a Way here
that makes a man, though courageous,
unable to stab into;
though strong,
unable to strike and hit.
Does Your Majesty alone have no interest in this?"
The King said:
"Excellent!
This is what I desire to hear."
Huì Àng said:
"That they cannot stab into,
cannot strike and hit—
this is still a disgrace.
I have a Way here
that makes a man, though courageous, dare not stab,
though strong, dare not strike.
Does Your Majesty alone have no interest in this?"
The King said:
"Excellent!
This is what I desire to know."
Huì Àng said:
"That they dare not stab,
dare not strike—
is not because they lack the intent.
I have a Way here
that makes a man fundamentally lack such intent.
Does Your Majesty alone have no interest in this?"
The King said:
"Excellent!
This is what I wish for."
Huì Àng said:
"Lacking the intent
still means not having a heart of love and benefit.
I have a Way here
that makes all men and women under heaven joyfully desire to love and benefit him.
This surpasses courage and strength,
standing above the four encumbrances.
Does Your Majesty alone have no interest in this?"
The King said: "This is what I desire to obtain."
Huì Àng replied:
"It is Kǒng and Mò.
Kǒng Qiū and Mò Dí,
though they possessed no land, were rulers;
though they held no office, were leaders.
All men and women under heaven craned their necks and stood on tiptoe, wishing to bring them peace and benefit.
Now, Your Majesty is the lord of a myriad chariots.
If you truly possess such intent,
then all within the four borders will obtain benefit from you.
This would far surpass Kǒng and Mò."
The King of Sòng had no reply.
Huì Àng hurried out.
The King of Sòng said to his attendants:
"Eloquent indeed!
The guest has used his persuasion to convince me."
The King of Sòng was a vulgar ruler,
yet his mind could still be convinced—
such is 'relying on circumstances.'
By relying on circumstances, the poor and lowly can overcome the rich and noble;
the small and weak can control the strong and great.
Tián Zàn, wearing patched clothing, went to see the King of Jīng.
The King of Jīng said:
"Why is your clothing so poor, sir?"
Tián Zàn replied:
"There is clothing worse than this."
The King of Jīng said:
"May I hear of it?"
He replied:
"Armor is worse than this."
The King said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"In winter it is cold,
in summer it is hot—
no clothing is worse than armor.
I, Zàn, am poor,
therefore my clothing is poor.
Now, Your Majesty is the lord of a myriad chariots,
your wealth and honor are unmatched,
yet you delight in clothing your people in armor—
I do not understand it.
Is it perhaps for righteousness' sake?
The matter of armor is the matter of war:
cutting men's necks,
carving out men's bellies,
destroying men's city walls,
executing men's fathers and sons—
its name is also most inglorious.
Is it perhaps for practical benefit?
If one schemes to harm others,
others will surely scheme to harm him;
if one schemes to endanger others,
others will surely scheme to endanger him.
The practical reality is also most unsafe.
Of these two,
I see nothing for Your Majesty to choose."
The King of Jīng had no reply.
Though his persuasion was not greatly implemented,
Tián Zàn can be said to have been able to establish his method.
As for the righteousness of reclining at ease,
he did not yet recognize it.
Guǎn Zhòng was captured in Lǔ.
Lǔ bound him and put him in a cage cart,
ordering laborers to cart and deliver him to Qí.
They sang as they pulled.
Guǎn Zhòng feared that Lǔ would stop and kill him,
and wished to reach Qí quickly.
Therefore, he said to the laborers:
"I will sing for you,
and you will chorus for me."
What he sang was suited for a fast pace.
The laborers did not tire,
and they covered the road very swiftly.
Guǎn Zhòng can be said to have been able to rely on circumstances.
The laborers obtained what they desired,
and he himself also obtained what he desired.
Using this method
to govern a state of ten thousand chariots,
achieving hegemony would still be insufficient—
Duke Huán would have found it difficult to go along with him.
15.6 "Bù Guǎng" (Not Neglecting Human Effort)
The sixth says:
The wise, when undertaking affairs, must rely on the timeliness.
Timeliness cannot be guaranteed to succeed,
therefore their human effort is not neglected.
Success is acceptable, failure is also acceptable.
They use what they are capable of to entrust what they are incapable of,
like a boat and a cart.
In the north there is a beast
named Jué.
Its front legs are like a rat's, its hind legs like a rabbit's.
When it hurries, it stumbles;
when it runs, it falls.
It often gathers sweet grass for the Qióngqióng Jùxū and gives it to them.
When Jué faces calamity or harm,
the Qióngqióng Jùxū will surely carry it on their backs and flee.
This is using what they are capable of to entrust what they are incapable of.
Bào Shū, Guǎn Zhòng, and Shào Hū
were three men who were close friends.
They wished together to stabilize the state of Qí,
believing that Prince Jiǔ would certainly be established.
Shào Hū said:
"We three men, regarding the state of Qí,
are like the legs of a tripod—
remove one and it will not stand.
Moreover, Xiǎo Bái certainly will not be established;
it would be better for the three of us to assist Prince Jiǔ."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"It cannot be done.
The people of the state despise the mother of Prince Jiǔ,
and by extension, Prince Jiǔ himself;
Prince Xiǎo Bái has no mother,
so the people pity him.
The outcome of affairs is unpredictable,
it would be better to have one man serve Prince Xiǎo Bái.
Whoever possesses the state of Qí will surely be one of these two princes."
Therefore, he ordered Bào Shū to tutor Prince Xiǎo Bái,
while Guǎn Zhòng and Shào Hū remained with Prince Jiǔ.
For Prince Jiǔ, external factors were inherently difficult to guarantee.
Even so,
Guǎn Zhòng's considerations were close to the mark.
If even this could not ensure his safety,
was it the will of Heaven?
Human efforts had been exhausted.
Qí attacked Lǐnqiū.
Zhào sent Kǒng Qīng to lead a force of dare-to-die soldiers to rescue it,
and in battle with the Qí army,
inflicted a great defeat upon them.
The Qí general was killed.
They captured two thousand chariots,
and gathered thirty thousand corpses to form two great mounds.
Nìng Yuè said to Kǒng Qīng:
"What a pity!
It would be better to return the corpses to attack them from within.
I have heard that
in ancient times, those skilled in warfare,
when the enemy was exhausted and submitted,
would withdraw their troops and leave the corpses,
so that the enemy, in retrieving the corpses, would deplete their resources,
their chariots and armor exhausted from battle,
their treasuries emptied for burials.
This is what is called attacking from within."
Kǒng Qīng said:
"What if the enemy, Qí, does not retrieve the corpses?"
Nìng Yuè said:
"If they fight and do not win, that is their first crime.
They lead men out but do not bring them back,
that is their second crime.
When corpses are offered to them and they do not take them,
that is their third crime.
The people will resent their superiors for these three reasons,
the superiors will have no means to command their subordinates,
the subordinates will have no means to serve their superiors.
This is what is called a double attack."
Nìng Yuè can be said to have understood the use of both civil and martial means.
Using martial means, one wins by force;
using civil means, one wins by virtue.
If both civil and martial means achieve victory,
what enemy would not submit?
Duke Wén of Jìn wished to assemble the feudal lords.
Jiù Fàn said:
"It cannot be done.
The world does not yet know Your Lordship's righteousness."
The Duke said:
"What should be done?"
Jiù Fàn said:
"The Son of Heaven, fleeing the troubles caused by Shū Dài,
has taken residence in Zhèng.
Why does Your Lordship not receive him,
thereby establishing great righteousness?
Moreover, it would enhance your reputation."
Duke Wén said:
"Am I capable of this?"
Jiù Fàn said:
"If the affair succeeds,
you will continue the civil achievements [of former rulers],
secure the martial accomplishments,
expand territory and secure borders—
all this lies herein.
If the affair does not succeed,
you will have mended the shortcomings of the Zhōu house,
relieved the difficulties of the Son of Heaven,
established teachings and left a lasting name—
all this lies herein.
Your Lordship should have no doubts."
Duke Wén heeded him,
and thus, with the Róng of Cǎozhōng and the Dí of Lítǔ,
settled the Son of Heaven in Chéngzhōu.
Thereupon, the Son of Heaven granted him the lands of Nányáng,
and he subsequently became hegemon of the feudal lords.
In undertaking affairs, righteousness and benefit,
to establish great achievements.
Duke Wén can be said to have been wise.
This was the strategy of Jiù Fàn.
Having been in exile for seventeen years,
returning to his state for four years and becoming hegemon—
were all his decisions like those of Jiù Fàn?
Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū assisted Duke Huán of Qí in managing affairs,
and the people of the eastern border regions of Qí often suffered hardship.
After Guǎn Zhòng died,
Shù Diāo and Yì Yá came to power,
and the people of the state often suffered even more, not knowing hardship,
unaware of suffering,
yet they ultimately became skilled artisans for the state of Qí,
with benefits extending to their descendants.
To understand great ritual,
even if one does not understand statecraft, it is acceptable.
15.7 "Valuing Adaptation"
The seventh discourse says:
Of the treasures of the Three Dynasties, none surpasses adaptation;
with adaptation, one is invincible.
Yǔ dredged the Three Rivers and Five Lakes,
opened the Yīquè Gorge,
channeled the land's waterways,
directing them east to the sea—
this was by adapting to the power of water.
Shùn, with one move, established a settlement;
with a second move, established a capital;
with a third move, established a state—
and Yáo abdicated the throne to him—
this was by adapting to the hearts of the people.
Tāng and Wǔ, with a thousand chariots, subdued Xià and Shāng—
this was by adapting to the desires of the people.
One who goes to Qín stands and arrives—
because there are chariots;
one who goes to Yuè sits and arrives—
because there are boats.
Qín and Yuè are distant journeys,
yet one arrives by standing still or sitting comfortably—
because one adapts to the tools.
King Wǔ sent someone to spy on Yīn,
who returned and reported to Qízhōu:
"Yīn is in chaos."
King Wǔ said:
"How far has the chaos reached?"
The reply was:
"Slanderers and villains prevail over the loyal and good."
King Wǔ said:
"Not yet."
He went again,
and returned to report:
"The chaos has increased."
King Wǔ said:
"How far?"
The reply was:
"The worthy have fled."
King Wǔ said:
"Not yet."
He went again,
and returned to report:
"The chaos is severe."
King Wǔ said:
"How far?"
The reply was:
"The common people dare not voice grievances or complaints."
King Wǔ said:
"Ah!"
He hurriedly informed Tàigōng.
Tàigōng replied:
"When slanderers and villains prevail over the loyal and good,
it is called 'slaughter';
when the worthy flee,
it is called 'collapse';
when the common people dare not voice grievances or complaints,
it is called 'punishment prevailing.'
The chaos has reached its peak,
it cannot be delayed any longer."
Therefore, he selected three hundred chariots,
three thousand tiger warriors,
and set the morning rendezvous for the day Jiǎzǐ,
and Zhòu was captured—
thus King Wǔ certainly knew he had no match.
By adapting to what he used,
what enemy could there be?
King Wǔ reached the Wěi River.
Yīn sent Jiāo Gé to observe the Zhōu army,
and King Wǔ received him.
Jiāo Gé said:
"Where is the Earl of the West going?
Do not deceive me."
King Wǔ said:
"I will not deceive you,
I am going to Yīn."
Jiāo Gé said:
"When will you arrive?"
King Wǔ said:
"I will arrive at the outskirts of Yīn on the day Jiǎzǐ,
you may report this."
Jiāo Gé departed.
It rained,
day and night without cease,
but King Wǔ pressed on without stopping.
The army commanders all advised him:
"The troops are weary,
we request a rest."
King Wǔ said:
"I have already ordered Jiāo Gé to report the date Jiǎzǐ to his lord.
If we do not arrive by Jiǎzǐ,
it will make Jiāo Gé untrustworthy.
If Jiāo Gé is untrustworthy,
his lord will surely kill him.
I press on to save Jiāo Gé from death."
King Wǔ indeed arrived at the outskirts of Yīn on the day of Jiǎzǐ.
The Yīn army had already formed their battle array beforehand.
Upon reaching Yīn,
they engaged in battle,
and achieved a great victory over them.
This was the righteousness of King Wǔ.
If one does what others desire,
and oneself does what others detest,
what benefit is there in forming the array first?
It merely allowed King Wǔ to reap without sowing.
When King Wǔ entered Yīn,
he heard that there was an elder in Yīn.
King Wǔ went to see him,
and asked him the reason for Yīn's downfall.
The elder of Yīn replied:
"If Your Majesty wishes to know,
then let us set midday as the appointed time."
King Wǔ and the Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, went early the next morning to meet at the appointed time,
but did not find him.
King Wǔ thought it strange.
The Duke of Zhōu said:
"I already understand.
This man is a gentleman.
Having served a ruler he could not approve of,
to then inform Your Majesty of his ruler's faults—
he could not bear to do it.
As for setting an appointment and not keeping it,
speaking without honesty,
this is the reason for Yīn's downfall.
He has already conveyed this to Your Majesty."
Now, those who observe the heavens,
examine the constellations to know the four seasons—
this is adaptation.
Those who calculate the calendar,
observe the moon's motion to know the new and full moons—
this is adaptation.
When Yǔ went to the naked country,
he entered naked and clothed himself upon leaving—
this is adaptation.
When Mòzǐ visited the King of Jīng,
he wore brocade and played the shēng—
this is adaptation.
When Confucius, through Mí Zǐxiá, sought an audience with Lady Lí—
this is adaptation.
When Tāng and Wǔ encountered a chaotic age,
faced a suffering people,
promoted their righteousness,
and achieved their success—
this is adaptation.
Therefore, adaptation leads to success,
while rigidity leads to clumsiness.
Those who adapt are invincible.
Even if a state is large,
and its people numerous,
what benefit is there?
15.8 "Examining the Present"
The eighth discourse says:
Why do rulers not model themselves on the laws of the former kings?
It is not that they are not worthy,
but because they cannot be modeled upon.
The laws of the former kings
have come down through past ages.
Some people have added to them,
others have subtracted from them—
how can they be modeled upon?
Even if no one had added or subtracted,
they still could not be modeled upon.
The terms of the East and of Xià,
the laws of ancient and modern times,
differ in language and vary in statutes.
Thus, many ancient terms are not understood in modern speech,
and many modern laws do not match ancient laws.
Peoples with different customs
are similar in this regard.
Their desires may be the same,
but their actions differ. The commands of a confused mouth are not understood,
just as boats, carts, clothing, caps, flavors, sounds, and colors differ.
Each person considers himself right,
and conversely slanders others.
Most scholars in the world are contentious,
their speech sharp and their arguments inverted.
They do not seek the truth of the matter,
but strive to slander each other,
taking victory as their aim.
How can the laws of the former kings
be modeled upon?
Even if they could be obtained,
they still could not be modeled upon.
All laws of the former kings
were suited to their time.
The times do not arrive together with the laws.
Even if the laws arrive today,
they still cannot be modeled upon.
Therefore, one should select the established laws of the former kings,
and model oneself on the basis upon which they made their laws.
What was the basis upon which the former kings made their laws?
The basis upon which the former kings made their laws was humanity.
And we ourselves are also human,
so by examining ourselves we can understand others,
by examining the present we can understand the past.
Past and present are one,
others and ourselves are alike.
A man of the Way
values using the near to know the distant,
using the present to know the past,
using what is seen to know what is unseen.
Thus, by observing the shadows beneath the hall,
he knows the course of the sun and moon, the changes of yīn and yáng;
by seeing the ice in a bottle of water,
he knows the cold of the world, the hibernation of fish and turtles;
by tasting one morsel of meat,
he knows the flavor of the whole pot, the seasoning of the whole tripod.
The people of Jīng wanted to attack Sòng,
and sent men first to mark the depth of the Yōng River.
The Yōng River suddenly rose,
but the people of Jīng did not know.
They followed the markers and crossed at night,
drowning more than a thousand men.
The army was thrown into panic, collapsing like city buildings.
When they first marked it, the river could be forded.
Now the water had changed and risen much higher,
yet the people of Jīng still followed the markers to guide them—
this is why they failed.
The rulers of the present age,
in modeling themselves on the laws of the former kings,
are similar to this.
Their time already differs from that of the former kings' laws,
yet they say,
"These are the laws of the former kings,"
and model themselves on them.
To govern in this way—
is it not lamentable?
Therefore, to govern a state without laws leads to chaos;
to hold fast to laws without change leads to absurdity.
Absurdity and chaos cannot sustain a state.
The world changes, the times shift—
changing the laws is appropriate.
It is like a good physician:
illnesses change in myriad ways,
and medicines also change in myriad ways.
If the illness changes but the medicine does not,
one who was formerly long-lived
would now become a short-lived child.
Therefore, in all undertakings one must act according to the law,
and those who change the laws must transform according to the times.
Following this principle, there will be no mistaken endeavors.
Now, those who dare not discuss the laws
are the common multitude;
those who defend them unto death
are the officials;
those who change the laws according to the times
are worthy rulers.
Thus, the seventy-two sages who possessed the world
all had different laws—
not because they sought to be contrary,
but because the times and circumstances differed.
Therefore it is said: a good sword is expected to cut,
not necessarily to be a Mòyé;
a good horse is expected to run a thousand lǐ,
not necessarily to be a Jì'áo.
That which achieves success and fame—
this is the former kings' "thousand-lǐ horse."
There was a man of Chǔ crossing a river.
His sword fell from the boat into the water.
He hastily notched the side of the boat, saying:
"This is where my sword fell from."
When the boat stopped,
he entered the water to search for it from the place he had notched.
The boat had already moved,
but the sword had not.
To search for a sword in this manner—
is it not foolish?
To use old laws to govern one's state is the same as this.
The time has already shifted,
yet the laws do not shift.
To govern in this way—
is it not difficult?
There was a man passing by a river
who saw someone about to throw an infant into the river.
The infant cried.
The man asked the reason.
He said:
"This child's father was a good swimmer."
Even if the father was a good swimmer,
would the son necessarily be a good swimmer?
To handle affairs in this manner is also bound to be absurd.
The way the state of Jīng conducts its governance
is similar to this.
16.1 "Foreknowledge"
First:
Whenever a state is about to perish,
those who possess the Way will inevitably depart first.
This holds true for both ancient and modern times.
The land follows the cities,
the cities follow the people,
and the people follow the worthy.
Thus, when a worthy ruler obtains the worthy, he obtains the people;
when he obtains the people, he obtains the cities;
when he obtains the cities, he obtains the land.
Now, does obtaining the land necessarily require treading upon it in person or persuading its people oneself?
It is merely a matter of grasping the essential point.
The Grand Historian of Xià, Zhōnggǔ,
took out the charts and laws of his state, held them, and wept.
As Jié of Xià grew increasingly deluded and confused,
and his tyranny and disorder worsened,
Grand Historian Zhōnggǔ then fled to Shāng.
Tāng was pleased and announced to the feudal lords:
"The King of Xià is without the Way,
tyrannizing and oppressing the common people,
exhausting their fathers and elder brothers,
humiliating his meritorious ministers,
disdaining the worthy and good,
abandoning righteousness and listening to slander.
The multitudes all harbor resentment,
and now a minister who upheld the laws
has voluntarily come to Shāng."
The Inner Scribe of Yīn, Xiàng Zhì, seeing that Zhòu was growing increasingly tyrannical, disordered, and deluded,
thereupon loaded the charts and laws onto a cart
and fled to Zhōu.
King Wǔ was greatly pleased
and announced to the feudal lords:
"The King of Shāng is in great disorder,
immersed in the virtue of wine,
keeping Jīzǐ at a distance,
while drawing close to women and favorites.
Dájǐ handles the governance,
rewards and punishments are without principle,
laws and regulations are not used,
three innocent men have been killed,
the people are greatly discontent,
and a minister who upheld the laws
has fled to the state of Zhōu."
The Grand Historian of Jìn, Tú Shǔ, observing the disorder in Jìn
and seeing the arrogance and lack of virtue and righteousness of the Duke of Jìn,
took the charts and laws and went to Zhōu.
Duke Wēi of Zhōu received him and asked,
saying:
"Among the states under Heaven, which will perish first?"
He replied:
"Jìn will perish first."
Duke Wēi asked his reason.
He replied:
"When your servant was recently in Jìn,
I dared not speak directly.
I showed the Duke of Jìn celestial portents—
the movements of the sun, moon, and stars were mostly irregular—
and he said:
'What can these do?'
I also showed him that human affairs were mostly unrighteous,
and the common people were all filled with suppressed resentment,
and he said:
'What harm can these do?'
I further showed him that neighboring states were not submissive
and the worthy and good were not promoted,
and he said:
'What injury can these cause?'
Being thus,
he does not understand the reasons for perishing.
Therefore, your servant says Jìn will perish first."
After three years,
Jìn indeed perished.
Duke Wēi again saw Tú Shǔ and asked him,
saying:
"Which will be next?"
He replied:
"Zhōngshān will be next."
Duke Wēi asked his reason.
He replied:
"Heaven gave birth to the people and established distinctions among them.
Having distinctions
is the righteousness of man,
that by which he differs from birds, beasts, deer, and elk,
and that upon which the relationships between ruler and minister, superior and inferior, are established.
The customs of Zhōngshān
make day into night
and continue night into day.
Men and women cling closely together,
constantly without rest,
indulging in licentiousness, confusion, comfort, and pleasure,
their songs and ballads fond of sorrow.
Their ruler does not know to detest this.
This is the atmosphere of a perishing state.
Therefore, your servant says Zhōngshān will be next."
After two years,
Zhōngshān indeed perished.
Duke Wēi again saw Tú Shǔ and asked him,
saying:
"Which will be next?"
Tú Shǔ did not reply.
Duke Wēi pressed him.
He replied:
"Your lordship will be next."
Duke Wēi then became fearful.
He sought out the elders of the state,
obtained Yì Shí and Tián Yì and treated them with ritual respect,
obtained Shǐ Lín and Zhào Pián to serve as remonstrating ministers,
and abolished thirty-nine oppressive decrees.
He reported this to Tú Shǔ.
He replied:
"Perhaps it will last until the end of your lordship's life!"
And said:
"Your servant has heard that:
When a state is about to flourish,
Heaven sends it worthy men and those who speak the utmost truth;
when a state is about to perish,
Heaven sends it disorderly men and those skilled in flattery."
When Duke Wēi died,
his body was placed in the temporary burial chamber,
and for nine months he could not be interred.
Zhōu then split into two.
Therefore, the words of those who possess the Way
cannot but be heeded.
On the Zhōu tripods, the Tāotiè is depicted:
it has a head but no body.
It devours men but cannot swallow them,
and the harm returns upon itself,
to illustrate retribution.
It is the same with doing evil.
When Bái Guī went to Zhōngshān,
the King of Zhōngshān wished to detain him,
but Bái Guī firmly declined
and departed by carriage.
He then went to Qí,
and the King of Qí also wished to detain him and offer him office,
but again he declined and left.
Someone asked him the reason.
He said:
"These two states are both about to perish.
From what I have learned, a state has five exhaustions.
What are called the five exhaustions?
They are:
When no one is trusted, then trust is exhausted;
when no one is praised, then reputation is exhausted;
when no one is loved, then kinship is exhausted;
when travelers have no provisions and residents have no food, then wealth is exhausted;
when one cannot employ others nor employ oneself, then achievement is exhausted.
If a state has these five,
it will inevitably perish without reprieve.
Both Zhōngshān and Qí correspond to this."
If the King of Zhōngshān and the King of Qí
had heard of the five exhaustions and reformed,
they would certainly not have perished.
Their calamity lay in not hearing,
or even if hearing, not believing.
Thus, the task of a ruler
lies solely in being good at listening.
As for ceding five cities to Zhào
and mobilizing all troops to resist the army at Jìshàng,
it was of no benefit.
This is to abandon that by which one survives
and create that by which one perishes.
16.2 Observing the Age
Second:
Although there are men who possess the Way under Heaven,
they are inherently few.
To have one such man within a thousand lǐ
is to have them shoulder to shoulder;
to have one sage in several generations
is to have them following on each other's heels.
The manner in which such men and sages arise
is so difficult as this,
yet order must await them.
How, then, can order be achieved?
Even if by chance there are such men,
one may not necessarily recognize them,
and not recognizing them is the same as having none.
This is why ages of order are short,
and ages of disorder are long.
Thus, true kings do not appear as a fourth,
and hegemons do not appear as a sixth;
perishing states look upon each other,
and imprisoned rulers succeed one another.
Obtaining such men would spare one this calamity.
The states enfeoffed by Zhōu numbered over four hundred,
and the submissive states over eight hundred,
yet none survive today;
even if any survive, they have all experienced destruction.
Worthy rulers know it is like this,
therefore they are cautious day by day,
to the end of their reigns.
It is like a mountain climber:
though he is already at a high place,
looking left and right,
he still sees towering mountains above him.
The way worthy individuals associate with others
is similar to this.
They themselves are already worthy,
their conduct is already lofty,
yet looking left and right,
they still see others as more worthy than themselves.
Thus, Duke Zhōu Dàn said:
"Those who are not as good as I am,
I do not associate with,
for they would burden me;
those who are equal to me,
I do not associate with,
for they would not benefit me."
Only the worthy must associate with those more worthy than themselves.
The reason worthy individuals can be associated with
is because they are treated with ritual propriety.
When the ruler is worthy and the world is well-governed,
then worthy individuals occupy high positions;
when the ruler is unworthy and the world is in chaos,
then worthy individuals are in low positions while flatterers advance. Now that the Zhōu house has perished,
the world has been abandoned.
No chaos is greater than having no Son of Heaven;
without a Son of Heaven, the strong overcome the weak,
the many oppress the few,
they attack each other with weapons,
finding no rest,
and flatterers advance,
the present age is experiencing this.
Therefore, in the present age, to seek men of the Way,
one must go to the shores of rivers and seas,
within mountains and valleys,
in remote, secluded, and isolated places;
only thus may one be fortunate enough to find them.
Tài Gōng fished at Zīquán,
encountering the era of Zhòu,
thus King Wén obtained him
and became king.
King Wén was a lord of a thousand chariots,
Zhòu was the Son of Heaven;
the Son of Heaven lost him,
while the lord of a thousand chariots gained him,
this is a matter of knowing or not knowing.
As for the multitudes of ordinary people,
they can be employed without being known,
and ordered without being treated with ritual propriety;
but as for men of the Way,
they must be treated with ritual propriety and must be known,
only then can their wisdom and abilities be fully utilized.
Yànzǐ went to Jìn,
and saw a man wearing his fur coat inside out, carrying fodder, resting by the road.
He thought him a gentleman,
and sent someone to ask him,
saying:
"Why have you come to this?"
The man replied:
"I was burdened by the people of Qí,
my name is Yuè Shífù."
Yànzǐ said:
"Alas!"
He immediately untied the left trace horse to ransom him,
and took him back in his carriage.
Upon reaching his residence,
Yànzǐ did not bid farewell before entering.
Yuè Shífù became angry,
and requested to sever ties.
Yànzǐ sent someone to respond to him, saying:
"I have never had dealings with you,
now I have saved you from distress,
is my treatment of you still not acceptable?"
Yuè Shífù said:
"I have heard that a gentleman may be constrained by those who do not know him,
but extends himself among those who know him.
This is why I request to sever ties."
Yànzǐ then came out to see him, saying:
"Earlier, I only saw your appearance,
now I see your will.
I have heard that one who examines reality does not dwell on reputation,
and one who observes conduct does not criticize words.
May I retract my words and not be rejected?"
Yuè Shífù said:
"Since you, sir, treat me with ritual propriety,
how dare I not respectfully comply?"
Yànzǐ then regarded him as a guest of honor.
Common people, when they have merit, become virtuous,
and when virtuous, become arrogant;
now Yànzǐ had the merit of saving someone from distress,
yet he instead humbled himself before him,
his distance from the common is indeed great.
This is the way to preserve merit completely.
Lièzǐ was impoverished,
his appearance showed signs of hunger.
A guest spoke of him to Zhèng Zǐyáng,
saying:
"Liè Yùkòu,
is a man of the Way.
Residing in your state yet impoverished,
are you not perhaps not fond of scholars?"
Zhèng Zǐyáng ordered an official to send him several tens of bundles of grain.
Lièzǐ went out to see the messenger,
bowed twice and declined.
After the messenger left,
Lièzǐ went inside.
His wife looked at him and beat her breast,
saying:
"I have heard that the wives and children of men of the Way
all enjoy ease and pleasure.
Now your wife and children show signs of hunger;
the ruler, recognizing his error, sent you food,
yet you, sir, again did not accept it.
Is this not fate?"
Lièzǐ laughed and said to her:
"The ruler does not know me himself,
but because of someone's words he sent me grain.
When he comes to condemn me,
he will also do so because of someone's words.
This is why I did not accept it."
In the end, the people indeed rebelled,
and killed Zǐyáng.
To accept another's support,
yet not die for their calamity is unrighteous;
to die for their calamity is to die for an unrighteous cause.
To die for an unrighteous cause
is perverse.
Lièzǐ avoided unrighteousness and removed perversity;
is this not far-sighted?
Moreover, he was suffering from hunger and cold,
yet still did not take improperly,
foreseeing the transformation.
Foreseeing the transformation and thus acting accordingly,
he was attuned to the essence of life and destiny.
16.3 "Knowing Connection"
Third:
A person's eyes, when they illuminate, see things;
when closed, it is the same as not seeing.
The means by which they illuminate
and the means by which they close are different.
A blind person has never illuminated,
thus has never seen;
a blind person's eyes have no means of connection.
Having no means of connection yet claiming to see is deceit.
Wisdom is also like this.
The means by which it connects wisdom and the means by which it connects unwisdom are the same,
but what it can connect to and what it cannot connect to are different.
The wise can connect to distant things,
the foolish can only connect to nearby things.
If one can only connect to nearby things yet is told of distant transformations,
how can they comprehend?
Having no means of comprehension,
even if the speaker is skilled,
they cannot be made to understand.
A Róng person saw someone spreading cloth and asked:
"Why make it so coarse?"
The person pointed to hemp and showed him.
The Róng person angrily said:
"Who would take such tangled stuff
to make something so coarse?"
Thus, a perishing state is not without wise scholars,
nor without worthy individuals,
but because its ruler has no means of connecting with them.
The trouble of having no means of connection
is that one considers oneself wise,
but wisdom certainly does not connect.
Now, without connection yet considering oneself wise
is delusion.
If so, then the state cannot be preserved,
and the ruler cannot be secure.
If wisdom has no means of connection,
yet one knows oneself to be unwise,
then one does not hear of states perishing,
nor of rulers being endangered.
Guǎn Zhòng fell ill.
Duke Huán went to ask him, saying:
"Zhòngfù's illness is grave;
what instruction do you have for me?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"The rustic people of Qí have a proverb:
'Those who stay do not carry burdens,
those who depart do not bury things.'
Now I am about to go on a long journey,
how can I be asked?"
Duke Huán said:
"I hope Zhòngfù will not decline."
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"I hope you will keep distant Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, Cháng Zhī Wū, and Wèi Prince Qǐfāng."
The Duke said:
"Yì Yá cooked his own son to please me;
is he still to be doubted?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Human nature
does not lack love for one's own child.
If he could bear to do that to his own son,
what would he not do to you, my lord?"
The Duke also said:
"Shù Diāo castrated himself to be close to me;
is he still to be doubted?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Human nature is such that
one does not love one's own body less;
if he could bear to mutilate his own body,
what would he not do to his lord?"
The Duke also said:
"Cháng Zhī Wū understands life and death thoroughly,
and can cure severe illnesses;
is he still to be doubted?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Life and death are fate,
severe illnesses are due to lapses.
If you do not accept your fate
and hold to the fundamentals,
but rely on Cháng Zhī Wū,
he will use this to do anything."
The Duke also said:
"The Wèi prince Qǐ Fāng has served me for fifteen years;
when his father died, he dared not return to mourn;
is he still to be doubted?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Human nature is such that
one does not love one's own father less;
if he could bear to abandon his own father,
what would he not do to his lord?"
The Duke said:
"Very well."
After Guǎn Zhòng died,
the Duke expelled them all.
His food lost its flavor,
his palace fell into disorder,
severe illnesses arose,
and the court lost its solemnity.
After three years,
the Duke said:
"Was not Zhòng Fù mistaken?
Who says Zhòng Fù was completely right?"
Thereupon, he summoned them all back and reinstated them.
The following year,
the Duke fell ill.
Cháng Zhī Wū came out from within and said:
"The Duke will pass away on such-and-such a day."
Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, and Cháng Zhī Wū joined in rebellion together.
They sealed the palace gates,
built high walls,
cut off access,
and forged the Duke's orders.
A woman climbed over the wall
and reached the Duke's place.
The Duke said:
"I want a drink."
The woman said:
"I cannot get anything."
The Duke said again:
"I want a drink."
The woman said:
"I cannot get anything."
The Duke said:
"Why?"
She replied:
"Cháng Zhī Wū came out from within and said:
'The Duke will pass away on such-and-such a day.'
Yì Yá, Shù Diāo, and Cháng Zhī Wū joined in rebellion together.
They sealed the palace gates,
built high walls,
cut off access,
so nothing can be obtained.
The Wèi prince Qǐ Fāng has taken forty communities and gone to Wèi."
The Duke sighed with emotion,
tears flowing as he said:
"Alas!
The sage's foresight
was indeed far-reaching!
If the dead have consciousness,
what face will I have to see Zhòng Fù?"
Covering his face with his sleeve, he died in the Shòu Palace.
Maggots flowed out from the door,
and the entrance was covered with a Yang Gate fan;
for three months he was not buried.
This was because he did not heed Guǎn Zhòng's words to the end.
Duke Huán did not belittle difficulties or dislike Guǎnzǐ;
he had no means to perceive.
Having no means to perceive,
he naturally rejected his loyal words and favored those he esteemed.
16.4 "Repenting of Errors"
The fourth says:
If a hole is eight fathoms deep, a man's arm certainly cannot reach the bottom;
why is this?
Because it does not reach.
Wisdom also has its limits.
Where it does not reach,
even if the speaker is eloquent,
and the principles are refined,
they cannot be seen.
Thus, Jīzǐ was trapped in Shāng,
and Fàn Lǐ drifted on the river.
Long ago, Duke Mù of Qín raised an army to launch a surprise attack on Zhèng.
Jiǎn Shū remonstrated, saying:
"It cannot be done.
I have heard that
in surprising a state or city,
with chariots one should not exceed a hundred lǐ,
with men one should not exceed thirty lǐ.
All rely on the vigor of their spirit and the abundance of their strength
to arrive,
so they can destroy the enemy when they engage,
and withdraw swiftly when they leave.
Now to march several thousand lǐ, crossing the territories of many feudal lords to surprise a state,
I do not see how it can succeed.
I urge you to reconsider carefully."
Duke Mù did not listen.
Jiǎn Shū saw off the army outside the gate,
weeping in mourning clothes,
saying:
"Army!
I see you depart but will not see you return."
Jiǎn Shū had two sons, Shēn and Shì,
who went with the army.
Jiǎn Shū said to his sons:
"If Jìn blocks the army, it will surely be at Yáo.
If you die, it will be either on the southern bank
or on the northern bank.
Make it easy for me to recover your bodies."
When Duke Mù heard of this,
he sent someone to reprimand Jiǎn Shū, saying:
"I am raising an army;
who knows how it will turn out?
Now you weep as you send them off;
this is weeping for my army."
Jiǎn Shū replied:
"I dare not weep for the army.
I am old,
and have two sons
who are both going with the army.
By the time they return,
if they are not dead, then I will surely be dead.
That is why I weep."
The army then set out.
Passing through Zhōu,
Wángsūn Mǎn watched from the side of the gate and said:
"Alas!
This army is sure to have flaws.
If it has no flaws,
I will never speak of the Way again.
Now Qín is no other
than a state established by the Zhōu house.
Passing by the Son of Heaven's city,
they should stow their armor and bundle their weapons,
dismount on both sides,
to show respect for the Son of Heaven.
Now they wear uniform armor and carry flags reversed;
those on the left do not touch the chariot rail in salute,
and those on the right leap onto their chariots—five hundred chariots thus.
Their strength is great indeed,
but they lack propriety.
How can they be without flaws?"
The army passed through Zhōu and went east.
Zhèng merchants Xián Gāo and Xī Shī were heading west to trade in Zhōu
when they encountered the Qín army on the road.
They said:
"Ah!
This army has come from afar;
it must be to surprise Zhèng."
They immediately sent Xī Shī back to report
and forged an order from the Earl of Zhèng to offer provisions, saying:
"My lord has long heard that your great state would arrive.
Since your great state did not come,
my lord and the soldiers have privately worried for your great state,
with nothing to do all day
but fear that your soldiers might be weary and your provisions exhausted.
How long it has been!
He sends his minister to offer provisions with jade disks
and a feast of twelve oxen."
The three Qín commanders replied:
"Our lord had no one to send,
so he sent his three ministers Bǐng,
Shù, and Shì to the eastern border to watch the road to Jìn.
We passed by and mistakenly entered the territory of your great state."
Not daring to firmly decline,
they bowed twice, touched their heads to the ground, and accepted.
The three commanders then grew fearful and plotted, saying:
"We have marched several thousand lǐ, crossing the territories of many feudal lords to surprise others,
but before we arrived, they already knew of it.
Their preparations must already be thorough."
They turned the army around and left.
At that time,
Duke Wén of Jìn had just died
and was not yet buried.
Xiān Zhěn said to Duke Xiāng:
"The Qín army must be attacked;
I request to attack them."
Duke Xiāng said:
"The former lord has passed away,
his corpse lies in the hall.
To see the Qín army's advantage and thus attack them,
is that not contrary to the way of a filial son?"
Xiān Zhěn said:
"They do not mourn our bereavement,
show no concern for our sorrow, and do not request passage.
This is to treat our lord as dead and weaken his orphan.
If we attack under such circumstances,
we can greatly strengthen ourselves.
I request permission to attack them."
Duke Xiāng had no choice but to consent.
Xiān Zhěn intercepted the Qín army at Xiáo and attacked them,
inflicting a great defeat,
capturing their three commanders and returning.
Duke Mù heard of this,
donned plain garments and faced the ancestral temple,
addressing the multitude to explain:
"Heaven did not favor the state of Qín,
causing me not to heed Jiǎn Shū's remonstrance,
leading to this calamity."
This Duke Mù did not wish to be defeated at Xiáo;
his wisdom was insufficient.
When wisdom is insufficient, there is no trust.
Yet words cannot be without trust.
The army's failure to return stems from this.
Thus, the harm of insufficient wisdom is great.
16.5 "Joy in Achievement"
The fifth says:
Great wisdom does not show its form,
great vessels are late to completion,
great sound is barely audible.
When Yǔ channeled the Jiāng River's waters,
the people gathered tiles and rubble.
When the task was accomplished,
the achievement established,
it became a benefit for ten thousand generations.
What Yǔ foresaw was far-reaching,
yet the people did not know it.
Therefore, one cannot deliberate on transformation and initiation with the people,
but can share joy in successful achievement.
When Confucius first gained employment in Lǔ,
the people of Lǔ chanted scornfully:
"In deerskin robes and knee-covers,
cast him away without fault;
in knee-covers and deerskin robes,
cast him away without blame."
After three years of service,
men walked on the right side of the road,
women walked on the left,
lost property,
the people did not pick up.
The application of great wisdom
is inherently difficult to surpass.
When Zǐ Chǎn first governed Zhèng,
he established field boundaries and ditches,
and regulated attire for capital and outlying areas.
The people chanted together:
"We have fields and lands,
yet Zǐ Chǎn taxes them.
We have clothes and caps,
yet Zǐ Chǎn stores them.
Whoever kills Zǐ Chǎn,
we will join them."
Three years later,
the people chanted again:
"We have fields and lands,
and Zǐ Chǎn enriches them.
We have sons and younger brothers,
and Zǐ Chǎn instructs them.
If Zǐ Chǎn dies,
who will succeed him?"
Had Duke Jiǎn of Zhèng and Duke Āi of Lǔ, facing the people's slander and criticism, thus not persisted in employing them,
then the state would surely have achieved no merit,
and Zǐ Chǎn and Confucius would have been incapable.
Not only incapable,
they could even have been punished among the people.
Nowadays, all praise Duke Jiǎn and Duke Āi as worthy,
praise Zǐ Chǎn and Confucius as capable.
These two rulers
understood the task of employing men.
When boats and carts first appeared,
three generations passed before people were at ease with them.
Is initiating goodness ever easy?
Therefore, listening without action leads to order.
The establishment of orderly governance
depends on the ruler's worthiness.
When Wèi attacked Zhōngshān,
Yuè Yáng commanded.
Having taken Zhōngshān,
he returned and reported to Marquis Wén,
with an expression of pride in his achievement.
Marquis Wén, aware of this,
ordered the archivist:
"Take all the writings presented by ministers and guests,
and bring them forth."
The archivist lifted two boxes and presented them.
He ordered the general to look:
the writings all concerned difficulties in attacking Zhōngshān.
The general retreated hastily,
faced north and bowed twice, saying:
"The capture of Zhōngshān
was not due to my strength,
but your lordship's merit."
At that time,
the scholars' discussions nearly reached a critical point;
had Zhōngshān not been taken,
why just two boxes?
An inch would have been lost.
Marquis Wén was a worthy ruler,
and even he was like this;
how much more so for a mediocre ruler?
The trouble with mediocre rulers is
they cannot refrain from action,
yet one cannot join them in steadfast action.
Whenever undertaking immutable tasks,
if spirit, will, sight, hearing, and actions are all aligned,
which minister would dare to doubt with what is not aligned?
All unified in action,
then no task will fail.
This is why Tāng and Wǔ achieved great merit against Xià and Shāng,
and why Gōu Jiàn could avenge his enemy.
Even small and weak states, unified in action, achieved this;
how much more so for the strong and great?
King Xiāng of Wèi was drinking with his ministers.
In the midst of revelry,
the king offered a toast to his ministers:
"May all my ministers attain their ambitions."
Shǐ Qǐ rose and replied:
"Among the ministers, some are worthy, some unworthy.
For the worthy to attain their ambitions is acceptable,
for the unworthy to attain their ambitions is not."
The king said:
"Let all be like Xīmén Bào as ministers."
Shǐ Qǐ replied:
"In Wèi's allocation of fields, it is one hundred mǔ per person,
yet in Yè alone it is two hundred mǔ,
because the land is poor.
The Zhāng River flows beside it, yet Xīmén Bào did not know to use it—
this shows his stupidity;
knowing yet not speaking—
this shows his disloyalty.
Stupidity and disloyalty
are not to be emulated."
The king of Wèi had no reply.
The next day,
he summoned Shǐ Qǐ and asked him:
"Can the Zhāng River still be used to irrigate the fields of Yè?"
Shǐ Qǐ replied:
"It can."
The king said:
"Why do you not do it for me?"
Shǐ Qǐ said:
"I fear your majesty cannot accomplish it."
The king said:
"If you can truly do it for me,
I will fully heed you."
Shǐ Qǐ respectfully agreed,
and said to the king:
"If I do it,
the people will greatly resent me.
At worst, I will die;
next, they will seize me.
Even if I die or am seized,
I hope your majesty will have another complete it."
The king said:
"Agreed."
He appointed him magistrate of Yè.
Shǐ Qǐ accordingly went to do it.
The people of Yè greatly resented it,
wishing to seize Shǐ Qǐ.
Shǐ Qǐ dared not appear and avoided them.
The king then had another complete it.
Once the water flowed,
the people greatly benefited,
and together sang:
"Yè has a sage magistrate,
at times Lord Shǐ,
who channeled the Zhāng River,
irrigated the lands of Yè,
turning age-old barren salt flats
into fields of rice and millet."
If the people knew what is feasible and what is not,
then there would be no use for it.
Worthy rulers and loyal ministers,
if they cannot guide the foolish and teach the ignorant,
then their names will not lead the future, nor their substance benefit the age.
Shǐ Qǐ was not unaware of transformation,
but acted out of loyalty to his lord.
King Xiāng of Wèi can be said to have been able to decide on goodness.
Truly able to decide on goodness,
even if the multitude clamors, one does not change.
The difficulty in establishing merit,
must surely arise from subtle distinctions.
The ruin and destruction of a state,
is also like this.
Therefore, within subtle distinctions,
one cannot fail to discern carefully.
A mediocre ruler uses subtle distinctions to stop at goodness,
while a worthy ruler uses subtle distinctions to achieve merit.
16.6 "Discerning the Subtle"
The sixth says:
If order and chaos, survival and destruction, were as distinct as high mountains and deep valleys,
as white chalk and black lacquer,
then there would be no use for wisdom,
and even a fool could manage.
However, order and chaos, survival and destruction are not like that.
They are as if knowable yet unknowable,
as if visible yet invisible.
Thus, wise scholars and worthy men together accumulate thoughts and worries to seek them out,
yet there still occurred the affair of Guǎn Shū and Cài Shū and the plot of the eight Eastern Yí states not to obey.
Therefore, order and chaos, survival and destruction,
their beginnings are like the autumn down.
If one discerns that autumn down,
then great matters will not go awry.
According to the laws of the state of Lǔ,
if a person from Lǔ became a servant or concubine to the feudal lords,
anyone who could ransom them,
would receive the payment from the state treasury.
Zǐgòng ransomed a man from Lǔ from the feudal lords,
and upon returning, declined and did not take the payment from the treasury.
Confucius said:
"Cì (Zǐgòng) is mistaken in this.
From now on,
people of Lǔ will not ransom others.
Taking the payment does no harm to one's conduct,
but not taking the payment means people will no longer ransom others."
Zǐlù rescued a drowning man,
and that man thanked him with an ox,
which Zǐlù accepted.
Confucius said:
"The people of Lǔ will certainly rescue drowning men."
Confucius perceived this from a small detail,
observing the transformation from afar.
There was a border town of Chǔ called Bēiliáng.
Its maidens and the maidens of the border town of Wú were picking mulberry leaves on the border,
and during play, a maiden from Bēiliáng was injured.
The people of Bēiliáng took their injured girl to reproach the people of Wú.
The people of Wú responded disrespectfully,
so in anger they killed them and left.
The people of Wú went to retaliate,
and slaughtered their entire household.
The Duke of Bēiliáng was enraged,
saying:
"How dare the people of Wú attack our town?"
He raised troops to counterattack,
and killed all, old and weak.
King Yímò of Wú heard of this and was angry,
sending men to raise troops and invade the border towns of Chǔ,
conquering and leveling them before leaving.
Wú and Chǔ thus became greatly hostile.
The Wú prince Guāng further led an army and fought the men of Chǔ at Jīfù,
greatly defeating the men of Chǔ,
capturing their commanders Pān Zǐchén, Xiǎo Wéizǐ, and Chén Xiàniè.
He then counterattacked and invaded Yǐng,
taking the wife of King Píng of Jīng and returning with her.
This was indeed the Battle of Jīfù.
In general, for maintaining a state,
the highest is to know the beginning,
the next is to know the end,
the next is to know the middle.
If one cannot do these three,
the state will certainly be endangered,
and one's person will certainly be reduced to extremity.
The "Classic of Filial Piety" says:
"High but not perilous,
this is how to long preserve nobility;
full but not overflowing,
this is how to long preserve wealth.
Wealth and nobility not leaving one's person,
only then can one protect the altars of soil and grain,
and harmonize his people."
Chǔ could not do this.
The Zhèng prince Guīshēng led an army to attack Sòng.
Sòng's Huá Yuán led an army to meet him at Dàjí,
with Yáng Zhēn as charioteer.
The next day they were to fight.
Huá Yuán killed sheep to feast the soldiers,
but Yáng Zhēn was not included.
The next day during the battle,
angrily he said to Huá Yuán:
"Yesterday's affair,
you were in control;
today's affair,
I am in control."
Thereupon he drove straight into the Zhèng army.
The Sòng army was utterly defeated,
and Huá Yuán was captured.
Now, if a crossbow trigger is off by a grain of rice, it will not release.
War,
is a great mechanism.
to thus be defeated and captured,
is it not fitting?
Therefore, in all warfare, one must be thoroughly familiar with and fully prepared in every aspect,
knowing the enemy and knowing oneself,
only then is it acceptable.
The Jì clan of Lǔ and the Hòu clan were fighting cocks.
The Hòu clan armored their cock,
and the Jì clan made metal spurs for theirs.
The Jì clan's cock did not win.
Jì Píngzǐ was angry,
and thereupon encroached upon the Hòu clan's residence to enlarge his own estate.
Hòu Zhāobó was angry,
and slandered him to Duke Zhāo,
saying:
"During the sacrifice at the temple of Duke Xiāng,
only two dancers were present,
all the rest were dancing at the Jì clan's.
The Jì clan's lawlessness and lack of respect for superiors has been long,
if not punished, they will certainly endanger the altars of soil and grain."
The Duke was angry,
without investigation,
he then sent Hòu Zhāobó to lead troops to attack the Jì clan,
and they entered their residence.
The Zhòngsūn and Shūsūn clans consulted together, saying:
"Without the Jì clan,
then our clans will die or be exiled any day."
Thereupon they raised armor and went,
breaching the northwest corner to enter,
the three clans becoming one,
Hòu Zhāobó was defeated and died.
Duke Zhāo was afraid,
and thereupon fled to Qí,
dying at Gānhóu.
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ listened to slander and did not discern its rightness,
he feared that with the state of Lǔ he could not overcome the Jì clan,
