but did not know that the Zhòng and Shū clans, fearing, shared the same trouble with the Jì clan.
This was not understanding the human heart.
Not understanding the human heart,
though one's position be尊贵,
what benefit is it for security?
Thinking that with the state of Lǔ he feared he could not overcome a single Jì clan,
how much more against three Jì clans?
Sharing the same hatred, they naturally help each other.
To misjudge matters to this extent is an error.
It was not only the Zhòng and Shū clans,
the entire state of Lǔ was afraid.
The entire state of Lǔ being afraid,
meant he was making an enemy of the whole state.
That he got as far as Gānhóu to die was still distant (i.e., he was fortunate to escape that far).
16.7 "Removing Prejudice"
The seventh says:
A Mohist from the east, Xièzǐ, was going west to see King Huì of Qín.
King Huì asked the Qín Mohist Tánggū Guǒ about him.
Tánggū Guǒ feared that the king would become close to Xièzǐ, considering him worthier than himself,
and replied:
"Xièzǐ
is a sophist from the east.
His character is very treacherous,
and he will exert himself in persuasion to win over the young lord."
The king thereupon harbored anger while waiting for him.
When Xièzǐ arrived,
and persuaded the king,
the king did not listen.
Xièzǐ was displeased,
and thereupon took his leave and departed.
In general, listening to words
is to seek goodness.
If what is said is good,
even if one exerts himself to win over the young lord,
what harm is there?
If what is said is not good,
even if one does not exert himself to win over the young lord,
what benefit is there?
Not taking goodness as sincere and honest,
but merely taking 'winning over the young lord' as perverse,
King Huì lost the means by which to listen.
Using one's mind like this,
though receiving guests may be laborious,
and ears and eyes may be worn out,
one still does not grasp the meaning.
This is how Shǐ Dìng was able to carry out his wickedness,
this is how Shǐ Dìng was able to disguise ghosts as men,
condemning and killing the innocent,
causing the ministers to be disturbed and chaotic,
and the state nearly to be greatly endangered.
When a person grows old,
their physical form increasingly declines,
yet their wisdom increasingly flourishes.
Now, as for King Huì growing old,
have both his form and wisdom declined?
King Wēi of Jīng studied texts under Shěn Yǐnhuá,
which Zhāo Lí detested.
King Wēi was fond of regulations.
There was a palace attendant who assisted with regulations.
Zhāo Lí said to King Wēi:
"All the people of the state say:
'The King is a disciple of Shěn Yǐnhuá.'"
The king was displeased,
and consequently distanced Shěn Yǐnhuá.
The palace attendant,
a petty man,
with a single statement caused King Wēi to cease hearing the methods of the former kings,
prevented scholars of literature from advancing,
and allowed Zhāo Lí to carry out his private schemes.
Therefore, the words of petty men
must not go unexamined.
Moreover, repeatedly provoking the ruler
is to clear the way for treacherous men;
once the treacherous path is cleared and wickedness is obstructed and repelled,
is that not difficult indeed?
For an arrow, when propelled, flies far;
water, when agitated, becomes swift;
a ruler, when provoked, becomes perverse;
and perversity means there will be no gentlemen.
That which cannot be provoked
surely only exists where there are pre-established standards.
There was an old man who had a neighbor.
There was a withered wútóng tree.
The neighbor's old man said the wútóng tree was not good,
and the neighbor promptly cut it down.
The old man then asked for it to use as firewood.
The man was displeased and said:
"A neighbor being so treacherous,
how can one be neighbors with him?"
This is a case of being blinded.
Whether he asked for it as firewood or did not ask,
this should not cast doubt on whether the withered wútóng tree was good or not.
There was a man of Qí who desired to obtain gold.
At dawn,
donning his clothes and hat,
he went to the place where gold was sold.
Seeing someone holding gold,
he snatched it and seized it.
The officers captured and bound him,
asking:
"People were all present there;
you snatched another's gold—
for what reason?"
In response to the officers, he said:
"I absolutely did not see any people;
I only saw the gold."
This is truly a great case of being blinded.
When a person is blinded,
they firmly take day for dusk,
white for black,
Yáo for Jié.
The harm caused by being blinded is also great.
The rulers of perished states,
were they all greatly blinded?
Therefore, all people must distinguish blindness before they can know;
distinguishing blindness then enables them to preserve their innate nature.
16.8 "Correct Designation"
The eighth says:
When designations are correct, there is order;
when designations are lost, there is chaos.
What causes designations to be lost
is excessive rhetoric.
When rhetoric is excessive, then the impermissible becomes permissible and the not-so becomes so,
the incorrect becomes correct and the not-wrong becomes wrong.
Therefore, the discourse of a gentleman
is sufficient to speak of the substance of the worthy and the emptiness of the unworthy, and that is all;
is sufficient to illustrate where order goes astray and whence chaos arises, and that is all;
is sufficient to understand the nature of things and what people obtain to live, and that is all.
Generally, in chaos,
form and designation do not correspond.
Even if the ruler is unworthy,
he still acts as if employing the worthy,
still acts as if listening to the good,
still acts as if doing what is permissible.
The trouble lies in calling worthy those who are merely unworthy,
calling good those who are merely wicked and depraved,
calling permissible those who are merely perverse and rebellious.
This is form and designation having different contents, and sound and substance being called differently.
With worthy and unworthy, good and wicked, permissible and perverse all confused,
what can be awaited but state chaos and personal danger?
King Mǐn of Qí was thus one who knew how to discourse about shì (scholars/officers) but did not know what is called a shì.
Therefore, when Yǐn Wén asked him the reason,
the king had nothing to reply.
This is why Gōng (or Wáng) Yùdān was trusted and Zhuō Chǐ was employed.
Employing Zhuō Chǐ and trusting Gōng (or Wáng) Yùdān—
was this not making enemies for oneself?
Yǐn Wén had an audience with the King of Qí.
The King of Qí said to Yǐn Wén:
"I greatly favor shì, yet in Qí there are no shì.
Why is this?"
Yǐn Wén said:
"I wish to hear what is called a shì?"
The king had nothing to reply.
Yǐn Wén said:
"Suppose there is a person here
who serves parents with filial piety,
serves his lord with loyalty,
associates with friends with trustworthiness,
and in his village conducts himself with fraternal duty.
Having these four kinds of conduct,
can he be called a shì?"
The King of Qí said:
"This is truly what is called a shì."
Yǐn Wén said:
"If Your Majesty obtained such a person,
would you be willing to make him a minister?"
The king said:
"That is my wish, but I cannot obtain one."
At that time, the King of Qí favored courage.
Yǐn Wén said:
"If such a person, in the court or temple,
were deeply insulted yet did not fight,
would Your Majesty still make him a minister?"
The king said:
"No.
A great officer who is insulted and does not fight
is thereby disgraced.
If disgraced, I would not make him a minister."
Yǐn Wén said:
"Even if insulted and not fighting,
he has not lost his four kinds of conduct.
Not losing his four kinds of conduct
means he has not lost that by which he is a shì.
When he has not lost that by which he is a shì, you would make him a minister;
when he loses that by which he is a shì, you would not make him a minister.
Then, was the shì you spoke of earlier not a shì?"
The king had nothing to reply.
Yǐn Wén said:
"Suppose there is a ruler here
who will govern his state.
If the people have faults, he condemns them;
if the people have no faults, he still condemns them.
If the people have crimes, he punishes them;
if the people have no crimes, he still punishes them.
And yet he resents that the people are difficult to govern—is that permissible?"
The king said:
"It is not permissible."
Yǐn Wén said:
"I privately observe the officials governing Qí,
and it is precisely like this."
The king said:
"If my governing of the state were truly like this,
then even if the people were not governed,
I would not resent it.
Perhaps it has not yet reached that point."
Yǐn Wén said:
"In speaking, I dare not be without explanation.
Allow me to explain.
Your Majesty's command says:
'Whoever kills a person shall die;
whoever injures a person shall be punished.'
If among the people there is one who, fearing Your Majesty's command,
is deeply insulted yet dares not fight,
he is upholding Your Majesty's command.
Yet Your Majesty says, 'One who is insulted and dares not fight
is thereby disgraced.'
Calling him disgraced
is not correct; this is condemning him though he has no fault.
Therefore, you consequently remove him from the register and do not make him a minister.
Not making him a minister
is punishing him. This is punishing him though he has no crime."
The King of Qí had nothing to reply.
His judgments were all like this;
therefore, the state was ruined and his person endangered.
He fled and went to Gǔ,
and then to Wèi.
King Mǐn of Qí was the leading lord among the Zhōu houses.
This is why Tàigōng grew old there.
Duke Huán once used this to become hegemon,
for Guǎn Zhòng's discrimination of name and substance was precise.
17.1 "Examining Distinctions"
The first says:
All rulers must examine distinctions,
then order can be achieved,
the paths of deceit, falsity, wickedness, and depravity can cease,
and noxious influences and severe maladies will have no way to arrive.
Governing the self and governing the state
are techniques of the same principle.
Now, when working the land collectively,
public labor is slow,
because people conceal their strength;
when land is divided, work is fast,
because there is no place to hide slowness.
The ruler also has his "land,"
and if ministers and ruler share the same "land,"
then ministers can conceal their wickedness,
and the ruler cannot avoid being burdened.
Generally, doing good is difficult,
but employing the good is easy.
How do we know this?
If a man races alongside a thoroughbred,
he cannot outrun the horse;
but if he sits in a chariot and employs the horse,
then the horse cannot outrun the man.
If a ruler enjoys managing the affairs of officials himself,
this is like racing alongside a thoroughbred—
he will surely fall short in many ways.
Now, the ruler also has his chariot;
if he does not leave his chariot,
then all the good will exhaust their strength and abilities,
flatterers, slanderers, thieves, and cunning sycophants will have no place to hide their treachery,
and the steadfast, upright, honest, loyal, and sincere will all strive and compete.
The ruler's chariot
is what he uses to ride upon things.
If he examines the principle of riding upon things,
he can possess the four extremes.
If he does not know how to ride upon things but relies on himself,
exerting his own intelligence and ability,
multiplying his commands and instructions,
and being fond of acting on his own—
if so, then all officials will be distressed and disturbed,
the young and old will overstep each other,
countless evils will arise together,
authority and power will be divided and shifted,
it cannot be brought to an end,
it cannot be taught—
this is the wind of a perishing state.
The reason why Wáng Liáng could drive horses
was that he controlled them precisely with the reins,
and the four horses dared not fail to exert their full strength.
An enlightened ruler
also has reins with which to direct his ministers.
What are these reins?
Correcting names and clarifying duties—
this is the rein of governance.
Therefore, examine the reality and scrutinize the name,
to seek the true situation;
listen to their words and observe their kind,
not allowing them to run wild and perverse.
When names often do not match reality and affairs often do not match their use,
the ruler cannot fail to scrutinize names and duties.
If he does not scrutinize names and duties,
it is like hating blockage but making it worse.
The responsibility for blockage
lies not with the ministers,
but with the ruler.
The ministers of Yáo and Shùn were not uniquely righteous,
nor were the ministers of Tāng and Yǔ uniquely loyal—
they grasped the method;
the ministers of Jié and Zhòu were not uniquely base,
nor were the ministers of Yōu and Lì uniquely wicked—
they lost the principle.
Suppose there is a person here
who asks for an ox but calls it a horse,
or asks for a horse but calls it an ox—
what he seeks will certainly not be obtained;
and if he then uses威严 and anger,
the officials will certainly complain and resent,
and the oxen and horses will certainly be disturbed and chaotic.
The hundred officials are like the many officers,
and the myriad things are like the herd of oxen and horses.
If names are not corrected,
and duties are not divided,
yet punishments are frequently used,
there is no greater chaos.
To praise someone as wise and understanding,
yet in reality they are confused and obstructed;
to commend someone as lofty and worthy,
yet they are filled with baseness and inferiority;
to extol someone as pure and white,
yet they follow with污秽 virtue;
to appoint someone with public law,
yet they act with greed and crookedness;
to employ someone for bravery,
yet they are stifled by weariness and cowardice—
these five cases
are all like calling an ox a horse,
or a horse an ox—
names are not correct.
Therefore, if names are not correct,
then the ruler will be anxious, toil, and labor hard,
and official positions will be troublesome, chaotic, and perverse.
The state's perishing,
the injury of its name,
arise from this.
That which one hopes will become whiter turns blacker, and the more one seeks it the less one obtains—
is this not the meaning here!
Therefore, the task of perfect governance
lies in correcting names.
If names are correct, the ruler will not be anxious and toil.
Not being anxious and toil, he will not harm the masters of his ears and eyes.
He inquires but does not command,
knows but does not act,
harmonizes but does not boast,
achieves but does not dwell.
What should stop does not move,
what should move does not stop;
he employs according to their form,
is not constrained by things,
and is unwilling to be driven.
Tranquil and impartial,
his spirit penetrates the six directions,
his virtue shines beyond the seas,
his mind observes the boundless,
his reputation flows without end.
This is called stabilizing nature in the great abyss,
named "non-being."
Therefore, attaining the Way, one forgets people,
and thus greatly attains people—
is this not the Way?
Knowing virtue, one forgets knowledge,
and thus greatly attains knowledge—
is this not virtue?
The highest knowledge does not rely on subtle signs,
tranquility makes subtle signs clear—
is this not clarity?
The great brightness does not attend to small affairs,
borrowing then manages affairs—
is this not borrowing?
No one can be capable in all things,
wholeness then makes one fully capable—
is this not wholeness?
Therefore, in wholeness, discard capability;
in borrowing, discard affairs;
in knowledge, discard subtle signs—
what is known becomes subtle.
If so, one can follow Heaven's will,
and one's vital energy can wander in the realm of silence,
one's form and nature can rest in the place of spontaneity.
Complete with the myriad things but not their master,
beneficence covers the world yet none know its origin—
even if one does not fully possess these five,
those who are fond of them are so.
17.2 "The Ruler's Preservation"
Second:
One who attains the Way must be tranquil.
Tranquility is without knowledge,
yet knowledge is without knowledge—
this can be spoken of as the way of the ruler.
Therefore it is said: inner desires not going out is called "barred,"
outer desires not entering is called "closed."
Both barred and closed:
Heaven's function is subtle,
having a level but not using it to level,
having a plumb line but not using it to straighten;
Heaven's great tranquility,
both tranquil and serene,
can make the world upright.
The body contains the mind,
the mind contains wisdom;
wisdom,
deeply hidden so that none can窥探 it.
The "Hóng Fàn" says:
"Heaven darkly aids the people below."
"Darkly" means
that by which it stimulates them.
Therefore it is said: without going out the door, one knows the world;
without looking out the window, one knows the Way of Heaven.
Those who go out farther
know less;
therefore, those of broad learning and strong memory are deficient,
affairs of ears and eyes and deep thought and consideration fail,
investigations of hardness and whiteness and debates on the无厚 are external.
Not going out
is the means by which one goes out;
not acting
is the means by which one acts.
This is called using yang to summon yang,
using yīn to summon yīn.
At the extreme of the Eastern Sea,
water reaches and returns;
under the summer heat,
it transforms into cold.
Therefore it is said: the vast Heaven has no form,
yet the myriad things are completed by it;
the most essential has no action,
yet the myriad things are transformed by it;
the great sage has no affairs,
yet all officials exhaust their abilities.
This is what is called teaching without teaching,
a decree without words.
Thus there is a way to know that the ruler is reckless,
by the appropriateness of his words;
there is a way to know that the ruler is deluded,
by the correctness of his words.
The ruler
takes inappropriateness as appropriate,
and takes incorrectness as correct.
Appropriateness and correctness do not lie with the ruler,
but with his ministers.
Therefore, the one who excels at being a ruler has no knowledge,
and next to him is the one who has no affairs.
Having knowledge means there will be inadequacy,
having affairs means there will be incompleteness.
Inadequacy and incompleteness
are why officials become doubtful,
and from where wickedness arises.
Nowadays, those who make carriages
require several officials to complete one.
Is governing a state merely like making a carriage?
It relies on the wisdom and abilities of the multitude;
one cannot secure a carriage with a single object or method.
Only one who can respond to the myriad without fixed methods, and who emerges to handle affairs,
is capable of this—only the one who possesses the Dào.
A rustic man from Lǔ sent a closed knot to King Yuán of Sòng.
King Yuán issued an order throughout the state,
summoning all skilled persons to come and unravel the knot.
No one could unravel it.
A disciple of Ér Shuō requested to go and unravel it.
He was able to unravel one part,
but could not unravel the other.
And he said:
"It is not that it can be unraveled and I am unable to do so,
but that it inherently cannot be unraveled."
They asked the rustic man from Lǔ.
The rustic man said:
"Indeed,
it inherently cannot be unraveled.
I made it and thus know it cannot be unraveled.
Now, without having made it, he knows it cannot be unraveled—
this means he is more skillful than I."
Therefore, one like Ér Shuō's disciple
used
"not unraveling" to unravel it.
The Grand Master Wén of Zhèng played the sè all day and then rose,
bowed twice before his sè and said:
"I learn from you,
I learn from the inexhaustible."
Therefore, one like Grand Master Wén
takes what is silent as his guide,
and thereby hits the mark.
Thus, pondering and worrying injure one's own heart;
clever schemes lead to one's own demise;
striving to display ability brings calamity upon oneself;
having a fixed position makes one reckless.
Therefore, the utmost spirit wanders freely, swift and sudden, and its form cannot be seen;
the utmost sage transforms practices and shifts customs, and none know whence he comes;
he departs from the world and separates from the crowd, yet there is nothing with which he does not harmonize;
he rules the people as the solitary and orphaned one, yet cannot be obstructed or blocked.
This way, the true nature of treachery and wickedness is apprehended, and treacherous, slanderous, flattering, and cunning people have no way to enter.
Whenever treacherous, wicked, and treacherous persons enter, there must be a cause.
What is the cause?
It is due to the ruler's actions.
If the ruler is fond of acting according to his own will,
then those in charge of duties will abandon their duties and flatter the ruler's actions.
Flattering the ruler's actions,
if there is fault, the ruler has no means to hold them accountable.
Thus, the ruler's authority diminishes daily, and the ministers gain power daily.
This results in movement where there should be stillness,
and stillness where there should be movement;
the honorable becomes lowly,
the lowly becomes honorable.
From this, such situations arise.
This is why states decline and why enemies attack them.
Xī Zhòng created the carriage,
Cāng Jié created writing,
Hòu Jì created agriculture,
Gāo Yáo created punishments,
Kūn Wú created pottery,
Xià Gǔn created city walls.
What these six men created was appropriate,
yet it is not the way of the ruler.
Therefore it is said: the creator brings disturbance,
the follower brings peace.
Only that way of rulership,
which comprehends the true nature of destiny,
can undertake the responsibility of the world without forcing it,
this is called the complete person.
17.3 "Relying on Methods"
Third:
All officials
are charged with maintaining order,
and held accountable for disorder.
Now, if there is disorder without accountability,
then disorder will grow ever greater.
If the ruler shows off his ability by being fond of harshness,
and prides himself on being fond of initiating,
and if ministers maintain their positions by not contending,
and gain favor by being obedient and compliant,
then the ruler is taking the place of the officials and acting as an official,
and the ministers are able to follow behind and advance their own careers.
When the roles of ruler and minister are not fixed,
even though the ears hear, they cannot listen;
even though the eyes see, they cannot perceive;
even though the mind knows, it cannot act.
Circumstances cause this.
All hearing by the ears depends on stillness;
all seeing by the eyes depends on clarity;
all knowing by the mind depends on principle.
If ruler and minister exchange their conduct,
then these three faculties of the ruler are rendered useless.
The ruler of a doomed state—
his ears are not incapable of hearing,
his eyes are not incapable of seeing,
his mind is not incapable of knowing.
But ruler and minister are in turmoil and disorder,
superior and inferior are not distinguished.
Even if he hears, what does he hear?
Even if he sees, what does he see?
Even if he knows, what does he know?
He rushes about relying merely on his ears.
This is what the foolish do not reach.
Not reaching it, they do not know;
not knowing, they do not believe.
One without bones cannot be made to know ice.
The ruler who possesses the land,
if he can examine these words,
then calamity will have no way to arrive.
Moreover, the ears, eyes, intelligence, and skill
are truly insufficient to rely on.
Only cultivating methods and practicing principles is reliable.
Hán Zhāo Lí Hóu inspected the sacrificial animal for the ancestral temple.
The pig was small,
so Zhāo Lí Hóu ordered the official to change it.
The official brought back this pig,
and Zhāo Lí Hóu said:
"Is this not the same pig as before?"
The official had no reply.
He ordered an officer to punish him.
An attendant asked:
"How did Your Majesty know?"
The ruler said:
"I knew by its ears."
Shēn Bù Hài heard of this
and said:
"How do we know he is deaf?
By the acuity of his hearing.
How do we know he is blind?
By the sharpness of his sight.
How do we know he is reckless?
By the appropriateness of his words.

Therefore it is said: eliminate hearing, and without anything to hear, one becomes truly perceptive; eliminate sight, and without anything to see, one becomes truly clear-sighted; eliminate knowledge, and without anything to know, one becomes truly impartial.
If these three are discarded and not employed, there will be order;
if these three are employed, there will be disorder."
This illustrates that ears, eyes, mind, and knowledge are insufficient to rely on.
Ears, eyes, mind, and knowledge—
the understanding they provide is very limited,
what they hear and see is very shallow.
To rely on shallow and limited understanding to broadly reside over the world, pacify different customs, and govern the myriad people—
such a theory certainly will not work.
Within ten lǐ, the ear cannot hear;
outside curtains and walls, the eye cannot see;
within a palace of three mǔ, the mind cannot know.
How then can one extend east to Kāi Wú, soothe Duō Yí in the south, subdue Shòu Mí in the west, and embrace Dān Ěr in the north?
What is to be done?
Therefore, the ruler of men
must examine these words.
Order and disorder, safety and danger, survival and ruin—
the Dào for them is fundamentally not twofold.
Therefore, the utmost wisdom discards wisdom;
the utmost benevolence forgets benevolence;
the utmost virtue is not virtue.
Without words, without thought,
remain still and await the time;
when the time comes, respond.
The one whose mind is at leisure prevails.
The principle of responding
is purity, tranquility, impartiality, and simplicity,
and correcting the beginning and end.
Thus ordering the guiding principles,
without initiation there is response,
without precedence there is following.
The ancient kings,
what they did was little,
what they relied on was much.
Following the natural course is the ruler's technique;
taking deliberate action is the minister's way.
Taking deliberate action leads to disturbance,
while following the natural course brings tranquility.
Winter brings cold,
summer brings heat—
what need has the ruler to intervene?
Thus it is said: The way of the ruler lies in having no knowledge and taking no action, yet being superior to having knowledge and taking action—
this is to grasp it.
An official requested instructions from Duke Huán of Qí.
Duke Huán said:
"Report it to Zhòngfù."
The official made another request.
The duke said, "Report it to Zhòngfù,"
and this happened three times.
A court attendant remarked:
"Once it's Zhòngfù,
twice it's Zhòngfù—
how easy it is to be ruler!"
Duke Huán said:
"Before I obtained Zhòngfù, it was difficult;
after I obtained Zhòngfù,
why should it not be easy?"
With Guǎn Zhòng, Duke Huán's affairs became greatly simplified—
how much more so with one who has attained the Way and its techniques!
When Confucius was in distress between Chén and Cài,
there was no vegetable soup to ladle,
and for seven days he tasted no grain,
sleeping by day.
Yán Huí sought rice,
obtained some, and cooked it.
When it was nearly done,
Confucius saw Yán Huí snatch some from the pot and eat it.
After a short while,
the food was cooked,
and Yán Huí presented it to Confucius to eat.
Confucius pretended not to have seen.
Confucius rose and said:
"Just now I dreamed of my late father;
I should offer him clean food before eating."
Yán Huí replied:
"That will not do.
A moment ago, soot from the stove fell into the pot;
to discard the food would be inauspicious,
so I snatched and ate it."
Confucius sighed and said:
"What one trusts are the eyes,
yet even the eyes cannot be trusted;
what one relies on is the mind,
yet even the mind is insufficient to rely on.
Disciples, remember this:
to know others is truly not easy."
Thus, knowing is not difficult;
what Confucius meant is that knowing people is difficult.
17.4 "Do Not Toil Personally"
Fourth:
If a person's intentions are good,
even without knowledge, they can become a leader.
Thus Lǐzǐ said:
"Without dogs, one cannot catch rabbits;
if rabbits transformed into dogs,
they would no longer be rabbits."
If a ruler enjoys performing the duties of his officials,
it resembles this.
His ministers will obscure him,
and others will try to stop him in time,
but if the ruler obscures himself, none dare stop him.
To personally perform officials' duties
is the height of self-obscuration.
A broom is used daily but not stored in a box;
thus, with use it wears out,
with action it grows dim,
with exertion it becomes weary.
Weariness, dimness, and weariness—these three are not the way of the ruler.
Dà Ráo created the sexagenary cycle;
Qián Rú created the lǔ shǒu method;
Róng Chéng created the calendar;
Xī Hé created solar observation;
Shàng Yí created lunar observation;
Hòu Yì created annual prognostication;
Hú Cáo created clothing;
Yí Yì created the bow;
Zhù Róng created markets;
Yí Dí created wine;
Gāo Yuán created dwellings;
Yú Xǔ created boats;
Bó Yì created wells;
Chì Jì created the mortar;
Chéng Yǎ created harnessing;
Hán Āi created charioteering;
Wáng Hài created ox-taming;
Shǐ Huáng created maps;
Wū Péng created medicine;
Wū Xián created divination.
These twenty offices
are what the sages used to govern the world.
The sage kings could not perform the tasks of these twenty offices,
yet they made these twenty offices exhaust their skill and fully employ their abilities—
this was because the sage kings were above them.
What the sage kings could not do was how they could do it;
what they did not know was how they knew it.
Nourish their spirit, cultivate their virtue, and transformation occurs—
must they toil their bodies, vex their minds, and weary their ears and eyes?
Therefore, the virtue of the sage kings
melts like the moon at its first emergence,
illuminating the six directions without exhaustion;
shining like the light of the sun,
transforming the myriad things without anything not proceeding.
Their spirit harmonizes with the Great One;
life is unbent,
and intention cannot be obstructed;
their essence penetrates to the spirits,
profound, subtle, mysterious, and wondrous,
with no form visible.
Today, facing south,
all evils rectify themselves,
and all under heaven return to their true nature;
the black-haired people all delight in their will, peacefully nurture their nature, and nothing is left undone.
Thus, one skilled at being ruler
devotes himself to serving the true nature of life,
and the hundred officials are already governed,
the black-haired people already drawn close,
and his name and title already illustrious.
Guǎn Zhòng reported to Duke Huán,
saying:
"Opening up fields and enlarging settlements,
reclaiming land and cultivating grain,
exhausting the benefits of the land's strength—
in this I am not equal to Níng Sù;
I request he be appointed as Grand Field Officer.
In ascending and descending, declining and yielding,
advancing and retreating with practiced ease—
in this I am not equal to Xí Péng;
I request he be appointed as Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Entering early and leaving late,
braving the ruler's countenance,
offering remonstrance with utmost loyalty,
not avoiding death,
not valuing wealth and honor—
in this I am not equal to Dōngguō Yá;
I request he be appointed as Grand Remonstrance Minister.
On broad plains and wide cities,
with chariots not entangling their tracks,
soldiers not turning their heels,
drums beating and the three-army soldiers looking upon death as returning home—
in this I am not equal to Wángzǐ Chéngfù;
I request he be appointed as Grand Marshal.
In deciding legal cases and achieving balance,
not killing the innocent,
not falsely accusing the guiltless—
in this I am not equal to Xián Zhāng;
I request he be appointed as Grand Judge.
If you, my lord, wish to govern the state and strengthen the military,
then these five men are sufficient;
if you, my lord, wish to become hegemon and king,
then Yí Wú is here."
Duke Huán said:
"Excellent."
He ordered the five men each to take up their duties,
receiving commands from Guǎn Zhòng.
In ten years,
he assembled the feudal lords nine times,
once rectifying all under heaven—
all due to the abilities of Yí Wú and these five men.
Guǎn Zhòng was a minister;
he did not undertake what he could not do,
but fully employed the abilities of these five men—
how much more should a ruler!
If a ruler understands that what he can and cannot do enables him to rule the people,
then obscure, deceitful, foolish, and dangerous words will all be restrained,
and the hundred officials and their departments will exhaust their strength and wisdom in their duties.
The Five Emperors and Three Kings in ruling the people
surely did not go beyond exhausting their strength and wisdom.
To rule others and know not to rely on one's own ability, courage, strength, sincerity, or trustworthiness—
this is close to it.
All rulers
abide in stillness and peace, entrust themselves to virtuous transformation, and listen for the essential.
If so, then form and nature become more abundant,
and ears and eyes grow more acute;
the hundred officials are careful in their duties,
and none dare be negligent;
each person attends to his own affairs,
thereby fulfilling his name.
When name and reality protect each other,
this is called understanding the Way.
17.5 "Understanding Measures"
The fifth says:
An enlightened ruler
does not need to observe all things in detail,
but understands what a ruler should grasp.
A ruler who possesses methods
does not personally handle everything,
but knows the essentials of the hundred officials.
Knowing the essentials of the hundred officials,
thus affairs are simplified and the state is well-governed.
Understanding what a ruler should grasp,
thus authority is concentrated and wickedness ceases.
When wickedness ceases, flatterers do not come,
and true circumstances become clear;
when true circumstances are not embellished,
then facts become evident.
This is called perfect governance.
In an age of perfect governance,
the people do not favor empty words and false rhetoric,
nor do they indulge in heretical teachings and baseless theories;
the worthy and the unworthy each return to their true nature.
They act according to their true feelings,
without embellishing their simplicity;
they are sincere, honest, and pure,
serving their superiors accordingly.
In this way, skill or clumsiness, foolishness or wisdom, courage or fear can be discerned.
Thus, official positions can be easily assigned,
and when positions are easily assigned, each person fits their role.
Therefore, those with duties remain content in their posts,
and do not engage in unnecessary discussions;
those without duties are judged by their actual achievements,
to verify their words.
When these two principles are carefully observed,
then useless words do not enter the court.
The ruler follows the true nature of life,
discarding personal likes and dislikes,
embracing emptiness and non-action as the foundation,
and listening to useful words in court.
The court is a place
where principles and righteousness are discussed together,
and laws and rules are established together.
When the ruler follows the true nature of life,
then scholars of principle and righteousness arrive,
the application of laws and rules is established,
corrupt and deceitful people retreat,
and those greedy, fraudulent, and hypocritical are kept at a distance.
Thus, the key to governing the world
lies in eliminating wickedness;
the key to eliminating wickedness
lies in managing officials;
the key to managing officials
lies in governing according to the Way;
the key to governing according to the Way
lies in understanding the nature of life.
Therefore, Zǐhuázi said:
"Be profound but not broad,
reverently uphold one thing,
and delight in rectifying one's nature.
Do not seek to encompass the multitude,
but strive to master one ability.
When this ability is fully mastered,
the four barbarians will be pacified.
Only by following the heavenly signs,
though not encompassing all, one encompasses all.
This is why Shénnóng endured long,
and why Yáo and Shùn became illustrious."
If a ruler considers himself wise and others foolish,
himself skillful and others clumsy,
then the foolish and clumsy will make requests,
and the skillful and wise will give orders.
If orders increase, requests will multiply,
and as requests multiply,
there will be endless requests.
Even if the ruler is skillful and wise,
he cannot know everything.
Being unable to know everything,
yet facing endless requests,
his methods will inevitably be exhausted.
If a ruler is repeatedly exhausted by his subordinates,
how can he rule over others?
If exhausted yet unaware of his exhaustion,
the danger is that he will instead become self-important,
this is called a ruler who is doubly obstructed,
and his state will not survive.
Therefore, a ruler who possesses the Way
relies on others without acting personally,
holds others accountable without giving orders,
discards thoughts and intentions,
remains calm and empty, awaiting
without interfering in words,
without seizing affairs,
supervising names and examining realities,
letting officials manage themselves,
taking not knowing as the Way,
and taking 'what to do' as the treasure.
Yáo said:
"How can one reach where the sun and moon shine?"
Shùn said:
"How can one subdue the lands beyond the four borders?"
Yǔ said:
"How can one govern Qīngqiū,
the strange transformations of Jiǔyáng, and the borders of the lands?"
During the time of Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
Rèn Dēng was appointed as magistrate of Zhōngmóu.
When reporting to the ruler,
he said to Xiāngzǐ:
"In Zhōngmóu, there is a scholar named Dǎn Xūjǐ,
I request an audience with him."
Xiāngzǐ met him and appointed him as a senior official.
The prime minister said:
"Perhaps you have only heard of him but not seen him?
To appoint a senior official so easily
is not the custom of the state of Jìn."
Xiāngzǐ replied:
"When I promoted Rèn Dēng,
I had already heard and seen him.
Now, regarding the person Rèn Dēng recommended,
I have also heard and seen him.
If this continues, there will be no end to hearing and seeing others."
Thus, he did not inquire further,
and appointed him as a senior official.
How did Xiāngzǐ appoint people?
He ensured that the worthy exerted their full efforts.
The danger for a ruler
lies in appointing people but not using them properly,
or using them while consulting with those who do not understand.
To cross a river, one relies on a boat;
to travel far, one relies on a steed;
to achieve hegemony, one relies on the worthy.
Yīyǐn, Lǚ Shàng, Guǎn Yíwú, and Bǎilǐ Xī
are the boats and steeds for achieving hegemony.
Setting aside fathers, brothers, sons, and nephews
is not to alienate them;
employing cooks, fishermen, butchers, enemies, servants, and slaves
is not to favor them;
it is the way to uphold the state and achieve merit and fame,
and it cannot be otherwise.
Just as a great craftsman building a palace
measures the size to know the amount of timber needed,
and estimates the work to know the number of laborers required.
Thus, when Xiǎochén and Lǚ Shàng were employed, the world knew that the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties would become kings;
when Guǎn Yíwú and Bǎilǐ Xī were employed,
the world knew that Qí and Qín would achieve hegemony;
how could it be only about steeds traveling far?
Those who achieve kingship and hegemony certainly have the right people,
and those who lose their states also have their people.
Jié employed Yáng Xīn,
Zhòu employed Èlái,
Sòng employed Táng Yāng,
Qí employed Sū Qín,
and the world knew they would perish.
To seek achievement without the right people
is like hoping for long nights on the summer solstice,
or shooting at fish while pointing at the sky and expecting to hit the target.
Even Shùn and Yǔ would find it difficult,
let alone ordinary rulers.
17.6 "Cautious Use of Power"
The sixth says:
To lose in strategy
and seek trust,
is doubtful.
To lose in power
and seek to preserve the state,
is perilous.
A fish large enough to swallow a boat,
on land cannot withstand ants.
When power is equal, none can command the others;
when influence is equal, none can annex the others;
when order and chaos are balanced, none can correct the others.
Therefore, small and large, light and heavy, few and many, order and chaos must be carefully examined,
for this is the gateway to fortune and misfortune.
All civilized states,
where boats and carriages can travel,
without the need for interpreters,
extend for three thousand lǐ.
The ancient kings
chose the center of the world to establish their state,
chose the center of the state to establish their palace,
and chose the center of the palace to establish their temple.
The land of the Son of Heaven
was a thousand lǐ square for the state,
to achieve the utmost in governance.
It was not that it could not be larger,
but larger is not as good as smaller,
and more is not as good as less.
To establish many fiefdoms
is not to favor the worthy privately,
but to facilitate power and preserve authority,
and to broaden righteousness.
When righteousness is broad and benefits are shared, there are no enemies.
Having no enemies brings peace.
Thus, looking at ancient times,
those who established many fiefdoms
enjoyed long-lasting fortune,
and their fame was illustrious.
Shénnóng ruled the world for seventeen generations,
sharing it with the world.
When a true king enfeoffs vassals,
the closer they are, the larger their territories;
the farther they are, the smaller their territories.
There are marquises on the seas with domains of only ten li.
Using the large to command the small,
using the heavy to command the light,
using the many to command the few—
this is how the true king treats the realm as his household and keeps it intact.
Thus it is said:
Using Téng and Fèi would be laborious;
using Zōu and Lǔ would be effortless;
using Sòng and Zhèng would be like galloping twice the distance in a day;
using Qí and Chǔ would be like lifting them and placing them on a net—that is all.
The greater the means employed,
the easier the desires are to fulfill.
If Tāng had lacked Yī,
or Wǔ had lacked Qí,
even with perfect virtue,
they could not have achieved success.
With the virtue of Tāng and Wǔ,
they still relied on understanding strategic advantage;
how much more so for those inferior to Tāng and Wǔ?
Therefore, using the large to nurture the small brings good fortune;
using the small to nurture the large leads to ruin.
Using the heavy to command the light brings compliance;
using the light to command the heavy brings calamity.
From this perspective,
to stabilize an age,
to secure the lives of the common people,
to have achievements recorded on vessels and plates,
and inscriptions engraved on pots and mirrors—
one’s strategic advantage cannot be too exalted,
and one’s substance cannot be too abundant.
Abundant substance and exalted advantage,
when controlled by worthy men,
can meet the challenges of a chaotic age—
yet even then, true kings are still few.
The people of the world
are destitute and suffering.
The more destitute and suffering the people are,
the easier it is for a true king to arise.
All true kings
are the salvation of the destitute and suffering.
On water, use boats;
on land, use carts;
on muddy paths, use sledges;
on sand, use skids;
in mountains,
use mountain chairs—
all follow the natural advantages.
Orders are carried out.
When rank is exalted, teachings are accepted;
when authority is established, treachery ceases.
This is the way to govern people.
Thus, for a ruler of ten thousand chariots to command one of a thousand is easy;
for a ruler of a thousand chariots to command a single household is easy;
for a single household to command one person is easy.
If one fails to recognize this,
even Yáo and Shùn could not succeed.
If feudal lords do not wish to be subjects of others
but have no alternative,
their strategic advantage is inconvenient—
then how can they avoid being subjects?
Weigh the heavy and light,
examine the large and small;
establishing many fiefs is how to make strategic advantage convenient.
A true king
is strategic advantage;
a true king
is strategic advantage without rival.
If strategic advantage has a rival, the true king is deposed.
One who understands that the small can surpass the large, and the few can surpass the many,
then understands being without rival.
Understanding being without rival keeps the ways of resemblance and suspicion at a distance.
Thus, the laws of the former kings
established the Son of Heaven without letting feudal lords suspect;
established feudal lords without letting ministers suspect;
established the rightful heir without letting concubines’ sons suspect.
Suspicion gives rise to contention;
contention gives rise to chaos.
Therefore, if feudal lords lose their positions, the world falls into chaos;
if ministers lack ranks, the court falls into chaos;
if wives and concubines are not distinguished, the household falls into chaos;
if rightful heirs and concubines’ sons are not separated, the clan falls into chaos.
Shènzǐ said:
"If a single rabbit runs loose,
a hundred men will chase it.
It is not that one rabbit is enough to be divided among a hundred men,
but because it is undetermined.
Because it is undetermined,
even Yáo would exhaust his strength,
let alone ordinary people.
If rabbits fill the market,
passersby will not even glance at them.
It is not that they do not want rabbits,
but because they are already determined.
Once determined,
even a lowly person will not contend.
Thus, governing the world or a state
lies solely in determining allotments."
King Zhuāng besieged Sòng for nine months;
King Kāng besieged Sòng for five months;
King Shēng besieged Sòng for ten months.
Chǔ besieged Sòng three times yet could not destroy it—
not because it was indestructible,
but because if Sòng attacked Chǔ,
when would it ever end?
All achievements that are established
differ based on worthiness or unworthiness, strength or weakness, order or chaos.
Lord Jiǎn of Qí had a minister named Zhūyù Yāng,
who remonstrated with Lord Jiǎn, saying:
"Chén Chéngcháng and Zǎiyǔ—
these two ministers deeply hate each other.
I fear they will attack each other.
If they attack each other and entrench themselves, it will endanger Your Highness.
I wish you would remove one of them."
Lord Jiǎn said:
"This is not something a petty person like you can understand."
Not long after,
Chén Chéngcháng indeed attacked Zǎiyǔ in the courtyard
and then Lord Jiǎn in the ancestral temple.
Lord Jiǎn sighed deeply and said:
"I failed to heed Yāng’s words,
and thus brought this calamity upon myself."
Losing the method,
lacking the advantage—
even if one regrets not listening to Yāng, it is the same as having no regret,
for this is not knowing to rely on what can be relied upon, but instead relying on what cannot be relied upon.
The Zhōu tripods bear images,
to make their principles penetrate.
Principles penetrating—
this is the way of the ruler.
17.7 "No Two"
The seventh says:
Listening to the debates of the masses to govern a state,
the state will be in peril before long.
How do we know this is so?
Lǎo Dān valued softness;
Kǒngzǐ valued benevolence;
Mò Dí valued frugality;
Guān Yǐn valued clarity;
Lièzǐ valued emptiness;
Chén Pián valued equality;
Yáng Shēng valued self;
Sūn Bìn valued strategic advantage;
Wáng Liào valued precedence;
Ér Liáng valued subsequence.
Having gongs and drums is to unify hearing;
having uniform laws and commands is to unify minds.
The wise may not use cleverness,
the foolish may not use clumsiness—
this is to unify the multitude.
The brave may not advance first,
the fearful may not lag behind—
this is to unify strength.
Thus, unity brings order;
division brings chaos.
Unity brings safety;
division brings danger.
To unify ten thousand differences,
so that foolish and wise, skilled and clumsy all exhaust their strength and abilities
as if emerging from a single opening—
is this not only possible for a sage?
Wisdom without method,
ability without teaching,
relying on forced haste and habitual practice—
is insufficient for accomplishment.
17.8 "Grasping Unity"
The eighth says:
Heaven and earth, yīn and yáng do not change,
yet they produce the ten thousand things in their differences.
The eye does not lose its sight,
and thus perceives the distinction between white and black;
the ear does not lose its hearing,
and thus hears the sounds of clear and turbid.
The true king grasps unity
and thereby rectifies the ten thousand things.
An army must have a general
to unify it;
a state must have a ruler
to unify it;
the world must have a Son of Heaven
to unify it;
the Son of Heaven must grasp unity
to consolidate it.
Unity brings order;
duality brings chaos.
Now, to drive a team of four horses,
if you have four men,
each holding a whip,
they cannot pass through the gate—because they are not unified.
The King of Chǔ asked Zhānzǐ about governing the state.
Zhānzǐ replied:
"I have only heard of cultivating oneself,
not of governing the state."
Did Zhānzǐ mean that the state requires no governance?
He believed that the foundation of governing the state lies in cultivating oneself.
When oneself is cultivated, the family is well-ordered;
when the family is well-ordered, the state is well-governed;
when the state is well-governed, the world is at peace.
Thus it is said: take oneself as the family,
take the family as the state,
take the state as the world.
These four things,
though different in position, share the same root.
Therefore, the affairs of the sage,
extended broadly, reach the limits of the cosmos and exhaust the sun and moon;
contracted narrowly, they do not go beyond the self.
A loving parent cannot transmit this to their child,
a loyal minister cannot instill this in their ruler;
only those with the inherent capacity can come close to it.
Tián Pián expounded the Way and its methods to the King of Qí.
The King of Qí responded to him:
"All I possess is the state of Qí;
I wish to hear about the governance of Qí."
Tián Pián replied:
"My words
contain no governance, yet they can lead to governance.
It is like a forest of trees:
there is no timber, yet timber can be obtained.
I hope Your Majesty will take up the governance of Qí yourself.
Pián has only spoken superficially;
speaking broadly,
how could it be limited to the governance of Qí alone?
Changes and responses come, yet all have their pattern;
following nature and employing things, nothing is inappropriate.
Péngzǔ attained longevity thereby,
the Three Dynasties flourished thereby,
the Five Emperors were illustrious thereby,
Shénnóng was vast thereby."
Wú Qǐ said to Shāng Wén:
"Serving a ruler indeed depends on fate, does it not!"
Shāng Wén said:
"What do you mean?"
Wú Qǐ said:
"Bringing order within the four borders,
establishing instruction and transformation,
changing customs and habits,
causing ruler and minister to have righteousness,
father and son to have proper order—
who is more worthy, you or I?"
Shāng Wén said:
"I am not your equal."
He said:
"Today, presenting credentials to become a minister,
one's lord feels secure and weighty;
today, returning the seal and resigning from office,
one's lord feels secure and light—
who is more worthy, you or I?"
Shāng Wén said:
"I am not your equal."
He said:
"When officers and horses are arrayed in formation,
horses matched against men,
men standing before horses,
taking up the drumstick and striking the drum once,
causing the soldiers of the three armies
to delight in death as if it were life—
who is more worthy, you or I?"
Shāng Wén said:
"I am not your equal."
Wú Qǐ said:
"In these three matters,
you are not my equal,
yet your position is above mine.
It is fate, this serving a ruler!"
Shāng Wén said:
"Good.
You have questioned me;
I shall also question you.
When the age changes and the ruler is young,
ministers suspect one another,
the common people are unsettled,
should it be entrusted to you?
Or entrusted to me?"
Wú Qǐ fell silent and did not reply.
After a short while, he said:
"To you."
Shāng Wén said:
"This is the reason I am placed above you."
Qǐ saw his own strengths,
but did not see his own weaknesses;
he knew wherein he was worthy,
but did not know wherein he was unworthy.
Thus he triumphed west of the Hé,
but was thwarted by Wáng Cuò;
he brought about great calamity,
and did not die a natural death.
Now, Wú triumphed over Qí,
but did not triumph over Yuè;
Qí triumphed over Sòng,
but did not triumph over Yān.
Therefore, of all who can preserve the state and keep themselves whole,
only they understand the transformations of strength and weakness, fullness and deficiency.
18.1 "Examining Responses"
It is said:
When a ruler utters words and displays expressions,
he cannot but be careful.
Generally, if a ruler is perceptive,
he does not wish to speak first.
When others initiate, he responds;
when others lead, he follows.
Taking their output as his input,
taking their words as their reputation,
he takes their substance to hold them accountable to their reputation.
Then those who speak will not dare to speak recklessly,
and the ruler grasps the essential.
Kǒng Sī requested to leave.
The ruler of Lǔ said:
"The rulers of the world are all like me;
where will you go?"
Kǒng Sī replied:
"I have heard that a gentleman is like a bird:
when startled, it takes flight."
The ruler of Lǔ said:
"If the ruler is unworthy, and all are like this,
to avoid the unworthy,
to encounter the unworthy,
do you consider yourself capable of judging the rulers of the world?"
Generally, when a bird takes flight,
it flees from the startled to the unstartled.
To flee from the startled to the unstartled
is not necessarily known.
To flee from the startled to the startled—
then why would the bird take flight?
Kǒng Sī's reply to the ruler of Lǔ was also mistaken.
King Huì of Wèi sent a man to say to Marquis Zhāo of Hán:
"That Zhèng was destroyed by the Hán clan;
I hope you will enfeoff its descendants.
This is what is called the principle of preserving the perishing and continuing the severed.
If you enfeoff them, you will gain great renown."
Marquis Zhāo was troubled by this.
Gōngzǐ Shíwǒ said:
"I request to go and reply to him."
Gōngzǐ Shíwǒ went to Wèi
and saw the King of Wèi, saying:
"Your great state commands our humble city to enfeoff the descendants of Zhèng;
our humble city dares not presume to do so.
Our humble city is a source of trouble for your great state.
In the past, Shēngshì, a descendant of Duke Chū,
was detained at Tóngdī when he became Duke of Jìn,
and your great state showed no pity.
Yet now you would have our humble city preserve the perishing and continue the severed;
our humble city dares not presume to do so."
The King of Wèi, ashamed, said:
"This was certainly not my intention;
please, sir, say no more."
This was to use unrighteousness to carry out unrighteousness.
Though the King of Wèi had no reply,
Hán's unrighteousness only grew greater.
Gōngzǐ Shíwǒ's argument
merely served to gloss over wrongs and persist in error.
King Zhāo of Wèi asked Tián Qū:
"When I was in the Eastern Palace,
I heard your discourse, saying:
'Becoming a sage is easy.'
Is this so?"
Tián Qū replied:
"This is what I advocated."
King Zhāo said:
"Then are you, sir, a sage?"
Tián Qū replied:
"To know someone is a sage before they have achieved merit
is like Yáo knowing Shùn;
to wait until they have achieved merit and then know they are a sage Shùn
is like a market person knowing the sage Shùn.
Now Qū has no merit,
yet Your Majesty asks Qū, 'Are you a sage?'
May I ask if Your Majesty is also a Yáo?"
King Zhāo had no reply.
Tián Qū's reply—
King Zhāo certainly did not say
"I know sages,"
but asked, "Are you, sir, a sage?"
He himself then used knowing sages to reply to King Zhāo.
King Zhāo did not possess what he claimed to possess,
and Tián Qū did not discern this.
King Huì of Zhào said to Gōngsūn Lóng:
"I have devoted myself to the cessation of warfare for over ten years, yet have not succeeded.
Is it impossible to cease warfare?"
Gōngsūn Lóng replied:
"The intention to cease warfare
is a heart that loves all under heaven equally.
To love all under heaven equally
cannot be done with empty reputation;
it must have its substance.
Now when Lìn and Líshí entered Qín's possession,
Your Majesty wore plain mourning garments and distributed cloth;
when attacking Qí in the east and gaining cities,
Your Majesty added delicacies to your meals and set out wine.
When Qín gained territory, Your Majesty distributed cloth;
when Qí lost territory, Your Majesty added delicacies—
this is not the heart of loving all equally.
This is why the cessation of warfare has not succeeded."
Suppose there were a person here who,
being rude and disrespectful, sought respect;
being partial and unfair, sought good order;
issuing vexatious commands and frequently changing them, sought tranquility;
being violent, cruel, and greedy, sought stability—
even Huángdì would find it difficult.
Lord Sì of Wèi wished to impose heavy taxes to accumulate grain,
but the people were not at ease.
He told Bó Yí about it, saying:
"The people are very foolish.
Accumulating grain
is intended to be for the people's benefit.
What difference does it make whether they store it themselves or it is kept by the ruler?"
Bó Yí said:
"Not so.
If it is with the people but the ruler does not know of it,
it is not as good as being with the ruler;
if it is with the ruler but the people do not know of it,
it is not as good as being with the people."
In general, when listening to matters, one must reflect them back upon oneself;
if one examines carefully, then there will be no orders that are not heeded.
A state that endures long becomes solid;
being solid, it is difficult to perish.
Now Yú, Xià, Yīn, and Zhōu no longer exist—
all because they did not know to reflect back upon themselves.
Gōngzǐ Tá was prime minister of Zhōu.
Shēn Xiàng persuaded him and he trembled.
Gōngzǐ Tá reproached him, saying:
"Master Shēn persuaded me and I trembled—
is this because I am prime minister?"
Shēn Xiàng said:
"I, Xiàng, am unworthy.
Nevertheless,
you, young master, became prime minister at twenty,
and when you see an old man you make him tremble—
may I ask, which is the fault?"
Gōngzǐ Tá had nothing to reply.
Trembling
is due to lack of familiarity;
making others tremble
is due to stern intimidation.
If one is reverent and restrained and people still tremble,
then the responsibility does not lie with the esteemed one.
Therefore, although people sometimes have their own failings,
still there is nothing to substitute for reverence and restraint.
One's own failings are not sufficient to cause difficulty;
using stern intimidation can do so.
18.2 "Weighty Speech"
Second:
The speech of a ruler
cannot but be cautious.
Gāozōng was the Son of Heaven.
Upon ascending the throne, during the mourning hut period,
he did not speak for three years.
The high ministers and grandees were fearful
and troubled by this.
Gāozōng then spoke, saying:
"With my single person rectifying the four quarters,
I only fear that my speech may not be fitting;
therefore I have not spoken."
The ancient Son of Heaven
valued speech to such an extent
that his words left nothing out.
King Chéng was at leisure with Táng Shū Yú.
Picking up a parasol tree leaf, he used it as a ceremonial tablet
and handed it to Táng Shū Yú, saying:
"I confer this upon you."
Shū Yú was pleased
and told Duke Zhōu about it.
Duke Zhōu requested an audience, saying:
"Is the Son of Heaven conferring a fief upon Yú?"
King Chéng said:
"I was just playing with Yú."
Duke Zhōu replied:
"Your servant has heard that
the Son of Heaven has no jesting words.
When the Son of Heaven speaks,
the scribes record it,
the musicians chant it,
and the officers cite it."
Thereupon he enfeoffed Shū Yú in Jìn.
Duke Zhōu Dàn may be said to have been skilled in persuasion.
With one citation he caused King Chéng to value speech even more,
clarified the duty of loving one's younger brother,
and strengthened the support of the royal house.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ, having established his government for three years,
did not attend court but was fond of riddles.
Chénggōng Jiǎ entered to remonstrate.
The king said:
"I have prohibited remonstrance;
now you come to remonstrate—
what is the reason?"
He replied:
"Your servant does not dare to remonstrate;
I wish to engage in riddles with Your Majesty."
The king said:
"Why not pose a riddle for me?"
He replied:
"There is a bird perched on a southern mound;
for three years it does not move, does not fly, does not cry—
what kind of bird is this?"
The king guessed it, saying:
"A bird perched on a southern mound—
its not moving for three years
is to settle its will and intent;
its not flying
is to grow its feathers and wings;
its not crying
is to observe the people's patterns.
Though this bird has not flown,
when it flies it will soar to the heavens;
though it has not cried,
when it cries it will startle people.
Jiǎ, you may leave;
I understand."
The next day at court,
he promoted five men
and dismissed ten men.
The assembled ministers were greatly pleased,
and the multitude of Chǔ congratulated one another.
Therefore the Odes say:
"Why so long?
There must be a reason.
Why so settled?
There must be a companion."
Does this refer to King Zhuāng?
Chénggōng Jiǎ's riddle
was worthier than Grand Steward Pǐ's persuasion.
Grand Steward Pǐ's persuasion
was heeded by Fūchāi,
and Wú became ruins;
Chénggōng Jiǎ's riddle
enlightened the King of Chǔ,
and Chǔ thereby became hegemon.
Duke Huán of Qí and Guǎn Zhòng planned to attack Jǔ.
The plan had not yet been put into action but was heard throughout the state.
Duke Huán found it strange, saying:
"I planned with Father Zhòng to attack Jǔ;
the plan has not yet been put into action but is heard throughout the state—
what is the reason?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"There must be a sage in the state."
Duke Huán said:
"Ah!
Among the laborers the other day,
there was one holding a shovel and looking upward—
perhaps it is he?"
He then ordered the laborers to resume work,
not allowing substitutions.
After a short while,
Dōngguō Yá arrived.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"This must be the one."
He then ordered the usher to escort him up,
and they stood on separate steps.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Was it you who spoke of attacking Jǔ?"
He replied:
"Yes."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ;
why did you speak of attacking Jǔ?"
He replied:
"Your servant has heard that the noble man is good at planning,
and the petty man is good at guessing.
I privately guessed it."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I did not speak of attacking Jǔ,
how did you infer it?"
The reply was:
"Your servant has heard that a gentleman has three expressions:
one that is radiantly joyful and good-humored
is the expression of bells and drums;
one that is sorrowfully pure and tranquil
is the expression of mourning garments;
one that is flushed and full,
with hands and feet tense and moving,
is the expression of war and arms.
The other day, your servant observed Your Lordship on the terrace,
flushed and full,
with hands and feet tense—
this was the expression of war and arms.
Your Lordship opened your mouth but did not close it; what
you spoke of was Jǔ;
Your Lordship raised your arm and pointed,
what you indicated was Jǔ.
Your servant privately considered that among the feudal lords who do not submit,
it is only Jǔ.
Therefore, your servant spoke of it."
In general, the ear hears through sound;
now, without hearing the sound,
but through his countenance and arm,
this is Dōng Guō Yá hearing not with his ears.
Although Duke Huán and Guǎn Zhòng were skilled at concealment,
they could not hide it.
Therefore, the sage hears the soundless,
sees the formless;
such were Zhān Hé, Tián Zǐfāng, and Lǎo Dān.
18.3 "Subtle Communication"
The third says:
Sages communicate without waiting for words;
there are those who speak before words.
There was a man by the sea who loved dragonflies;
every morning he would stay by the sea,
following the dragonflies as they played;
the dragonflies that came
numbered in the hundreds without end,
before, behind, left, and right were all dragonflies;
he played with them all day without leaving.
His father told him:
"I hear the dragonflies all follow where you stay;
catch some and bring them,
I will play with them."
The next day he went to the sea,
and no dragonflies came.
Shèng Shū addressed Duke Zhōu Dàn, saying:
"The court is small and the crowd large;
speaking slowly will not be heard,
speaking quickly will let others know;
shall I speak slowly?
Or speak quickly?"
Duke Zhōu Dàn said:
"Speak slowly."
Shèng Shū said:
"There is a matter here,
and speaking subtly will not make it clear,
not speaking will not accomplish it;
shall I speak subtly?
Or not speak?"
Duke Zhōu Dàn said:
"Do not speak."
Thus, Shèng Shū was able to persuade without speaking,
and Duke Zhōu Dàn was able to listen without words;
this is called listening without words.
Plans without words,
affairs unheard,
though Yīn hated Zhōu,
they could find no fault.
The mouth does not speak,
but communicates with subtlety;
though Zhòu had many suspicions,
he could not know.
The eye sees the formless,
the ear hears the soundless;
though the merchants of Shāng were many,
they could not spy.
Sharing dislikes and likes,
intentions all having desires,
even as the Son of Heaven,
one cannot separate from them.
Confucius met Wēn Bó Xuězǐ,
and left without speaking.
Zǐgòng said:
"Our master has long wished to see Wēn Bó Xuězǐ;
now he has seen him but did not speak;
what is the reason?"
Confucius said:
"As for that man,
at a glance the Way is present;
there is no need for words."
Thus, without seeing the person, one knows his intent;
seeing the person, his heart and intent are both revealed;
it is the harmony of Heaven's accord.
When sages know each other,
how could they wait for words?
Bái Gōng asked Confucius:
"Can one speak subtly with others?"
Confucius did not respond.
Bái Gōng said:
"What is it like to throw a stone into water?"
Confucius said:
"A diver can retrieve it."
Bái Gōng said:
"What is it like to pour water into water?"
Confucius said:
"When the Zī and Shéng rivers merge,
Yì Yá can taste and know."
Bái Gōng said:
"Then, can one not speak subtly with others?"
Confucius said:
"Why not?
Only those who understand what words mean can do so."
Bái Gōng did not grasp it.
To understand what words mean is not to rely on words for meaning.
Words belong to the category of meaning.
Those who seek fish get wet,
those who chase beasts run;
it is not for pleasure.
Thus, the highest words abandon words,
the highest action is non-action.
What shallow wisdom contends over is trivial;
Bái Gōng did not attain it.
This is why Bái Gōng died in the prison cell.
Duke Huán of Qí assembled the feudal lords;
the people of Wèi arrived late.
The duke held court and plotted with Guǎn Zhòng to attack Wèi;
after court, he entered his chambers.
Consort Wèi saw the lord,
descended the hall and bowed twice,
pleading for the crime of the lord of Wèi.
The duke said:
"I have no grievance against Wèi;
why do you plead?"
She replied:
"Your concubine observed Your Lordship's entry:
your steps were high, your spirit strong,
with the intent to attack a state;
seeing your concubine, your expression changed—
it is to attack Wèi."
The next day, the lord held court,
bowed to Guǎn Zhòng and advanced him.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Has Your Lordship abandoned Wèi?"
The duke said:
"How did you know, Father Zhòng?"
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Your Lordship's court bow was reverent,
and your speech was slow;
seeing your minister, you showed a ashamed expression;
thus your minister knew."
The lord said:
"Good.
Father Zhòng governs the outside,
my lady governs the inside;
I know I will never be laughed at by the feudal lords."
What Duke Huán concealed was not spoken;
now Guǎnzǐ discerned it through appearance and voice,
and the lady through gait and spirit;
though Duke Huán did not speak,
it was like a torch in the dark night.
Duke Xiāng of Jìn sent an envoy to Zhōu, saying:
"Our humble lord is bedridden with illness;
divination with the guardian turtle said:
'Sān Tú is causing misfortune.'
Our humble lord sends his humble minister to request passage to pray for blessings."
The Son of Heaven permitted it.
At court,
after the rituals for the envoy were completed,
the guest departed.
Cháng Hóng said to Liú Kānggōng:
"To pray for blessings at Sān Tú,
and receive rites from the Son of Heaven—
this is a gentle and auspicious affair;
yet the guest had a martial expression;
likely there is another matter;
I hope you prepare for it."
Liú Kānggōng then alerted his chariots and soldiers to await them.
Jìn indeed sent the sacrificial party first,
then ordered Yángzǐ to lead one hundred twenty thousand troops to follow,
crossing at Jíjīn,
attacking Liáoruǎn, Liáng, and Mánshì,
and destroying these three states.
This is when form and name do not match,
which the sage scrutinizes;
Cháng Hóng was discerning indeed.
Thus, words are insufficient to decide small matters;
only those who understand what words mean can do so.
18.4 "Divergence of Words and Meaning"
The fourth says:
Words are used to convey meaning.
When words and meaning are separated,
it is ominous.
The custom of a disordered state
is that there are many rumors,
and they do not care about the facts,
striving to slander each other,
striving to praise each other,
slander and praise form factions,
the mouths of the multitude fill the sky,
the worthy and the unworthy are not distinguished.
To govern a state in this way,
even a worthy ruler would be confused by it,
how much more so an unworthy one?
The trouble with the confused
is that they do not consider themselves confused.
Therefore, within confusion there is clarity,
within darkness there is illumination.
The rulers of perished states
do not consider themselves confused,
thus they are all like Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì.
Yet there are states that perish,
but there is no second way about it.
In the state of Zhèng, many people posted writings to criticize each other.
Zǐchǎn ordered that no writings be posted,
Dèng Xī delivered them.
Zǐchǎn ordered that no writings be delivered,
Dèng Xī attached them to other things.
If the orders are endless,
then Dèng Xī's responses will also be endless.
This is a case where right and wrong are indistinguishable.
When right and wrong are indistinguishable,
and yet rewards and punishments are applied,
the more severe the punishments,
the greater the disorder.
This is a prohibition in governing a state.
Therefore, to argue but not accord with principle is deceitful;
to be clever but not accord with principle is fraudulent.
Deceitful and fraudulent people
are those whom the former kings punished.
Principle is
the foundation of right and wrong.
The Wěi River was very high,
and a rich man of Zhèng drowned.
Someone recovered the corpse.
The rich man's family requested to ransom it,
but the person demanded a very high price.
They told Dèng Xī about it.
Dèng Xī said:
"Be at ease.
He certainly cannot sell it to anyone else."
The person who had the corpse became worried
and told Dèng Xī.
Dèng Xī again replied to him:
"Be at ease.
They certainly have nowhere else to buy it."
Those who harm loyal ministers
are similar to this.
If a minister achieves no merit and wins no support from the people,
they use his lack of merit and support to harm him;
if he achieves merit and wins support from the people,
they then use his merit and support to harm him.
A ruler without standards
has no way to understand this—
is this not悲哀?
Bǐgān and Chánghóng died because of this,
Jīzǐ and Shāngróng were reduced to poverty because of this,
Zhōugōng and Shàogōng were doubted because of this,
Fànlǐ and Zǐxū were exiled because of this.
Life and death, survival and perishment, safety and danger
all arise from this.
When Zǐchǎn governed Zhèng,
Dèng Xī made every effort to oppose him.
He made an agreement with the people who had lawsuits:
for a major lawsuit, one garment;
for a minor lawsuit, a short jacket and trousers. The people who offered garments, short jackets, and trousers to learn litigation
were too many to count.
They turned wrong into right,
and right into wrong.
Right and wrong had no standard,
and what was permissible and impermissible changed daily.
Whoever they wanted to win would win,
whoever they wanted to condemn would be condemned.
The state of Zhèng fell into great disorder,
and the people's mouths were filled with clamor.
Zǐchǎn was troubled by this,
so he had Dèng Xī killed and his corpse exposed.
Only then did the people's hearts submit,
right and wrong were settled,
and laws were implemented.
People of the present age
mostly desire to govern their states well,
but none of them punish those like Dèng Xī.
This is why the more they desire order, the greater the disorder becomes.
In Qí, there was a man who served another.
When the one he served encountered trouble, he did not die for him.
He met an old acquaintance on the road.
The old acquaintance said:
"So you did not die after all?"
He replied:
"Indeed.
In all cases, serving another is for profit.
To die is not profitable,
so I did not die."
The old acquaintance said:
"How can you still show your face to people?"
He replied:
"Do you think that by dying one can still show one's face to people?"
This story has been passed down several times.
Not dying for one's lord or superior
is greatly unrighteous,
yet his words still cannot be refuted.
That words are insufficient to decide matters is clear.
Words are
the expression of intention.
To examine the expression and discard the intention is perverse.
Therefore, the ancients,
when they grasped the intention, would discard the words.
Those who listen to words use the words to observe the intention.
If after listening to the words the intention cannot be known,
then they are no different from deceptive words.
There was a man from Qí named Chúnyú Kūn
who persuaded the King of Wèi with a policy of alliance (zòng).
The King of Wèi found him eloquent,
prepared ten carriages,
and was about to send him to Jīng.
As he was taking his leave and about to depart,
he persuaded the King of Wèi with a policy of horizontal alliance (héng).
The King of Wèi then stopped his mission.
He lost the intention of the vertical alliance,
and also failed in the matter of the horizontal alliance.
Having many abilities is not as good as having few abilities;
being eloquent is not as good as being ineloquent.
The Zhōu tripod depicts Chuí biting his finger—
the former kings thereby showed that great cleverness should not be pursued.
18.5 "Licentious Speech"
The fifth says:
Without words, there is no way to communicate,
but following words leads to disorder.
Within disordered words, there are yet more words—
this refers to the mind.
If words do not deceive the mind,
then one is close to it.
All words
are to convey the mind.
If words and mind are separated,
and those above have no way to verify them,
then those below will often say one thing and do another,
or do one thing and say another.
When words and actions contradict each other,
there is no greater inauspiciousness.
At the meeting of Kōngxióng,
Qín and Zhào made a pact with each other.
The pact said:
"From now on,
whatever Qín wishes to do,
Zhào will assist;
whatever Zhào wishes to do,
Qín will assist."
Not long after,
Qín raised troops to attack Wèi,
and Zhào wished to rescue it.
The King of Qín was displeased
and sent someone to reproach the King of Zhào, saying:
"The pact says:
'Whatever Qín wishes to do,
Zhào will assist;
whatever Zhào wishes to do,
Qín will assist.'
Now Qín wishes to attack Wèi,
yet Zhào instead wishes to rescue it—
this is not according to the pact."
The King of Zhào told this to Lord Píngyuán.
Lord Píngyuán told it to Gōngsūn Lóng.
Gōngsūn Lóng said:
"You can also send an envoy to reproach the King of Qín, saying:
'Zhào wishes to rescue it,
yet now the King of Qín alone does not assist Zhào—
this is not according to the pact.'"
Kǒng Chuān and Gōngsūn Lóng debated each other at Lord Píngyuán's residence.
Their discussion was profound and disputatious,
reaching the topic of "three ears of Zāng."
Gōngsūn Lóng argued very persuasively about Zāng having three ears,
but Kǒng Chuān did not respond.
After a short while,
he took his leave and went out.
The next day,
Kǒng Chuān attended court.
Píngyuán Jūn said to Kǒng Chuān:
"In the past, Gōngsūn Lóng's words were extremely sophistical."
Kǒng Chuān said:
"Indeed.
He nearly made it so that a sheep has three ears.
Nevertheless, it is truly difficult.
I wish to ask you a question:
To say a sheep has three ears is extremely difficult yet actually false,
to say a sheep has two ears is extremely easy yet actually true.
I do not know whether you will follow what is easy and true?
Or will you follow what is difficult and false?"
Píngyuán Jūn did not respond.
The next day,
he said to Gōngsūn Lóng:
"You should no longer debate with Kǒng Chuān."
Jīng's Pillar of State Zhuāng Bó ordered his father to observe the sun.
"The sun,"
he said, "is in the sky";
"Observe what it is like?"
He said, "Perfectly round";
"Observe the time,"
he
said, "the present moment."
He ordered the usher to "harness the carriage,"
who said, "There are no horses."
He ordered the attendant to "fetch the cap,"
who said, "It is presented above."
Asked about "the horse's teeth,"
the groom said, "Twelve incisors and thirty molars."
There was a man who guaranteed his servant would not flee,
the servant fled,
Zhuāng Bó adjudicated the case,
and the guarantor was found not guilty.
In Sòng there was a man named Chéngzǐ
who lost a black garment.
He searched for it on the road,
saw a woman wearing a black garment,
grabbed her and would not let go,
wanting to take her garment,
saying:
"Today I lost a black garment."
The woman said:
"Although you lost a black garment,
this one was truly made by me myself."
Chéngzǐ said:
"You had better quickly give me the garment.
What I lost before
was a lined black garment.
Now your garment
is an unlined black garment.
Using an unlined black garment to replace a lined black garment,
aren't you getting an advantage?"
The King of Sòng said to his Chancellor Táng Yāng:
"The people I have killed are many,
yet my ministers grow increasingly unafraid.
What is the reason for this?"
Táng Yāng replied:
"Those whom Your Majesty punishes
are entirely the wicked.
Punishing the wicked,
the good therefore remain unafraid.
If Your Majesty wishes your ministers to be afraid,
it would be better not to distinguish between the good and the wicked but to punish them from time to time.
If so, then your ministers will be afraid."
Not long after,
the Lord of Sòng killed Táng Yāng.
Táng Yāng's reply
was worse than no reply at all.
Huìzǐ formulated laws for King Huì of Wèi.
When the laws were completed,
he showed them to the various people.
The people all approved of them.
He presented them to King Huì,
and King Huì approved of them.
He showed them to Zhái Jiǎn.
Zhái Jiǎn said:
"They are good."
King Huì said:
"Good, but can they be implemented?"
Zhái Jiǎn said:
"They cannot."
King Huì said:
"Good yet cannot be implemented;
what is the reason?"
Zhái Jiǎn replied:
"Now those lifting large logs
call out 'yúxú' in front,
and those behind also respond.
This is good for lifting large logs.
Is it that there are no melodies like those of Zhèng and Wèi?
Yet they are not as suitable as this.
A state is also like a large log."
18.6 《Bùqū》
The sixth says:
Those who are discerning may think they have attained the Way, but they have not.
Nevertheless,
in their response to things,
their arguments are difficult to exhaust.
Though their arguments may be exhausted,
whether they bring fortune or calamity is still unknowable.
If discernment is used to comprehend principles and clarify righteousness,
then discernment brings fortune;
if discernment is used to embellish wrongdoing and delude the foolish,
then discernment brings calamity.
In ancient times, skilled charioteering was valued
for pursuing the violent and restraining the wicked.
