King Huì of Wèi said to Huìzǐ:
"Those who held states in high antiquity
were necessarily worthy men.
Now I am truly not equal to you, sir.
I wish to hand over the state to you."
Huìzǐ declined.
The king again firmly requested, saying:
"I have no one here to give the state to,
but by transmitting it to a worthy man,
the people's hearts of greed and contention will cease.
I wish you, sir, would consent to this for my sake."
Huìzǐ said:
"If it is as the king says,
then I, Shī, cannot consent.
The king is firmly the lord of ten thousand chariots.
To give the state to another is still permissible.
Now I, Shī,
am a commoner.
To be able to have the state of ten thousand chariots and decline it—
this would make the cessation of greedy and contentious hearts even greater."
King Huì said to Huìzǐ:
"Those who held states in ancient times
were necessarily worthy men."
When a great officer received it, the worthy one was Shùn;
this was wanting Huìzǐ to be Shùn.
When one declined it, the worthy one was Xǔ Yóu;
this was Huìzǐ wanting to be Xǔ Yóu.
When one transmitted it, the worthy one was Yáo;
this was King Huì wanting to be Yáo.
The actions of Yáo, Shùn, and Xǔ Yóu
were not merely transmitting to Shùn and Xǔ Yóu declining;
their other conduct matched this.
Now they lacked their other qualities,
yet wanted to be Yáo, Shùn, and Xǔ Yóu.
Therefore, King Huì wore a cloth cap and was detained in Juàn;
King Wēi of Qí nearly did not receive him;
Huìzǐ changed his clothes and cap,
rode in a carriage and fled,
nearly not escaping the borders of Wèi.
Generally, one's own actions cannot be done by luck;
they must be sincere.
Kuāng Zhāng said to Huìzǐ in front of the King of Wèi:
"Locusts, borers, and stem-borers—
when farmers catch them, they kill them.
What is the reason?
Because they harm the crops.
Now in your travels, sir,
at most several hundred chariots,
several hundred men on foot;
at least several tens of chariots,
several tens of men on foot.
These are people who do not plow yet eat.
Their harm to the crops is also great."
King Huì said:
"Huìzǐ Shī
finds it difficult to respond to you with words.
Nevertheless,
let him speak his mind.
Huìzǐ said:
'Now in building city walls,
some wield large rammers on the wall,
some carry baskets and hurry below the wall,
some hold markers and sighting poles to observe well.
As for me, Shī,
I am one who holds the markers and sighting poles.
Make a skilled weaver transform into silk,
she cannot work silk;
make a great carpenter transform into wood,
he cannot work wood;
make a sage transform into a farmer,
he cannot manage farmers.
I, Shī, am one who manages farmers.'
Why do you compare me, Shī, to borers and stem-borers?"
Huìzǐ governed Wèi taking this as fundamental,
his governance was not good governance.
During King Huì's time,
there were fifty battles and twenty defeats,
those killed were innumerable,
great generals and beloved sons were captured.
The folly of his grand methods
was laughed at by all under heaven.
When his faults were exposed,
he requested the Grand Historian of Zhōu to change his recorded name.
They besieged Hándān for three years but were unable to capture it.
The officers and people were exhausted and weary,
the state treasury was empty,
and armies from all under Heaven arrived from four directions.
The masses criticized and slandered,
the feudal lords did not praise,
they apologized to Zhái Jiǎn and instead listened to his counsel,
and only then did the altars of soil and grain survive.
Precious treasures were scattered and lost,
territory was reduced on all four sides,
and the state of Wèi declined from then on.
The title of Zhòngfù is a great name,
yielding the state is a great act.
To persuade with what is not listened to or believed,
and to listen in such a manner,
cannot be called skillful.
To govern without skill,
there is no greater harm to all under Heaven,
yet it is fortunate that only Wèi listened.
To regard harming all under Heaven as an act,
and to regard governing as a name,
is Kuāng Zhāng’s criticism—
is that not indeed appropriate?
Bái Guī had just met Master Huì,
and Master Huī persuaded him with forceful arguments,
but Bái Guī had no response.
Master Huī left.
Bái Guī told others:
“There was a man who had just taken a bride.
When the bride arrived,
she ought to have been calm, reserved, with downcast eyes and graceful steps.
A servant boy was holding a torch too high,
and the bride said:
‘The torch is held too high.’
Upon entering the gate,
there was a depression in the threshold,
and the bride said:
‘Fill it in,
or it will injure people’s feet.’
This is not an inconvenience to the household,
but it is rather excessive.
Now, Master Huī’s acquaintance with me is still new,
yet his persuasion of me is rather excessive.”
Master Huī heard this and said:
“That is not so.
The Odes say:
‘A joyous and reverent gentleman
is the parent of the people.’
‘Joyous’ means great,
‘reverent’ means elder.
The virtue of a gentleman,
being both elder and great,
makes him the parent of the people.
When parents teach their children,
must they wait long?
Why compare me to a bride?
Does the Odes say
‘a joyous and reverent bride’?”
To criticize filth because of filth,
to criticize perversity because of perversity,
is to make the critic and the criticized alike.
Bái Guī said:
“Master Huī’s acquaintance with me is still new,
yet his persuasion of me is rather excessive.”
Master Huī heard and criticized him,
and thereby considered himself as his parent—
his fault is even greater than Bái Guī’s, and is also rather excessive.
18.7 “Appropriate Speech”
The seventh says:
Bái Guī said to the King of Wèi:
“Using the Dǐng of Shìqiū to cook chicken,
if too much broth is added, it becomes bland and inedible;
if too little broth is added, it becomes scorched and undercooked;
yet to look at it, it is grand and beautiful but utterly useless.
Master Huī’s words
are similar to this.”
Master Huī heard this and said:
“That is not so.
Suppose the three armies were starving and placed beside the Dǐng,
and it was just made into a Zèng,
then nothing would be more suitable than this Dǐng.”
Bái Guī heard this and said:
“If it is utterly useless,
does that mean one merely adds a Zèng to it?”
Bái Guī’s argument contradicts itself,
and he belittles the King of Wèi excessively.
To say that Master Huī’s words are grand and beautiful but utterly useless
is to say that the King of Wèi regards utterly useless words as those of a Zhòngfù,
and thus regards useless words as beautiful.
Gōngsūn Lóng persuaded King Zhāo of Yān to disband the army.
King Zhāo said:
“Very good.
I wish to discuss this with you, my guest.”
Gōngsūn Lóng said:
“I suspect that Your Majesty will not do it.”
The King said: “Why?”
Gōngsūn Lóng said:
“Previously, Your Majesty wished to defeat Qí,
and among the scholars of all under Heaven,
those who wished to defeat Qí,
Your Majesty fully supported them;
those who knew Qí’s strategic passes, strongholds, and the relations between its ruler and ministers,
Your Majesty fully supported them;
even if they knew but did not wish to defeat Qí,
Your Majesty still did not support them;
and in the end, they indeed defeated Qí and achieved merit.
Now Your Majesty says, ‘I greatly desire to disband the army.’
Yet the scholars of the feudal lords
in Your Majesty’s own court
are all skilled in using troops.
Therefore, I know that Your Majesty will not do it.”
The King had no response.
Sīmǎ Xǐ challenged a Mohist master before the King of Zhōngshān regarding the condemnation of offensive warfare,
saying:
“Is it not offensive warfare that you, sir, advocate?”
The Mohist master said:
“Yes.”
Sīmǎ Xǐ said:
“Now the King raises troops to attack Yān—
will you, sir, condemn the King?”
The Mohist master replied:
“Then does the Chancellor approve of attacking?”
Sīmǎ Xǐ said:
“Yes.”
The Mohist master said:
“Now Zhào raises troops to attack Zhōngshān—
will the Chancellor approve of that?”
Sīmǎ Xǐ had no response.
Lù Shuō said to Zhōu Pō:
“If you, sir, do not love Zhào,
all under Heaven will surely follow.”
Zhōu Pō said:
“I indeed wish for all under Heaven to follow.
If all under Heaven follow, it benefits Qín.”
Lù Shuō responded:
“Then do you, sir, wish for Qín’s benefit?”
Zhōu Pō said:
“I wish for it.”
Lù Shuō said:
“If you, sir, wish for it,
then why not work for it to follow?”
Wèi ordered Mèng Áng to cede the lands of Jiàng, Fèn, and Ānyì to the King of Qín.
The King was pleased,
and ordered Qǐ Jiǎ to request from the King of Wèi that Mèng Áng be made Minister over the Masses.
The King of Wèi was displeased,
and responded to Qǐ Jiǎ:
“Áng is my minister.
I would rather make Zāng Minister over the Masses
than use Áng.
I hope His Majesty will instruct someone else.”
Qǐ Jiǎ left,
and encountered Mèng Áng in the court,
saying:
“How did your affair go?”
Qǐ Jiǎ said:
“You are held in very low esteem by your lord.
Your lord said:
‘I would rather use Zāng as Minister over the Masses
than use you.’”
Mèng Áng entered for an audience,
and said to the King of Wèi:
“What did the envoy from Qín say?”
The King said:
“He requested that you be made Minister over the Masses.”
Mèng Áng said:
“How did Your Majesty respond?”
The King said:
“I would rather use Zāng
than use Áng.”
Mèng Áng sighed deeply and said:
“No wonder Your Majesty is controlled by Qín.
Why does Your Majesty doubt Qín’s goodwill toward me?
To order an ox to carry the document for Jiàng, Fèn, and Ānyì to Qín,
even an ox would be treated well.
Though I am unworthy,
am I alone inferior to an ox?
Moreover, Your Majesty ordered three generals to precede me, saying, ‘Treat Áng as you would your own person’—
that was to honor me.
Now to belittle me twice,
and order me to bear responsibility—
though I am capable, could I possibly manage?”
After three days,
the King of Wèi then listened to Qǐ Jiǎ.
Whenever a ruler grants a high office to someone,
it is because it is beneficial.
Now, having ceded a small portion of the state’s territory,
and thereby obtaining a high office,
what land will be left to provide?
High office is what ministers desire.
Mèng Áng allowed Qín to obtain what it desired,
and Qín also allowed Mèng Áng to obtain what he desired.
The debt has been repaid;
what further obligation remains?
Even if Wèi were strong, it could not demand payment where no debt is owed,
let alone when it is weak.
For the King of Wèi to appoint Mèng Áng as Minister of Education
in order to evade his own obligation was unskillful.
When the King of Qín declared himself Emperor,
the Magistrate of Xūyáng, Xǔ Wǎn, deceived the King of Wèi,
and the King of Wèi was about to go to Qín.
Wèi Jìng said to the King:
"Which is more important, Hénèi or Liáng?"
The King said:
"Liáng is more important."
He then asked:
"Which is more important, Liáng or your own person?"
The King said:
"My own person is more important."
He then said:
"If Qín were to demand Hénèi,
would Your Majesty give it to them?"
The King said:
"I would not."
Wèi Jìng said:
"Hénèi is the least important in these three comparisons,
while your own person is the most important.
Qín demanded the least important, and Your Majesty refused;
yet now it demands the most important, and Your Majesty is willing to comply.
I privately believe this is not a course Your Majesty should take."
The King said:
"Very true."
He then halted his journey.
Although Qín achieved a great victory at Chángpíng,
it took three years to decide the battle,
its soldiers and people were weary,
and its grain supplies were depleted.
At that time,
if the two Zhōu had been preserved intact,
and their northern territories had remained,
and if Wèi had seized Táo and reduced Wèi,
gaining six hundred lǐ of territory,
with such a strategic advantage,
yet entering Qín too early—
why wait for Wèi Jìng's persuasion?
To enter when one should not enter
brings calamity; likewise,
to have the opportunity to enter and yet not enter
also brings calamity. The timing of
whether to enter or not
must be carefully considered.
18.8 "Being Equipped"
The eighth says:
Suppose Yì or Péng Méng were here with the Fánruò bow,
but without a bowstring,
they would certainly be unable to hit the target.
Hitting the target does not depend solely on the string,
yet the string is the means by which the bow hits the target.
Achieving merit and fame also requires the means.
Without the proper means,
even if one's worth surpasses that of Tāng or Wǔ,
one will toil without achieving merit.
Tāng was once constrained in Yībó,
King Wǔ was once in distress in Bìchéng,
Yī Yǐn was once trapped in the kitchen,
and Tàigōng once lived in obscurity fishing.
It was not that their worth had declined,
nor that their wisdom had become foolish;
they simply lacked the means.
Therefore, in all achievements of merit and fame,
even the worthy must have the means before they can succeed.
Mìzǐ Jiàn was to govern Dǎnfù,
but he feared that the ruler of Lǔ would listen to slanderers
and prevent him from implementing his methods.
As he was about to take his leave and depart,
he requested two close officials from the ruler of Lǔ
to accompany him to Dǎnfù.
When the local officials all came to court,
Mìzǐ Jiàn ordered the two officials to write.
As the officials were about to write,
Mìzǐ Jiàn would frequently tug and shake their elbows from the side.
The officials' writing turned out poorly,
and Mìzǐ Jiàn would become angry with them.
The officials were greatly troubled by this,
and asked to leave and return home.
Mìzǐ Jiàn said:
"Your writing is very poor;
you had better return."
The two officials returned and reported to the ruler,
saying:
"Mìzǐ is impossible to write for."
The ruler asked:
"Why?"
The officials replied:
"Mìzǐ had us write,
but he constantly tugged and shook our elbows.
When the writing was bad, he became very angry.
The other officials all laughed at Mìzǐ.
This is why we asked to leave."
The ruler of Lǔ sighed deeply and said:
"Mìzǐ used this to admonish me for my lack of virtue.
I have interfered with Mìzǐ
and prevented him from implementing his methods;
this must have happened many times.
Were it not for these two men,
I would have nearly committed an error."
Thereupon, he sent a trusted envoy
to Dǎnfù,
instructing him to tell Mìzǐ:
"From now on,
Dǎnfù is not mine to govern,
but yours.
Whatever benefits Dǎnfù,
you may decide and act upon it.
Report the essentials every five years."
Mìzǐ respectfully agreed,
and thus was able to implement his methods in Dǎnfù.
After three years,
Wūmǎ Qí, wearing coarse short garments and a worn fur coat,
went to observe the transformation in Dǎnfù.
He saw a night fisherman
who, upon catching fish, would release them.
Wūmǎ Qí asked him:
"Fishing is done to catch fish.
Now you catch them and release them;
why is that?"
The fisherman replied:
"Mìzǐ does not wish people to catch small fish.
What I release are small fish,
so I let them go."
Wūmǎ Qí returned and reported to Confucius, saying:
"Mìzǐ's virtue has reached its peak.
He makes the common people act in the dark
as if under the threat of severe punishment.
May I ask how Mìzǐ achieved this?"
Confucius said:
"I once said to him:
'Sincerity in this leads to punishment in that.'
Mìzǐ must have implemented this method in Dǎnfù."
That Mìzǐ was able to implement this method
was because the ruler of Lǔ later understood it.
The reason the ruler of Lǔ later understood it
was that Mìzǐ had prepared in advance.
But having prepared in advance—
was success necessarily guaranteed?
This was due to the worthiness of the ruler of Lǔ.
A three-month-old infant
does not know to desire carriages and official caps placed before it,
nor does it know to fear axes and executioners placed behind it.
Yet the love of a compassionate mother reaches it—
this is due to sincerity.
Therefore, where there is sincerity, it aligns with true feeling;
where there is essence, it connects with Heaven.
When one connects with Heaven,
even the natures of water, wood, and stone
can be moved,
let alone beings with blood and qi.
Thus, in all persuasion and governance, nothing is more important than sincerity.
Hearing someone speak sorrowfully
is not like seeing them weep;
hearing someone speak angrily
is not like seeing them fight.
If persuasion and governance lack sincerity,
they will not spiritually move people's hearts.
19.1 "Transcending Custom"
The first says:
What the world lacks
is principle and righteousness;
what it has in excess
is recklessness and compromise.
The nature of the people
is to value what is lacking
and disdain what is in excess.
Therefore, the conduct of commoners and ministers,
pure, clean, honest, and aligned with the standard,
becomes more honorable the more impoverished they are.
Even in death,
the world holds them in higher esteem—
because they embody what is lacking.
Yet if measured by the standard of principle and righteousness,
even Shénnóng and Huángdì
could be found fault with,
not to mention Shùn and Tāng alone.
Fēitù and Yāoniǎo
were famous steeds of antiquity,
yet their abilities still had shortcomings.
Therefore, if one selects timber solely by the marking line,
the palace chambers will never be completed.
Shùn offered the throne to his friend, the farmer of Shíhù.
The farmer of Shíhù said:
"How toilsome and laborious is the conduct of the sovereign!
He is a man who relies on his strength."
Considering Shùn's virtue insufficient,
thereupon the husband carried his belongings on his back,
the wife led their child, and they entered the sea,
leaving and never returning for the rest of their lives.
Shùn also offered the throne to his friend, Běirén Wúzé.
Běirén Wúzé said:
"How strange is the conduct of the sovereign!
He dwelt among the fields and furrows,
yet wandered into Yáo's gate.
Not content with this alone,
he now wishes to stain me with his disgraceful actions.
I am ashamed of it."
And he threw himself into the deep waters of Cānglǐng.
When Tāng was about to attack Jié,
he consulted Biàn Suí.
Biàn Suí declined, saying:
"This is not my affair."
Tāng said:
"Who then is suitable?"
Biàn Suí said:
"I do not know."
Tāng then consulted Wù Guāng.
Wù Guāng said:
"This is not my affair."
Tāng said:
"Who then is suitable?"
Wù Guāng said:
"I do not know."
Tāng said:
"What about Yī Yǐn?"
Wù Guāng said:
"He is strong and capable of enduring disgrace.
I know nothing else about him."
Tāng then plotted with Yī Yǐn to attack Jié of Xià,
conquered him,
and offered the throne to Biàn Suí.
Biàn Suí declined, saying:
"When the sovereign attacked Jié,
he consulted me;
he must have considered me a traitor.
Having defeated Jié, he offers me the throne;
he must consider me greedy.
I was born in a chaotic age,
and now a man without principle comes again to disgrace me.
I cannot bear to hear such things repeatedly."
Thereupon he threw himself into the Yǐng River and died.
Tāng then offered the throne to Wù Guāng, saying:
"The wise plan it,
the brave accomplish it,
the benevolent occupy it—
this is the way of antiquity.
Why do you not take the position?
I beg to serve as your minister."
Wù Guāng declined, saying:
"To depose one's sovereign
is not righteous.
To kill the people
is not benevolent.
Others endure the difficulties,
while I enjoy the benefits—
this is not honest.
I have heard it said:
'If it is not righteous,
do not accept the benefit;
in an age without principle,
do not tread upon its soil.'
How much less should I accept such honor?
I cannot bear to witness this for long."
Thereupon he tied a stone to himself and sank into the Mù River.
Thus, men like the farmer of Shíhù,
Běirén Wúzé,
Biàn Suí, and Wù Guāng
regarded the empire as something beyond the six directions,
which ordinary men could not perceive;
they regarded honor and wealth
as things that, even if obtainable,
they would certainly not rely upon.
With lofty integrity and stern conduct,
they delighted solely in their own principles,
and no external thing could harm them.
Not stained by profit,
not constrained by power,
they were ashamed to dwell in a turbid age.
Such was the integrity of these four gentlemen.
As for Shùn and Tāng,
they encompassed and accommodated all,
acting only when compelled by necessity,
responding according to the times,
taking love and benefit as their foundation,
and considering the myriad people as their righteousness.
They were like anglers:
fish have sizes large and small,
bait must be suitable and appropriate,
and the float has its movements and stillness.
When Qí and Jìn were at war,
a young man from Píng'ē lost his halberd but obtained a spear.
He retreated and left,
feeling dissatisfied,
and said to a passerby:
"Having lost a halberd and gained a spear,
may I return home?"
The passerby said:
"A halberd is a weapon,
a spear is also a weapon.
Losing a weapon and gaining a weapon—
why may you not return?"
As he went on his way,
his heart still dissatisfied,
he met Shū Wúsūn, an orphan from Gāotáng,
stopped before his horse and said:
"In today's battle,
I lost a halberd and gained a spear.
May I return home?"
Shū Wúsūn said:
"A spear is not a halberd,
a halberd is not a spear.
Losing a halberd and gaining a spear—
how can that offset your responsibility?"
The young man from Píng'ē said:
"Alas!
I must return to the battle.
If I hurry, I may still catch up."
Thereupon he fought and died.
Shū Wúsūn said:
"I have heard it said:
'A gentleman who involves another in peril
must share his hardship.'"
He swiftly galloped after him,
and also died without returning.
Had such men commanded troops,
they would certainly not have fled;
had they stood by a ruler's side,
they would certainly have died for righteousness.
Now they died without great achievement—
because their responsibilities were small.
Those with small responsibilities
do not understand great ones.
How can we know today that under heaven there are no men like the young man of Píng'ē and Shū Wúsūn?
Therefore, if a ruler desires to obtain honest gentlemen,
he must diligently seek them.
During the time of Duke Zhuāng of Qí,
there was a gentleman named Bīn Bēijù.
He dreamed of a strong man,
wearing a white silk cap,
a crimson-trimmed lower garment,
a coarse cloth robe,
new plain shoes,
and a black sword scabbard,
who followed him, shouting at him,
spat in his face,
and he awoke in fright—
only a dream.
He sat the entire night, deeply troubled.
The next day, he summoned his friend and told him:
"From youth I have valued courage,
and at sixty have suffered no humiliation.
Last night I was insulted.
I shall seek out this figure.
If I find him, all will be well;
if not, I shall die."
Each morning he stood with his friend at the crossroads,
but after three days without success,
he withdrew and took his own life.
To call this attending to essential matters would be incorrect.
Nevertheless,
his heart's refusal to be humiliated
is something that can be esteemed.
19.2 "Lofty Righteousness"
The second says:
In a gentleman's personal conduct,
his actions must be grounded in righteousness,
his deeds must sincerely embody righteousness.
Though the world may call him impoverished,
he is truly prosperous;
if his deeds do not sincerely embody righteousness,
his actions are not grounded in righteousness,
though the world may call him prosperous,
he is truly impoverished.
Thus, a gentleman's prosperity and poverty
differ from those of the world.
Therefore, he accepts reward only when merit warrants it,
and accepts punishment only when guilt warrants it.
If a reward is undeserved,
even if offered, he must decline it;
if a punishment is truly deserved,
even if pardoned, he will not evade it.
Considering the state's interests,
he must benefit its long-term stability.
Long-term stability for the ruler
must align with inner reflection, and only when his heart feels no shame does he act.
Confucius visited Duke Jǐng of Qí.
Duke Jǐng offered him the fief of Lǐnqiū to support him.
Confucius declined and did not accept it.
Upon leaving, he said to his disciples:
"I have heard that a gentleman should receive emolument only for his achievements.
Now I advised Duke Jǐng,
but before he has put my advice into practice, he bestows Lǐnqiū upon me.
His failure to understand Qiū is truly profound."
He ordered his disciples to hasten the harnessing of the carriage,
took his leave, and departed.
Confucius was a commoner.
His office in Lǔ was that of Minister of Justice.
Yet the ruler of a state of ten thousand chariots could not compare with his conduct.
The assistants of the Three Kings were not more illustrious than he.
Was this not because his choices in accepting or refusing were never made lightly?
Master Mòzǐ sent Gōngshàng Guò to Yuè.
Gōngshàng Guò spoke of Master Mò's doctrines,
and the King of Yuè was pleased.
He said to Gōngshàng Guò:
"If your master would be willing to come to Yuè,
I beg to grant him the lands of the former state of Wú,
the shores of the Yīn River,
and three hundred registered communities,
to enfeoff the Master."
Gōngshàng Guò went back and reported this to Master Mòzǐ.
Master Mòzǐ said:
"In your observation of the King of Yuè,
do you think he is able to heed my words and employ my Way?"
Gōngshàng Guò said:
"I fear he is not yet able."
Master Mò said:
"Not only does the King of Yuè not understand Dí's intentions,
but even you do not understand Dí's intentions.
If the King of Yuè heeds my words and employs my Way,
Dí would measure his body for clothing,
and gauge his stomach for food,
comparing himself to a guest or a commoner,
and would not dare seek office.
If the King of Yuè does not heed my words and does not employ my Way,
even if he gave me the whole of Yuè,
I would have no use for it.
If the King of Yuè does not heed my words and does not employ my Way,
and I were to accept his state,
then I would be selling righteousness.
If one is to sell righteousness, why must it be in Yuè?
Even in the Central States it would be possible."
For all men, one cannot but carefully consider such matters.
The rustics of Qín,
for the sake of small profit,
bring lawsuits against their own brothers,
and are harsh with their own kin.
Yet here was one who, when he could have obtained a state,
feared it would compromise his righteousness and declined it.
He can be said to have been capable of maintaining his conduct.
The distance between him and the rustics of Qín is indeed great.
The men of Jīng and the men of Wú were about to do battle.
The Jīng army was small,
the Wú army was large.
The Jīng general Zǐ Náng said:
"If I engage the men of Wú in battle,
I will certainly be defeated.
To defeat the king's army,
dishonor the king's name,
and diminish his territory—
a loyal minister cannot bear to do such a thing."
Without reporting back to the king, he retreated.
When he reached the outskirts,
he sent a man to report to the king, saying:
"I beg to die."
The king said:
"The general retreated
because he considered it advantageous.
Now if it was truly advantageous,
why should the general die?"
Zǐ Náng said:
"If one who retreats is without guilt,
then ministers who serve kings in later generations
will all rely on the pretext of disadvantage and imitate my retreat.
If this happens, then Jīng will ultimately be subjugated by the world."
Thereupon he fell upon his sword and died.
The king said:
"Let me fulfill the general's righteousness."
He then had a three-inch coffin of tong wood made for him,
and placed an axe upon it to parade through the state.
The trouble with rulers is that
when they survive, they do not know why they survive;
when they perish, they do not know why they perish.
This is why survival and perish come about so frequently.
The vastness of Yì and Qí,
and the submission of the ten thousand states,
arose from this.
Jīng has existed as Jīng for forty-two generations.
It has experienced the rebellions of Gānxī and Lord Bái; it has experienced the evasions of Zhèng Xiù and Zhōu Hóu.
Yet it still remains a great state of ten thousand chariots.
Is this not because it sometimes had ministers like Zǐ Náng?
Zǐ Náng's integrity
served not only to inspire the ministers of his own generation.
During the time of King Zhāo of Jīng,
there was an officer
named Shí Zhǔ.
His character was such that
he was impartial, upright, and without selfishness.
The king appointed him to administer justice.
At that time, there was a murderer in the court.
Shí Zhǔ pursued him,
and found it was his own father.
He turned his carriage around and returned.
Standing in the court, he said:
"The murderer
is your servant's father.
To enforce the law upon one's father—
I cannot bear it.
To show favoritism toward a guilty person
and thereby nullify the state's laws—
that cannot be done.
To fail in upholding the law, one must submit to punishment.
This is the duty of a minister."
Thereupon he prostrated himself before the executioner's axe,
begging the king for death.
The king said:
"You pursued but did not catch him.
Must you necessarily submit to punishment?
You may resume your duties."
Shí Zhǔ declined, saying:
"Not to show partiality to one's kin
cannot be called filial piety.
To serve one's lord by perverting the law
cannot be called loyalty.
For the lord to order his pardon
is the grace of a superior.
Not daring to nullify the law
is the conduct of a minister."
He did not move from before the axe,
and died by it in the king's court.
To uphold the law rightly, one must die if one perverts it.
His father violated the law, yet he could not bear to punish him.
The king pardoned him, yet he would not accept.
As a minister, Shí Zhǔ
can be said to have been both loyal and filial.
19.3 "Esteeming Virtue"
The Third Discourse:
For ruling the world and the state,
nothing is better than relying on virtue,
nothing is better than practicing righteousness.
Through virtue and righteousness,
the people are encouraged without rewards,
and wickedness ceases without punishments.
This was the governance of Shénnóng and Huángdì.
Through virtue and righteousness,
even the vastness of the four seas,
the waters of the great rivers,
cannot withstand it;
the height of Tàihuà Mountain,
the perils of Kuàijī Mountain,
cannot obstruct it;
the training of Hélǘ,
the troops of Sūn and Wú,
cannot oppose it.
Therefore, the kings of antiquity
had virtue that permeated heaven and earth,
and spread across the four seas.
East, west, south, and north,
to the farthest reaches illuminated by the sun and moon,
under the covering heaven and supporting earth,
love and hatred were not concealed,
empty of self-interest and impartial.
The common people all followed them as their enemies, yet did not know why they did so.
This is called complying with Heaven.
Their teachings transformed appearances and altered customs, yet none knew from whom they received them.
This is called complying with human nature.
Therefore, the men of antiquity,
though their persons were hidden, their achievements were illustrious;
though their forms perished, their names were renowned.
Their doctrines spread and their transforming influence was vigorous.
Benefit extended throughout the world, yet the people were unaware of it.
How could they have necessarily relied on severe punishments and generous rewards?
Severe punishments and generous rewards—
this is the governance of a declining age.
The Sānmiáo did not submit.
Yǔ requested to attack them.
Shùn said:
"Virtue will suffice."
He practiced virtue for three years,
and the Sānmiáo submitted.
Confucius, hearing of this, said:
"If one comprehends the essence of virtue,
then even Mèngmén and Tàiháng would not be considered perilous.
Therefore it is said: The speed of virtue
is swifter than sending a message by post-horse relay."
In the Bright Hall of Zhōu,
metal vessels were placed behind,
to show that virtue comes first and martial force afterward.
Did Shùn perhaps resemble this?
His concealment of martial force connects to Zhōu.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn banished the crown prince because of Lì Jī.
Crown Prince Shēnshēng resided in Qūwò,
Prince Chóng'ěr resided in Pú,
and Prince Yíwú resided in Qū.
Lì Jī said to the crown prince:
"In the past, the lord dreamed of Jiāngshì."
The crown prince made offerings and sent food to the duke,
but Lì Jī switched it.
When the duke was about to taste the food,
Jī said:
"It came from afar;
please have someone taste it first."
The person who tasted it died,
and the dog that ate it died,
so the duke condemned the crown prince.
The crown prince refused to defend himself,
saying:
"Without Lì Jī,
the lord would not rest peacefully,
nor eat with relish."
Then he died by his own sword.
Prince Yíwú fled from Qū to Liáng.
Prince Chóng'ěr fled from Pú to Dí.
Leaving Dí, he passed through Wèi,
and Duke Wén of Wèi treated him without courtesy.
Passing through Wǔlù, he went to Qí,
but Duke Huán of Qí had died.
Leaving Qí, he went to Cáo,
where Duke Gòng of Cáo observed his fused ribs,
and made him bare his chest to catch fish in a pond.
Leaving Cáo, he passed through Sòng,
and Duke Xiāng of Sòng treated him with added courtesy.
Going to Zhèng,
Duke Wén of Zhèng showed him no respect,
and Bèi Zhān admonished, saying:
"Your servant has heard that a worthy ruler does not drive the desperate to extremity.
Now, the followers of the Jìn prince
are all worthy men.
If you do not treat him with courtesy,
it would be better to kill him."
The lord of Zhèng did not listen.
Leaving Zhèng, he went to Jīng,
and King Chéng of Jīng treated him disdainfully.
Leaving Jīng, he went to Qín,
and Duke Mù of Qín helped him enter [Jìn].
Once Jìn was settled,
he raised an army to attack Zhèng,
demanding Bèi Zhān.
Bèi Zhān said to the lord of Zhèng:
"It would be better to hand me over to him."
The lord of Zhèng said:
"This is my fault."
Bèi Zhān said:
"Kill me to save the state,
and I am willing."
Bèi Zhān entered the Jìn army,
and Duke Wén was about to boil him alive.
Bèi Zhān leaned against the cauldron and cried out:
"Let all officers and soldiers of the three armies listen to Zhān:
from now on,
let there be no one loyal to his lord,
for those loyal to their lord will be boiled alive."
Duke Wén apologized to him,
withdrew the army,
and returned him to Zhèng.
Moreover, Bèi Zhān was loyal to his lord, and thus his lord was spared from Jìn's menace;
he acted righteously in Zhèng, and thus was pleased by Duke Wén.
Therefore, the benefits of righteousness are vast.
The Mohist leader Mèng Shèng
was on good terms with Yángchéng Jūn of Jīng.
Yángchéng Jūn ordered him to guard his fief,
breaking a jade pendant to make a tally,
agreeing:
"Act only when the tallies match."
When the King of Jīng died,
the ministers attacked Wú Qǐ,
with armed conflict at the mourning site,
and Yángchéng Jūn was involved,
so Jīng held him guilty.
Yángchéng Jūn fled,
and Jīng confiscated his fief.
Mèng Shèng said:
"I received charge of another's fief,
and with him had a tally.
Now the tally is not presented,
and my strength cannot prevent [the confiscation],
yet if I do not die for it,
it is unacceptable."
His disciple Xú Ruò admonished Mèng Shèng, saying:
"If dying would benefit Yángchéng Jūn,
then dying is acceptable.
But if it brings no benefit,
and cuts off the Mohist line in the world,
it is unacceptable."
Mèng Shèng said:
"Not so.
My relationship with Yángchéng Jūn
is either that of teacher or friend,
or else that of minister.
If I do not die,
from now on,
those seeking strict teachers will certainly not look to the Mohists,
those seeking worthy friends will certainly not look to the Mohists,
and those seeking good ministers will certainly not look to the Mohists.
Dying is how I practice Mohist righteousness and continue its cause.
I will bequeath the leadership to Tián Xiāngzǐ of Sòng.
Tián Xiāngzǐ is a worthy man;
why worry about the Mohist line being cut off?"
Xú Ruò said:
"If it is as you say, Master,
then I, Ruò, ask to die first to clear the way."
Then he fell forward, dying before [Mèng Shèng].
Mèng Shèng then sent two men to convey the leadership to Tián Xiāngzǐ.
Mèng Shèng died,
and one hundred eighty disciples died with him.
Three men delivered the order to Tián Xiāngzǐ,
then wished to return to die with Mèng Shèng in Jīng.
Tián Xiāngzǐ stopped them, saying:
"Master Mèng has already passed the leadership to me;
you should obey."
Yet they returned and died with him.
The Mohists considered disobeying the leader as impermissible.
Severe punishments and generous rewards
are insufficient to achieve this.
Nowadays, those who speak of governance
mostly rely on severe punishments and generous rewards;
this is like the ways of antiquity.
19.4 "Using the People"
Fourth:
In general, when using the people,
the highest method is through righteousness,
the next is through rewards and punishments.
If righteousness is insufficient to make them die [for you],
and rewards and punishments insufficient to make them advance or withdraw,
then to be able to use one's people under such conditions
has never occurred in ancient or modern times.
The people are not always usable,
nor always unusable;
only by attaining the proper way is it possible.
Hé Lú used no more than thirty thousand troops in warfare,
and Wú Qǐ used no more than fifty thousand.
For a state with ten thousand chariots,
even thirty or fifty thousand is still many.
Yet now, externally they cannot repel enemies,
internally they cannot defend the state.
It is not that their people are unusable,
but that they do not know how to use them.
Not knowing how to use them,
even if the state is large,
its position advantageous,
and its soldiers numerous,
what good is it?
In antiquity, many had the world yet perished,
because their people would not serve them.
The theory of using the people
must be thoroughly understood.
A sword does not cut by itself,
a carriage does not move by itself;
something makes them do so.
Planting wheat yields wheat,
planting millet yields millet;
no one finds this strange.
Using the people also has its seed;
if one does not examine the seed,
yet expects the people to be usable,
no delusion is greater.
In the time of Yǔ,
there were ten thousand states in the world;
by the time of Tāng, there were over three thousand states,
and now none of them remain,
all because they could not use their people.
The people not being usable
is due to rewards and punishments not being sufficient.
Tāng and Wǔ used the people of Xià and Shāng,
and knew how to use them.
Guǎn [Zhòng] and Shāng [Yāng] also used the people of Qí and Qín,
and knew how to use them.
The usability of the people has its reason;
grasping that reason,
there is no way the people cannot be used.
Using the people has its guiding threads and its main rope.
Pull one thread,
and all meshes rise;
pull the main rope,
and all meshes open.
What are the guiding threads and main rope for the people?
Desires and aversions.
What is desired and what is aversed?
Desire is for honor and profit,
aversion is for disgrace and harm.
Disgrace and harm serve as the substance of punishment,
honor and profit serve as the substance of reward.
If both reward and punishment have substance,
then the people will be fully utilized.
Hélǘ tested his people at Wǔhú,
swords were all placed on their shoulders,
blood flowed on the ground, almost unstoppable;
Gōujiàn tested his people in his palace,
the people competed to enter fire and water,
more than a thousand died,
only then did he strike the gong to make them retreat;
this is because reward and punishment had substance.
Mòyé does not change for the brave or the fearful,
the brave use it skillfully,
the fearful use it clumsily,
this is a matter of ability or inability.
The people of Sùshā
attacked their own ruler
and submitted to Shénnóng.
The people of Mìxū
bound their own lord
and went over to Wénwáng.
Tāng and Wǔ were not only able to use their own people,
but also able to use people who were not their own.
To be able to use people who are not one's own,
even if the state is small,
the troops few,
achievements and fame can still be established.
In ancient times, many rose from commoners to stabilize an age,
all were able to use what was not originally theirs.
The mindset of using what is not one's own
must be examined at its root.
The way of the Three Dynasties is not twofold,
it takes trust as its guiding principle.
A man of Sòng who was traveling
found his horse would not advance,
so he beheaded it and threw it into the Xī River.
He then set out again, and his horse would not advance,
so he beheaded it and threw it into the stream.
He did this three times.
Even Zàofù's method of intimidating horses
could not surpass this.
Without understanding Zàifù's way,
and merely imitating his intimidation,
is of no benefit to charioteering.
Unworthy rulers
are similar to this.
Without understanding the proper way,
and merely increasing their intimidation,
the more intimidation they employ,
the less the people will be used.
Rulers of perished states
mostly used intimidation to command their people.
Thus, intimidation cannot be entirely absent,
but it is insufficient to rely on exclusively.
It is like salt in flavoring:
all use of salt
depends on something,
if improper, it ruins what it depends on and becomes inedible.
Intimidation is likewise:
it must depend on something,
only then can it be effective.
On what does it depend?
It depends on love and benefit.
When the heart of love and benefit is understood,
then intimidation can be effective.
If intimidation is too severe, the heart of love and benefit diminishes,
and when the heart of love and benefit diminishes while only harsh intimidation is applied,
the ruler is sure to incur blame.
This is why the Yīn and Xià dynasties perished.
The ruler holds advantageous power and official position.
Occupying official position,
wielding advantageous power,
one cannot fail to examine this.
To achieve prohibition without prohibiting,
is only possible for those who deeply understand this discourse.
19.5 "Appropriate Intimidation"
The fifth says:
The ancient kings in employing their people
were like driving fine horses:
with light burdens and fresh reins,
they wanted to run but could not,
thus they achieved a thousand lǐ.
Those skilled at using their people are likewise.
The people pray day and night to be employed but cannot be,
if they are obtained for the ruler's use,
the people's rush to him
is like releasing accumulated water from a thousand-rèn ravine—
who could withstand it?
The Zhōushū says:
"If the people are treated well, they are nurtured;
if not treated well, they become enemies."
To have enemies in multitude
is worse than having none.
Lìwáng, the Son of Heaven,
had enemies in multitude,
thus he was exiled to Zhì,
disaster extended to his descendants,
and were it not for Shàogōng Hǔ, he would have had no posterity.
The rulers of the present age
mostly desire multitude,
but do not know how to treat them well;
this multiplies their enemies.
If not treated well, they are not truly possessed.
To possess them must stem from the heart's love for them;
merely having their form cannot be called possession.
Shùn was a commoner yet possessed the world.
Jié was the Son of Heaven,
yet could not rest secure—
this arises from this.
The discourse on possession and non-possession
must be thoroughly understood.
Tāng and Wǔ comprehended this discourse,
thus their achievements and fame were established.
Ancient rulers of the people
governed them with benevolence and righteousness,
secured them with love and benefit,
guided them with loyalty and trust,
striving to eliminate their calamities,
thinking to bring them fortune.
Thus the people's relation to the ruler
is like a seal to clay:
press it square, and it is square;
press it round, and it is round.
It is like the five grains to the earth:
they must correspond to their kind,
and multiply a hundredfold.
This is why the Five Emperors and Three Kings were invincible.
Their persons have ended,
yet later generations are transformed as if by spirits—
their human affairs were carefully attended.
When Wèi Wǔhóu resided in Zhōngshān,
he asked Lǐ Kè:
"Why did Wú perish?"
Lǐ Kè replied:
"Because it fought frequently and won frequently."
Wǔhóu said:
"Fighting frequently and winning frequently
is the fortune of a state.
Yet solely for this it perished—
what is the reason?"
He replied:
"Frequent fighting exhausts the people;
frequent victory makes the ruler arrogant.
With an arrogant ruler employing exhausted people,
for a state not to perish
is rare in the world.
Arrogance leads to wantonness;
wantonness leads to exhausting things.
Exhaustion leads to resentment;
resentment leads to extreme schemes.
When both superior and inferior reach extremes,
Wú's demise was still late—
this is why Fūchāi himself met his end at Gānsuì."
Dōngyě Jì displayed his charioteering to Zhuānggōng,
advancing and retreating as straight as a line,
turning left and right as perfect as a compass.
Zhuānggōng said:
"Excellent!"
and thought even Zàofù could not surpass it.
He made him circle a hundred times and still wanted more.
Yán Hé encountered him
and entered for an audience.
Zhuānggōng said:
"Did you meet Dōngyě Jì?"
He replied:
"Yes,
I met him.
His horses are sure to fail."
Zhuānggōng said:
"How will they fail?"
Shortly after,
Dōngyě Jì's horses failed and returned.
Zhuānggōng summoned Yán Hé and asked him:
"How did you know they would fail?"
Yán Hé replied:
"His advancing and retreating as straight as a line,
turning left and right as perfect as a compass—
even Zàofù's charioteering
could not surpass it.
When I met him earlier,
his horses' strength was already exhausted,
yet he still demanded more from them—
this is how I knew they would fail."
Therefore, when a disorderly state employs its people,
it does not consider their inherent nature,
nor does it reflect on their true feelings.
It wearies them with excessive instruction and blames them for not understanding;
it repeatedly issues commands and criticizes them for not obeying;
it creates great dangers and punishes them for not daring to face them;
it imposes heavy responsibilities and penalizes them for not being able to bear them.
When the people advance, they desire rewards;
when they retreat, they fear punishment.
Knowing that their abilities are insufficient,
they then resort to deception to cope.
Once they resort to deception,
the ruler further punishes them for it.
Thus, punishment begets more punishment,
and mutual enmity between superiors and inferiors
arises from this.
Therefore, when rituals are excessive, they lack dignity;
when tasks are numerous and burdensome, they yield no achievement;
when commands are harsh, they go unheeded;
when prohibitions are many, they cannot be enforced.
The prohibitions of Jié and Zhòu
were too numerous to count,
so the people suffered and they themselves were slain—
this is the extreme,
the inability to wield authority appropriately.
Zǐyáng, in his extreme fondness for severity,
had a man who broke a bow out of fear of certain death for his fault,
and so, taking advantage of a mad dog,
he assassinated Zǐyáng—this is the extreme.
The Zhōu tripod bears the image of a thief,
with a very long, curved shape,
both top and bottom bent,
to illustrate the ruin brought by extremity.
19.6 "On Desires"
The sixth says:
If the people have no desires,
even a worthy ruler cannot employ them.
Those without desires
regard being the Son of Heaven as no different from being a cart-puller;
they regard possessing the world as no different from having not an inch of land;
they regard being as long-lived as Péngzǔ as no different from being a child who dies young.
The Son of Heaven is of the highest nobility,
the world is of the greatest wealth,
Péngzǔ is of the longest life—
if one truly has no desires, then these three are insufficient to motivate.
A cart-puller is of the lowest station,
having not an inch of land is of the greatest poverty,
a child who dies young is of the shortest life—
if one truly has no desires, then these three are insufficient to deter.
But if there is a single desire,
then north to Dàxià,
south to Běihù,
west to Sānwēi,
east to Fúmù,
one will not dare to act recklessly;
facing bright blades,
braving flying arrows,
charging into fire and water,
one will not dare to retreat;
rising early at dawn,
striving to plow and labor diligently,
enduring toil and hardship,
one will not dare to rest.
Thus, those with many desires
can be employed in many ways;
those with few desires
can be employed in few ways;
those without desires
cannot be employed at all.
Even if people have many desires,
if the ruler has no means to direct them,
though people may attain their desires,
they still cannot be employed.
The way to enable people to attain their desires
must be carefully examined.
A skilled ruler
can enable people to attain endless desires,
so people can be employed endlessly.
Among the states of the Mányí with inverted tongues, strange customs, and different practices,
their clothing, hats, and belts,
their palaces, dwellings, and residences,
their boats, carts, and tools,
their sounds, colors, and flavors are all different,
yet they are driven by desires in the same way.
The Three Kings could not change this;
though they could not change it, they achieved success—
because they followed Heaven's way.
Jié and Zhòu could not depart from it;
though they could not depart from it, their states perished—
because they opposed Heaven's way.
Opposing it without knowing they were opposing it,
they sank into custom.
Long sinking without breaking free makes it seem like nature;
whether it is nature or not-nature
must be thoroughly understood.
Those who have not heard the Way—
how can they rid themselves of what is not nature?
Without the means to rid themselves of what is not nature,
then desires are never rectified.
If desires are not rectified,
applied to cultivating oneself, it leads to premature death;
applied to governing a state, it leads to ruin.
Thus, the sage kings of old,
carefully followed Heaven's way and acted upon desires,
so the people were all obedient,
and achievements were all established.
The sage kings held to the One,
and the Four Barbarians all came—
this is what is meant.
Holding to the One is of the highest nobility.
The highest nobility is invincible.
The sage kings relied on being invincible,
so the people's fate was tied to them.
A pack of dogs living together
are all calm and without conflict,
but throw them a roasted chicken,
and they will fight over it—
some breaking their bones,
some snapping their tendons—
because the means for conflict exist.
Where means for conflict exist, conflict arises;
where means for avoiding conflict exist, non-conflict arises.
To adopt means for avoiding conflict and yet fight over them—
not one state in ten thousand does this.
In general, a well-governed state makes its people strive to act righteously;
a disorderly state makes its people strive to act unrighteously.
A strong state makes its people strive to be gladly employed;
a weak state makes its people compete to not be employed.
The difference between striving to act righteously and gladly being employed, and striving to act unrighteously and competing to not be employed—
in terms of fortune and calamity,
heaven cannot cover it,
earth cannot bear it.
When Duke Wén of Jìn attacked Yuán,
he set a deadline of seven days with his troops.
When seven days passed and Yuán had not surrendered,
he ordered withdrawal.
A spy came out and said:
"Yuán is about to surrender."
The army officers said:
"Please wait."
The duke said:
"Trust is the treasure of the state.
To gain Yuán but lose this treasure—
I will not do it."
So he withdrew.
The next year he attacked again,
setting a deadline with his troops to take Yuán before returning.
The people of Yuán, hearing of this, surrendered.
The people of Wèi, hearing of it,
considered Duke Wén's trustworthiness supreme,
and submitted to Duke Wén.
Thus it is said,
"Attacking Yuán, he gained Wèi"—
this is what is meant.
It was not that Duke Wén did not wish to gain Yuán,
but gaining Yuán through untrustworthiness
was不如 not gaining it at all.
Gaining it through sincere trustworthiness—
those who submitted were not just Wèi.
Duke Wén may be said to have known how to seek desires.
19.7 "Valuing Trustworthiness"
The seventh says:
All rulers must be trustworthy.
Trustworthy and again trustworthy—
who would not draw close?
Thus the Zhōu Shū says:
"Sincerely, oh sincerely!"
Meaning that without trust, no task can be fulfilled.
Thus, the merit of trust is great.
When trust is established, empty words can be rewarded.
If empty words can be rewarded,
then all within the six directions becomes one's own treasury.
Where trust reaches,
all can be controlled.
Controlling but not using—
it belongs to others;
controlling and using—
it belongs to oneself.
When it belongs to oneself,
then all things of heaven and earth are fully employed.
If a ruler understands this discourse,
his kingship will not be long in coming;
if a minister knows this discourse,
he can become an assistant to a king.
If heaven's movements are untrustworthy,
the year cannot be completed;
if earth's movements are untrustworthy,
The virtue of spring is the wind;
if the wind is not trustworthy,
its blossoms will not flourish;
if the blossoms do not flourish, then fruits will not grow.
The virtue of summer is heat;
if the heat is not trustworthy,
the soil will not be fertile;
if the soil is not fertile, then growth and maturation will not be refined.
The virtue of autumn is rain;
if the rain is not trustworthy,
the grains will not be firm;
if the grains are not firm, then the five crops will not succeed.
The virtue of winter is cold;
if the cold is not trustworthy,
the earth will not be hard;
if the earth is not hard, then freezing and sealing will not be complete.
As vast as heaven and earth are,
and as transformative as the four seasons are,
they still cannot accomplish things without trustworthiness;
how much more so in human affairs?
If ruler and minister are not trustworthy,
then the common people will criticize and slander,
and the state will not be peaceful.
If officials in their posts are not trustworthy,
then the young will not fear the elders,
and the noble and lowly will despise each other.
If rewards and punishments are not trustworthy,
then the people will easily violate the laws,
and cannot be commanded.
If friends in social interactions are not trustworthy,
then they will be scattered, depressed, and resentful,
unable to be close to each other.
If the various artisans are not trustworthy,
then tools and implements will be crude and counterfeit,
and vermilion lacquer and dyes will not be genuine.
That which can be with one at the beginning,
and can be with one at the end,
which can be honored and prosperous with,
and can be humble and impoverished with—
is it not only trustworthiness?
Trustworthy and again trustworthy,
layered upon one's person,
then one connects with heaven.
Governing people with this,
then sweet rain and sweet dew will descend,
and cold and heat, the four seasons, will be timely.
Duke Huán of Qí attacked Lǔ.
The people of Lǔ did not dare to engage in battle lightly,
so he withdrew fifty lǐ from the state of Lǔ and established a border.
Lǔ requested to be treated as a marquis within the passes and submit,
and Duke Huán agreed.
Cáo Guì said to Duke Zhuāng of Lǔ:
"Would you rather die and die again,
or would you rather live and live again?"
Duke Zhuāng said:
"What do you mean?"
Cáo Guì said:
"If you listen to my words,
the state will surely expand greatly,
and your person will surely be safe and happy—
this is to live and live again.
If you do not listen to my words,
the state will surely perish,
and your person will surely be endangered and disgraced—
this is to die and die again."
Duke Zhuāng said:
"I ask to follow."
Thereupon, the next day, when they were about to swear the covenant,
Duke Zhuāng and Cáo Guì both carried swords and went up to the altar.
Duke Zhuāng seized Duke Huán with his left hand,
and with his right drew his sword to press against himself,
saying:
"The state of Lǔ is several hundred lǐ from the border;
now it is only fifty lǐ from the border—
there is also no life left.
Since death is equal,
let me be slain before you, my lord."
Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shū advanced,
but Cáo Guì pressed his sword between the two steps and said:
"Moreover, the two lords are about to change plans;
let none advance."
Duke Zhuāng said:
"If the border is set at the Wèn River, then it is acceptable;
if not, then I ask to die."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Use land to protect the lord,
not use the lord to protect land.
My lord, please agree to it."
Thereupon, they set the border south of the Wèn River,
and swore a covenant with him.
Upon returning, [Duke Huán] wanted not to give [the land].
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"That will not do.
Others specifically coerced you, my lord, and you swore a covenant without knowing it—
this cannot be called wise.
Facing difficulty and being unable not to listen—
this cannot be called courageous.
Agreeing and then not giving—
this cannot be called trustworthy.
Without wisdom, without courage, without trustworthiness—
having these three,
one cannot achieve merit and fame.
Give it;
though you lose land, you still gain trustworthiness.
With four hundred lǐ of land, you show trustworthiness to the world—
my lord, you still gain."
Duke Zhuāng was an enemy;
Cáo Guì was a villain.
If one is trustworthy even with enemies and villains,
how much more so with those who are not enemies or villains?
That the nine assemblies were assembled,
and that the one rectification was heeded—
all arose from this.
Guǎn Zhòng can be said to be able to adapt to circumstances.
Turning disgrace into honor,
turning poverty into prosperity—
though he lost before,
he can be said to have gained afterward.
Things inherently cannot be perfect.
19.8 "The Difficulty of Recommendation"
The eighth says:
To recommend someone as perfect is inherently difficult—
such is the nature of things.
People injure Yáo with the name of being unkind,
Shùn with the title of demeaning his father,
Yǔ with the intention of coveting position,
Tāng and Wǔ with the scheme of exile and regicide,
and the Five Hegemons with deeds of invasion and seizure.
From this perspective,
can things ever be perfect?
Therefore, the noble person demands of others according to human standards,
but demands of himself according to righteousness.
Demanding of others according to human standards makes it easy to be satisfied;
being easily satisfied wins people.
Demanding of oneself according to righteousness makes it difficult to do wrong;
being difficult to do wrong refines conduct.
Therefore, one can bear heaven and earth and still have surplus.
The unworthy are not like this:
they demand of others according to righteousness,
but demand of themselves according to human standards.
Demanding of others according to righteousness makes it difficult to please;
being difficult to please loses closeness.
Demanding of oneself according to human standards makes it easy to act;
being easy to act leads to careless conduct.
Therefore, even the vastness of the world cannot contain them;
their persons meet danger, and their states meet destruction.
Such were the actions of Jié, Zhòu, Yōu, and Lì.
A foot of wood must have knots,
an inch of jade must have flaws.
The former kings knew that things cannot necessarily be perfect,
so they selected what was essential and valued taking one aspect.
The Jìsūn clan seized the ducal house.
Confucius wanted to explain methods but was kept at a distance,
so he accepted support and spoke conveniently,
and the state of Lǔ criticized him.
Confucius said:
"The dragon eats in the clear and swims in the clear;
the chī eats in the clear and swims in the turbid;
the fish eats in the turbid and swims in the turbid.
Now, I, Qiū, am not as good as the dragon above,
nor like the fish below—
I, Qiū, am perhaps the chī."
Those who wish to achieve merit—
can they always meet the plumb line?
Those who rescue the drowning get wet;
those who pursue fugitives run.
The brother of Marquis Wén of Wèi was named Jì Chéng;
his friend was named Zhái Huáng.
Marquis Wén wanted to make one of them chancellor but could not decide,
so he asked Lǐ Kè.
Lǐ Kè replied:
"If you, my lord, wish to appoint a chancellor,
then ask whether Yuè Téng or Wángsūn Gǒuduān is more worthy?"
Marquis Wén said:
"Good."
He considered Wángsūn Gǒuduān unworthy,
and Zhái Huáng had recommended him;
he considered Yuè Téng worthy,
and Jì Chéng had recommended him;
therefore, he made Jì Chéng chancellor.
In general, when speaking to one's lord about others,
one cannot but be cautious.
Jì Chéng was a brother;
Zhái Huáng was a friend;
and yet he still did not know them—
how could he know Yuè Téng and Wángsūn Gǒuduān?
Knowing the distant and lowly,
but not knowing the close and familiar—
there is no principle in this being natural.
If it is natural and yet one decides on the chancellor wrongly,
then Lǐ Kè's reply to Marquis Wén was also wrong.
Though both were wrong,
it is like metal compared to wood:
even if metal is soft, it is still harder than wood.
Lord Mèngcháng asked Bái Guī:
"The reputation of Marquis Wén of Wèi surpasses that of Duke Huán,
yet his achievements do not match those of the Five Hegemons. Why is this?"
Bái Guī replied:
"Marquis Wén took Zǐxià as his teacher,
befriended Tián Zǐfāng,
and respected Duàngān Mù.
This is why his reputation surpasses that of Duke Huán.
But when divining for a chancellor, he asked:
'Between Chéng and Huáng, which one is suitable?'
This is why his achievements do not match those of the Five Hegemons.
The chancellor is
the leader of all officials.
In selecting one, the desire is for broad consideration.
Yet now, in his selection, he did not look beyond these two men.
This is far from even employing one's enemy.
Moreover, teachers and friends
are a matter of public principle;
relatives and favorites
are a matter of private comfort.
To let the private prevail over the public
is the governance of a declining state.
Nevertheless, the reason his name and honor are illustrious
is that he was assisted by these three gentlemen."
Nìng Qì wished to seek service with Duke Huán of Qí.
Impoverished and with no means to advance himself,
he thus became a merchant, driving a cart to Qí,
and spent the night outside the outer city gate.
Duke Huán was going out to the suburbs to welcome a guest.
The city gates were opened at night,
and carts were cleared from the path.
Torches burned brightly,
and his attendants were numerous.
Nìng Qì, feeding his ox, stood beneath his cart,
gazed at Duke Huán, and felt sorrow.
He struck the ox's horn and sang urgently.
Duke Huán heard him,
patted his attendant's hand, and said:
"How extraordinary!
This singer is no ordinary man."
He ordered him to be taken in a following carriage.
Duke Huán returned,
and upon arrival,
his attendants made a request on Nìng Qì's behalf.
Duke Huán bestowed upon him robes and a cap,
and was about to receive him.
When Nìng Qì had his audience,
he advised Duke Huán on governing within the borders.
The next day, he had another audience,
and advised Duke Huán on ruling All Under Heaven.
Duke Huán was greatly pleased,
and intended to employ him.
The assembled ministers objected, saying:
"This visitor is a man of Wèi.
Wèi is not far from Qí.
Would it not be better, my lord, to send someone to inquire about him?
If he is truly a worthy man,
it will not be too late to employ him."
Duke Huán said:
"That is not so.
If we inquire,
we risk learning of minor faults.
To let a man's minor faults
cause us to lose sight of his great excellence
— this is how rulers lose the scholars of All Under Heaven."
In general, when listening, there must be a basis.
Now, I listened and did not inquire further,
which accords with that basis.
Moreover, men are inherently difficult to be perfect;
one must weigh matters and employ their strengths.
In raising men to office,
Duke Huán understood this.
20.1 "Relying on the Ruler"
It is said:
In the nature of man,
claws and teeth are insufficient for self-defense,
skin and flesh insufficient to withstand cold and heat,
sinews and bones insufficient to pursue advantage and avoid harm,
and courage insufficient to repel the fierce and restrain the violent.
Yet he still manages all things,
controls the birds and beasts,
and subdues the cunning creatures.
Cold, heat, dryness, and dampness cannot harm him.
Is this not only because he first makes preparations
and also because he gathers in groups?
That groups can gather
is because they benefit each other.
The benefit arising from the group
is where the Way of the Ruler is established.
Therefore, when the Way of the Ruler is established, benefit arises from the group,
and human preparations can be perfected.
In high antiquity, there were no rulers.
The people lived together in groups,
knowing their mothers but not their fathers.
There was no distinction between relatives, brothers, husbands and wives, men and women;
no principles of high and low, elder and younger;
no rituals of advance and retreat, bowing and yielding;
no convenience of clothing, shoes, belts, dwellings, or stores;
no preparations of tools, boats, carts, city walls, or defensive barriers.
These were the troubles of having no ruler.
Therefore, the duty between ruler and minister
cannot be unclear.
Since the earliest ages,
many states under Heaven have perished,
yet the Way of the Ruler has not been abandoned,
because All Under Heaven benefits from it.
Therefore, those who are not true rulers are cast aside,
and those who practice the Way of the Ruler are established.
What is the Way of the Ruler?
It is to benefit, and to make clear what benefits the myriad things.
East of Fēibīn,
in the lands of the Yí and Huì peoples,
in the dwellings of Dàjiě, Língyú, Qí, Lùyě, Yáoshān, Yángdǎo, and Dàrén,
many have no ruler. South of the Yáng and Hàn rivers,
in the regions of the Bǎiyuè,
in the lands of Bìkǎizhū, Fūfēng, and Yúmí,
in the states of Fùlóu, Yángyú, and Huāndōu,
many have no ruler. West of the Dī, Qiāng, Hūtáng, and Líshuǐ,
in the riverlands of the Bó people, Yěrén, and Piānzuó,
in the villages of Zhōurén, Sònglóng, and Tūrén,
many have no ruler. North of Yànmén,
in the states of Yīngsǔn, Suǒzhì, and Xūkuī,
in the lands of Tāotiè and Qióngqí,
in the place of Shūnì,
in the dwellings of Dān'ěr,
many have no ruler. These are the four directions where there are no rulers.
Their people are like deer, birds, and beasts.
The young lord it over the old,
the old fear the strong,
the powerful are considered worthy,
the violent and arrogant are honored.
Day and night they injure each other,
without rest,
until their kind is exhausted.
The sages, deeply perceiving this trouble,
therefore, for the long-term consideration of All Under Heaven,
deemed nothing better than establishing the Son of Heaven;
for the long-term consideration of a state,
deemed nothing better than establishing a ruler.
Establishing a ruler is not to fawn upon the ruler;
establishing the Son of Heaven is not to fawn upon the Son of Heaven;
establishing officials and chiefs is not to fawn upon officials and chiefs.
When virtue declines and the age is disordered,
then the Son of Heaven seeks profit from All Under Heaven,
the feudal lords seek profit from their states,
officials and chiefs seek profit from their offices.
This is why states rise and fall in succession,
and why disorder and calamity arise from time to time.
Therefore, loyal ministers and incorruptible gentlemen,
inwardly admonish their ruler's faults,
and outwardly die for the duty of a minister.
Yù Ràng wished to kill Zhào Xiāngzǐ.
He shaved off his beard and eyebrows,
mutilated himself to change his appearance,
and became a beggar, going to beg at his wife's place.
His wife said:
"His appearance does not resemble my husband,
but why does his voice so closely resemble my husband's?"
He then swallowed charcoal to become hoarse,
to change his voice.
His friend said to him:
"The path you have chosen is extremely difficult and will bring no success.
To say you have determination is correct,
but to say you are wise is not.
With your talent, if you sought service with Xiāngzǐ,
Xiāngzǐ would certainly favor and keep you close.
Once close, you could carry out your desire.
This would be very easy and certain to succeed."
Yù Ràng laughed and replied:
"That would be avenging a former patron upon a later patron,
injuring a new ruler for the sake of an old ruler.
Nothing creates greater confusion in the duty between ruler and minister than this;
it would negate the very reason for my actions.
All that I am doing
is to make clear the duty between ruler and minister,
not to follow the easy path."
Zhù Lìshū served Lord Áo of Jǔ.
Believing himself unrecognized,
he left and lived by the sea.
In summer, he ate water caltrops and foxnuts;
in winter, he ate acorns and chestnuts.
When Lord Áo of Jǔ faced calamity,
Zhù Lìshū bade farewell to his friend and went to die for him.
His friend said:
"You left because you believed yourself unrecognized.
Now you go to die for him.
This shows there is no difference between being recognized and unrecognized."
Zhù Lìshū said:
"Not so.
I left because I thought he did not understand me.
Now that he is dead, if I do not go and die for him,
it would indeed mean that he understood me.
I will die to shame those rulers of later generations who do not understand their ministers,
thereby stimulating the conduct of rulers,
and strengthening the integrity of sovereigns.
When conduct is stimulated and integrity strengthened,
loyal ministers are fortunate to be recognized.
When loyal ministers are recognized, the way of the ruler is secured."
20.2 "Cháng Lì"
The second says:
Those who are scholars of the world
consider the long-term benefit of the world,
and firmly position themselves to uphold it:
Even if the benefit is doubled today,
but is not advantageous for the future,
they do not act;
even if peace is long-lasting,
but only benefits their own descendants,
they do not proceed.
From this perspective,
Chén Wúyǔ's shamefulness is also grave,
compared with Bóchéng Zǐgāo,
Zhōu Gōngdàn, and Róng Yí,
their forms may be the same, but the difference in their choices,
is it not far?
Yáo governed the world,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo was established as a feudal lord.
Yáo passed it to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo resigned from being a feudal lord and tilled the land.
Yǔ went to see him,
and he was plowing in the field.
Yǔ hurried to stand downwind and asked him,
saying:
"When Yáo ordered the world,
you, sir, were established as a feudal lord,
now it has come to me and you resign,
what is the reason?"
Bóchéng Zǐgāo said:
"In Yáo's time,
without rewards the people were encouraged,
without punishments the people were in awe,
the people did not know resentment,
did not know pleasure,
contentedly like infants.
Now rewards and punishments are frequent,
yet the people contend for profit and are not submissive,
virtue declines from this,
profit arises from this,
the disorder of later generations begins from this.
Why don't you go, sir,
do not trouble over my farming."
He harmoniously covered the seeds,
and did not look back.
To be a feudal lord,
the name is illustrious,
the reality is ease and pleasure,
descendants all receive its benefits,
Bóchéng Zǐgāo did not need to ask to know this,
yet he resigned from being a feudal lord,
to prevent the disorder of later generations.
Xīn Kuān saw Lǔ Mùgōng and said:
"I now know that our former lord Zhōu Gōng was not as wise as Tàigōng Wàng in enfeoffment.
In the past, Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed at Yíngqiū,
a place by the sea, blocked by mountains, high, perilous, and secure,
therefore the land daily expanded,
descendants increasingly flourished.
Our former lord Zhōu Gōng was enfeoffed at Lǔ,
without the perils of mountains, forests, valleys, or gorges,
feudal lords could reach it from all sides,
therefore the land daily diminished,
descendants increasingly declined."
Xīn Kuān left,
Nángōng Kuò entered to see.
The duke said:
"Now Kuān has criticized Zhōu Gōng,"
his words were like this.
Nángōng Kuò replied:
"Kuān is young,
and does not understand.
Have you alone not heard King Chéng's statement on establishing Chéngzhōu?
His words said:
'I alone,
reside in Chéngzhōu.
I alone,
if I do good, it is easily seen,
if I do evil, it is easily punished.'
Therefore it is said
the good obtain it, the evil lose it,
this is the ancient way.
Would the worthy desire their descendants to rely on the perils of mountain forests to long persist in unrighteousness?
Petty man, Kuān!
Now if sparrows and swallows plan for swans and phoenixes,
they certainly cannot succeed.
What they seek,
are gaps between tiles,
shaded places under eaves;
compared to one flight covering a thousand miles,
if virtue is not abundant, righteousness not great, they do not reach its outskirts.
Ignorant and lowly people,
when they plan for the worthy,
are also like this.
Foolishly slandering and criticizing,
is it not lamentable?"
Róng Yí left Qí for Lǔ,
the weather extremely cold and he arrived after the gates closed,
with one disciple he lodged outside the outer wall,
the cold grew even more severe,
he said to his disciple:
"If you give me your clothes,
I will live;
if I give you my clothes,
you will live.
I am a scholar of the state.
I cherish life for the sake of the world;
you are an unworthy person,
not worth cherishing.
You give me your clothes."
The disciple said:
"Since I am an unworthy person,
how can I give clothes to a scholar of the state?"
Róng Yí sighed deeply and said:
"Alas!
The Way will not be realized."
He took off his clothes and gave them to the disciple,
and died at midnight,
the disciple then lived.
To say Róng Yí could certainly stabilize an age,
that is not known;
but as for his heart desiring to benefit others,
it could not be surpassed.
He understood the distinction of benevolence and love,
therefore he could demonstrate his righteousness by certain death.
20.3 "Zhī Fēn"
The third says:
The accomplished scholar
understands the distinction between life and death.
Understanding the distinction between life and death,
then profit and harm, survival and perish cannot confuse him.
Therefore Yànzǐ, when making a covenant with Cuī Zhù, faced the place of death yet did not change his righteousness;
Yánlíng Jìzǐ, the people of Wú wished to make him king but he refused;
Sūn Shū'áo three times became prime minister yet was not pleased,
three times left the prime ministership yet was not troubled;
all had something they understood.
Having something understood, then things cannot confuse them.
In Jīng there was Cì Fēi,
who obtained a precious sword at Gānsuì,
returning, crossed the river,
reaching midstream,
two flood dragons flanked and encircled his boat.
Cì Fēi said to the boatman:
"Have you ever seen two flood dragons encircling a boat and both surviving?"
The boatman said:
"I have not seen it."
Cì Fēi rolled up his sleeves, bared his arms, drew his precious sword and said:
"These are rotten flesh and decayed bones in the river.
To abandon the sword to preserve oneself,
why would I cherish that!"
Thereupon he leapt into the river and stabbed the flood dragons,
killed them and returned to the boat,
all in the boat survived.
The king of Jīng heard of it,
appointed him to hold the guī tablet.
Confucius heard of it and said:
"How excellent!
Not abandoning the sword for rotten flesh and decayed bones,
is this not referring to Cì Fēi?"
Yǔ went south to inspect the regions,
crossed the river,
a yellow dragon carried the boat.
The people in the boat,
were pale with fright.
Yǔ looked up at the sky and
laughed, saying:
"I receive the mandate from heaven,
exerting myself to nourish the people.
Life is nature,
death is fate.
What concern do I have with the dragon?"
The dragon lowered its ears and tail and left.
Thus Yǔ understood the distinction between life and death, the principle of profit and harm.
All living beings and things
are transformations of yīn and yáng.
Yīn and yáng
are created by Heaven and formed thereby.
Heaven inherently has periods of decline, deficiency, abandonment, and dormancy,
as well as times of flourishing, fullness, proliferation, and growth;
humans likewise have times of hardship, poverty, oppression, and scarcity,
as well as periods of abundance, fulfillment, success, and attainment.
These are all manifestations of Heaven and the principles of things,
inevitable and unavoidable patterns.
The ancient sages did not allow personal emotions to harm their spirit,
but remained composed and awaited their fate.
When Yànzǐ made a covenant with Cuī Zhù,
the oath stated:
"May those who do not side with the Cuī clan but instead with the Gōngsūn clan suffer misfortune."
Yànzǐ bowed to drink the blood,
then looked up and cried out to Heaven:
"May those who do not side with the Gōngsūn clan but instead with the Cuī clan suffer this misfortune."
Cuī Zhù was displeased,
pointed a spear at his chest,
and hooked a halberd around his neck,
saying to Yànzǐ:
"If you change your words,
then I will share the state of Qí with you;
if you do not change your words,
then this is the end."
Yànzǐ said:
"Cuīzǐ!
Have you not read the Book of Songs?
The Book of Songs says:
'Luxuriant are the creepers,
spreading over branches and stems.
Kindly and gentle is the noble man,
seeking blessings without deviating.'
How could I, Yīng, deviate to seek blessings?
You may decide for yourself."
Cuī Zhù said:
"This is a worthy man;
he cannot be killed."
He withdrew his weapons and left.
Yànzǐ took hold of the carriage strap and mounted,
and as his driver was about to speed away,
Yànzǐ placed his hand on the driver's hand and said:
"Steady!
Do not lose composure.
Haste does not necessarily bring life,
nor does slowness necessarily bring death.
The deer is born in the mountains, yet its life hangs in the kitchen.
Now my life
also hangs in the balance."
Yànzǐ can be said to have understood fate.
Fate
is something whose reasons are unknown, yet it is as it is;
human efforts, wisdom, and cleverness in action have no part in it.
Thus, fate
cannot be approached and obtained,
nor can it be avoided and escaped.
A true scholar of the state knows it is like this,
and therefore makes decisions based on righteousness and accepts it calmly.
Bái Guī asked Zhōu Gōngzǐ Xiàhòu Qǐ:
"The integrity of treading the straight line,
the ambition of ascending to the four heights,
and the affairs of the three states of Jìn—
these are the heroes of the world.
Living in Jìn,
I have repeatedly heard of Jìn's affairs.
But I have never heard of the integrity of treading the straight line or the ambition of ascending to the four heights;
I wish to hear of them."
Xiàhòu Qǐ said:
"I am but a humble man;
how am I worthy of such questions?"
Bái Guī said:
"I hope you will not decline, my lord."
Xiàhòu Qǐ said:
"If one believes something should be done,
then one does it;
once done,
the world cannot stop it.
If one believes something should not be done,
then one refrains;
once refrained,
the world cannot compel it."
Bái Guī said:
"Can profit not compel it?
Can authority not stop it?"
Xiàhòu Qǐ said:
"If life itself cannot compel them,
then how can profit be enough to compel them?
If death cannot stop them,
then how can harm be enough to stop them?"
Bái Guī had no reply.
Xiàhòu Qǐ took his leave and departed.
In general, the way to employ the worthy and the unworthy differs;
the unworthy are employed through rewards and punishments,
while the worthy are employed through righteousness.
Thus, a worthy ruler employs his subordinates through righteousness,
carefully examines rewards and punishments,
and then both the worthy and unworthy are fully utilized.
20.4 "Summoning of Like Kinds"
The fourth says:
Like kinds summon one another,
like energies combine,
and like sounds resonate.
Thus, when the gōng note is struck, other gōng notes respond;
when the jué note is struck, other jué notes resonate.
Dragons summon rain,
forms chase shadows.
The origins of fortune and misfortune,
the common people attribute to fate,
but how can they know their source?
