(They do not know their origins.)
Thus, when a state is in chaos, it is not merely chaotic;
it inevitably summons invaders.
Chaos alone does not necessarily lead to destruction,
but summoning invaders leaves no means of survival.
In general, the use of military force
is for benefit
and for righteousness.
Attacking chaos leads to submission,
and submission benefits the attacker;
attacking chaos is righteous,
and righteousness brings honor to the attacker.
With both honor and benefit,
even a mediocre ruler would do it,
let alone a worthy ruler?
Thus, ceding territory, offering treasures, presenting weapons, using humble words, or submitting
are insufficient to stop an attack;
only good governance is sufficient.
With good governance, those seeking benefit will not attack,
and those seeking fame will not invade.
In general, when people attack or invade,
it is either for benefit or for fame.
If they can gain neither fame nor benefit,
even if the state is powerful,
they will not attack.
The origins of military force are ancient:
Yáo fought at the shores of the Dānshuǐ River
to subdue the southern barbarians;
Shùn repelled the Miáo people,
changing their customs;
Yǔ attacked Cáo and Wèi,
subdued Ào and Yǒuhù,
to implement his teachings.
The three kings and earlier rulers
all used military force.
It is used in times of chaos
and ceased in times of order.
To attack a well-governed state
brings the greatest misfortune;
to fail to punish chaos
brings the longest harm to the people.
This is the transformation of order and chaos,
the origin of civil and military affairs.
Civil affairs are a sign of love,
military affairs are a manifestation of hatred.
Love and hatred follow righteousness,
civil and military affairs have their constants,
and this is the foundation of the sage.
It is like the sequence of cold and heat:
when the time comes, events arise accordingly.
The sage cannot create the time,
but can adapt affairs to the time.
Affairs adapted to the time achieve great merit.
Shì Yǐnchí, envoy of Chǔ to Sòng,
was hosted by Sīchéng Zǐhǎn.
The wall of the southern neighbor
protruded in front and was not straight;
the drainage from the western neighbor
flowed through his palace without stopping.
Shì Yǐnchí asked the reason.
Sīchéng Zǐhǎn said:
"The southern neighbor is a craftsman
who makes leather shoes.
I intended to relocate him.
His father said:
'I have relied on making shoes to feed my family for three generations.
If we are relocated now,
those in Sòng who seek shoes will not know where to find us.
We will have nothing to eat.
I hope the prime minister will consider our lack of food.'
For this reason,
I did not relocate him.
The western neighbor's land is high,
while my palace is low,"
The drainage channel passing by my residence is beneficial,
therefore I did not prohibit it."
Shǐ Yǐn Chí returned to Jīng,
and the King of Jīng was about to raise troops to attack Sòng.
Shǐ Yǐn Chí remonstrated with the King of Jīng, saying:
"Sòng cannot be attacked.
Its ruler is worthy,
and its minister is benevolent.
A worthy ruler can win the people's hearts,
and a benevolent minister can employ men of talent.
If the state of Jīng attacks it,
will it not be fruitless and become a laughingstock of the world!"
Therefore, he abandoned Sòng and attacked Zhèng instead.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"To cultivate virtue in the court and repel the enemy a thousand miles away—
is this not referring to Sīchéng Zǐ Hǎn?"
Sòng was situated among three great states of ten thousand chariots.
During Zǐ Hǎn's time,
there was no mutual aggression,
and the borders expanded in all four directions.
He served as minister to Duke Píng, Duke Yuán, and Duke Jǐng until the end of his life.
Was this not due to his benevolence and moderation?
Thus, the merit of benevolence and moderation is great indeed.
Therefore, the Mingtáng had thatched roofs and reed pillars,
and earthen steps of three levels,
to demonstrate frugality.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was about to launch a surprise attack on Wèi
and sent Shǐ Mò to observe it,
giving him a deadline of one month.
He returned only after six months.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Why did it take so long?"
Shǐ Mò said:
"To seek profit but incur harm—
is this not due to a lack of scrutiny?
Now, Qú Bóyù serves as minister,
Shǐ Qiū assists him,
Confucius is a guest,
and Zǐ Gòng gives commands before the ruler,
all of which are highly respected.
The Yì says:
'Disperse the crowd,
supreme good fortune.'
'Disperse' means worthy men,
'crowd' means the multitude,
'supreme' means the beginning of good fortune;
'disperse the crowd, supreme good fortune' means
there are many worthy assistants."
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ halted his troops and did not move.
All planning involves doubt.
When in doubt, one should follow righteousness to decide matters.
Following righteousness to decide matters ensures plans are not flawed,
and if plans are not flawed, reputation and reality will follow.
When a worthy ruler takes action,
must he wait until banners fall and generals perish to know victory or defeat?
Examine the principle, and gain or loss, honor or disgrace, will be determined.
Thus, what the Three Dynasties valued
was nothing more than worthiness.
20.5 "Dá Yù"
Fifth:
All humans have three hundred and sixty joints,
nine orifices, five viscera, and six bowels.
The skin and flesh should be close-knit,
the blood vessels should flow freely,
the sinews and bones should be firm,
the mind and will should be harmonious,
and the vital energy should circulate.
If this is so, then illness will have no place to reside, and evil will have no way to arise.
When illness lingers and evil arises,
it is because the vital energy is obstructed.
Thus, when water is obstructed, it becomes stagnant;
when trees are obstructed, they become infested;
when grass is obstructed, it becomes withered.
A state also has obstructions.
When the ruler's virtue does not circulate,
and the people's desires are not expressed,
this is the obstruction of the state.
If the state's obstruction persists for long,
then all evils will arise together,
and myriad disasters will gather and emerge.
Mutual resentment between superiors and inferiors
arises from this.
Therefore, the sage kings valued heroic scholars and loyal ministers
because they dared to speak frankly and resolve obstructions.
King Lì of Zhōu oppressed the people,
and the people of the state all criticized him.
Duke Shào reported this, saying:
"The people cannot endure your commands."
The king sent the Wei shamans to monitor those who criticized,
and when caught, they were killed.
The people of the state dared not speak,
and on the roads, they communicated with their eyes.
The king was pleased
and told Duke Shào:
"I can silence criticism."
Duke Shào said:
"This is blocking it,
not silencing it.
To block the mouths of the people
is worse than blocking a river;
if a river is dammed and bursts,
the damage will be great.
The people are like this.
Therefore, those who govern rivers dredge them to guide the flow,
and those who govern the people encourage them to speak.
Thus, when the Son of Heaven hears governance,
he has the high ministers and officials offer upright remonstrance,
the learned and well-informed present poems,
the blind offer admonitions and the masters recite,
the commoners convey their words,
the close ministers exhaust their counsel,
and relatives supplement and scrutinize,
after which the king deliberates.
Thus, nothing good is overlooked below,
and no mistaken actions are taken above.
Now, Your Majesty blocks the mouths of those below
and perpetuates the faults above,
which I fear will bring worry to the altars of soil and grain."
The king did not listen.
After three years,
the people of the state exiled the king to Zhì.
This is the ruin caused by obstruction.
Obstruction means
the absence of yang.
The Zhōu tripod depicts a rat,
with a horse stepping on it,
to symbolize the absence of yang.
The absence of yang
is the custom of a perishing state.
Guǎn Zhòng hosted a banquet for Duke Huán.
As dusk fell,
Duke Huán, enjoying himself, called for candles.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"I divined for the day,
but not for the night.
Your Lordship may leave."
The duke was displeased,
saying:
"Father Zhòng is old now,
how much longer can I enjoy myself with Father Zhòng?
Let us continue into the night."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Your Lordship is mistaken.
Those who indulge in flavors are shallow in virtue,
and those who sink into pleasure will face sorrow in return;
if one is negligent in youth, one loses opportunities,
and if one slackens in old age, one loses reputation.
I am now urging Your Lordship to exert yourself—
how can you sink into wine?"
Guǎn Zhòng can be said to have established proper conduct.
All conduct deteriorates through pleasure,
yet now, amid pleasure, he urged greater discipline;
conduct is corrupted by indulgence,
yet now, though the ruler wished to stay, he did not permit it.
He upheld his will and followed principle,
unchanged by indulgence or pleasure,
in serving his ruler.
This is why Duke Huán achieved hegemony.
Liè Jīngzǐgāo's conduct was heeded by King Mǐn of Qí.
He wore fine clothes of eastern cloth,
a white silk cap,
and shoes with upturned toes.
He deliberately walked in the morning rain, shaking his sleeves as he descended the hall,
and asked his attendant:
"How do I look?"
The attendant said:
"You are handsome and beautiful."
Liè Jīngzǐgāo then walked over and looked into a well,
and saw the wretched appearance of an ugly man.
He sighed deeply and said:
"The attendant flatters me because my conduct is heeded by the King of Qí.
How flattering is that?
Moreover, when one's conduct is heeded by a ruler of ten thousand chariots,
people's flattery is even more extreme.
If one has no mirror to reflect upon,
one's ruin and demise are not far off.
Who, then, can serve as a mirror?
Only the scholars!
Everyone likes a mirror that shows their true self,
but dislikes scholars who reveal their true selves.
The mirror's reflection of oneself is of minor merit,
while the scholar's reflection of oneself is of great merit.
To gain the minor
and lose the major
is to lack understanding of categories."
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Jué loves me,
but Duó does not love me.
When Jué remonstrates with me,
he does so where there are no others;
when Duó remonstrates with me,
he delights in confronting me before a crowd,
and always makes me look bad."
Yǐn Duó replied:
"Jué loved the ruler's ugliness,
but did not love the ruler's faults;
Duó loves the ruler's faults,
but does not love the ruler's ugliness.
I have heard from a physiognomist teacher,
that those with thick faces and earthy complexions endure ugliness.
If I did not confront you among people,
I feared you would not change."
This shows Jiǎnzǐ's worthiness.
When a ruler is worthy, his ministers' words are incisive.
If Jiǎnzǐ were not worthy,
Duó would ultimately not dwell in the land of Zhào,
let alone remain by Jiǎnzǐ's side?
20.6 "Conduct and Circumstances"
The sixth says:
The conduct of a ruler differs from that of a commoner.
When circumstances are unfavorable,
and the times are inopportune,
one may serve an enemy to seek survival.
To hold the lives of the people,
to hold the lives of the people,
is a heavy responsibility,
and cannot be treated as a matter of personal gratification.
Therefore, if a commoner acts thus,
he will be condemned by the state,
and not tolerated in his village.
Yáo abdicated the empire to Shùn.
Gǔn, as a feudal lord,
angrily said to Yáo:
"He who attains the Way of Heaven becomes emperor;
he who attains the Way of Earth becomes one of the Three Dukes.
Now I have attained the Way of Earth,
yet you do not make me one of the Three Dukes."
He considered Yáo mistaken in judgment.
Desiring to become one of the Three Dukes,
he grew angry and fierce as a wild beast,
wishing to cause rebellion.
Aligning the horns of beasts,
he could form a city wall;
raising their tails,
he could form banners.
Summoned, he would not come,
but roamed the wilderness to trouble the emperor.
Shùn then executed him at Yǔshān,
dismembering him with the Wú knife.
Yǔ did not dare to resent this,
but instead served Shùn,
holding office as Minister of Works,
to regulate floods and waters,
his face dark and swarthy,
his steps not crossing each other,
his breath stifled and blocked,
all to satisfy the emperor's heart.
In the past, Zhòu acted without principle,
killing Méi Bó and mincing him into paste,
killing Guǐ Hóu and drying him into jerky,
to feast the feudal lords in the temple.
King Wén wept and sighed over this.
Zhòu feared his rebellion,
and wanted to kill King Wén and destroy Zhōu.
King Wén said:
"Though a father may be without principle,
how dare a son not serve his father?
Though a ruler may be unkind,
how dare a minister not serve his ruler?
Which king may be rebelled against?"
Zhòu then pardoned him.
The world heard of this,
and considered King Wén as one who revered superiors and pitied inferiors.
The Odes say:
"Only this King Wén,
cautious and reverent,
brightly served the High God,
and thus secured much happiness."
Qí attacked Sòng.
The King of Yān sent Zhāng Kuí to lead Yān troops to follow,
and the King of Qí killed him.
The King of Yān heard this,
tears streaming down in rows,
summoned his officials and told them:
"I initiated this affair, and Qí killed my envoy;
I request to raise troops and attack Qí."
The officials received the order.
Fán Yóu came forward for an audience,
and protested, saying:
"I wished to serve you because you were a worthy king.
Now you are not a worthy ruler,
I wish to resign and not be your minister."
King Zhāo said:
"Why is this?"
He replied:
"During the rebellion at Sōngxià,
our former ruler, due to unrest, abandoned his ministers.
You endured the pain and served Qí
because your strength was insufficient.
Now Kuí is dead, and you attack Qí;
this means you regard Kuí as more worthy than our former ruler."
The king said:
"Yes."
"I ask the king to halt the troops."
The king said:
"Then what should be done?"
Fán Yóu replied:
"I ask the king to don plain white garments, vacate the palace, and dwell in the suburbs,
send an envoy to Qí,
as a guest to apologize,
saying:
'This is entirely my fault.
The great king is a worthy ruler;
how could he kill all the envoys of feudal lords?
Yet only the envoy of Yān died;
this is because our humble state chose its man carelessly.
I wish to change and beg for forgiveness.'"
The envoy went to Qí.
The King of Qí was feasting grandly,
with many attendants and officials present,
and a great crowd of courtiers.
He then ordered the envoy to come forward and report.
The envoy reported how the King of Yān was greatly fearful and begged for forgiveness.
When finished,
he repeated it,
to show off to the attendants and officials.
He then sent a minor envoy to order the King of Yān to return to his palace.
This is why they were defeated at Jìshàng,
and Qí was left empty.
The seventy cities,
without Tián Dān, would hardly have been recovered.
King Mǐn, with the great state of Qí, grew arrogant and cruel;
Tián Dān, with the city of Jímò, achieved merit.
The Odes say:
"If you wish to destroy something,
you must first pile heavy burdens upon it;
if you wish to topple something,
you must first raise it high."
Is this not what it means?
Piled high but not destroyed,
raised high but not toppled—
is this only for those who possess the Way?
King Zhuāng of Chǔ sent Wén Wúwèi to Qí.
Passing through Sòng,
he did not first request permission.
On his return,
Huá Yuán said to Duke Zhāo of Sòng:
"Going, he did not request permission;
returning, he does not request permission;
this treats Sòng as a wild frontier.
During the hunting assembly of Chǔ,
he whipped your servant at Mèngzhū.
I request to execute him."
So they killed Wén Wúwèi at the dike of Yángliáng.
King Zhuāng was just trimming his sleeves,
and hearing this, said:
"Alas!"
He threw down his sleeves and rose,
his shoes catching up to him in the courtyard,
his sword catching up at the gate,
his carriage catching up at the market of Púshū,
then encamped in the suburbs,
raising troops to besiege Sòng for nine months.
The people of Sòng exchanged children to eat,
and split bones for fuel.
The Duke of Sòng bared his shoulder and held a sacrificial animal,
submitting and reporting his distress,
saying:
"If the great state will forgive and consider us,
we will obey all commands."
King Zhuāng said:
"Sincere are the words of the Duke of Sòng."
He then withdrew forty li,
and encamped at the gate of Lúmén,
thus making peace and returning.
The root of all affairs lies with the ruler.
The ruler's flaw
lies in prioritizing affairs and neglecting people;
neglecting people leads to affairs reaching an impasse.
Now, when a minister dies unjustly,
and the ruler personally leads troops to avenge it,
this can be said not to neglect people.
The Duke of Sòng submitted and reported his distress, and the troops withdrew;
this can be said not to reach an impasse.
Those who feasted with feudal lords at Hànyáng and celebrated their return—
did they advance and retreat by righteousness?
Mere strength is insufficient to achieve this.
20.7 "Arrogance and Wilfulness"
The seventh says:
The ruler of a doomed state
is inevitably arrogant,
inevitably considers himself wise,
and inevitably underestimates others.
Arrogance leads to neglecting scholars;
considering oneself wise leads to autocracy;
underestimating others leads to lack of preparedness.
Lack of preparedness invites disaster;
autocracy endangers one’s position;
neglecting scholars causes obstruction.
To avoid obstruction, one must respect scholars;
to keep one’s position secure, one must win the support of the masses;
to avoid inviting disaster, one must be fully prepared.
These three are the great principles for a ruler.
Duke Lì of Jìn was extravagant and dissolute,
fond of listening to slanderers,
and wanted to remove all his high ministers and replace them with his attendants.
Xú Tóng said to Duke Lì:
"You must first kill the three Xìs.
Their clan is large and has incurred much resentment;
removing a large clan will eliminate pressure."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
He then sent Chángyú Jiǎo to kill Xì Chōu, Xì Qí, and Xì Zhì at court and display their corpses.
Thereafter, Duke Lì went on an excursion to the house of Jiànglìshì,
where Luán Shū and Zhōngháng Yǎn seized and imprisoned him.
No feudal lord came to his rescue,
and none of the common people mourned him.
Three months later, they killed him.
The trouble with a ruler
lies in knowing how to harm others,
but not knowing that harming others inappropriately will instead rebound upon himself.
Why is this?
Because his wisdom is short.
Short wisdom means he does not understand transformation;
he who does not understand transformation brings danger upon himself.
Marquis Wǔ of Wèi, when his plans were successful,
would roll up his sleeves and loudly declare in court:
"No minister’s considerations match mine!"
After standing for a while,
he would repeat it several times.
Lǐ Kuī hurried forward and said:
"In the past, King Zhuāng of Chǔ, when his plans were successful
and he achieved great merit,
would retire from court with a worried expression.
His attendants asked:
'Your Majesty has achieved great merit,
yet you retire from court with a worried expression;
may we ask the reason?'
The King said:
'Zhònghuǐ had a saying,
which I, the unworthy one, appreciate.
It says:
"Among the virtues of feudal lords,
he who can take others as his teacher will become king;
he who can take others as friends will survive;
he who chooses those inferior to himself will perish."
Now, given my lack of virtue,
and that none of my ministers’ plans match mine,
am I not doomed to perish?
That is why I am worried.'"
Lǐ Kuī continued:
"This is what a hegemon or king worries about,
yet you alone boast of it—
is this acceptable?"
Marquis Wǔ said:
"Well said."
The trouble with a ruler
lies not in underestimating himself,
but in overestimating himself.
Overestimating himself leads to rejecting advice;
rejecting advice leads to the exhaustion of his sources.
Lǐ Kuī may be said to have been able to admonish his ruler well,
for with one statement he made Marquis Wǔ better understand the way of ruling people.
King Xuān of Qí built a great hall,
covering over a hundred mǔ,
with three hundred doors in the main chamber.
Despite Qí’s great size,
it took three years to complete the preparations, yet it remained unfinished.
None of the ministers dared to admonish the King.
Chūn Jū asked King Xuān:
"The King of Jīng abandoned the rituals and music of the former kings and took pleasure in lightness;
may I ask if the state of Jīng had a ruler?"
The King said:
"It had no ruler."
"With thousands of worthy ministers, yet none dared to admonish him;
may I ask if the state of Jīng had ministers?"
The King said:
"It had no ministers."
"Now, Your Majesty builds a great hall,
covering over a hundred mǔ,
with three hundred doors in the main chamber.
Despite Qí’s great size,
it has taken three years to prepare, yet it remains unfinished.
None of the ministers dare to admonish you;
may I ask if Your Majesty has ministers?"
The King said:
"I have no ministers."
Chūn Jū said:
"I request to take my leave."
He hurried out.
The King said:
"Master Chūn!
Master Chūn, come back!
Why did you admonish me so late?
I will stop the project now."
He immediately summoned the scribe and said:
"Write this down:
I, the unworthy one,
was fond of building a great hall,
and Master Chūn stopped me."
Admonition must not be taken lightly.
Those who dare not admonish
do not lack the desire to do so.
What Chūn Jū desired was the same as others,
but his method of entering into it was different.
If King Xuān had lacked Chūn Jū,
he would have nearly become a laughingstock to the world.
From this, it can be argued that
rulers who lose their states
are often like King Xuān,
but the problem lies in lacking a Chūn Jū.
Therefore, when loyal ministers admonish,
they must also consider the method of entry;
this cannot be taken lightly,
for it is the root of success and failure.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ drowned Luán Jiǎo in the river,
saying:
"I once favored music and beauty,
and Luán Jiǎo provided them.
I once favored palaces, towers, and pavilions,
and Luán Jiǎo built them.
I once favored fine horses and skilled drivers,
and Luán Jiǎo procured them.
Now, for six years, I have favored scholars,
yet Luán Jiǎo has never recommended a single one.
This is to encourage my faults and suppress my virtues."
Thus, someone like Jiǎnzǐ
was able to later hold his ministers accountable with reason.
Holding ministers accountable with reason
means the ruler can be led to do good,
but not to do wrong;
he can be led to be upright,
but not to be crooked.
This was the flourishing teaching of the Three Dynasties.
20.8 "Observing External Signs"
The eighth says:
In general, when assessing people’s minds
and observing the transmission of events,
one must not be superficial,
and one must not be shallow.
Heaven is high,
yet the sun, moon, stars, clouds, and rain never cease;
Earth is vast,
yet springs, plants, trees, fur, feathers, naked creatures, and scaled creatures never rest.
All that dwell between Heaven and Earth, within the six directions,
strive for mutual peace and benefit,
while those who cause mutual harm and danger
are innumerable.
Human affairs are likewise.
Events follow the mind;
the mind follows desires.
Those whose desires are without measure
have minds without measure;
those whose minds are without measure,
their actions become unknowable.
The human mind is hidden and difficult to perceive,
deep as an abyss and difficult to fathom.
Therefore, the sage focuses on events.
The reason the sage surpasses others lies in foreknowledge;
foreknowledge must examine signs and manifestations.
Without signs and manifestations, to desire foreknowledge,
even Yáo and Shùn would be no different from ordinary people.
Signs may be easy,
manifestations may be difficult,
but the sage cannot be misled,
while ordinary people have no way to attain it.
Having no way to attain it, they consider it divine,
or consider it luck.
It is neither divine nor luck;
it is the inevitable pattern of things.
Hòu Chéngzǐ and Wú Qǐ came close to this.
Hòu Chéngzǐ was sent by Lǔ on a mission to Jìn.
Passing through Wèi,
Right Minister Gǔ Chén detained him and offered him wine.
Music was played, but he took no pleasure in it;
when the wine was at its height, he presented him with a jade disc.
Upon returning,
Hòu Chéngzǐ passed through again but did not bid farewell.
His servant said:
"Earlier, Right Minister Gǔ Chén offered you wine with great joy;
now, why do you pass through again without bidding farewell?"
Hòu Chéngzǐ said:
"He stopped and toasted me,
showing his joy with me;
he arranged music but did not enjoy it,
indicating his worries to me;
when the wine was flowing freely, he sent me off with a jade disc,
entrusting it to me.
If we view it from this perspective,
is Wèi about to have turmoil?"
Thirty lǐ beyond Wèi,
he heard of Nìng Xǐ's rebellion breaking out,
and Right Minister Gǔ Chén died in it.
He turned his carriage back and approached,
performed three libations and then returned.
Upon arrival,
he sent someone to fetch Gǔ Chén's wife and children,
housed them in a separate residence,
shared his salary to feed them,
and when their son grew up, returned the jade disc to him.
Confucius heard of this and said:
"One whose wisdom allows for subtle counsel and whose benevolence allows for entrusting wealth—
this must refer to Hòu Chéngzǐ!"
Hòu Chéngzǐ's observation of Right Minister Gǔ Chén
was profound and marvelous;
he did not observe his actions but observed his intent—
this can be called the ability to observe people.
Wú Qǐ governed west of the Hé River,
when Wáng Cuò slandered him to Marquis Wǔ of Wèi,
Marquis Wǔ sent someone to summon him.
When Wú Qǐ reached Ànmén,
he stopped his carriage to rest,
gazed toward the west of the Hé River,
and tears streamed down in rows.
His servant said to him:
"I have observed your ambition in secret—
you regard abandoning the world as discarding a sandal.
Now, leaving the west of the Hé River, you weep—
why is that?"
Wú Qǐ wiped his tears and replied:
"You do not understand.
If the ruler truly knew me,
and allowed me to fully utilize my abilities,
Qín could certainly be destroyed,
and the west of the Hé River could become a kingdom.
Now, the ruler listens to slanderers' words,
and does not know me;
the west of the Hé River will soon belong to Qín,
and Wèi will decline from this point on."
Wú Qǐ indeed left Wèi and entered Jīng,
and after a while, the west of the Hé River was entirely annexed by Qín,
Wèi declined day by day,
and Qín grew increasingly powerful.
This is why Wú Qǐ foresaw it and wept.
In ancient times, those skilled at judging horses:
Hán Fēng judged by the mouth and teeth,
Má Zhāo judged by the cheeks,
Zǐnǚ Lì judged by the eyes,
Wèi Jì judged by the whiskers,
Xǔ Bǐ judged by the rump,
Tóu Fá Hè judged by the chest and ribs,
Guǎn Qīng judged by the lips and nostrils,
Chén Bēi judged by the thighs and feet,
Qín Yá judged by the front,
Zàn Jūn judged by the rear.
All these ten individuals
were master craftsmen of the world;
their methods of judgment differed,
but by observing a single characteristic of a horse,
they could discern the height of its joints,
the smoothness or roughness of its hooves,
the firmness or brittleness of its build,
and the length of its endurance.
Not only is judging horses like this—
people also have characteristics,
and events and states likewise have characteristics.
Sages know a thousand years into the past,
and a thousand years into the future—
not by mere conjecture,
but because there are sources for it.
Green charts and silk banners
arise from this.
21.1 "Kāichūn"
First, it is said:
When spring begins and thunder sounds, hibernating insects stir;
when timely rain falls, grasses and trees grow;
when eating, drinking, and living conditions are suitable, the nine orifices, hundred joints, and thousand vessels all flow smoothly.
When a king enriches his virtue,
accumulates all goodness,
then phoenixes and sages all come to him.
Gòng Bó Hé cultivated his conduct,
loved the worthy and benevolent,
and all within the seas came to rely on him.
During the troubles of King Lì of Zhōu,
when the Son of Heaven was absent,
all under heaven came to plead with him.
This illustrates how things respond to one another—
thus it is said: actions lead to completion.
Skillful persuaders are the same;
when words exhaust reason, gains, losses, benefits, and harms are determined—
how could it be for the sake of one person's words?
When Marquis Huì of Wèi died,
the burial date was set.
Heaven sent heavy snow,
reaching up to the eyes of oxen.
Many ministers advised the crown prince,
saying:
"With snow this heavy,
if we proceed with the burial,
the people will surely suffer greatly,
and official expenses may also be insufficient.
We request to postpone the date and choose another day."
The crown prince said:
"As a son,
to not carry out the former king's burial
due to the people's hardship and official expenses—
this is unrighteous.
Do not speak of this again."
None of the ministers dared to advise further,
so they informed Xī Shǒu.
Xī Shǒu said:
"I have no way to speak of it.
Perhaps only Lord Huì can do so?
I request to inform Lord Huì."
Lord Huì said:
"Very well."
He rode to see the crown prince and said:
"The burial date is set."
The crown prince said:
"Indeed."
Lord Huì said:
"In the past, King Jì Lì was buried at the foot of Wōshān,
and Luán water eroded his tomb,
exposing the front of his coffin.
King Wén said:
'Ah!
Our former ruler surely wished to see his ministers and people once more,
thus he made the Luán water reveal it.'
Thereupon, he had the coffin brought out and set up a court for it,
allowing the people to see it,
and after three days, reburied it—
this was King Wén's righteousness.
Now, the burial date is set,
but the snow is heavy,
reaching up to the eyes of oxen,
making travel difficult.
If the crown prince insists on the scheduled date,
might it not seem like you desire a hasty burial?
I hope the crown prince will change the date.
The former king surely wishes to linger a while to comfort the state and pacify the black-haired people,
thus he made the snow fall heavily.
By postponing and choosing another date,
this would be King Wén's righteousness.
If you do not do this,
does it mean you are ashamed to emulate King Wén?"
The crown prince said:
"Very well.
I respectfully postpone the date
and choose another burial day."
Master Huì not only successfully persuaded,
but also enabled the crown prince of Wèi, before burying his former ruler, to have a discourse on King Wén's righteousness.
To discourse on King Wén's righteousness and show it to all under heaven—
is this a minor achievement?
When the Hán clan walled Xīnchéng,
the deadline was fifteen days to complete it.
Duàn Qiáo served as Minister of Works.
One county was two days late,
so Duàn Qiáo arrested its official and imprisoned him.
The prisoner's son ran to inform Fēngrén Zǐgāo, saying:
"Only you, sir, can save my father from death—
I entrust this to you, sir."
Fēngrén Zǐgāo said:
"Very well."
He then went to see Duàn Qiáo
and climbed the wall with him.
Fēngrén Zǐgāo looked left and right and said:
"How magnificent this wall is!
A great achievement indeed.
You are sure to receive a generous reward.
From ancient times to the present,
for achievements as great as this,
and yet to avoid punishment or execution—
this has never happened."
After Fēngrén Zǐgāo left,
Duàn Qiáo sent someone at night to release the official from his bonds and set him free.
Thus it is said: Fēngrén Zǐgāo spoke for him,
yet concealed his own purpose in doing so;
Duàn Qiáo listened and acted,
concealing his own actions in doing so.
Persuasion carried out with such subtlety—
Fēngrén Zǐgāo can indeed be called skilled at persuasion.
Shū Xiàng's younger brother Yángshé Hǔ was a friend of Luán Yíng.
Luán Yíng committed a crime against Jìn,
and Jìn executed Yángshé Hǔ.
Shū Xiàng was made a slave and imprisoned.
Qí Xī said:
"I have heard that when petty men attain positions,
not to contend is inauspicious;
when a gentleman is in distress,
not to rescue him is inauspicious."
So he went to see Fàn Xuānzǐ and persuaded him,
saying:
"I have heard that those who excel at governing a state
do not overstep in rewards nor are lax in punishments.
If rewards overstep, one fears they will reach the dissolute;
if punishments are lax, one fears they will reach the gentleman.
Rather than the misfortune of erring,
it is better to err by rewarding the dissolute,
than to err by punishing the gentleman.
Thus, in Yáo's punishments,
he executed Gǔn at Yú but employed Yǔ;
in Zhōu's punishments,
he executed Guǎn and Cài but made Zhōu Gōng his minister;
this was not being lax in punishments."
Xuānzǐ then ordered the officials to release Shū Xiàng.
Those who rescue others from peril,
undertaking danger and hardship without avoiding trouble and disgrace,
may still not succeed.
Now Qí Xī discussed the virtue of the former kings,
and Shū Xiàng was thereby spared.
Can learning ever be considered sufficient?
Many cases are like this.
21.2 "Examining the Worthy"
The second says:
Suppose there is an excellent physician here,
who treats ten people and cures nine;
the reason people seek him out is by the tens of thousands.
Thus, when the worthy achieve merit and fame,
they are certainly like the excellent physician,
yet rulers of men do not know to urgently seek them out;
is this not a mistake?
Now in matters of warfare,
bravery, strength, auspicious days, divination, and prayers are of no use;
the skilled are certain to win.
Achieving merit and fame is likewise;
the essential lies in obtaining the worthy.
Wèi Wénhóu took Bǔ Zǐxià as his teacher,
befriended Tián Zǐfāng,
and treated Duàngān Mù with respect;
the state was well-governed and his person was at ease.
The worthy rulers of the world,
must they necessarily toil their bodies and trouble their thoughts?
They merely grasp the essential.
When frost, snow, rain, and dew come in season,
then all things are nurtured,
the people are well-ordered,
and sickness, disease, and calamities depart.
Thus it is said that Yáo's demeanor was like loosely draped robes,
meaning he had few affairs.
Mìzǐ Jiàn governed Dānfù,
plucking his zither,
never descending from his hall, yet Dānfù was well-governed.
Wūmǎ Qī went out at the stars
and returned at the stars,
day and night without rest,
personally attending to affairs,
and Dānfù was also well-governed.
Wūmǎ Qī asked Mìzǐ the reason.
Mìzǐ said:
"My method is called employing others;
your method is called employing effort.
Employing effort is therefore toilsome;
employing others is therefore easy."
People say Mìzǐ was indeed a gentleman,
easing his four limbs,
preserving his ears and eyes,
calming his mind and spirit,
and the hundred officials thereby governed affairs.
He merely employed his methods.
Wūmǎ Qī was not so;
he wore out his vitality and exhausted his essence,
toiling his hands and feet,
troubling with instructions and commands,
and though he governed, he still did not reach the ultimate.
21.3 "Awaiting the Worthy"
The third says:
Now those who catch cicadas by torchlight
focus on making their torch bright
and shaking the tree.
If the torch is not bright,
even if they shake the tree,
what good is it?
A bright torch does not depend solely on the torch itself,
but on the darkness.
In the present age, the world is very dark;
if a ruler of men can make his virtue bright,
then the scholars of the world
will flock to him
like cicadas rushing toward a bright torch.
A state does not become secure by chance,
nor does fame become illustrious by chance;
it must obtain worthy scholars.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ was sitting by day,
and sighed deeply, saying:
"How strange!
I have wished to attack Wèi for ten years,
yet Wèi remains unassailed."
An attendant said:
"With Zhào's greatness
attacking Wèi's smallness,
if my lord does not wish it, that is one thing.
If my lord wishes it,
I request to be ordered to attack it."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"It is not as you say.
Wèi has ten scholars in my domain.
If I were to attack it,
these ten men would say it is unjust,
and if I attack,
then I would be acting unjustly."
Thus, in Jiǎnzǐ's time,
Wèi used these ten men to halt Zhào's troops,
lasting throughout Jiǎnzǐ's lifetime.
Wèi can be said to have known how to employ men;
by retaining ten scholars, the state gained security.
Jiǎnzǐ can be said to have delighted in following remonstrance;
heeding ten scholars, he avoided the name of invading the small and seizing the weak.
Wèi Wénhóu passed by Duàngān Mù's alley and bowed to his crossbar.
His driver said:
"Why does my lord bow?"
He said:
"Is this not Duàngān Mù's alley?
Duàngān Mù is a worthy man;
how dare I not bow?
Moreover, I have heard that Duàngān Mù has never been willing to exchange himself for me;
how dare I be arrogant toward him?
Duàngān Mù shines with virtue,
I shine with territory;
Duàngān Mù is rich in righteousness,
I am rich in wealth."
His driver said:
"Then why does my lord not make him prime minister?"
Thereupon, the lord requested to make him prime minister,
but Duàngān Mù would not accept.
So the lord then bestowed a salary of a million,
and from time to time went to inquire after him.
Thereupon, the people of the state were all pleased,
and together they chanted:
"Our lord loves rectitude,
hence he honors Duàngān Mù;
our lord loves loyalty,
hence he exalts Duàngān Mù."
Not long after,
Qín raised troops wishing to attack Wèi.
Sīmǎ Táng remonstrated with the ruler of Qín, saying:
"Duàngān Mù is a worthy man,
and Wèi treats him with respect;
all under heaven have heard of it.
Would it not be inadvisable to attack with troops?"
The ruler of Qín thought this right,
so he halted his troops
and ceased, not daring to attack.
Wèi Wénhóu can be said to have excelled at using troops.
I have heard that when a gentleman uses troops,
no one sees his form,
yet his achievement is already complete;
this is what is meant.
When a rustic uses troops,
the drumbeats are like thunder,
the shouts shake the earth,
dust fills the sky,
flying arrows are like rain,
carrying the wounded and bearing the dead,
treading on intestines and wading through blood,
the innocent people who die could fill a marsh,
yet the survival of the state and the life or death of the ruler are still unknown;
this is far removed from benevolence and righteousness.
21.4 "Examining Purpose"
The fourth says:
The person is that for the sake of which one acts;
the world is that by means of which one acts.
Examine that for the sake of which and that by means of which, and then the relative importance becomes clear.
Suppose there is a person here
who cuts off his head to exchange for a hat,
or kills his person to exchange for clothes;
the world would certainly consider him deluded.
Why is this?
The crown is used to adorn the head,
clothing is used to adorn the body.
Now, if one were to kill what is adorned in order to obtain the means of adornment,
then one would not understand what one is doing.
The way people in the world pursue profit
is similar to this.
Endangering one’s life, harming one’s health, cutting one’s throat, or severing one’s head in order to chase after profit—
then they, too, do not understand what they are doing.
Tàiwáng Dǎnfù dwelled in Bīn.
The Dí people attacked him.
He offered them hides and silk, but they would not accept;
he offered them pearls and jade, but they still refused.
What the Dí people sought was territory.
Tàiwáng Dǎnfù said:
"To dwell alongside another man’s elder brother and yet kill his younger brother,
to live alongside another man’ father and yet kill his son—
I cannot bear to do such a thing.
You should all strive to remain here.
What difference is there between being my subject and being a subject of the Dí people?
Moreover, I have heard it said:
‘Do not use that by which one nurtures life to harm that which is nurtured.’"
Taking his staff, he departed.
The people linked together and followed him,
and thus he established a state at the foot of Qíshān.
Tàiwáng Dǎnfù may be said to have been capable of honoring life.
One who is capable of honoring life,
even if noble and wealthy, does not use his means of nurture to injure his body;
even if poor and lowly, does not allow profit to burden his form.
Now, if one receives the noble rank and emoluments of one’s ancestors,
one is certain to regard losing them as a grave matter.
Yet life—that from which one originates—has existed for a long time,
and one lightly discards it.
Is this not deluded?
Hán and Wèi were contending over encroached-upon territory.
Zǐhuázi went to see Zhāolíhóu.
Zhāolíhóu had a worried expression.
Zǐhuázi said:
"Suppose now that a covenant inscription from all under heaven were placed before you,
and its words said:
‘If you seize it with your left hand, your right hand will be crippled;
if you seize it with your right hand, your left hand will be crippled.
Yet whoever seizes it is certain to possess all under heaven.’
Would you, my lord, seize it?
Or would you not?"
Zhāolíhóu said:
"I would not seize it."
Zǐhuázi said:
"Very good.
From this perspective,
your two arms are more important than all under heaven,
and your body is more important than your two arms.
Hán is far less important than all under heaven.
Now, what you are contending over
is far less important than Hán.
Why then do you, my lord, persistently distress your body and harm your life by worrying over it, unable to find peace?"
Zhālíhóu said:
"Excellent.
Many have instructed me,
but I have never before heard such words."
Zǐhuázi may be said to have understood what is light and what is heavy.
Understanding what is light and what is heavy,
therefore his judgment was not mistaken.
Zhōngshān Gōngzǐ Móu said to Zhānzǐ:
"My body is upon the rivers and seas,
yet my mind dwells beneath the palace gate-towers of Wèi.
What is to be done?"
Zhānzǐ said:
"Value life.
If you value life, you will regard profit lightly."
Zhōngshān Gōngzǐ Móu said:
"Although I know this,
I am still unable to master myself."
Zhānzǐ said:
"If you cannot master yourself, then indulge it.
The spirit takes no offense
at one who cannot master himself yet forcibly refrains from indulgence.
This is called ‘doubly wounding.’
A doubly wounded person does not belong to the category of those who live long."
21.5 "Ài Lèi" (Loving One’s Own Kind)
The fifth says:
To be benevolent toward other creatures,
but not benevolent toward humans,
does not qualify as benevolence;
to be not benevolent toward other creatures,
but benevolent solely toward humans,
still qualifies as benevolence.
Benevolence
means being benevolent toward one’s own kind.
Therefore, a benevolent person, in relation to the people,
if something can benefit them,
there is nothing he will not do.
"The Teachings of Shénnóng" says:
"If there are men of an age fit for labor who do not plow,
then someone in the world may suffer hunger because of it;
if there are women of an age fit for labor who do not spin,
then someone in the world may suffer cold because of it."
Therefore, he personally plowed,
and his wife personally spun,
in order to demonstrate his commitment to securing benefits for the people.
Worthy men do not avoid the roads within the seas,
but from time to time come and go to the courts of kings and dukes,
not because they seek profit,
but because they make the people their task.
If a ruler is capable of making the people his task,
then the world will turn to him.
To be a true king does not necessarily require strong armor, sharp weapons, selected troops, and trained soldiers;
it does not necessarily require destroying others’ city walls, killing their officers and people.
The kings of high antiquity were many,
and their affairs were all different.
But in addressing the urgent needs of their time, caring for the people’s benefit, and eliminating harm to the people, they were the same.
Gōngshū Bān constructed tall scaling ladders,
intending to attack Sòng.
Mòzǐ heard of this,
set out from Lǔ,
tore his garments to wrap his feet,
traveling day and night without rest,
and after ten days and ten nights reached Yǐng.
He saw the King of Jīng and said:
"I am a humble man from the north.
I have heard that Your Majesty is about to attack Sòng.
Is it true?"
The king said:
"It is."
Mòzǐ said:
"Is it that you will attack only if you are certain to obtain Sòng? Or is it that you will attack even if you do not obtain Sòng and it is moreover unrighteous?"
The king said:
"If I am certain not to obtain Sòng,
and it is moreover unrighteous,
then why would I attack?"
Mòzǐ said:
"Very good.
In my view, Sòng is certainly unobtainable."
The king said: "Gōngshū Bān
is the most skillful craftsman in the world.
He has already made the devices for attacking Sòng."
Mòzǐ said:
"Allow me to have Gōngshū Bān try to attack,
and allow me to try to defend."
Thereupon, Gōngshū Bān set up his devices for attacking Sòng,
and Mòzǐ set up his preparations for defending Sòng.
Gōngshū Bān attacked nine times,
and Mòzǐ repelled him nine times.
He could not enter.
Therefore, Jīng ceased its attack on Sòng.
That Mòzǐ was able to use his techniques to defend against Jīng and avert the disaster for Sòng
is what this refers to.
There has never been a sage king or a penetrating scholar who did not act for the benefit of the people.
In high antiquity, before Lóngmén had been opened,
before Lǚliáng had been breached,
the river issued from Mèngmén,
greatly overflowing and flowing backward,
so that there were no hills, fertile plains, level fields, or high mounds—
all were submerged.
It was called the Great Flood.
Yǔ thereupon dredged the rivers and breached the channels,
creating the barrier of Pénglí,
drying out the eastern lands.
Those he saved numbered eighteen hundred states.
This was the achievement of Yǔ.
In toiling diligently for the people,
none suffered hardship like Yǔ.
Kuāng Zhāng said to Huìzǐ:
"Your doctrine advocates abolishing honor,
yet now you are making the King of Qí a true king.
How contradictory is this?"
Huìzǐ said:
"Suppose there were a person here
who was determined to strike the head of his beloved child.
A stone could be used to substitute for it."
Kuāng Zhāng said:
"Would you take it to substitute,
or would you not?
I would substitute the stone.
The child’s head is what is important;
the stone is what is unimportant.
To strike what is unimportant in order to spare what is important—
would that not be acceptable?"
Kuāng Zhāng said:
"The reason the King of Qí employs troops without cease, attacks others without end—
what is the cause?" Huìzǐ said:
"At best, he could become a true king;
next best, he could become a hegemon.
Now, if by making the King of Qí a true king I can prolong the lives of the black-haired people,
spare the people from death,
this is using a stone to substitute for the head of a beloved child.
Why would I not do it?
When the people are cold, they desire fire;
when hot, they desire ice;
when dry, they desire moisture;
when damp, they desire dryness.
Cold and heat, dryness and dampness are opposites,
yet in benefiting the people they are one.
Is benefiting the people only a single way?
It is simply a matter of suiting the time."
21.6 "Valuing Swiftness"
The sixth says:
In strength, suddenness is valued;
in wisdom, swiftness is valued.
If the result is the same, speed is superior;
if victory is the same, delay is inferior.
The reason for valuing a fine steed
is that it can cover a thousand lǐ in a single day.
If it takes ten days to fetch it,
it is no different from a nag.
The reason for valuing an arrow
is that it arrives at the sound of the bowstring.
If it takes a whole day to arrive,
it is no different from not arriving at all.
Wǔ Qǐ said to the King of Jīng:
"What Jīng has in excess is land;
what it lacks is people.
Now, Your Majesty uses what is lacking to augment what is already in excess.
I cannot condone such an action."
Thereupon, he ordered the nobles to go and populate the vast, empty lands.
They all suffered greatly from this.
When the King of Jīng died,
the nobles all returned.
The corpse lay in the hall,
and the nobles together shot at Wǔ Qǐ.
Wǔ Qǐ cried out:
"I will show you how I use troops!"
He pulled out the arrows and fled,
then lay over the corpse, stuck the arrows in it, and quickly said:
"The ministers are rebelling against the king!"
Wǔ Qǐ died.
Moreover, according to the laws of the state of Jīng,
anyone who raises arms against the king's corpse
is subject to severe punishment,
extending to the extermination of three clans.
The wisdom of Wǔ Qǐ
can be called swift indeed.
When Duke Xiāng of Qí ascended the throne,
he hated Gōngsūn Wúzhī
and stripped him of his stipend.
Wúzhī was displeased
and killed Duke Xiāng.
Prince Jiǔ fled to Lǔ,
and Prince Xiǎobái fled to Jǔ.
Later, the people of the state killed Wúzhī,
and with no ruler,
both Prince Jiǔ and Prince Xiǎobái returned.
They arrived together
and vied to be the first to enter the ducal residence.
Guǎn Zhòng drew his bow and shot at Prince Xiǎobái,
hitting his belt hook.
Bào Shū drove the chariot,
and Prince Xiǎobái feigned death.
Guǎn Zhòng, thinking Xiǎobái was dead,
reported to Prince Jiǔ:
"Be at ease.
Prince Xiǎobái is already dead."
Bào Shū then swiftly drove ahead and entered first,
so Prince Xiǎobái was able to become ruler.
Bào Shū's wisdom in responding to the arrow shot by making Prince Xiǎobái feign death
was like the swiftness of an arrow.
Lord Wǔ of Zhōu sent someone to assassinate Líng Kuī in Eastern Zhōu.
Líng Kuī feigned death
and ordered his son to quickly cry out:
"Who has stabbed my father?"
The assassin, hearing this,
thought he was dead.
Zhōu, considering him untrustworthy,
thereupon severely punished him.
The Zhào clan attacked Zhōngshān.
Among the people of Zhōngshān was a man of great strength named Wúqiū Yù.
Clad in iron armor and wielding an iron staff, he fought,
and wherever he struck, nothing remained unbroken;
wherever he charged, nothing remained unbreached.
He threw chariots against chariots,
and men against men.
He nearly reached the commander's position before he died.
22.1 "Acting with Caution"
The first says:
One cannot but be thorough in one's actions.
If one is not thorough,
it is like plunging into a deep ravine:
even regret is of no avail.
The noble man plans his actions considering righteousness;
the petty man plans his actions considering profit,
and thus brings about disadvantage.
He who understands the advantage of disadvantage
can be spoken to about principle.
King Píng of Jīng had a minister named Fèi Wújí,
who envied Crown Prince Jiàn
and wanted to remove him.
The king took a wife for Jiàn from Qín, and she was beautiful.
Wújí urged the king to take her for himself.
After the king had taken her,
he became estranged from the crown prince.
Wújí said to the king:
"When Jìn was hegemonic,
it was close to the central states,
while Jīng was remote.
Therefore, we could not contend with it.
It would be better to greatly fortify Chéngfù and station the crown prince there,
to seek influence in the north,
while Your Majesty secures the south.
This is the way to gain the world."
The king was pleased
and had the crown prince reside in Chéngfù.
After a year,
Wújí slandered him, saying:
"Jiàn and Liányǐn Shē are planning to rebel beyond the Fāngchéng wall."
The king said:
"He is already my son.
What more could he seek?"
Wújí replied:
"He resents the matter of his wife.
Moreover, he considers himself like the ruler of Sòng,
with Qí and Jìn assisting him.
He intends to harm Jīng,
and the affair is already arranged."
The king believed him
and had Liányǐn Shē arrested.
Crown Prince Jiàn fled.
Left Yin Xì Wǎn
was liked by the people of the state.
Wújí also wanted to kill him.
He said to Lìngyǐn Zǐcháng:
"Xì Wǎn wishes to invite Lìngyǐn for a drink."
He also said to Xì Wǎn:
"Lìngyǐn wishes to drink at your house."
Xì Wǎn said:
"I am a lowly man.
I am not worthy to receive Lìngyǐn.
If Lìngyǐn must come and honor me,
how shall I entertain him?"
Wújí said:
"Lìngyǐn is fond of armor and weapons.
You should bring them out and place them at the gate.
When Lìngyǐn arrives,
he will certainly look at them.
Afterward,
you can present them as a gift."
On the day of the feast,
Xì Wǎn placed armor and weapons beside the gate.
Wújí then said to Lìngyǐn:
"I nearly brought disaster upon Lìngyǐn.
Xì Wǎn intends to kill Lìngyǐn.
Armor is at the gate."
Lìngyǐn sent someone to look,
and it was true.
He then attacked Xì Wǎn
and killed him.
The people of the state were greatly resentful,
and all who acted criticized Lìngyǐn.
Shěn Yǐn Shù said to Lìngyǐn:
"That Wújí is a slanderer of Jīng.
He caused the loss of Crown Prince Jiàn,
killed Liányǐn Shē,
and blinded the king's eyes and ears.
Now Lìngyǐn employs him again,
killing many innocents,
and arousing great condemnation.
Disaster will soon reach Lìngyǐn."
Lìngyǐn Zǐcháng said:
"This is my fault.
How dare I not make amends?"
He then killed Fèi Wújí
and exterminated his entire clan,
to appease the state.
To act without considering righteousness,
to know how to harm others but not know that others may harm oneself,
and thus to bring about the extermination of one's clan—
this refers to Fèi Wújí!
Cuī Zhù and Qìng Fēng plotted to kill Duke Zhuāng of Qí.
When Duke Zhuāng died,
they established Duke Jǐng in his place,
with Cuī Zhù as his minister.
Qìng Fēng also wanted to kill Cuī Zhù and replace him as minister.
Thereupon, he incited Cuī Zhù's sons,
making them contend for the succession.
Cuī Zhù's sons fought among themselves in private.
Cuī Zhù went to see Qìng Fēng and told him.
Qìng Fēng said to Cuī Zhù:
"Stay here for now.
I will raise troops to kill them."
He then ordered Lú Mǎn Piè to raise troops and execute them.
They killed all of Cuī Zhù's wives, children, and relatives,
burned his house,
and reported to Cuī Zhù:
"I have already executed them."
Cuī Zhù had nowhere to return to
and thereupon hanged himself.
Qìng Fēng served as prime minister to Duke Jǐng.
Duke Jǐng suffered under him.
Qìng Fēng went out hunting.
Duke Jǐng, along with Chén Wúyǔ, Gōngsūn Zào, and Gōngsūn Chài, plotted against Qìng Fēng.
Qìng Fēng fought with his followers,
but was not victorious,
and fled to Lǔ.
The people of Qí held this against Lǔ,
so he left Lǔ and went to Wú,
where the king gave him Zhūfāng.
King Líng of Jīng heard of this,
led the feudal lords to attack Wú,
besieged Zhūfāng,
captured it,
and seized Qìng Fēng.
He had him bear the axe and execution block,
and paraded him before the armies of the feudal lords,
ordering him to call out:
"Let no one be like Qìng Fēng of Qí,
who murdered his ruler and weakened his orphan,
causing his high ministers to perish."
Then they killed him.
Huángdì was noble, yet he died;
Yáo and Shùn were worthy, yet they died;
Mèng Bēn was brave, yet he died;
all men inevitably die.
But one like Qìng Fēng
can be said to have died a double death.
His person was mutilated,
and his kin could not remain whole,
all because of his conduct of malice.
Generally, when men of disorder act,
at first they assist each other,
but later they inevitably come to hate each other.
Those who act for righteousness are not like this.
At first they associate with each other,
in time they trust each other,
and finally they become close,
so that later generations take them as a model.
22.2 "The Absence of Righteousness"
Second:
The former kings reached the ultimate in their judgments.
Therefore, righteousness is the beginning of all affairs,
the root of all benefit,
and what men of middling intelligence cannot reach.
Not reaching it, they do not know it;
not knowing it, they pursue profit.
But pursuing profit inherently cannot be certain.
Gōngsūn Yāng, Zhèng Píng, Xù Jīng, and Gōngsūn Jié are examples of this.
If one acts according to righteousness, then no affair will be neglected.
When one minister conspires with another minister to do evil,
some may still join him.
How much more so when a ruler conspires with his ministers to act righteously—
who would not join him?
Not only his ministers,
but all under heaven will join him.
Gōngsūn Yāng, in relation to Qín,
was not a father or elder brother,
nor did he have any old connection;
he was employed for his ability.
Wishing to fulfill the responsibility placed upon him,
he had no means other than attack,
and so he became a general for Qín and attacked Wèi.
Wèi sent Prince Áng to command and oppose him.
When Gōngsūn Yāng resided in Wèi,
he had been on good terms with Prince Áng.
He sent a man to say to Prince Áng:
"All my travels and desire for honor
were for your sake, Prince.
Now Qín orders Yāng to command,
and Wèi orders you, Prince, to oppose him.
How can we bear to fight each other?
You, Prince, speak to your lord,
and Yāng will request to speak to my lord as well,
and we will both withdraw our armies."
Then, as they were about to return,
he sent a man to say to the Prince:
"After returning, we may not meet again for some time.
I wish to sit with you, Prince, and take leave before parting."
The Prince said:
"Agreed."
The Wèi officers argued with him, saying:
"It cannot be done."
The Prince did not listen,
and so they sat together.
Gōngsūn Yāng then used hidden troops, chariots, and cavalry to capture Prince Áng.
Duke Xiào of Qín passed away,
and King Huì ascended the throne.
Because of this, he doubted Gōngsūn Yāng's conduct
and wished to punish him.
Gōngsūn Yāng, with his private followers and mother, returned to Wèi.
Xiāng Cī would not receive him,
saying:
"Because of your betrayal of Prince Áng,
I have no way to know your character."
Therefore, a gentleman must be careful in his own conduct.
Zhèng Píng was a minister to the King of Qín,
and a friend of Yìnghóu.
He deceived his friend and betrayed his lord
for the sake of profit.
When he was a general for Qín,
there was nothing the world honored that he did not possess—
such was his weight.
What is gained through weight,
will inevitably be lost through lightness.
He left his position as a Qín general
and entered Zhào and Wèi.
There was nothing the world despised that he did not do,
nothing shameful that he did not do.
His conduct was despicable and shameful,
and he lacked the weight of a Qín general.
How could he avoid ruin?
Zhào urgently sought Lǐ Kǎi.
Lǐ Kǎi told Xù Jīng to go with him to Wèi,
to seek out Gōngsūn Yǔ.
Gōngsūn Yǔ met them and brought them in.
Xù Jīng then informed the Wèi officers to have them arrested.
Xù Jīng thereby became a Grandee of the Fifth Rank in Zhào.
No one would share the court with him,
and his descendants could not form friendships.
Gōngsūn Jié was involved in the affair of Yīn Jūn,
but turned and reported it to Chancellor Chūlǐ,
thereby becoming a Grandee of the Fifth Rank in Qín.
His achievement was not insignificant,
yet he could not enter the three capitals.
How much more so for one without such achievement but with such conduct?
22.3 "Resemblance and Doubt"
Third:
What causes great confusion in people
must be the resemblance between things.
What jade workers worry about
is stones that resemble jade;
what sword appraisers worry about
is swords that resemble the Wú Gān sword;
what worthy rulers worry about
is men of broad learning and eloquent speech who resemble the truly understanding.
A ruler who will lose his state resembles the wise;
a minister who will lose his state resembles the loyal.
Similar things
are what greatly confuse the foolish,
and what the sage gives extra consideration to.
Therefore, Mòzǐ wept when he saw a fork in the road.
The Zhōu capital at Fēnghào was near the Róng people.
They made a pact with the feudal lords
to build high watchtowers along the royal road,
placing drums atop them
so the sound could be heard from far and near.
If the Róng invaders arrived,
the drums would be passed along to give warning,
and the troops of the feudal lords would all come to rescue the Son of Heaven.
Once, when the Róng invaders came,
King Yōu beat the drums,
and the troops of the feudal lords all arrived.
Bāosì was greatly pleased
and delighted by it.
King Yōu wanted to make Bāosì laugh,
so he repeatedly beat the drums.
The troops of the feudal lords came several times, but there were no invaders.
Later, when the Róng invaders truly came,
King Yōu beat the drums,
but the troops of the feudal lords did not come.
King Yōu himself
then died at the foot of Lìshān,
becoming a laughingstock for all under heaven.
This is a case of losing the true invaders because of the false ones.
The worthy may have small faults that lead to great faults.
Bāosì's ruin
caused King Yōu to love small pleasures, leading to great destruction.
Thus, body and soul parted,
the Three Dukes and Nine Ministers fled,
this was why Bāosì died,
and why King Píng moved east,
and why Duke Xiāng of Qín and Duke Wén of Jìn labored for the king and were granted lands.
North of Liáng was the Líqiū district,
where there was a strange ghost
skilled at imitating the appearance of people's sons, nephews, and brothers.
An old man of the town went to the market and returned drunk.
The ghost of Líqiū imitated the appearance of his son,
supported him along the way, and tormented him.
The old man returned home,
sobered up, and scolded his son,
saying:
"I am your father.
Can it be said I am not kind?
I was drunk,
and you tormented me along the way.
Why?"
His son wept and knocked his head on the ground, saying:
"A calamity!
There was no such thing.
That day I went to collect a debt from a man in the eastern town—you can ask him."
His father believed it,
and said:
"Ah!
That must be the strange ghost;
I have indeed heard of such things."
The next day, he deliberately went to drink in the marketplace again,
intending to encounter and stab it.
The following morning, he went to the marketplace and got drunk.
His real son, fearing that his father would be unable to return,
went to meet him.
The old man saw his real son,
drew his sword, and stabbed him.
The old man's judgment was confused by one who resembled his son,
and he killed his own true son.
To be misled by those who resemble true scholars and thus lose the genuine ones—
this is the wisdom of the old man of Líqiū.
Signs of similarity and doubt
must be carefully examined.
Such examination must be conducted by the right person.
If Shùn were the charioteer,
Yáo on the left,
and Yǔ on the right,
upon entering the marshes, they would still ask the shepherd boys;
upon entering the waters, they would still ask the fishermen.
Why is this?
Because these people possess precise knowledge.
When sons closely resemble each other,
their mothers can always recognize them—
because they know them precisely.
22.4 "Consistency in Action"
The fourth discourse states:
What the former kings detested most
was nothing more than the unknowable.
If things are unknowable, then the relationships between ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brother, friend and friend, and husband and wife will deteriorate.
If all ten relationships deteriorate,
no disorder could be greater.
All human relationships rely on these ten bonds for stability.
If these ten bonds are abandoned, then humans are no different from deer, tigers, and wolves;
the more courageous among them will merely be subdued.
If things are unknowable, then there will be no secure ruler, no joyful parents,
no honored elder brothers, no close friends, and no respected husbands.
Being powerful and large does not necessarily lead to kingship,
but a true king must be powerful and large.
What does a king rely on to achieve this?
He relies on his authority and his benefits.
Without power and size, his authority is not authoritative, and his benefits are not beneficial.
If his authority is not authoritative, it is insufficient to enforce prohibitions;
if his benefits are not beneficial, they are insufficient to encourage actions.
Therefore, a worthy ruler must ensure that his authority and benefits are unmatched,
so that his prohibitions will certainly be heeded,
and his encouragements will certainly be followed.
With unmatched authority and benefits,
one who cares for the people's sufferings and acts in a knowable manner will become king;
with unmatched authority and benefits,
one who acts in an unknowable manner will perish.
If a small and weak state is unknowable,
then powerful states will suspect it.
It is human nature not to love what one suspects.
If a small and weak state is not loved by the great, it cannot survive.
Therefore, the way of the unknowable,
if practiced by a king, leads to ruin;
if practiced by a powerful state, leads to danger;
if practiced by a small and weak state, leads to extinction.
When a traveler sees a large tree,
he will certainly remove his outer garment, hang his hat, lean his sword, and rest beneath it.
A large tree is not a relative or close friend of humans,
yet one feels so at ease beneath it—
because it is trustworthy.
A giant tree on a hilltop
is used by people as a meeting point—
because it is easily recognizable.
How much more should this apply to scholars?
If scholars' righteousness is knowable,
then they can certainly be relied upon.
How much more does this apply to powerful states?
If a powerful state is truly knowable,
then its kingship is not difficult to achieve.
People use boats
because they can float and not sink;
the world honors gentlemen
because they can act righteously and not wickedly.
When Confucius divined,
he obtained the hexagram "Bì."
Confucius said:
"This is not auspicious."
Zǐgòng asked:
"The 'Bì' hexagram is also good;
why do you say it is not auspicious?"
Confucius replied:
"White should be white,
black should be black.
What is good about 'Bì'?"
Therefore, what worthy men detest in things
is nothing more than having no fixed place.
What the world detests most
is nothing more than the unknowable.
If something is unknowable,
even thieves will not make appointments with it,
and robbers will not conspire with it.
Thieves and robbers are great villains,
yet they still require partners.
How much more is this true for those who wish to achieve great merit?
To achieve great merit,
so that all under heaven will lightly encourage and assist them,
one must ensure that scholars are knowable.
22.5 "Seeking Talent"
The fifth discourse states:
To stabilize oneself,
bring security to the state,
and bring order to the world,
worthy men are essential.
In ancient times, those who possessed the world
numbered seventy-one sages.
Observing the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
from Duke Yǐn of Lǔ to Duke Āi—twelve generations—
the methods by which they gained or lost it
were the same.
Gaining worthy men,
the state will invariably be secure,
and its name will invariably be honored;
losing worthy men,
the state will invariably be endangered,
and its name will invariably be disgraced.
The former kings sought worthy men by all means,
even to the humblest and lowliest,
the most distant and laborious.
If Yú had followed Gōngzhīqí's advice and Wú had followed Wǔ Zǐxū's counsel,
these two states
could have survived to this day.
Thus, a state can achieve longevity.
If someone could increase a person's lifespan,
then everyone would desire it.
Now, there is a way to give longevity to a state,
yet rulers do not seek it—
this is a grave error.
Yáo passed the world to Shùn,
honored him among the feudal lords,
gave him his two daughters in marriage,
made his ten sons serve him,
and personally requested to face north and pay homage to him—
this is the utmost humility.
Yīyǐn was a servant in the kitchen;
Fùyuè was a convict in Yīn.
Both later became chief ministers to the Son of Heaven—
this is the utmost lowliness.
Yǔ traveled east to the land of Fúmù,
to the regions of Rìchū, Jiǔjīn, and Qīngqiāng,
to the places of dense forests,
to the mountain of Mǐntiān,
to the villages of Niǎogǔ and Qīngqiū,
and to the state of Hēichǐ;
he traveled south to the states of Jiāozhǐ, Sūnpǔ, and Xùmán,
to the mountains of Dānsù, Qīshù, Fèishuǐ, Piāopiāo, and Jiǔyáng,
to the dwellings of the Yǔrén and Luǒmín peoples,
and to the land of immortality;
he traveled west to the state of Sānwēi,
beneath the Wūshān mountains,
among the people who drank dew and inhaled qi,
to the mountain of accumulated gold,
and to the lands of Gònghóng, Yībì, and Sānmiàn;
he traveled north to the state of Rénzhèng,
to the farthest reaches of Xiàhǎi,
to the heights of Héngshān,
to the state of Quǎnróng,
to the wilderness of Kuāfù,
to the territory of Yújiāng,
and to the mountains of accumulated water and accumulated stone.
He never slackened,
worried for his black-haired people,
his complexion became dark and swarthy,
his orifices and organs blocked,
his steps could not cross each other,
all in his search for worthy men,
desiring to exhaust the earth's benefits—
this is the utmost labor.
He obtained five men—Táo, Huàyì, Zhēnkuī, Hénggé, and Zhījiāo—to assist Yǔ.
Thus, their achievements were inscribed on metal and stone, recorded on plates and vessels.
In the past, Yáo visited Xǔyóu in the marsh of Pèi,
and said:
"When ten suns shine, yet a tiny torch is not extinguished—
is this not laborious?
If you, Master, were to become the Son of Heaven,
the world would already be well-governed.
I beg to entrust the world to you, Master."
Xǔ Yóu declined, saying:
"Is it because the world is not well-governed?
Yet it is already well-governed.
Is it for my own sake?
The wren builds its nest in the forest,
occupying no more than a single branch;
the mole drinks from the river,
filling no more than its belly.
Return to your lord!
What use have I for the world?"
Thereupon he went to the foot of Jīshān,
on the north bank of the Yǐng River,
plowed the fields for sustenance,
and throughout his life never showed any desire to govern the world.
Thus, when a worthy ruler treats the worthy,
nothing obstructs them;
relatives, loved ones, close associates, and old friends
do not harm them;
therefore, the worthy gather.
Where the worthy gather,
heaven and earth do not bring ruin,
ghosts and spirits do not cause harm,
human affairs do not require scheming—
this is the fundamental principle of the five constants.
When Gāo Zǐ was suspected by the multitude of seizing the state,
he summoned Nángōng Qián and Kǒng Bóchǎn, and the public criticism ceased.
When the people of Jìn wished to attack Zhèng,
they sent Shū Xiàng on a diplomatic mission
to observe whether it had capable men or not.
Zǐchǎn composed a poem for him, saying:
"If you cherish me and think of me,
lift your skirts and wade the Wěi;
if you do not think of me,
are there no other men?"
Shū Xiàng returned and said:
"Zhèng has capable men;
Zǐchǎn is there,
so it cannot be attacked.
Qín and Jīng are nearby,
and the poem reveals a different intent;
it cannot be attacked."
Thus, the people of Jìn abandoned their plan to attack Zhèng.
Confucius said:
"The Book of Songs says:
'There is no competition like having men.'
With one utterance from Zǐchǎn, the state of Zhèng was spared."
22.6 "Examining Traditions"
The sixth discourse:
When hearing transmitted words, one must examine them,
for after several transmissions, white becomes black,
and black becomes white.
Thus, a dog resembles a jué,
a jué resembles a macaque,
a macaque resembles a human,
but humans and dogs are far apart.
This is why fools make great errors.
To hear and scrutinize brings fortune;
to hear without scrutiny
is worse than not hearing at all.
Duke Huán of Qí heard about Guǎn Zhòng from Bào Shū,
and King Zhuāng of Chǔ heard about Sūnshū Áo from Shěn Yǐn Shì—
they scrutinized,
and thus their states became hegemons among the feudal lords.
King of Wú heard about King Gōujiàn of Yuè from Grand Steward Pǐ,
and Zhì Bó heard about Zhào Xiāngzǐ from Zhāng Wǔ—
they did not scrutinize,
and thus their states perished and they themselves died.
Whenever hearing words, one must thoroughly deliberate,
and regarding people, one must verify with reason.
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Confucius:
"I heard that Yuèzhèng Kuí had one foot—
is it true?"
Confucius said:
"Long ago, Shùn wished to use music to spread teachings throughout the world,
so he ordered Chónglí to select Kuí from among the common people and recommend him.
Shùn appointed him as Yuèzhèng.
Kuí then rectified the six pitch standards,
harmonized the five notes,
to communicate the eight winds,
and the world was greatly subdued.
Chónglí wished to seek more men,
but Shùn said:
'Music is the essence of heaven and earth,
the regulator of success and failure.
Thus, only sages can harmonize the root of music.
Kuí can harmonize it,
and thereby pacify the world.
One like Kuí is sufficient.'
Thus, it is said 'Kuí, one is sufficient,'
not that he had one foot."
The Dīng family of Sòng
had no well at home and had to fetch water from outside,
often requiring one person to stay out.
When they dug a well at home,
they told others:
"We dug a well and gained one person."
Someone heard and transmitted it, saying:
"The Dīng family dug a well and obtained a person."
The people of the state spoke of it,
and it reached the ears of the ruler of Sòng.
The ruler of Sòng sent someone to ask the Dīng family,
and they replied:
"We gained the service of one person,
not that we obtained a person from the well."
To seek ability in such a manner
is worse than not hearing at all.
When Zǐxià went to Jìn,
passing through Wèi,
he heard someone reading historical records say:
"The Jìn army crossed the river with three pigs."
Zǐxià said:
"That is incorrect;
it is 'jǐhài.'
The character 'jǐ' resembles 'three,'
and 'pig' resembles 'hài.'"
When he arrived in Jìn and inquired,
it was indeed said: "The Jìn army crossed the river on the jǐhài day."
Words often appear false yet are true,
and often appear true yet are false.
The boundary between right and wrong
must be distinguished—
this is what the sages were cautious about.
How, then, to be cautious?
By following the nature of things and human feelings to examine what one hears, one will attain it.
23.1 "Valuing Straightforwardness"
The first discourse:
What worthy rulers value most is scholars.
The reason they value scholars
is for their ability to speak straightforwardly.
When speech is straightforward, the crooked becomes apparent.
The flaw of rulers
is desiring to hear the crooked while disliking straightforward speech.
This is like blocking the source yet wanting water—
how can water come?
This is devaluing what they desire and valuing what they dislike—
how can what they desire come?
Néng Yì went to see King Xuān of Qí.
King Xuān said:
"I have heard that you value straightforwardness—
is this true?"
He replied:
"How can Yì be straightforward?
Yì has heard that those who value straightforwardness
do not dwell in disordered states,
nor do they meet with corrupt rulers.
Now that I personally meet Your Majesty,
and my household resides in Qí,
how can Yì be straightforward?"
King Xuān angrily said:
"A rustic scholar!"
and intended to punish him.
Néng Yì said:
"In my youth, I admired such deeds;
in adulthood, I practice them.
Why can Your Majesty not tolerate a rustic scholar,
to highlight what he values?"
The king then spared him.
If one like Néng Yì were to speak cautiously by the ruler's side,
he would certainly not flatter the ruler.
Not flattering the ruler—
would the ruler gain little from this?
This is what worthy rulers seek,
and what unworthy rulers detest.
Hú Yuàn advised King Mǐn of Qí:
"The tripods of Yīn were displayed in the court of Zhōu,
its altar was covered by Zhōu's screen,
the music of its shields and axes
accompanies people's wanderings.
The music of a perished state
should not reach the ancestral temple;
the altar of a perished state
should not see the sky;
the vessels of a perished state displayed in court
serve as a warning.
Your Majesty must strive.
Do not let Qí's great bell be displayed in court,
do not let Tàigōng's altar be covered by a screen,
do not let Qí's music fill people's wanderings."
The King of Qí did not accept this.
Hú Yuàn left and wept for the state for three days,
saying:
"Those who leave early
wear fine hemp and ramie;
those who leave late
fill the prisons.
Now I see the people wandering eastward in confusion, not knowing where to go."
The King of Qí asked his official,
"What is the law for one who mourns the state?"
The official said,
"Beheading."
The king said,
"Carry out the law."
The official set up the execution block and axe at the Eastern Gate,
not wishing to kill him,
but hoping he would flee.
Hú Yuàn heard of this and hurriedly went to pass by.
The official said,
"The law for mourning the state is beheading.
Is the venerable sir old or confused?"
Hú Yuàn said,
"Why would I be confused?"
Thereupon he then spoke, saying:
"There is one who came from the south,
a minnow entering while a whale takes residence,
causing our court to become weeds and our state to become ruins.
Yīn had Bǐgān,
Wú had Zǐxū,
Qí has Hú Yuàn.
Having not heeded such words,
you now behead me at the Eastern Gate.
Let each beheading make me a third alongside those two men!"
Hú Yuàn did not delight in being beheaded,
but the state was already in chaos,
the ruler was already perverse,
and grieving for the altars of soil and grain and the people,
therefore he uttered such words.
Uttering such words was not balanced discourse,
but was intended to save [the state] from ruin,
and was inherently fraught with danger.
This is why Chù Zǐ left him,
and why Dá Zǐ died for him.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ attacked Wèi, approaching its outer walls,
leading the troops himself.
When battle was joined,
he stood far off,
moreover staying beneath a rhinoceros-hide screen and shield,
and when he beat the drum the officers did not rise [to attack].
Jiǎnzǐ threw down the drumstick and sighed, saying:
"Alas!
Have the officers' swiftness and vigor deteriorated to such a state?"
The messenger Zhú Guò, removing his helmet and holding his spear crosswise, advanced and said:
"Your servant has heard that
it is also a case of the ruler's inability,
what deterioration do the officers have?"
Jiǎnzǐ, flushing with anger, changed countenance and said:
"I have no one to command,
and you yourself are leading these multitudes;
you personally say I am incapable.
If you have an explanation it is acceptable,
if not, you die."
He replied, saying:
"In the past, our former lord, Duke Xiàn, upon ascending the throne for five years,
annexed nineteen states,
using these same officers.
Duke Huì, upon ascending the throne for two years,
was licentious, violent, and arrogant,
personally fond of jade-like women.
The people of Qín attacked us,
and we retreated seventy lǐ from Jiàng,
using these same officers.
Duke Wén, upon ascending the throne for two years,
steered them with courage,
therefore after three years the officers were all resolute and daring;
at the battle of Chéngpú,
he five times defeated the men of Jīng;
besieged Wèi and took Cáo,
captured Shíshè;
settled the Son of Heaven in his position,
and achieved a revered name under heaven;
using these same officers.
It is also a case of the ruler's inability to lead them,
what deterioration do the officers have?"
Jiǎnzǐ then left the rhinoceros-hide screen and shield and stood where arrows and stones could reach,
and with one drumbeat the officers all mounted the walls.
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Rather than obtaining a thousand chariots for me,
it is not as good as hearing one word from the messenger Zhú Guò."
The messenger Zhú Guò can be said to have been capable of remonstrating with his ruler.
On the field of battle,
just as the drums were being used,
with rewards not increased,
punishments not made heavier,
with one word he made the officers all gladly die for their superior.
23.2 "Straightforward Remonstrance"
The second says:
When words reach their extreme, [the ruler] becomes angry;
when angry, the speaker is in danger.
If not a worthy, who would willingly confront danger?
And if not a worthy,
