he will be seeking profit.
One who seeks profit,
what benefit is there in confronting danger?
Therefore, an unworthy ruler has no worthies.
Having no worthies, he does not hear extreme words;
not hearing extreme words, treacherous men form cliques and all evils arise in full.
If it is like this, then there is no means to survive.
Whenever a state survives,
and a ruler is secure,
there must be a reason for it.
Not knowing the reason,
even if it survives it will inevitably perish,
even if secure it will inevitably be endangered.
Therefore, the reason cannot but be discussed.
Duke Huán of Qí, Guǎn Zhòng, Bào Shū, and Nìng Qī were drinking together.
When the wine was at its height,
Duke Huán said to Bào Shū:
"Why do you not rise and offer a toast to me?"
Bào Shū, holding up a cup, advanced and said:
"May my lord not forget fleeing and residing in Jǔ,
may Guǎn Zhòng not forget being bound and in Lǔ,
may Nìng Qī not forget feeding oxen and dwelling beneath a cart."
Duke Huán left his mat, bowed twice, and said:
"If I and my great officers can all not forget the master's words,
then the altars of soil and grain of Qí will be fortunate not to be endangered."
At this time,
one could speak extreme words with Duke Huán.
Being able to speak extreme words with him,
therefore one could assist him in becoming hegemon.
King Wén of Jīng obtained the Rúhuáng dog and the Yuǎnlù arrows,
and went hunting in Yúnmèng,
not returning for three months;
he obtained the woman of Dān,
became licentious,
and for a full year did not hold court.
Bǎo Shēn said:
"The former king divined and made me his guardian,
and it was auspicious.
Now the king has obtained the Rúhuáng dog and Yuǎnlù arrows,
hunts in Yúnmèng,
and does not return for three months;
he has obtained the woman of Dān,
become licentious,
and for a full year has not held court.
The king's crime deserves flogging."
The king said:
"Since leaving the swaddling clothes, I have been ranked among the feudal lords;
I wish to request a change and avoid flogging."
Bǎo Shēn said:
"Your servant receives the former king's command,
and dares not abandon it.
If the king does not accept flogging,
it is abandoning the former king's command.
Your servant would rather incur punishment from the king,
than incur punishment from the former king."
The king said:
"I respectfully assent."
Then he drew out a mat,
and the king prostrated himself.
Bǎo Shēn bound fifty thin thorn branches,
knelt and placed them on the king's back,
doing this twice,
then said to the king, "Rise."
The king said:
"Since I have the name of being flogged once,
then carry it out properly."
Bǎo Shēn said:
"Your servant has heard that for a gentleman, it is shameful;
for a petty man, it is painful.
If shame does not change him,
what benefit is there in pain?"
Bǎo Shēn hurried out,
wishing to cast himself into the deep pool,
and requested the death penalty.
King Wén said:
"This is my fault.
What crime has Bǎo Shēn committed?"
The king then changed his conduct,
summoned Bǎo Shēn,
killed the Rúhuáng dog,
broke the Yuǎnlù arrows,
and banished the woman of Dān.
Afterwards, the state of Jīng annexed thirty-nine states.
That the state of Jīng was expanded to this extent
was due to the strength of Bǎo Shēn and the achievement of extreme words.
23.3 "Knowing Transformation"
The third says:
Those who serve others with bravery do so unto death;
if they have not died yet speak of death,
it is not worth discussing;
regarding death, even if one knows it, it is the same as not knowing.
What is valuable about wisdom in general
is that it values knowing transformation.
The deluded ruler is not like this.
Before transformation arrives, he does not know;
when transformation has already arrived,
even if he knows, it is uniformly the same as not knowing.
There are matters that can be overlooked,
and there are matters that cannot be overlooked.
When it comes to personal death and the destruction of the state,
how can these be overlooked?
This is what wise rulers value,
and deluded rulers disregard.
When it is disregarded,
how can the state avoid peril?
How can the ruler himself avoid distress?
The path of peril and distress,
leading to personal death and the destruction of the state,
lies in not foreseeing changes beforehand.
King Fūchāi of Wú was an example of this.
It was not that Wǔ Zǐxū failed to foresee the changes;
he remonstrated, but his advice was not heeded.
Therefore, Wú became ruins,
and the disaster reached even Hélǘ.
When King Fūchāi of Wú was about to attack Qí,
Wǔ Zǐxū said:
"It must not be done.
Between Qí and Wú,
customs are different,
and languages are not mutually intelligible.
If we obtain their land, we cannot settle it;
if we obtain their people, we cannot command them.
Between Wú and Yuè,
the territories are adjacent,
the lands connect and border each other,
customs are the same,
and languages are mutually intelligible.
If we obtain their land, we can settle it;
if we obtain their people, we can command them.
The same is true for Yuè regarding us.
The situation between Wú and Yuè is one of irreconcilable opposition.
Yuè, in relation to Wú,
is like a disease of the heart and abdomen.
Even if it does not act,
the injury is deep and internal.
Qí, in relation to Wú,
is like a skin rash.
It is not troublesome when it heals,
and moreover, it causes no real injury.
Now, to abandon Yuè and attack Qí
is like fearing a tiger yet stabbing a wild boar.
Even if you are victorious,
the subsequent calamity will be endless."
Grand Steward Pǐ said:
"It must not be so.
The reason Your Majesty's commands do not prevail among the superior states
is because of Qí and Jìn.
If Your Majesty attacks Qí and is victorious,
then move the troops to confront Jìn.
Jìn will certainly obey your commands.
Thus, in one move, Your Majesty will subdue two states,
and your commands will surely prevail among the superior states."
Fūchāi considered this correct.
He did not heed Wǔ Zǐxū's words,
but employed Grand Steward Pǐ's plan.
Wǔ Zǐxū said:
"If Heaven is going to destroy Wú,
then it will make Your Majesty victorious in battle.
If Heaven is not going to destroy Wú,
then it will make Your Majesty defeated in battle."
Fūchāi did not listen.
Wǔ Zǐxū, with sleeves flung back and striding high, left the court,
saying:
"Alas!
Thorns and brambles are sure to grow in the court of Wú!"
Fūchāi raised an army to attack Qí,
fought at Àilíng,
and greatly defeated the Qí army.
Upon returning, he put Wǔ Zǐxū to death.
As Wǔ Zǐxū was about to die, he said:
"Ah!
How I wish I could keep one eye to see the Yuè people enter Wú!"
Then he committed suicide.
Fūchāi then took his corpse and cast it into the river,
gouged out his eyes,
and displayed them on the eastern gate,
saying:
"How will you see the Yuè people enter my state?"
After several years,
Yuè took revenge on Wú,
devastated the state,
ended its lineage,
destroyed its altars of soil and grain,
razed its ancestral temples,
and Fūchāi himself was captured.
As Fūchāi was about to die, he said:
"If the dead have consciousness,
what face will I have to see Wǔ Zǐxū in the underworld?"
Then he covered his face with a cloth and died.
Before calamity arrives,
it cannot be foretold;
once calamity has arrived,
even if one knows, it is too late.
Therefore, Fūchāi's feeling of shame before Wǔ Zǐxū
was worse than not knowing at all.
23.4 "Exceeding Reason"
The fourth discourse:
The rulers of perished states share one common trait.
Though the times may differ,
and their affairs may vary,
the reason for their common destruction
is indulgence in improper pleasures.
Indulgence in improper pleasures makes preservation impossible.
Mounds of distiller's grains and pools of wine,
forests of meat and racks for roasting,
carved pillars and shackling feudal lords—
these are improper.
Executing the daughter of Guǐhóu to take her jade,
cutting off the shins of waders to examine their marrow,
killing Méi Bó and sending his minced flesh to King Wén—
these are improper.
King Wén outwardly accepted it and informed the feudal lords.
Building the Xuán chamber,
constructing the Qǐng palace,
slicing open pregnant women to observe their fetuses,
killing Bǐgān to examine his heart—
these are improper.
Confucius, hearing of this, said:
"If his orifices had been clear, Bǐgān would not have died."
These were the reasons for the downfall of Xià and Shāng.
Duke Líng of Jìn was without principle.
He shot pellets at people from a tower to watch them dodge;
he had a cook stew bear's paws until they were undercooked,
then killed him,
and ordered women to carry the corpse past the court to display his might—
this was improper.
Zhào Duǎn repeatedly remonstrated, but he would not listen.
The duke hated him,
and sent Jùmí to assassinate him.
Jùmí saw him,
but could not bear to kill him,
saying:
"He does not forget reverence and respect;
he is the lord of the people.
To assassinate the lord of the people is disloyal;
to abandon the ruler's command is untrustworthy.
Faced with either, I would rather die."
Then he dashed himself against a locust tree in the court and died.
When King Mǐn of Qí, having lost his state, was dwelling in Wèi,
he said to Gōng Yùdān:
"What kind of ruler am I?"
Yùdān replied:
"Your Majesty is a worthy ruler.
I have heard that in ancient times there were those who relinquished the world without a trace of regret.
I have heard of their reputation,
and in Your Majesty I see the reality.
Your Majesty was renowned as the Eastern Emperor,
and truly distinguished in the world.
Having left your state and dwelling in Wèi,
your appearance is full and content,
your complexion radiant,
with no thought of your lost state."
The king said:
"Excellent!
Dān understands me.
Since I left my state and dwelt in Wèi,
my waistband has increased by three notches!"
The King of Sòng built the Nièdì terrace,
filled leather sacks with blood,
hung them high,
shot arrows at them wearing armor,
from below,
so the blood poured down and flowed on the ground.
His attendants all congratulated him, saying:
"Your Majesty's worthiness surpasses even Tāng and Wǔ.
Tāng and Wǔ conquered men,
but now Your Majesty conquers Heaven.
Worthiness can go no further than this."
The King of Sòng was greatly pleased,
and drank wine.
When someone in the chamber shouted 'Long live the king!',
all in the hall responded.
Once those in the hall had responded,
all below the hall responded.
Those hearing it in the courtyard outside the gate
did not dare not to respond.
This was improper.
23.5 "Obstruction"
The fifth discourse:
The kings of perished states
cannot be spoken to directly.
If they cannot be spoken to directly,
then their faults never reach their ears,
and goodness never comes to them of itself.
When goodness does not come of itself, there is obstruction.
During the time of Duke Mù of Qín,
the Róng were powerful.
Duke Mù of Qín sent them sixteen female musicians and an excellent cook.
The Róng king was greatly delighted.
Because of this,
he feasted repeatedly,
day and night without cease.
When his attendants mentioned that Qín invaders were coming,
he would draw his bow and shoot at them.
The Qin invaders indeed arrived,
the Rong king was drunk and lay beneath the wine vessel,
and in the end they captured him alive, bound and tied.
Before capture, it was unknowable;
after capture, it was again unknowable.
Even the most skilled persuaders are like this—
why is that?
When Qi attacked Sòng,
the king of Sòng sent someone to scout where the Qi invaders had reached.
The messenger returned
and said:
"The Qi invaders are near,
and the people are terrified."
The attendants all said to the king of Sòng:
"This is what is called 'the flesh itself brings worms.'
Given Sòng's strength
and Qi's military weakness,
how could this be?"
The king of Sòng, enraged, had the messenger wrongfully executed.
He sent another person to observe the Qi invaders;
the messenger reported as before,
and the king of Sòng again angrily had him wrongfully executed.
This happened three times.
Afterward, he sent yet another person to observe.
The Qi invaders were near,
and the people were terrified.
The messenger encountered his elder brother,
who said:
"The state is in extreme peril;
where are you going?"
His younger brother replied:
"I am going to observe the Qi invaders for the king,
unexpectedly they are so near,
and the people are terrified like this.
Now I am privately worried that those who previously observed the Qi invaders
all reported that the invaders were near and died for it.
If I now report the truth,
I will die;
if I do not report the truth,
I fear I will also die.
What should I do?"
His elder brother said:
"If you report the truth,
you will die ahead of those who will perish,
and perish ahead of those who will flee."
Thereupon, he reported to the king:
"I have no idea where the Qi invaders are.
The people are very peaceful."
The king was greatly pleased.
The attendants all said:
"Those who died earlier deserved it."
The king bestowed much gold upon him.
When the invaders arrived,
the king himself leaped into his chariot and fled at full speed,
while this man became wealthy in another state.
When climbing a mountain and looking at oxen, they appear like sheep;
looking at sheep, they appear like piglets.
An ox's nature is not like a sheep's,
nor is a sheep's nature like a piglet's;
it is the perspective from which one views them that distorts them.
Yet to become angry at the oxen and sheep for appearing small
is the height of madness.
To act madly in dispensing rewards and punishments
is why the Dài clan perished.
The king of Qi wanted Chúnyú Kūn to tutor the crown prince,
but Kūn declined, saying:
"I am unworthy
and insufficient to shoulder such a great responsibility.
Your Majesty should instead select an elder of the state and appoint him."
The king of Qi said:
"Do not decline.
How could I demand that you make the crown prince exactly like me?
I was inherently born with these qualities.
Could you make the crown prince like Yáo for me?
Or like Shùn?"
Generally, for persuasion to succeed,
the one without wisdom must listen to the wise,
and the one who is wrong must accept what is right.
Now, if one considers oneself more worthy than Yáo and Shùn,
how could they possibly heed persuasion?
Persuasion will certainly not enter.
One will not hear how to preserve the ruler.
King Xuān of Qi enjoyed archery
and liked others to say he was strong enough to use a powerful bow.
The bow he actually used did not exceed three dàn,
yet he showed it to his attendants.
The attendants all tried to draw it,
but stopped halfway,
and all said:
"This is no less than nine dàn;
who but the king could use such a bow?"
King Xuān's reality
was that he used no more than three dàn,
yet for his entire life he believed he used nine dàn.
Is this not lamentable?
If not for upright men, who could avoid flattering the ruler?
The upright men of the world
are few and cannot overcome the many—
such is the norm.
Thus, the rulers of disordered states
suffer from mistaking three dàn for nine dàn.
23.6 "Yuán Luàn"
The sixth says:
Disorder must have degrees;
there are five great disorders,
three minor disorders,
and three disturbances of rebellion.
Therefore, the Odes say:
"Do not pass by the gate of disorder,"
to keep far from it.
Consider blessings not yet arrived,
consider misfortunes that exceed them,
to thereby preserve oneself intact.
King Wǔ obtained it through martial means,
maintained it through civil means,
laid down spears and unstrung bows,
showing the world he would not use arms—
this is how he preserved it.
Duke Xiàn of Jìn installed Lí Jī as his consort
and made Xī Qí his crown prince;
Lǐ Kè led the people of the state to attack and kill them.
Xún Xī installed his younger brother, Prince Zhuó;
after the burial,
Lǐ Kè again led the people of the state to attack and kill him.
Thus, Jìn was left without a ruler.
Prince Yíwú heavily bribed Qín with land to seek entry;
Duke Mù of Qín led an army to install him,
and the people of Jìn established him as ruler—
this was Duke Huì.
Once Duke Huì was settled in Jìn,
he betrayed Qín's kindness and did not give the land.
Duke Mù of Qín led an army to attack Jìn;
Duke Huì of Jìn confronted him,
and they fought the people of Qín at Hányuán.
The Jìn army was greatly defeated;
Qín captured Duke Huì and returned,
imprisoning him at Língtái.
In the tenth month,
they made peace with Jìn,
returned Duke Huì, and took his crown prince, Yǔ, as a hostage.
Crown Prince Yǔ escaped and returned.
When Duke Huì died,
Yǔ was established as ruler—
this was Duke Huái.
Duke Mù of Qín was angered by his escape and return;
he raised an army to support Prince Chóng'ěr and attack Duke Huái,
killing him at Gāoliáng,
and established Chóng'ěr—
this was Duke Wén.
Duke Wén distributed alms,
revived the neglected and stagnant,
relieved the destitute and needy,
saved from disasters and calamities,
prohibited licentiousness and evil,
reduced taxes and levies,
pardoned crimes and offenses,
moderated the use of vessels and implements,
employed the people according to the seasons,
defeated the Jīng people at Chéngpú,
secured King Xiāng,
lifted the siege of Sòng,
withdrew the garrison from Gǔ,
and both internally and externally, all submitted—
only then did the disorder in Jìn cease.
Thus, when Duke Xiàn listened to Lí Jī,
drew close to Liáng Wǔ and Yōu Shī,
and killed Crown Prince Shēnshēng,
five great calamities followed:
three rulers died violently,
one ruler was captured,
ministers, nobles, and officials died by the hundreds,
and calamity lasted for twenty years.
Since ancient times,
disorder has never been singular,
yet the trouble with those who cause disorder
is that they all say it is only one,
for their considerations of affairs differ in nature.
When considerations of affairs differ in nature,
it is because minds differ.
Therefore, all who stir disorder
rarely escape personal calamity.
24.1 "Bù Gǒu"
The first says:
In the affairs of the worthy,
though noble, they do not act carelessly;
though trusted, they do not flatter themselves;
they must accord with principle before acting,
and must align with righteousness before undertaking—
this is the conduct of loyal ministers.
What worthy rulers delight in,
even unworthy rulers, though unworthy, also delight in,
not because they dislike the reputation.
Though a ruler may be unworthy,
his delight in the reputation of loyal ministers is the same as that of a worthy ruler;
but in practicing the reality, he differs from a worthy ruler.
Because they differ, their achievements, fame, misfortune, and blessings also differ.
Because they differ, Wǔ Zǐxū was delighted in by Hé Lǘ but detested by Fū Chāi;
Bǐ Gān was detested in Shāng while alive but delighted in by Zhōu after death.
King Wǔ arrived at the outskirts of Yīn,
and his reins fell off.
Five attendants were driving before him,
but none were willing to fix them,
saying:
"What we serve our lord with is not fixing reins."
King Wǔ then released the white feather in his left hand,
and the yellow battle-axe in his right hand,
and with effort fixed the reins himself.
When Confucius heard of this, he said:
"This is why these five men became assistants to a true king,
but would not be tolerated by an unworthy ruler."
Thus, there are times when the Son of Heaven cannot overcome the common people,
and times when the realm cannot overcome a state with a thousand chariots.
Duke Mù of Qín met Yóu Yú of the Róng tribe,
was pleased with him and wanted to keep him,
but Yóu Yú refused.
Duke Mù reported this to Jiǎn Shū.
Jiǎn Shū said:
"My lord, report this to the Internal Scribe Liào."
The Internal Scribe Liào replied:
"The Róng people are not versed in the five tones or the five flavors,
so why not send him gifts?"
Duke Mù sent him sixteen female musicians and an excellent cook.
The Róng king was delighted,
became confused and fell into great disorder,
indulging in drinking,
day and night without rest.
Yóu Yú repeatedly remonstrated but was not heeded,
so in anger he defected to Duke Mù.
Jiǎn Shū was not incapable of doing what the Internal Scribe Liào did,
but his sense of righteousness would not allow it.
Duke Mù was able to make his ministers sometimes uphold their proper righteousness,
and thus avenged the shame of Xiáo,
extending his power west to Héyōng.
Duke Mù of Qín appointed Bǎilǐ Xí as his chancellor.
When Jìn sent Shū Hǔ and Qí sent Dōngguō Jiǎn to Qín,
Gōngsūn Zhī requested an audience with them.
The duke said:
"Is receiving guests
your responsibility?"
He replied:
"No."
"Did the chancellor send you?"
He replied:
"No."
The duke said:
"Then what you are doing is not your duty.
Qín is a remote and uncultured state,
where the Róng and Yí tribes serve us.
Even when officials perform their own duties,
we still fear being laughed at by the feudal lords.
Now you are doing what is not your duty;
withdraw, and you will be judged and punished."
Gōngsūn Zhī left,
and presented his case to the Bǎilǐ clan.
Bǎilǐ Xí pleaded for him.
The duke said:
"Is this what you heard from the chancellor?
If Zhī is innocent, why plead for him?
If he is guilty, why plead for him?"
Bǎilǐ Xí returned,
and declined Gōngsūn Zhī's request.
Gōngsūn Zhī moved,
and presented his case in the street.
Bǎilǐ Xí ordered the officials to carry out his punishment.
To define duties and assign offices,
this is what the ancients used as their model.
Now Duke Mù has followed this,
so is it not fitting that he became hegemon of the Western Róng?
Duke Wén of Jìn was about to attack Yè.
Zhào Cuī explained the strategy for defeating Yè,
and Duke Wén employed it,
indeed defeating Yè.
Upon returning,
he prepared to grant rewards.
Cuī said:
"Will my lord reward the root?
Or reward the branch?
If you reward the branch, then the cavalrymen will remain;
if you reward the root, then I heard it from Xì Zǐhǔ."
Duke Wén summoned Xì Zǐhǔ and said:
"Cuī explained how to defeat Yè,
and Yè has been defeated.
I am about to reward him,
but he said:
'I heard it from Zǐhǔ,
so please reward Zǐhǔ.'"
Zǐhǔ said:
"Speaking is easy,
but acting is difficult.
I was merely the one who spoke."
The duke said:
"Do not refuse."
Xì Zǐhǔ did not dare to firmly decline,
and so accepted the reward.
In general, when granting rewards, one should be broad,
for breadth brings more assistance.
Now Hǔ was not the one who personally spoke,
yet the reward still reached him.
This is why even those distant and unrelated will exhaust their abilities and wisdom.
Duke Wén of Jín had been in exile for a long time,
and upon returning, amidst the remnants of great disorder,
he was still able to become hegemon.
Was it not due to this?
24.2 "Praising Ability"
The second says:
The worthy treat others according to their character,
the average according to their deeds,
and the unworthy according to their wealth.
To obtain ten fine horses
is not as good as obtaining one Bó Lè;
to obtain ten fine swords
is not as good as obtaining one Ōu Yě;
to obtain a thousand lǐ of land
is not as good as obtaining one sage.
Shùn obtained Gāo Yáo and Shùn received him;
Tāng obtained Yī Yǐn and gained the people of Xià;
King Wén obtained Lǚ Wàng and subdued Yīn Shāng.
To obtain a sage,
can it be measured in lǐ?
Guǎn Zhòng was bound and imprisoned in Lǔ.
Duke Huán wanted to appoint Bào Shū as chancellor.
Bào Shū said:
"If my lord wishes to become hegemon and king,
then Guǎn Yíwú is there,
and I am not his equal."
Duke Huán said:
"Yíwú is my enemy,
the one who shot me.
It cannot be."
Bào Shū said:
"Yíwú shot people for his own lord.
If my lord can obtain and employ him,
then he will also shoot people for you."
Duke Huán did not listen,
and insisted on appointing Bào Shū.
Bào Shū firmly declined and recommended him instead,
and Duke Huán finally listened.
Thereupon, he sent someone to inform Lǔ:
"Guǎn Yíwú is my enemy,
and I wish to obtain him and personally deal with him."
The lord of Lǔ agreed,
and had officials cover his fists with leather,
glue his eyes shut,
place him in a leather sack,
and put him in a carriage.
When they reached the border of Qí,
Duke Huán sent someone to meet him with a court carriage,
purified him with torch fire,
and anointed him with a sacrificial pig.
He entered the state with him alive,
ordered the officials to prepare the ancestral temple, set out mats and tables, and presented him,
saying:
"Since I heard Yíwú's words,
my eyes have become clearer,
my ears have become sharper.
I dare not keep this to myself,
and dare to report it to my ancestors."
Then, turning, he commanded Guǎnzǐ:
"Yíwú, assist me."
Guǎn Zhòng retreated,
bowed twice and touched his head to the ground,
received the command, and left.
Guǎn Zhòng governed Qí,
and whenever affairs were accomplished with merit,
Duke Huán would first reward Bào Shū,
saying:
"The one who enabled Qí to obtain Guǎnzǐ
was Bào Shū."
Duke Huán can be said to have understood how to grant rewards.
In general, when granting rewards, one should aim at the root,
for if the root is addressed, errors will have no way to arise.
Sūnshū Áo and Shěnyǐnjīng were friends.
Shū Áo traveled in Yǐng for three years,
yet his reputation remained unknown,
and his virtuous conduct unheard.
Shěnyǐnjīng said to Sūnshū Áo:
"To explain righteousness and be heeded,
to have methods and strategies trusted and implemented,
enabling one's lord to rise to kingliness above,
or to hegemony below,
I am not your equal.
But to adapt to the world and connect with customs,
to explain righteousness and harmonize evenly,
to suit the lord's heart,
you are not my equal.
Why don't you return to farming?
I will travel on your behalf."
Shěn Yǐnjīng traveled in Yǐng for five years.
The King of Jīng wanted to make him Prime Minister.
Shěn Yǐnjīng declined, saying:
"Among the humble people of Qīsī, there is one named Sūnshū Áo,
a sage.
Your Majesty must employ him.
I am not his equal."
The King of Jīng then sent a royal carriage to welcome Shū Áo and made him Prime Minister.
In twelve years, King Zhuāng became hegemon.
This was due to the efforts of Shěn Yǐnjīng.
No achievement is greater than advancing the worthy.
24.3 "Self-Knowledge"
The third says:
To know what is straight and level,
one must have a marking line and plumb line.
To know what is square and round,
one must have a compass and square.
If a ruler wishes to know himself,
he must have upright men.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven establishes assistants and advisors,
appoints tutors and guardians,
in order to point out his faults.
Now, people inherently cannot know themselves,
and a ruler is even more so.
Whether one survives or perishes, is safe or in danger,
do not seek it externally;
the task lies in self-knowledge.
Yáo had a drum for those wishing to remonstrate;
Shùn had a wooden board for criticism;
Tāng had officials to correct his faults;
King Wǔ had a warning drum.
Yet they still feared they might not know themselves.
Now, the worthy are not like Yáo, Shùn, Tāng, or Wǔ,
and there are ways to obscure and block [criticism].
How then can they know themselves?
King Chéng of Jīng and King Zhuāng of Qí, lacking self-knowledge, were killed.
The King of Wú and Zhì Bó, lacking self-knowledge, perished.
Sòng and Zhōngshān, lacking self-knowledge, were destroyed.
Duke Huì of Jìn and Zhào Kuò, lacking self-knowledge, were captured.
Zuāntú, Páng Juān, and Crown Prince Shēn, lacking self-knowledge, died.
Therefore, no failure is greater than lacking self-knowledge.
When the Fàn clan was destroyed,
a commoner obtained one of their bells.
He wanted to carry it and run away,
but the bell was too large to carry.
So he tried to break it with a hammer.
The bell clanged loudly.
Fearing others would hear it and take it from him,
he hastily covered his own ears.
It is understandable to fear others hearing it,
but to fear hearing it oneself is absurd.
For a ruler to dislike hearing about his faults,
is this not similar?
Disliking others hearing about his faults is still somewhat understandable.
(But disliking hearing about his faults himself is absurd.)
Marquis Wén of Wèi held a banquet
and ordered all his ministers to discuss him.
Some said his lordship was wise.
When it came to Rèn Zuò's turn,
Rèn Zuò said:
"Your lordship is an unworthy ruler.
Having obtained Zhōngshān, you did not enfeoff it to your brother,
but instead enfeoffed it to your son.
From this, I know your lordship is unworthy."
Marquis Wén was displeased,
and it showed on his face.
Rèn Zuò hurriedly left.
Next was Dí Huáng.
Dí Huáng said:
"Your lordship is a worthy ruler.
I have heard that when a ruler is worthy,
his ministers' words are straightforward.
Just now, Rèn Zuò's words were straightforward.
Therefore, I know your lordship is worthy."
Marquis Wén, pleased, said:
"Can he be brought back?"
Dí Huáng replied:
"Why not?
I have heard that a loyal minister exhausts his loyalty,
and dares not stray far to avoid death.
Zuò is probably still at the gate."
Dí Huáng went to look,
and Rèn Zuò was indeed at the gate.
He summoned him by the ruler's order.
Rèn Zuò entered.
Marquis Wén descended the steps to welcome him,
and from then on treated Zuò as a guest of honor.
Had Marquis Wén lacked Dí Huáng,
he would have nearly lost a loyal minister.
To comply with the ruler's heart in order to highlight the worthy—
was this not Dí Huáng?
24.4 "Appropriate Rewards"
The fourth says:
The people have no way to know Heaven directly.
They know Heaven through the movements of the four seasons, cold and heat, sun, moon, and stars.
When the movements of the four seasons, cold and heat, sun, moon, and stars are proper,
then all living beings with blood and breath find their proper place and live peacefully.
Ministers also have no way to know their ruler directly.
Ministers know their ruler through the rewards, punishments, ranks, and emoluments he bestows.
If the ruler's bestowal of rewards, punishments, ranks, and emoluments is appropriate,
then close and distant, worthy and unworthy, all will exert their strength and be of use.
When Duke Wén of Jìn returned to his state,
he rewarded those who followed him in exile,
but Táo Hú was not included.
His attendants said:
"My lord, you have returned to the state and family.
Ranks and emoluments have been bestowed three times,
yet Táo Hú is not included.
May we ask the reason?"
Duke Wén said:
"Those who assisted me with righteousness and guided me with ritual—
I consider them deserving of the highest reward.
Those who taught me with goodness and strengthened me with worthiness—
I consider them deserving of the second reward.
Those who opposed my desires and repeatedly pointed out my faults—
I consider them deserving of the lowest reward.
These three are for rewarding meritorious ministers.
As for rewarding the laboring servants of Tángguó,
then Táo Hú would be first."
The Zhou historian Xīng heard of this and said:
"The Duke of Jìn will likely become hegemon!
In the past, the sage kings put virtue before force.
The Duke of Jìn fits this."
When the young ruler of Qín's consort employed the eunuch Biàn,
the multitude of worthies were displeased and hid themselves.
The common people were resentful and criticized their superiors.
Prince Lián was in exile in Wèi.
Hearing of this,
he wished to enter [Qín].
He followed his ministers and people to the pass at Zhèngsuǒ.
Yòuzhǔ Rán guarded the pass
and would not let him enter,
saying:
"I have a principle of loyalty:
I cannot serve two masters.
Please strive to leave, my prince."
Prince Lián left
and entered Dí territory.
He went to the Yānshì Pass,
and Jūn Gǎi let him in.
The consort heard of this,
was greatly alarmed,
and ordered officers to raise troops,
commanding them:
"There are bandits at the border."
When the troops and officers first set out,
they all said, "Let's go attack the bandits."
Midway, they changed their tune, saying:
"We are not attacking bandits.
We are welcoming our rightful lord."
Prince Lián then came with the troops.
They reached Yōng,
surrounded the consort,
and she committed suicide.
Prince Lián was established [as ruler],
becoming Duke Xiàn.
He resented Yòuzhǔ Rán and intended to punish him severely,
while feeling grateful to Jūn Gǎi and wishing to reward him richly.
Jiān Tū objected, saying:
"This cannot be done.
There are many Qín princes abroad.
If you do this, then ministers will compete to bring in exiled princes.
This is not beneficial for the ruler."
Duke Xiàn considered this correct.
Therefore, he pardoned Yòuzhǔ Rán's offense,
bestowed upon Jūn Gǎi the rank of Guāndàfū,
and rewarded the guards of the pass with twenty dàn of rice each.
Duke Xiàn can be said to have known how to use rewards and punishments.
Generally, rewards are not given out of affection,
nor punishments out of hatred.
They are used to observe the outcome.
If the outcome is good,
even if one hates the person, reward him.
If the outcome is not good,
even if one loves the person, punish him.
This is how the former kings brought order out of chaos and ensured safety.
24.5 "Concentrating the Will"
The fifth says:
The former kings had great tasks.
They removed what harmed them.
Therefore, what they desired, they surely obtained;
what they hated, they surely eliminated.
This is how they established their achievements and fame.
Mediocre rulers are not like this.
They have great tasks but cannot remove what harms them.
This is why they are incapable of success.
The ability to remove harmful factors from one's tasks, or the inability to do so—
this is what distinguishes the worthy from the unworthy.
If a river deer runs swiftly,
even a horse cannot catch up;
what allows it to be caught later
is its habit of looking back.
A fine steed can travel a thousand li in a day,
because the carriage is light;
if heavily loaded, it cannot go even a few li,
due to the burden.
When a worthy person undertakes affairs,
one never hears of them achieving no merit;
yet if their fame is not greatly established and their benefits do not extend to the world,
it is because fools and incompetents bear the responsibility.
Winter and summer cannot both be severe,
weeds and crops cannot both flourish,
when new grain ripens, old grain is depleted,
all creatures with horns lack upper teeth,
trees with abundant fruit are necessarily low,
those who use their intellect narrowly achieve no success—
this is the way of Heaven.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven does not dwell in perfection,
does not dwell in extremity,
does not dwell in fullness.
Perfection must lead to deficiency,
extremity must lead to reversal,
fullness must lead to loss.
The former kings knew that things cannot have two great aspects simultaneously,
so they selected their tasks
and dwelled in what was appropriate.
Kǒngzǐ, Mòzǐ, and Nìng Yuè
were all scholars of common birth.
Considering the affairs of the world,
they believed there was nothing like the methods of the former kings,
so they studied them day and night.
Whatever was beneficial to learning,
they did not fail to do;
whatever was not beneficial to learning,
they refused to do.
It is said that Kǒng Qiū and Mò Dí
recited and practiced their studies by day,
and at night personally saw King Wén and the Duke of Zhōu, Dàn, to question them.
With such focused intent,
what affair would they not comprehend?
What task would they not accomplish?
Thus it is said: “Refine and master it,
and even spirits will inform you.”
It is not that spirits inform you,
but that you have refined and mastered it.
If here were a precious sword and fine horse,
you would never tire of admiring them,
nor weary of gazing upon them.
But with precious conduct and excellent principles,
if you practice them once and never again,
desiring personal safety
and illustrious fame—
is that not difficult?
Nìng Yuè was a humble man from Zhōngmóu.
Suffering the toil of plowing and farming,
he said to his friend:
“What can I do to avoid this hardship?”
His friend replied:
“Nothing is better than study.
Study for thirty years, and you will achieve success.”
Nìng Yuè said:
“Let me do it in fifteen years.
When others rest,
I will not dare to rest;
when others sleep,
I will not dare to sleep.”
After fifteen years, Duke Wēi of Zhōu took him as his teacher.
An arrow is swift, yet it does not exceed two li—
because it stops;
walking is slow, yet it covers a hundred stages—
because it does not stop.
Now, with Nìng Yuè’s talent and long perseverance,
his becoming a teacher to feudal lords—
is that not fitting?
Yǎng Yóujī and Yǐn Rú
were both masters of the six arts.
The Chǔ court once had a divine white gibbon;
none of Chǔ’s skilled archers could hit it,
so the King of Chǔ asked Yǎng Yóujī to shoot it.
Yǎng Yóujī straightened his bow, took his arrows, and went;
before shooting, he had already struck it in his mind;
when he released the arrow, the gibbon fell in response—
thus Yǎng Yóujī had the ability to hit the mark before shooting.
Yǐn Rú studied charioteering for three years without mastering it;
distressed by this,
he dreamed at night of receiving the “autumn drive” from his teacher.
The next day, when he went to see him,
his teacher looked at him and said:
“It is not that I begrudge you the technique,
but I feared you were not yet ready.
Today I will teach you the autumn drive.”
Yǐn Rú retreated,
faced north, bowed twice, and said:
“Last night I dreamed of receiving it.”
He first told his teacher about the dream,
and the dream was indeed of the autumn drive.
These two gentlemen can be said to have mastered learning;
they can be said to have done no harm to it—
this is why they are observed by later generations.
24.6 “Valuing Appropriateness”
The sixth says:
Great fame and renown
cannot be forcibly sought;
they must follow the proper way.
Governing things lies not in the things but in people;
governing people lies not in affairs but in the ruler;
governing the ruler lies not in the ruler but in the Son of Heaven;
governing the Son of Heaven lies not in the Son of Heaven but in desires;
governing desires lies not in desires but in nature.
Nature is the root of all things;
it cannot be lengthened,
nor shortened,
but must follow its inherent tendencies—
this is the principle of Heaven and Earth.
When raw flesh is exposed, crows and magpies gather;
when a cat is in the hall, mice scatter;
when mourning garments are displayed, people know of bereavement;
when yú and sè are set out, people know of music;
Tāng and Wǔ cultivated their conduct, and the world followed;
Jié and Zhòu neglected their conduct, and the world rebelled—
how could it depend on their words?
The gentleman examines only what lies within himself.
In Chǔ, there was a skilled physiognomist
whose predictions never missed,
and his reputation spread throughout the state.
King Zhuāng met and questioned him.
He replied:
“I am not able to read people’s faces,
but I can observe their friends.
Observing a commoner,
if his friends are all filial, brotherly, pure, cautious, and law-abiding,
then such a person
will surely see his family prosper daily,
and his person honored daily—
this is what is called an auspicious person.
Observing one who serves a ruler,
if his friends are all sincere, trustworthy, virtuous, and fond of goodness,
then such a person
will surely serve his ruler better daily,
and his office advance daily—
this is what is called an auspicious minister.
Observing a ruler,
if his court has many worthies,
his attendants are mostly loyal,
and when the ruler errs,
they all contend and remonstrate,
then such a ruler
will see his state grow more secure daily,
his person more honored daily,
and the world more submissive daily—
this is what is called an auspicious ruler.
I am not able to read people’s faces,
but I can observe their friends.”
King Zhuāng approved of this,
and thereupon urgently gathered scholars,
never slackening day or night,
and thus became hegemon over the world.
Therefore, when a worthy ruler occasionally encounters men of culture and art,
it is not merely to possess them,
but to accomplish great tasks.
Affairs, whether great or small,
are fundamentally interconnected.
Hunting and galloping,
archery and dog racing—
worthies do not refrain from these,
but by engaging in them, their wisdom daily increases;
incompetent rulers engage in them, and their wisdom daily becomes confused.
The Records say:
“With arrogant and confused affairs,
what can one await but ruin?”
There was a ruler fond of hunting
who spent long days without catching game.
Returning home, he was ashamed before his family;
going out, he was ashamed before his friends and community.
Considering the reason for his failure,
he realized his dogs were poor.
Wanting good dogs,
he lacked the means due to poverty.
Thereupon, he returned and diligently farmed;
diligent farming enriched his family,
family wealth allowed him to seek good dogs,
good dogs enabled him to catch game frequently,
and his hunting harvests often surpassed others’.
It is not only hunting—
all affairs are like this.
No hegemon or king has achieved hegemony or kingship without first “farming”—
this has never occurred, past or present.
This is how worthies and incompetents differ.
What worthies and incompetents desire is the same as others’;
Yáo, Jié, Yōu, and Lì were all thus,
but their ways of pursuing it differed.
Therefore, a wise ruler examines matters,
and if he deems them unfeasible,
he does not act;
if he deems them feasible,
he thus acts upon them.
In acting, he must follow the proper way,
so that nothing can harm him.
This is how achievements differ ten-thousandfold.
25.1 "Seeming Contrary but Conforming"
First it is said:
Many affairs seem contrary but are in fact conforming,
and many seem conforming but are in fact contrary.
One who understands that what seems conforming may be contrary, and what seems contrary may be conforming,
can then discuss transformation.
The extreme of length turns to shortness,
the extreme of shortness turns to length—
this is the way of Heaven.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ wanted to attack Chén,
and sent someone to observe it.
The envoy said:
"Chén cannot be attacked."
King Zhuāng asked:
"Why?"
He replied:
"Its city walls are high,
its moats are deep,
and its stores are abundant."
Níng Guó said:
"Chén can be attacked.
Now Chén is a small state,
yet its stores are abundant—
this means its taxes are heavy,
so the people resent their superiors.
Its city walls are high,
its moats are deep—
this means the people's strength is exhausted.
If we raise troops to attack it,
Chén can be taken."
King Zhuāng heeded him and thus took Chén.
The reason Tián Chéngzǐ has been able to possess the state until now
is that he had an elder brother named Wánzǐ,
who was both benevolent and courageous.
The Yuè people raised an army to punish Tián Chéngzǐ, saying:
"Why did you kill your lord and seize the state?"
Tián Chéngzǐ was troubled by this.
Wánzǐ requested to lead the officers and gentry to meet the Yuè army,
asking that they must fight,
and in fighting they must be defeated,
and in defeat he must die.
Tián Chéngzǐ said:
"That you must fight Yuè is acceptable,
but fighting must lead to defeat,
and defeat must lead to death—
I am doubtful of this."
Wánzǐ said:
"Your possession of the state
has caused the common people to resent their superiors,
and the worthy and good either die for it or ministers suffer disgrace.
In my view,
the state is already imperiled.
Now the Yuè people have raised an army,
and I will fight them.
If we fight and are defeated, the worthy and good will all perish,
and those who do not die will not dare return to the state.
You and the orphans will remain in the state.
In my view,
the state will surely be secure."
Wánzǐ departed,
and Tián Chéngzǐ wept as he sent him off.
Death and defeat
are what people detest,
yet here they are turned into security—
is there only one way?
Therefore, what rulers heed and what scholars learn
cannot but be broad.
When Yǐn Duó was at Jìnyáng,
he made a request of Zhào Jiǎnzǐ.
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Go and level those ramparts.
I will be going there,
and if I go and see the ramparts,
they will remind me of Zhōngxíng Yín and Fàn Jíshè."
Duó went and increased them instead.
When Jiǎnzǐ went up to Jìnyáng,
he saw the ramparts and angrily said:
"Ah!
Duó has deceived me."
Thereupon, he encamped in the suburbs,
intending to send someone to execute Duó.
Sūn Míng came forward to remonstrate, saying:
"In my private opinion,
Duó should be rewarded.
Duó's words were certainly:
'Seeing pleasure leads to extravagance and excess,
seeing worry leads to diligence and order—
this is the way of people.
Now if you, my lord, see the ramparts and remember troubles and perils,
how much more so will your ministers and people?
To benefit the state and profit the ruler,
even if it means sharing in guilt,
Duó will do it.
Those who follow orders to gain favor—
many can do that,
and how much more so Duó?'
I ask you to consider this."
Jiǎnzǐ said:
"Without your words,
I would have nearly erred."
Thereupon, he rewarded Yǐn Duó with the reward for averting calamity.
For a ruler,
the highest is that joy and anger must follow principle;
the next is that if they do not follow principle,
they must be frequently corrected.
Even if one does not reach great worthiness,
this is still enough to rise above a corrupt age.
Jiǎnzǐ achieved this.
The flaw of rulers of the age
is to feel shame at not knowing yet boast of self-reliance,
to prefer stubbornly persisting in error and detest listening to remonstrance,
leading to peril.
No shame is greater than that of peril.
25.2 "Distinguishing Categories"
Second it is said:
To know what one does not know is superior.
The flaw of those who err
is not knowing yet considering themselves knowing.
Many things seem of a kind but are not so, hence the ruin of states and suffering of people never cease.
Now among herbs, there are shēn and lěi;
eating either alone will kill a person,
but eating them combined increases longevity;
ten thousand jǐn will not kill.
Lacquer is soft, water is soft,
but combining two softs makes them hard;
when wetted they become dry.
Gold is soft, tin is soft,
but combining two softs makes them hard;
when heated they become soft.
Some become dry when wetted,
some become soft when heated—
categories are not always predictable.
Small squares and large squares are of a kind,
small horses and large horses are of a kind,
but small wisdom is not of the same kind as great wisdom.
There was a man of Lǔ named Gōngsūn Chuò
who told people:
"I can raise the dead."
People asked him how.
He replied:
"I am originally able to cure hemiplegia;
now if I double the medicine for hemiplegia, I can raise the dead."
Things certainly exist that can be used for the small but not for the large,
that can be used for the half but not for the whole.
A sword appraiser said:
"The white makes it hard,
the yellow makes it tough;
yellow and white mixed makes it both hard and tough—
a fine sword."
An objector said:
"The white makes it not tough,
the yellow makes it not hard;
yellow and white mixed makes it neither hard nor tough.
Moreover, if soft it will curl,
if hard it will break.
A sword that breaks and curls—
how can it be a sharp sword?"
The nature of the sword is unchanged,
yet some consider it fine,
some consider it poor—
explanation causes this.
Therefore, if one uses intelligence to listen to explanations, then false explanations cease;
if one does not use intelligence to listen to explanations, then Yáo and Jié are indistinguishable.
This is what troubles loyal ministers,
and why the worthy are cast aside.
Righteousness—if practiced in small measure, brings small fortune;
if practiced in great measure, brings great fortune.
With calamity it is not so—
a small calamity is not as good as having none.
One shooting at a target wants to hit the small mark,
one shooting at game wants to hit the large beast.
Things are certainly not fixed—
how can they be predicted?
Gāoyáng Yīng was about to build a house,
and the craftsman said to him:
"It cannot be done yet.
The wood is still green;
applying plaster on top of it
will surely cause it to warp.
Using green wood to build a house,
though good now,
will certainly fail later."
Gāoyáng Yīng said:
"Not so.
According to what you have said,
the house will not collapse.
For wood becomes stronger as it dries,
and clay becomes lighter as it dries.
Using what is increasingly strong to bear what is increasingly light will not lead to collapse."
The craftsman had no words to reply,
and so, accepting the order, he built it.
When the house was first completed, it was fine,
but later it indeed collapsed.
Gāoyáng Yīng was fond of petty cleverness,
but did not understand the greater principle.
A fine steed like Lǜ'ěr, with the sun at its back, runs westward;
by evening, the sun is before it.
The eyes certainly have things they do not see,
the intellect certainly has things it does not know,
and calculation certainly has limits it cannot reach.
Not understanding the reasons why things are as they are,
the sages established systems accordingly,
without forcing things by mental effort.
25.3 "Having Standards"
Third it is said:
A worthy ruler, having standards by which to listen,
therefore does not err.
Having standards by which to listen,
then he cannot be deceived,
cannot be flustered,
cannot be intimidated,
cannot be made joyful.
With the knowledge of ordinary men,
if they are not confused by what they already know,
but are confused by what they do not yet know,
then men are easily deceived,
can be flustered,
can be intimidated,
can be made joyful,
because their knowledge is not discerning.
A guest asked Jìzǐ:
"How do you know Shùn's ability?"
Jìzǐ said:
"Yáo had already brought order to the world,
and Shùn spoke of governing the world in a way that matched his own tally,
therefore I know his ability."
"Even if you know this,
how do you know he did not act for private gain?"
Jìzǐ said:
"All those capable of governing the world
must certainly comprehend the essential nature of life and destiny.
(Those who comprehend the essential nature of life and destiny,)
should be without selfishness.
In summer, one does not wear fur robes,
not out of love for the robes,
but because warmth is abundant.
In winter, one does not use a fan,
not out of love for the fan,
but because coolness is abundant.
The sage's lack of selfishness
is not out of love for nobility,
but from moderation within himself.
Moderating oneself,
even a greedy and corrupt mind can be stopped,
how much more so for a sage?"
Xǔ Yóu was not forceful,
but had that which he comprehended.
Having that which he comprehended, the profit of greed and corruption was external to him.
The disciples and followers of Confucius and Mòzǐ filled the world,
all using the methods of benevolence and righteousness to instruct the world,
yet these methods were nowhere practiced.
If the teachers' methods still could not be practiced,
how much less so what they taught?
Why is this?
The methods of benevolence and righteousness are external.
Using the external to overcome the internal,
an ordinary man on foot cannot do it,
how much less so a ruler?
Only by comprehending the essential nature of life and destiny
do the methods of benevolence and righteousness practice themselves.
The former kings could not know everything,
but by holding to the One, the myriad things were ordered.
What prevents men from holding to the One
is the disturbance of things.
Therefore it is said: penetrate the perversity of intention,
untangle the confusion of the mind,
remove the burdens of virtue,
clear the obstructions of the Way.
Nobility, wealth, prominence, dignity, fame, and profit—these six
are perversities of intention.
Appearance, movement, expression, manner, bearing, and will—these six
are confusions of the mind.
Dislike, desire, joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure—these six
are burdens of virtue.
Wisdom, ability, withdrawal, approach, acceptance, and rejection—these six
are obstructions of the Way.
If these four sets of six do not agitate within the breast, then one is correct.
Being correct, one is tranquil;
being tranquil, one is clear and bright;
being clear and bright, one is empty;
being empty, one does nothing, and yet there is nothing that is not done.
25.4 "Division of Functions"
Fourth it is said:
The former kings used what was not theirs
as if it were their own,
comprehending the way of rulership.
Now the ruler,
dwelling in emptiness, clothed in plainness, and without wisdom,
therefore can make the multitude wise;
wisdom returning to non-ability,
therefore can make the multitude able;
ability holding to non-action,
therefore can make the multitude act.
Without wisdom, without ability, without action—
this is what the ruler holds to.
Those rulers who are confused are not like this.
They force their wisdom with wisdom,
force their ability with ability,
force their action with action.
This is to occupy the function of a minister.
Occupying the function of a minister yet wishing to avoid obstruction,
even Shùn could not do it.
King Wǔ had five assistants.
King Wǔ, regarding the affairs of these five men, had no ability,
yet the world all says:
"It was King Wǔ who took the world."
Therefore King Wǔ took what was not his
as if it were his own,
comprehending the way of rulership.
Comprehending the way of rulership,
then he could make the wise plan,
could make the brave exert themselves,
could make the eloquent speak.
Now with horses,
Bólè examines them,
Zàofǔ drives them,
and the worthy ruler rides them,
covering a thousand lǐ in a day,
without the toil of driving or examining, yet having the achievement—
this is knowing what to ride.
Now when a host invites guests,
and when the wine is in full swing,
there is singing, dancing, drumming, se-playing, and yú-blowing,
the next day they do not bow to those who pleased them with music,
but bow to the host,
because the host made them do it.
The former kings' establishment of merit and fame
is similar to this.
Employing the multitude of abilities and the multitude of worthies,
great merit and fame are established in the world.
It is not given to the assistants,
but to their ruler,
because the ruler made them do it.
Consider building a palace:
one must certainly employ a skilled craftsman.
Why?
It is said:
"If the craftsman is not skilled, the palace will not be good."
Now the state is a weighty thing;
if it is not well-governed,
is it merely like a palace?
A skilled craftsman building a palace
must use a compass to make circles,
must use a square to make angles,
must use a level and line to make things straight and true.
When the work is completed,
one does not know the compass, square, or line,
but praises the skilled craftsman.
When the palace is completed,
one does not know the skilled craftsman,
but all say:
"Excellent!
This is the palace of such-and-such lord, such-and-such king."
This cannot but be examined.
Rulers who do not comprehend the way of rulership are not like this.
They themselves, acting as others' models, cannot do it;
employing the worthy, they dislike them;
consulting with the unworthy, they deliberate with them.
This is why merit and fame are harmed,
and the state endangered.
Dates
belong to the jujube tree;
fur robes
belong to the fox.
Eating the dates of the jujube,
wearing the fur of the fox,
the former kings certainly used what was not theirs
as if it were their own.
Tāng and Wǔ in a single day completely possessed the people of Xià and Shāng,
completely possessed the lands of Xià and Shāng,
completely possessed the wealth of Xià and Shāng.
Using their people to bring stability, no one in the world dared
(to dare) to endanger them;
using their lands to enfeoff, no one in the world dared to be displeased;
using their wealth to reward, everyone in the world competed to be encouraged.
Without expending anything from Yì or Qízhōu,
the world praised them as supremely benevolent and supremely righteous,
because they understood how to use what was not originally theirs.
Báigōng Shèng obtained the state of Jīng,
but could not distribute the contents of its treasuries to the people.
After seven days,
Shí Qǐ entered and said:
"Disaster is upon us.
If you cannot distribute it to the people, then burn it,
do not let others use it to harm us."
Báigōng again could not do it.
After nine days,
Shè Gōng entered,
then issued the goods from the Grand Treasury to give to the masses,
brought out the weapons from the High Armory to distribute to the people,
and thereby attacked him.
After nineteen days, Báigōng died.
Now, to desire to possess a state that is not one's own,
can be called the height of greed;
being unable to act for others,
and also unable to act for oneself,
can be called the height of folly.
To liken Báigōng's stinginess,
it is like an owl loving its chicks.
Duke Líng of Wèi, in cold weather, had a pond dug.
Wǎn Chūn remonstrated, saying:
"In cold weather to start a labor service,
I fear it will harm the people."
The Duke said:
"Is the weather cold?"
Wǎn Chūn said:
"My lord wears a fox-fur robe,
sits on a bear-skin mat,
and has a stove in the corner of the room,
therefore you are not cold.
Now the people wear torn clothes they cannot mend,
and broken sandals they cannot weave.
My lord may not be cold,
but the people are cold."
The Duke said:
"Well said."
And ordered the labor service stopped.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
"My lord was digging the pond,
unaware that the weather was cold,
yet Chūn knew it.
Because Chūn knew it and you ordered it stopped,
the credit will go to Chūn,
and the resentment will go to you, my lord."
The Duke said:
"Not so.
This Chūn,
was a commoner of the state of Lǔ,
and I promoted him.
The people have not yet seen his worth,
now I will let the people see it through this.
(It is said) Moreover, if Chūn has goodness, it is mine to have,
is Chūn's goodness not also my goodness?"
Duke Líng's judgment regarding Wǎn Chūn
can be said to understand the way of a ruler.
The ruler inherently has no specific duties,
but assigns duties according to office.
Skill or clumsiness is for the subordinates,
rewards and punishments are according to law;
what then does the ruler have to do?
If it is like this, then those who receive rewards feel no personal debt,
and those who face punishment bear no resentment,
each person reflects on themselves,
this is the pinnacle of governance.
25.5 "Establishing Distinctions"
The fifth says:
In all governance, one must first establish distinctions.
Ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife—
when these six, ruler, minister, father, son, husband, wife, are in their proper positions,
then subordinates do not overstep their bounds and superiors do not act arbitrarily,
the young are not rebellious and the elders are not negligent.
Metal and wood have different functions,
water and fire have distinct natures,
yīn and yáng are not the same,
yet in benefiting the people they are one.
Therefore, distinction is what brings stability to unity,
and unity is what endangers distinction.
The distinction between unity and difference,
the separation between noble and base,
the principle of elder and younger—
these are what the former kings were careful about,
and they are the key to order and chaos.
Now, an archer who focuses on a hair's breadth will miss the wall,
a painter who focuses on a single strand will distort the face;
this speaks to examining the root.
If the root is not examined,
even Yáo and Shùn could not bring order.
Therefore, all disorder
must begin close at hand and then extend afar,
must begin at the root and then reach the branches.
Order is likewise.
Therefore, Bǎilǐ Xī stayed in Yú and Yú perished,
stayed in Qín and Qín became hegemon;
Xiàng Zhì stayed in Shāng and Shāng was destroyed,
stayed in Zhōu and Zhōu became kingly.
Bǎilǐ Xī's staying in Yú—
his wisdom was not folly;
Xiàng Zhì's staying in Shāng—
his statutes were not bad;
it was because they lacked the root.
His staying in Qín—
his wisdom was not increased;
his staying in Zhōu—
his statutes were not improved;
it was because they had the root.
What is called the root,
is the establishment of distinctions.
Qí ordered Zhāng Zǐ to lead troops and, together with Hán and Wèi, attack Jīng.
Jīng ordered Táng Miè to lead troops and resist them.
The armies faced each other,
for six months without engaging in battle.
Qí ordered Zhōu Zuì to urge Zhāng Zǐ to fight quickly,
his words were very harsh.
Zhāng Zǐ replied to Zhōu Zuì, saying:
"To kill me or pardon me,
to destroy my family,
the king can get this from me.
To fight when one should not fight,
or not to fight when one should fight,
the king cannot get this from me."
They faced the Jīng army across the Cǐ River.
Zhāng Zǐ sent men to observe where the river could be forded;
the Jīng men shot at them,
they could not get near the water.
There was a grass-gatherer by the water,
who told the Qí scout,
saying:
"The shallows and depths of the river are easy to know.
Where the Jīng men guard heavily,
are all the shallow places;
where they guard lightly,
are all the deep places."
The scout carried the grass-gatherer to see Zhāng Zǐ.
Zhāng Zǐ was very pleased,
and thereupon trained his troops and at night suddenly attacked the place the Jīng men heavily guarded,
and indeed killed Táng Miè.
Zhāng Zǐ can be said to have understood the distinction of a general.
Hán Zhāolíhóu went out hawking,
one trace was slack.
Zhāolíhóu, sitting in the chariot,
said to his driver:
"Is not one trace slack?"
His driver said:
"It is."
Upon reaching the lodge,
Zhāolíhóu shot birds.
His right-hand attendant adjusted one trace,
making it even.
After Zhāolíhóu had finished shooting,
they harnessed the horses and returned.
Getting into the chariot,
after a short while,
he said:
"Earlier one trace was slack,
now it is even,
why is that?"
His right-hand attendant answered from behind:
"Just now your servant adjusted it."
Zhāolíhóu arrived,
and questioned the chariot officer.
Both avoided their quarters.
Therefore, the way of acting on one's own authority and presumptuous judgment, even if correct,
is not followed by a worthy ruler.
Suppose there is a person here,
who, by acting on forged orders, can save the state,
who, in weighing light and heavy, is as accurate as a steelyard,
who, in making squares and circles, is as precise as compasses and square,
this person would be skilled and clever,
yet not worthy of being taken as a model.
The law
is what is common to all,
what the worthy and unworthy alike exert their strength by.
When plans arise from what cannot be used,
when actions arise from what cannot be shared,
this is what the former kings discarded.
25.6 "Being Careful About Small Things"
The sixth says:
The superior is honored, the inferior is lowly.
Being lowly, one cannot observe the superior through minor matters.
Being honored, one becomes unrestrained;
being unrestrained, one belittles minor matters;
belittling minor matters, the superior lacks the means to understand the inferior.
The inferior lacks the means to understand the superior.
When superior and inferior do not understand each other,
the superior criticizes the inferior,
and the inferior resents the superior.
The nature of a minister
is such that he cannot serve one whom he resents;
the nature of a ruler
is such that he cannot love one whom he criticizes;
this is the great mutual loss of the Way between superior and inferior.
Therefore, a worthy ruler is attentive to minor matters in order to discern likes and dislikes.
A great dike may harbor termites,
yet it can flood cities and drown people;
a chimney may leak a single spark,
yet it can burn palaces and consume stores;
a general may issue one mistaken order,
yet his army can be destroyed and he himself killed;
a ruler may utter one mistaken word,
yet his state can be ruined and his name disgraced,
becoming a laughingstock for later generations.
Duke Xiàn of Wèi invited Sūn Línfǔ and Níng Zhí to dine.
Wild geese gathered in the park,
and the gamekeeper reported it.
The duke went to the park to shoot the geese.
The two men waited for the ruler;
the day grew late,
and the duke did not arrive.
When he came, he did not remove his fur cap before meeting the two men.
The two men were displeased,
drove out Duke Xiàn,
and set up Gōngzǐ Qián.
When Duke Zhuāng of Wèi was established,
he wished to drive out Shí Pǔ.
He ascended a tower to look out,
saw the Róng district and asked about it, saying:
"What is that place?"
The attendant said:
"It is the Róng district."
Duke Zhuāng said:
"I am of the Jī surname.
How dare the Róng people dwell within the state?"
He ordered their dwellings seized,
and ravaged their district.
When the Jìn people attacked Wèi,
the people of the Róng district joined with Shí Pǔ to kill Duke Zhuāng,
and set up Gōngzǐ Qǐ.
This is failing to examine minor matters.
People do not stumble on mountains,
but stumble on anthills.
When Duke Huán of Qí assumed the throne,
in three years he made three statements,
and the world praised him as worthy,
and all his ministers were pleased.
He banished beasts that eat meat,
banished birds that eat grain,
and removed nets with silk meshes.
Wú Qǐ governed Xīhé,
wishing to demonstrate his trustworthiness to the people.
One evening he set up a marker outside the south gate,
and issued an order in the city, saying:
"Tomorrow, if anyone can topple the marker outside the south gate,
he will be appointed senior grand master."
The next day grew late,
and no one had toppled the marker.
The people said to each other:
"This surely cannot be trusted."
One man said:
"Let me try to topple the marker.
At worst, I will not receive the reward—
what harm is there?"
He went and toppled the marker,
then came to see Wú Qǐ.
Wú Qǐ personally received him and sent him out,
appointing him senior grand master.
That evening he again set up a marker,
and again issued the same order in the city.
The people of the city guarded the gate and contended to topple the marker,
but the marker was planted more firmly,
and no one could obtain the reward.
From then on,
the people trusted Wú Qǐ's rewards and punishments.
When rewards and punishments are trusted by the people,
what undertaking will not succeed?
Is it only in military affairs?
26.1 "The Demeanor of the Scholar"
The first says:
The scholar is neither partial nor partisan,
gentle yet firm,
empty yet substantial.
His appearance is bright and not cunning,
as if he has lost his oneness.
He disregards minor matters and focuses his will on the great,
seeming lacking in courage yet cannot be intimidated,
firm and resolute, bold and daring, yet cannot be insulted or harmed;
facing peril and traversing difficulties, he abides by righteousness without overstepping;
facing south and calling himself "the solitary one," he is not arrogant or grandiose;
today ruling the people, he desires to subdue lands beyond the seas;
his standards are very high, and he does not rely on petty gains;
his ears and eyes transcend vulgar customs, and he can bring stability to the age;
he does not seek wealth and honor, nor does he shun poverty and lowliness;
his virtuous conduct honors principle, and he is ashamed to use clever deceit;
broad and generous, not calculating, yet his heart is very stern;
difficult to sway with material things, and he will never bend recklessly.
This is the demeanor of a scholar of the state.
In Qí there was a man skilled at judging dogs.
His neighbor borrowed from him to buy a dog that catches rats.
After a full year he obtained one,
and said:
"This is a fine dog."
His neighbor kept it for several years,
but it did not catch rats.
He informed the judge.
The judge said:
"This is a fine dog.
Its ambition lies in deer, elk, boars, and stags,
not in rats.
If you want it to catch rats, you must fetter it."
His neighbor fettered its hind legs,
and the dog then caught rats.
The spirit of a noble steed,
the ambition of a swan or wild goose—
if there is something that truly resonates in the human heart, it is sincerity.
Humans are likewise.
If one truly possesses it, the spirit responds in others;
how can words suffice to convey it?
This is called wordless speech.
A visitor came to see Tián Pián.
His attire conformed to the rules,
his advances and retreats followed the proper measure,
his gait was graceful and elegant,
his speech was deferential and quick.
Tián Pián listened to him to the end and then dismissed him.
The visitor left,
and Tián Pián saw him off with his eyes.
A disciple said to Tián Pián:
"Is the visitor
a scholar?"
Tián Pián said:
"I fear he is not a scholar.
What the visitor now conceals,
is what the scholar practices;
what the scholar conceals,
is what the visitor practices.
I fear the visitor is not a scholar."
Thus, if a torch illuminates one corner,
the room is partially without light;
if the bones and joints mature early,
the orifices become haggard and worn,
and the body will surely not grow tall;
if the multitude lacks strategic plans,
begging for caution in what is seen,
there will be many troubles and no goodness;
the will will surely not be impartial,
and one cannot achieve merit;
loving to gain and hating to give,
even if the state is large, one cannot become king;
calamities and disasters will arrive daily.
Therefore, the demeanor of the gentleman
is pure like the jade of Zhōngshān,
sturdy like the trees on the hills.
Diligent and careful, cautious and respectful of transformation,
yet unwilling to be self-satisfied;
sincere and earnest in choices and rejections, without wavering,
and the heart is very simple and plain.
Táng Shàng reached the age for becoming a clerk,
and an old acquaintance thought Táng Shàng desired it,
and told Táng Shàng so.
Táng Shàng said:
"It is not that I cannot become a clerk,
but I am ashamed to do so."
His old acquaintance did not believe him.
When Wèi besieged Hándān,
Táng Shàng persuaded King Huì and lifted the siege,
and was given Bóyáng.
His old acquaintance then believed he was ashamed to be a clerk.
After some time had passed,
his old acquaintance made a request on behalf of his elder brother.
Táng Shàng said:
"When the ruler of Wèi dies,
I will have your elder brother replace him."
His old acquaintance turned around, bowed twice, and believed him.
To distrust what is trustworthy,
and to trust what is not trustworthy—
this is the folly of the foolish.
To understand human sentiments,
yet be unable to rid oneself of them,
to act as a ruler in such a state,
what benefit is there even if one possesses the entire realm?
Thus, there is no greater failure than foolishness.
The peril of foolishness
lies in the certainty of self-reliance.
Self-reliance leads to the foolish and ignorant flocking to congratulate him.
To possess a state in such a manner,
is no better than having none at all.
In ancient times, the practice of yielding to the worthy
arose from this.
It was not because they despised their own descendants,
nor was it to seek fame and take pride in it,
but to return to the essence of governance.
26.2 "Devotion to Greatness"
The second says:
Let us examine the records of antiquity:
the ministers who assisted the Three Kings
all enjoyed illustrious reputations,
and their achievements were all secure,
because their merits were great.
The ministers who served mediocre rulers
desired fame and achievement just as those who served the Three Kings did,
yet their reputations were all tarnished,
and their achievements were all precarious,
because they lacked merit.
They all worried about not being esteemed within their own state,
but did not worry about their ruler not being esteemed throughout the realm.
This is why they sought glory but ended up with disgrace,
sought security but ended up in peril.
Confucius said:
"Swallows and sparrows compete for a favorable spot under the same roof,
mother and offspring feed one another,
contentedly delighting in each other's company,
believing themselves to be secure.
When the chimney cracks,
and the roof beams catch fire,
the swallows and sparrows show no change in expression.
Why is this?
They do not know that disaster is about to befall them.
Is this not foolish?
Among those who serve as ministers, few avoid the wisdom of swallows and sparrows.
Those who serve as ministers,
advancing their ranks, emoluments, and wealth,
fathers, sons, and brothers colluding within a single state,
contentedly delighting in each other's company,
yet endangering their altars of soil and grain—
their situation is as precarious as the chimney,
yet they remain unaware until the end.
Their wisdom is no different from that of swallows and sparrows.
Thus it is said:
'When the realm is in great chaos,
no state is secure;
when a state is in complete chaos,
no family is secure;
when a family is in complete chaos,
no individual is secure.'
This is what it means.
Thus, the security of the small
must depend on the great;
the security of the great
must depend on the small.
Small and great, humble and noble,
mutually support one another,
and only then can all attain what they delight in."
Bó Yí advised Lord Sì of Wèi on the art of kingship.
Lord Sì replied to him:
"What I possess is a state of a thousand chariots,
and I wish to receive your instruction accordingly."
Bó Yí responded:
"Wū Huò could lift a thousand jūn,
how much more a single jīn?"
Dù Hè advised Zhāowén Jūn of Zhōu on securing the realm.
Zhāowén Jūn said to Dù Hè:
"I wish to learn how to secure Zhōu."
Dù Hè responded:
"If what I say cannot be implemented,
then Zhōu cannot be secured;
if what I say can be implemented,
then Zhōu will secure itself."
This is what is called securing through not securing.
The Lord of Zhèng asked Bèi Zhān:
"I have heard of your principle,
not dying for one's lord,
not perishing for one's lord.
Is it truly so?"
Bèi Zhān responded:
"It is so.
If one's words are not heeded,
and one's way is not practiced,
then one certainly does not serve the lord.
If one's words are heeded and one's way is practiced,
then why would there be death or perishing?"
Thus, Bèi Zhān's not dying or perishing
was wiser than dying or perishing.
In the past, Shùn wished to subdue the lands beyond the seas but did not succeed,
yet he achieved enough to become an emperor.
Yǔ wished to become emperor but did not succeed,
yet he achieved enough to rule the lands within the seas.
Tāng and Wǔ wished to succeed Yǔ but did not succeed,
yet they achieved enough to rule over all accessible lands.
The Five Hegemons wished to succeed Tāng and Wǔ but did not succeed,
yet they achieved enough to become leaders among the feudal lords.
Confucius and Mòzǐ wished to practice the Great Way in the world but did not succeed,
yet they achieved enough to attain illustrious honor.
Though the great righteousness was not fully realized,
there was still achievement in it.
Therefore, one must devote oneself to great endeavors.
26.3 "Prioritizing Agriculture"
The third says:
The way the ancient sage kings guided their people
was to prioritize agriculture.
Engaging the people in agriculture was not merely for the benefit of the land,
but to honor their spirit.
When the people engage in agriculture, they become simple;
when they are simple, they are easy to employ;
when they are easy to employ, the borders are secure,
and the ruler's position is exalted.
When the people engage in agriculture, they become steadfast;
when they are steadfast, they have few private disputes;
when they have few private disputes, public laws are established,
and efforts become unified.
When the people engage in agriculture, their production is abundant;
when their production is abundant, they are reluctant to relocate;
when they are reluctant to relocate, they remain in their place until death without second thoughts.
If the people abandon the root and pursue the branches, they become unruly;
if they are unruly, they cannot be relied upon for defense,
nor for warfare.
If the people abandon the root and pursue the branches, their production becomes limited;
if their production is limited, they become prone to migration;
if they are prone to migration,
then when the state faces calamity,
they all have distant aspirations,
with no intention to stay.
If the people abandon the root and pursue the branches, they become fond of cleverness;
if they are fond of cleverness, they become deceitful;
if they are deceitful, they manipulate laws and decrees,
turning right into wrong,
and wrong into right.
Hòujì said:
"The reason for emphasizing plowing and weaving
is to make them the fundamental teachings."
Therefore, the Son of Heaven personally leads the feudal lords to plow the imperial fields,
and the high officials and scholars all have their duties.
Thus, during the farming season,
no farmers are seen in the capital,
to teach the people to respect the produce of the land.
The queen leads the nine concubines to raise silkworms in the suburbs,
and to tend mulberry trees on public fields.
Thus, in spring, autumn, winter, and summer, there are tasks of hemp, flax, silk, and cocoons,
to encourage the teachings for women.
Therefore, men do not weave yet are clothed,
women do not plow yet are fed,
men and women exchange their labors,
to nurture life,
this is the system of the sages.
Thus, they respect the seasons and cherish the days,
not resting until old age,
not ceasing unless ill,
not abandoning their tasks until death.
On superior fields,
one man feeds nine people.
On inferior fields,
one man feeds five people.
This can be increased,
but not decreased.
One man works the land,
ten people are fed,
and the six domestic animals are all included.
This is the great way of utilizing the land.
Thus, during the farming season,
no earthworks are undertaken,
no military campaigns are launched,
commoners do not hold capping ceremonies, marry wives, marry off daughters, or hold sacrificial feasts,
nor do they gather crowds for drinking,
farmers who have not been reported to the authorities
dare not privately hire laborers,
for it harms the season.
Then, field prohibitions are established:
unless of the same surname,
farmers do not go out to marry,
women do not marry outside,
to stabilize agriculture.
There are five field prohibitions:
if the land has not been cleared and prepared,
do not handle hemp,
do not remove manure.
When one's age is not yet advanced,
one dares not create gardens or parks.
When one's strength is insufficient,
one dares not dig channels to farm.
Farmers dare not engage in trade,
nor dare they undertake different tasks.
This is because it harms the proper season.
Afterwards, prohibitions for the four seasons are established:
In the mountains, one dares not cut down timber or fell trees,
in the marshes, people dare not burn vegetation or harm life,
nets and traps dare not be taken out the door,
large fishing nets dare not enter the deep waters,
and unless one is the boat officer of the marshes,
one dares not claim rights by name,
for it harms the proper timing.
If the people do not exert themselves in farming,
their households will become impoverished and livestock scarce,
the state will be difficult to govern,
the three doubts will reach their extreme,
this is called turning away from the root and opposing the rules,
leading to the ruin and destruction of the state.
All people from seven feet in height and above,
are assigned to the three offices.
Farmers focus on grain,
artisans on tools,
traders on goods.
If the seasonal tasks are not coordinated,
this is called great misfortune.
If they are deprived by earthworks,
this is called obstruction,
endless worries and anxieties,
and they will surely lose their chaff.
If they are deprived by water projects,
this is called leakage,
loss following joy,
and neighboring states will come to plunder.
If they are deprived by military affairs,
this is called cruelty,
calamity extending throughout the year,
and no scythes or sickles will be raised.
If the people's seasons are repeatedly taken away,
great famine will come.
Plows will lie idle in the fields,
some will chat or sing,
morning will turn to dusk,
and much grain will be lost.
All know the branches,
but none know the true root.
26.4 "Rèn Dì"
Fourth:
Hòu Jì said:
