Can you turn hollows into mounds?
Can you conceal the poor soil and cover it with shade?
Can you make our soil tranquil and let the furrows bathe the earth?
Can you preserve moisture, stabilize the land, and make it suitable?
Can you prevent weeds from spreading excessively?
Can you make your fields all filled with gentle breezes?
Can you make the stalks have numerous joints and sturdy stems?
Can you make the ears large, firm, and even?
Can you make the grain round with thin husks?
Can you make the rice plentiful, rich, and strong to eat?
What if you cannot?
The general principles of farming:
Hard soil should be made soft,
soft soil should be made firm.
Resting land should be worked,
worked land should be rested.
Poor soil should be enriched,
rich soil should be made lean.
Compact soil should be loosened,
loose soil should be compacted.
Wet soil should be dried,
dry soil should be moistened.
On high fields, abandon the ridges;
on low fields, abandon the furrows.
Plow five times and weed five times,
must be thorough and complete.
The depth of planting,
must reach the moist soil,
so that large weeds do not grow,
and there are no pests like borers or locusts.
This year, fine millet;
next year, fine wheat.
Thus, a six-foot plowshare,
is used to form ridges;
its width is eight inches,
used to form furrows;
the weeding hoe handle is one foot,
this is its measure;
the hoe blade is six inches,
used to space the crops.
Land can be made fertile,
and can also be made poor.
When manuring, it must be done with moisture,
to make the seedlings firm and the soil porous;
when weeding, it must be done in drought,
to make the land fertile and the soil loose.
Weeds are cleared in the great month.
Fifty-seven days after the winter solstice,
the calamus begins to grow,
calamus is the first of all grasses to sprout,
then farming begins.
At the end of early summer,
when the three-leaf plant dies, harvest the barley.
When the summer solstice arrives,
the bitter vegetable dies and the sow thistle grows,
then plant hemp and beans,
this tells the people the earth's treasures are exhausted.
When grasses grow and hide, and the sun is at its peak,
when the pig's head plant grows and wheat has no leaves,
then engage in storing,
this tells the people it is the end.
Observe the five seasons: see growth and plant,
see death and harvest.
Heaven determines the seasons,
earth produces wealth,
they do not consult the people.
In fruitful years, bury offerings in the earth;
in barren years, bury offerings in the earth.
Do not miss the people's seasons,
do not make them toil.
Those below know the tools of poverty and wealth,
all act when the time comes,
and stop when thirsty for time.
Thus, the strength of the old and weak can be fully mobilized,
their labor takes half a day,
but the results can be doubled.
Those who do not understand affairs,
act prematurely before the time comes,
long for it after the time has passed,
neglect it when it is present,
and drive their people away from it.
Once the people are driven away,
they long for the good season,
this is the lowest way of undertaking tasks.
Labor becomes bitter,
not knowing high or low,
the people then become displaced.
Planting early grain does not yield early grain,
planting late grain does not yield late grain,
thus grain is scarce and effort wasted.
26.5 "Biàn Tǔ"
Fifth:
The principles of farming:
must begin with the hard soil,
because it has little moisture and later dries out;
must be thorough with the soft soil later,
because only when it is thoroughly treated later will it be timely;
loose soil is weeded,
hard soil is plowed,
moisten the soft soil and then treat it;
high fields should be covered,
low fields should be drained of all water.
Do not allow the three thieves to occupy the land:
When the four sequences are disordered and mixed,
large furrows and small ridges,
become like the gills of a blue fish,
seedlings like straight hunting lines,
this is theft by the land;
after sowing, if there are no rows,
plowed but not growing,
then the seedlings steal from each other;
if not weeded, they become overgrown,
if weeded, they become sparse,
then weeds steal from them.
Therefore, eliminate these three thieves,
and then grain can be abundant.
What is called farming today,
laboring without harvest:
the early ones are ahead of time,
the late ones miss the time,
cold and heat are unregulated,
the crops then suffer many disasters
and fruits.
As for the fields,
if high and precarious, moisture is lost,
if sloping, they become ridges,
exposed to wind, they wither,
if piled high, they are uprooted,
if cold, they wither,
if hot, they shrivel,
five or six deaths at once,
thus they cannot produce for the future.
They do not all sprout together but all die together.
The empty crops die first,
and then many pests steal in.
From a distance they appear abundant,
but up close they are hollow.
The farmer knows his field is easy to work,
but does not realize his crops are sparse and unsuitable;
he knows the boundaries of his field are cleared,
but does not realize his crops occupy hollow ground;
if not weeded, they become overgrown;
if weeded, they become hollow—
this is what harms the matter.
Therefore, the ridges should be broad and level,
the furrows small, deep, and clear;
below they receive moisture,
above they receive sunlight,
and then all will grow.
Crops should sprout in fine soil
and be planted in firm ground.
Be careful with the seeds:
do not make them too dense,
nor too sparse.
When applying soil,
do not let it be insufficient,
nor let it be excessive.
When the soil is worked after sowing,
one must focus on covering them.
If the covering is upright,
the upright ones will surely sprout first.
If the soil application is even,
the even ones will surely grow firm.
Thus, if the ridges are broad and level,
the base stems will not be lost;
for those growing in the ground,
divide the ground into five parts.
Stems grow in rows,
thus they grow swiftly;
the weak do not harm each other,
thus they swiftly become large.
Horizontal rows must be aligned,
vertical rows must be straight.
Straighten the rows,
let the wind pass through,
break open the center,
so cool breezes lead.
When seedlings are weak, they should be isolated;
when they grow, they should live together;
when ripe, they should support each other.
Therefore, group them in threes,
and there will be much grain.
The trouble with all grain crops is
they do not all sprout together but all die together.
Thus, those that sprout early yield fine rice,
those that sprout late become chaff.
Therefore, when weeding,
foster the elder and remove the younger.
In fertile soil, do not let them grow too densely;
in poor soil, do not let them cluster together.
If fertile and too dense, there will be much chaff;
if poor and clustered, many will die.
Those who do not understand crops:
when weeding, remove the elder and nurture the younger,
do not harvest the grain but harvest the chaff,
above and below are unsettled,
then many crops die.
In thick soil, sprouts cannot break through;
in thin soil, they wither and do not develop.
Dark-colored clay soil,
firm soil planted gently,
avoid tilling and eliminate hidden pests,
so that farming succeeds.
26.6 “Examining the Seasons”
The sixth says:
In all farming principles,
timeliness is the treasure:
if trees are felled at the wrong time,
they will either break or tassel;
if crops mature but are not harvested,
they will surely meet natural disaster.
Crops are made by humans,
grow from the earth,
and are nourished by heaven.
Therefore, when planting crops, allow space for feet;
when weeding, allow space for the hoe;
when handling, allow space for hands.
This is called the way of farming.
Thus, timely grain
has long stalks and tassels,
large roots and slender stems,
sparse nodes and large tassels;
its grains are round with thin husks;
its rice is plump and eating it strengthens;
such crops are not blown down by wind.
Those planted too early
have stems and leaves with awns and short crossbars,
large tassels but stolen fragrance,
full grains but not fragrant.
Those planted too late
have stems and leaves with awns and drooping tips,
tassels closed and green falling,
much chaff and not full.
Timely millet
has awned stems and drooping lower parts,
tassels with long awns,
round grains and thin husks,
easy to pound,
and eating it is not greasy but fragrant;
such crops do not become sticky.
Those planted too early
have large roots and flowers,
slender stems that do not thrive,
withered leaves and short tassels.
Those planted too late
have small stems and long fibers,
short tassels and thick husks,
small grains, astringent and not fragrant.
Timely rice
has large roots and preserved stems,
long stalks and sparse nodes,
tassels like horse tails,
large grains without awns,
round grains and thin husks,
easy to pound and fragrant to eat;
such crops do not choke.
Those planted too early
have large roots and stems and leaves opposing each other,
short stalks and short tassels,
much chaff and thick husks,
thin grains and many awns.
Those planted too late
have slender stems and do not multiply,
thick husks and much chaff, hollow grains,
cannot wait until fully ripe,
but die facing the sky.
Timely hemp
must have awns and be long,
sparse nodes and bright color,
small roots and firm stems,
thick fibers and even,
ripens late with much glory,
grows again day and night;
such crops are not attacked by locusts.
Timely beans
have long stems and short feet,
their fine pods group in twos and sevens,
many branches and numerous nodes,
competing leaves and abundant pods,
large beans are round,
small beans are round and fragrant,
heavy when weighed,
eating them is satisfying and fragrant;
such crops are not worm-eaten.
Those planted too early
must be long and vine-like,
floating leaves and sparse nodes,
small pods and not full.
Those planted too late
have short stems and sparse nodes,
hollow roots and not full.
Timely wheat
has long stalks and black necks,
groups in twos and sevens per row,
and is dense,
thin glumes and red color,
heavy when weighed,
eating it is extremely fragrant and satisfying,
makes people’s skin glossy and strong;
such crops do not have maggots.
Those planted too early
before summer rains arrive, rot moves,
maggots and many diseases,
next, sheep-like nodes.
Those planted too late
have weak seedlings and green-blue tassels,
pale color and fine awns.
Therefore, timely crops thrive,
untimely crops are stunted.
If stems are similar and weighed,
timely ones are heavier,
with more grain.
If equal amounts of grain are pounded,
timely ones yield more rice.
If equal amounts of rice are eaten,
timely ones endure hunger.
Therefore, crops that are grown in their proper season,
have a fragrant aroma,
a sweet taste,
and their vital energy is robust.
Consuming them for a hundred days,
one's ears and eyes become sharp,
the mind becomes wise and discerning,
the four limbs grow strong,
no harmful energy can invade,
and the body remains free from ailments and calamities.
Huángdì said:
"When the four seasons are not in harmony,
it is enough to rectify the five grains."
